name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: When Disaster Strikes, Medicaid Work Rules Add Barriers for Potential Enrollees
description: New work rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed last year, have put Medicaid enrollees living in disaster-struck counties at risk of losing health insurance.
text:
This story was reported by Ashley Mizuo
A month after Hurricane Lowell hit the island of Kauaʻi, downed trees, construction crews, and damaged homes dotted the neighborhoods. At the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort, where over 100 workers were laid off, heaps of sand blanketed the grounds, and the drained pool’s concrete deck crumbled into the beach, just steps away from the ocean.
On Kauaʻi, unemployment claims jumped from 69 before the September hurricane to about 1,800 nearly two weeks afterward, with widespread layoffs in the tourism industry amid a sharp decline in visitors. The number of Medicaid applications submitted by island residents jumped by about 50% in the following month, according to the Hawaiʻi Department of Human Services.
In times of emergencies, Medicaid provides a critical safety net for people to maintain healthcare coverage. But new work rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed last year, have put Medicaid enrollees living in disaster-struck counties at risk of losing health insurance. The law requires many nondisabled adults enrolled in Medicaid in 43 states and Washington, D.C., to work, volunteer, or attend school at least 80 hours a month, with eligibility checks starting in January.
In most states, residents impacted by a disaster can be granted a short-term exemption from Medicaid work requirements. Eligibility largely relies on a federal law that allows the president to issue a disaster or emergency declaration and authorizes federal assistance, but any declaration can take months or may not come at all.
Those who live in counties affected by natural disasters may not need to comply with the work rules — one of several carve-outs intended to provide limited, short-term exceptions. However, it’s unclear whether those who lost jobs after Hurricane Lowell would be eligible for that exemption so many months later. The Trump administration hasn’t offered clear guidance on how long a state can apply the natural disaster exemption to enrollees.
Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, and her boyfriend were laid off by Sheraton and are getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work. The union that represents the hotel’s hospitality workers secured them three months of health insurance. If Ganotisi isn’t hired back to her housekeeping job by then, she plans to apply for Medicaid, the federal-state program that provides health coverage to people with low incomes or disabilities.
Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, was laid off by the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort after it sustained significant damage from Hurricane Lowell. Her family is getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work.  (Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News)
Hawaiʻi Gov. Josh Green, a Democrat and practicing physician, emphasized the importance of quickly issuing disaster declarations, especially as changes to Medicaid are set to take effect. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services allowed states to delay enforcing the work requirements until next July, but states are still expected to implement eligibility checks by Jan. 1.
“It would be devastating if suddenly 40,000 or 50,000 people didn’t have their Medicaid benefits,” he said. “It could affect our rural hospitals, our nurse practitioners, our doctors, so timeliness is key.”
Hawaiʻi officials said they will keep people who don’t meet the work requirements enrolled until July.
At least 34 states, plus Washington, D.C., plan to adopt the optional hardship exemptions to those work requirements. So far, four states — Indiana, Iowa, Missouri, and Ohio — do not plan to adopt the exemptions, according to KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. All four were issued disaster declarations for severe storms and flooding this summer.
CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster told KFF Health News in a statement that states can request a longer duration for a hardship exemption if they can prove that barriers to demonstrating work requirements persist in disaster areas.
Tom Cotter, CEO of Health Response Alliance, a nonprofit focused on improving healthcare access in disasters, said that when people lose coverage they end up using emergency rooms and charitable clinics, among the few places that will treat patients regardless of their ability to pay.
“All of these are really stretched thin during an emergency because their patient load goes way up,” he said. “That makes it even more expensive for the healthcare system that is being otherwise also burdened for the disaster.”
With additional work requirements, “it is going to slow the economic recovery of any particular community,” Cotter said. “It’s going to require people to be thinking about how they’re paying for healthcare when they have a lot of other things to worry about.”
Nebraska Work Requirements Begin
Once the president declares a disaster or emergency, the short-term hardship exception applies for the full month the disaster took place. Eligibility can apply retroactively after a disaster declaration, and enrollees can be reimbursed for expenses from previous months.
Nebraska implemented Medicaid work requirements early, in May, offering states a preview of how the hardship declaration might provide relief. For Nebraskans, that relief was delayed.
It took three months for Trump to declare a federal disaster for March and April wildfires. For severe storms, tornadoes, and flooding that occurred in May, he didn’t declare a federal disaster until August.
Six Nebraskans impacted by the disasters lost coverage because they did not comply with work requirements. In October, the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services reported it was reprocessing their eligibility now that they qualify for a hardship exemption.
Sarah Maresh, director of the Health Care Access program at the nonprofit advocacy group Nebraska Appleseed, said the early rollout of the Medicaid work requirements has been marred by uncertainty.
“This is part of the confusion that comes with the Medicaid work requirements, because it applies differently depending on your situation,” she said. “I think it’ll be very challenging for new applicants.”
Local economies and businesses can take years to recover after a natural disaster. About 90% of businesses fail within two years after being struck by disaster, according to the U.S. Small Business Administration. Housing shortages can hamper business recovery as employees repair their homes or are displaced to areas farther from work. Three years after the 2023 Maui wildfires that killed over 100 people, recovery is ongoing, with most storefronts still shuttered in what was once a bustling area.
After CMS published rules governing the exceptions to the work requirements, several Democratic states sued the agency. Their lawsuit cited the narrow time frame for securing natural disaster exceptions. The complaint argued that the lack of guidance burdens state Medicaid agencies determining eligibility.
In its response filing, CMS wrote that the restrictions ensure the exemption applies only when a disaster affects Medicaid enrollees’ ability to comply with work requirements.
Construction crews lined the roads on Kauaʻi a month after Hurricane Lowell, clearing debris and repairing damaged businesses, homes, and infrastructure.  (Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News)
Disaster Delays, Denials
In Trump’s second term, he has denied nearly a quarter of disaster and emergency declaration requests as of mid-November, a denial rate higher than that of any other presidential administration in more than two decades, KFF Health News found. While decision wait times have increased across the country, they’re more acute in states with Democratic governors. Those states experienced both significantly higher denial rates and longer decision times than states with Republican governors, according to 2026 analyses from The Associated Press and Politico’s E&E News.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied any politicization in Trump’s decisions on disaster relief. She wrote that his response to requests from states ensures appropriate use of taxpayer money and that federal funds are used to “supplement — not substitute” states’ obligations to respond to disasters.
The presidential major disaster declaration for Kauaʻi was the state’s sixth disaster or emergency declaration this year. As of November, Hawaiʻi had received more disaster and emergency declarations than any other state in 2026. Trump’s disaster declaration for a 6.0-magnitude earthquake that damaged over 300 homes on Hawaiʻi Island took about three months.
A month after Hurricane Lowell in September 2026, sand still covered the grounds of the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort.  (Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News)
Other states have waited longer for disaster declarations. New Mexico, where the Democratic Party controls the governor’s office and majorities in both legislative chambers, had one of the longest wait times for a decision — nine months for a presidential disaster declaration for severe storms and flooding in September 2025. Illinois, which also has a Democratic trifecta, waited over seven months and was denied. The state has yet to secure any major disaster declarations during Trump’s second term, despite several attempts.
Some who lost their jobs and don’t qualify for Medicaid have few resources to help them.
Oscar Cardova worked at The Terrace Hanalei, a restaurant on Kauaʻi’s North Shore that was significantly damaged in the hurricane. When the restaurant closed, he lost his employer-provided health insurance. Although he has a work permit visa from Peru, he was denied Medicaid because of his immigration status.
Cardova and his wife, Yesenia, live in their van. Yesenia has astigmatism and, without insurance, she will need to pay for glasses out-of-pocket, Cardova said. The cost is expected to be about $500.
The couple planned to work for two more years in the U.S. before returning to Peru. A month after the hurricane, they were still struggling to find work. In search of more job opportunities, they considered moving to Honolulu.
“Right now, we’re just surviving,” Cardova said. “We’re waiting to see what happens before making other decisions, because we can’t keep living like this.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC leaders plan to hike 100 miles to raise awareness of food insecurity
description: The hike will take place with nonprofit Hunters for the Hungry, which donates local venison to food pantries.
text:
A partnership between the state Department of Natural Resources and nonprofit Hunters for the Hungry is meant to raise awareness of a program to fight food insecurity with donated venison. (Photo courtesy of Liz Julian/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)State leaders will hike 100 miles over 10 days in an effort to raise awareness about food insecurity, according to the Department of Natural Resources.
The 100 Miles for the Hungry expedition will begin Jan. 8 and go through Orangeburg, Bamberg, Barnwell and Allendale counties, according to the agency.
The state agency is partnering with Hunters for the Hungry, a Spartanburg-based nonprofit that provides deer killed and donated by hunters to food banks, churches and other places where people might get free meals.
For 30 days, a nonprofit leads hikes and floats across SC. The goal is conservation.

The nonprofit pays the processing fees to turn the deer into venison before packaging and freezing it, executive director Rick Counts told the SC Daily Gazette.
Throughout the expedition, state leaders and members of Hunters for the Hungry will talk to local residents, businesses and churches about how to donate venison or volunteer to get food to people who might not have enough, Counts said.
The goal is to raise awareness of food insecurity, he said.
“This is a way to shine some light on the areas of the state that don’t get as much notoriety and press on what they need,” Counts said.
In 2023, roughly 14% of people in the state were food insecure, according to the most recent data from the Department of Public Health. Rural Allendale County has the highest rate of food insecurity, with more than 20% of residents lacking consistent access to healthy food, according to the agency.
The Department of Natural Resources often encourages hunters to donate extra deer to Hunters for the Hungry by dropping off carcasses at participating processing sites. The deer must have a state-issued tag to show they were legally hunted, according to the nonprofit.
Promotions from the agency have helped the nonprofit in the past, Counts said. When DNR shared a map of processors, a facility in Dillon County realized the area wasn’t covered and called Counts asking how to help sign up, he said.
Having as many processors involved across the state as possible is important because the nonprofit tries to keep donations local, so hunters can help their own communities, Counts said.
“We try to keep that deer meat in that county as much as possible,” he said.
This year, hunters received an extra tag for a doe when buying the regular deer tags in an effort to better balance the state’s population of deer. Most hunters don’t kill more than one doe each season, but having too many can disrupt local ecosystems, according to the agency.
If hunters already have as much venison as they plan to eat, state leaders encourage using as many of the tags as possible and donating the extra meat to Hunters for the Hungry.
“Most people, they’ve filled their freezers by now,” Counts said. “With our program, they can still go hunting and donate their does.”
The idea of hiking to raise awareness is similar to a program DNR runs with nonprofit South Carolina 7.
Every year, state officials, volunteers and members of the public walk, float and kayak more than 300 miles in an effort to get people outside and promote conservation.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska wildlife disease discoveries show new risks for people
description: When a woman showed up at his Fairbanks clinic in 2015 with what she thought was a spider bite, accompanied by hard-to-pin-down illness symptoms, Dr. Zachary Werle suspected the ailment was something highly unusual. He was right. A sample he sent to the state virology lab, then forwarded to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control […]
text:
Aren Gunderson, mammal collection manager at the University of Alaska Museum of the North, pulls out a drawer containing vole specimens on Feb. 6, 2025. The voles are museum’s collection of more than 130,000 mammal specimens. Within the collection, scientists found a northern red-backed vole found in Denali National Park in the 1990s that contained viable borealpox virus, proving that the virus has been in Alaska as least as far back as then. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)When a woman showed up at his Fairbanks clinic in 2015 with what she thought was a spider bite, accompanied by hard-to-pin-down illness symptoms, Dr. Zachary Werle suspected the ailment was something highly unusual.
He was right. A sample he sent to the state virology lab, then forwarded to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention national lab, revealed a completely new-to-science orthopoxvirus strain. It was dubbed Alaskapox.
What ultimately raised Werle’s suspicions and prompted him to send samples for testing was something called lymphangitis, “which is where there was a tracking or streaking or redness and inflammation where the infection was following the lymphatic channels,” he said. There were also some additional lesions that emerged on the patient’s skin, in somewhat similar fashion to an outbreak of shingles, which is a viral disease.
 

Dr. Zachary Werle, the Fairbanks clinician who made the first diagnosis of the disease initially called Alaskapox, then renamed borealpox. (Photo provided by Foundation Health Partners)
 

	For five years, that case was a one-off. Then in 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, another patient came into Werle’s office with what she thought was a staph infection.
“I immediately recognized the similarities to the first case from 2015. I said, ‘Hey, I think I have an idea what this is,’” he recalled.
After then, a handful of patients trickled into Werle’s Tanana Valley Clinic with the same issues. Although their symptoms were unpleasant, all six Fairbanks-area residents diagnosed with Alaskapox from 2015 to 2023 recovered. Patients were mostly adults, though there was one 3-year-old child, Werle said. They had manageable illnesses, which were uncomfortable but not serious enough for hospitalizations, he said.
As cases emerged, state health officials alerted clinicians to keep an eye out for the ultra-rare disease that, though not expected to cause serious trouble for healthy people, might be more dangerous for people with compromised immune systems.
That warning proved prescient. In January 2024, a 69-year-old man from the Kenai Peninsula south of Anchorage, with an immune system weakened by cancer treatments, died from the infection.
The disease is now called borealpox, reflecting scientists’ conviction that it is found beyond Alaska.
The global total of diagnosed borealpox cases now stands at nine, with two new Fairbanks-area cases identified this year at Werle’s practice.
Borealpox is among the world’s most recently identified zoonotic diseases, a term for diseases that can leap between animal species and people. It is a growing list that includes several potentially deadly diseases such as COVID-19, Zika and Ebola.
Borealpox is now known to be circulating in small mammals, particularly red-backed voles, a species of burrowing animals found in almost all of Alaska and beyond in North America. The virus or antibodies indicating its past presence were also found in other small mammals, like squirrels, shrews and at least one house mouse.
 

A northern red-backed vole is seen in this undated photo. Red-backed voles, which are known to be carriers of the borealpox virus, are plentiful and found in almost all regions of Alaska. (Photo by Jim Dau/provided by Alaska Department of Fish and Game)
 

	That conclusion came after researchers from the CDC, the Alaska Department of Health and the University of Alaska conducted searches in the wild over successive summers. They live-trapped and tested numerous types of small mammals in the woods around Fairbanks. Later, they extended their trap-and-test search to the Kenai Peninsula.
Along with the live-trapping effort, scientists at the University of Alaska Museum of the North went through the facility’s store of over 130,000 mammals to see if any in the past were carrying the virus.
The museum search hit pay dirt: proof that the virus dates back nearly three decades. A red-backed vole collected in 1998 from Denali National Park and stored as part of the museum’s vast collection was shown to be carrying a viable borealpox virus.
The large number of red-backed voles and their short lifespans, which are typically only about a year, help explain why the borealpox virus was so readily found in that species, said Link Olson, curator of mammals at the University of Alaska Museum of the North. Voles acquiring the virus may not have had enough time to outlive it, Olson said.
The degree to which the virus is circulating in longer-lived animals is now an important area of study. Olson and his colleagues are focusing on red squirrels, which generally live for five years in the wild.
“They live longer, and if they are exposed and survive, they will continue to mount an antibody response,” Olson said. “The downside of that type of testing is that it has to be a very fresh specimen, so none of these tissue samples from 30 years ago are amenable to serum testing.”
However, if any of the preserved red squirrels had active borealpox infections when they died, DNA tests can detect those, he added.
 

A northern red-backed vole scampers through a forested area of the Kenai Peninsula. (Photo by Colin Canterbury/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)
 

	Exactly why borealpox is emerging now is unknown. There are too few documented cases to make any determinations beyond theories, according to scientists who are researching it.
One of those theories is that people are more susceptible to picking up pox viruses circulating in the environment because smallpox vaccines are no longer routine, now that that once-deadly disease is considered eradicated.
“The hypothesis that keeps popping up time and time again is that that coincides with the first generation or two of people who are not routinely vaccinated for smallpox,” Olson said.
Werle believes that is a logical explanation. Routine vaccination for smallpox stopped around 1980.
“We have a whole new generation of people enjoying the outdoors who don’t have that innate smallpox immunity through vaccination,” he said.
Other theories link borealpox’s appearance to climate change.
A 2025 study by an international team that included UAF researchers suggested that permafrost thaw may be a factor in borealpox, as it is for some other pathogens. A 2024 paper in The Lancet, a medical journal, suggested another possible factor: warmer winters that might be enabling a longer reproduction season and thus a population boom for red-backed voles.
A similarity in the cases to date is seasonal timing. All of the known human infections occurred in the summer or fall seasons, when people become busier in their outdoor recreation pursuits and food-gathering activities like hunting and berry-picking.

Ripe raspberries hang from a branch in this undated photo. (Photo provided by the University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension Service)

Berry-picking, a popular late-summer and fall Alaska activity, was a common theme, Werle said.
“My personal theory on that is, potentially, some of these small rodents may be eating on raspberries or other berries that people also are picking and consuming,” he said. So people sticking their hands into raspberry patches and getting scratched up may be getting exposed to the virus. “If a small animal has defecated or urinated as they’re climbing those branches to chew on those berries.”
Another common theme is care for pets, particularly cats. Cats are widely implicated in the transmission to humans of another pox virus, cowpox, Werle noted. That makes it logical to add cats to the list of suspected borealpox remission sources, he said. “If you have a cat that’s a mouser and is out catching rodents and then rubbing on someone’s skin as it’s greeting them, that could also be another potential source,” he said.
It is also logical to assume that borealpox is much more widespread beyond the Fairbanks area, Denali and Kenai Peninsula, Werle said.
Olson said the museum currently has over 2,000 small mammal specimens in deep freeze that were donated by Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage. The plan is to start testing those, he said.
Werle expects those tests to turn up some positives.
“I think they’re going to find more of it,” he said. “I think this is something that’s just right under our noses.”
People, wildlife and the environment
 

Two caribou walk along the Hulahula River in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in 2019. (Photo by Alexis Bonogofsky/U.S. Fish and WIldlife Service)
 

	The study of borealpox falls under the One Health approach that connects humans, animals and the environment. Examined through the One Health approach, zoonotic diseases are of concern to people in Alaska not just because of the possibility of human infection but also because the risks to wildlife populations are important to rural and mostly Indigenous residents’ food security and culture.
Of particular concern in Alaska are caribou populations.
Caribou herds are in decline across the Arctic, a concern for rural residents who depend on hunting. Climate change is cited as a key factor, but so are various diseases, which themselves could be linked to climate change.
One example is a bacterium called Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, which causes a skin infection called erysipelas. In people, the infection turns skin red and is sometimes referred to as “St. Anthony’s fire.” The bacterium affects domestic livestock. And in recent years, it has been showing up in caribou herds, Canada and Greenland — with a suggested link to climate change, according to a 2022 study by U.S. and Canadian researchers from institutions that included the Alaska Department of Fish and Game.
The study found that seroprevalence, the term that refers to antibody presence in the blood from a prior infection, increased in summers following winters with rain-on-snow or icing events. Warmer winters produce rain-on-snow and icing events.
Also studying caribou, among other animals, is Jayne Ellis, who teaches wildlife pathology in the UAF Veterinary Medicine Program.

The exterior of the Alaska state virology lab on the University of Alaska Fairbanks campus is seen on June 23, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

Ellis, herself a graduate of UAF’s veterinary collaboration with Colorado State University, specializes in animal disease. She has been among those researching the spread of highly pathogenic avian influenza into wild terrestrial Alaska mammal populations, for example. Currently, she and her research partners are tracking a respiratory disease affecting caribou and moose, especially young animals, in different parts of the state.
She is a leader of UAF’s One Health Wildlife Laboratory, where she and other researchers are studying numerous other animal health conditions.
Those include zoonotic diseases of concern carried by voles, the plentiful mammals that are known to be carriers of borealpox. Ellis and her colleagues trapped several in the summer of 2025 and examined them for other diseases and pathogens.
The tiny animals, now under scrutiny for their role in spreading borealpox, had not gotten much attention until recently, she said.
“They’re minimally studied because people don’t really care about them,” she said. “But also, you know, they go everywhere, so they interact with wildlife, they interact with domestic animals, and then they go into people’s houses. And so they’re a big risk in terms of a vector for a zoonotic disease.”
Prominent among the troublesome zoonotic pathogens they found in the voles was bartonella, a type of bacteria that causes the disease bartonellosis.
It is commonly called “cat scratch disease” or “cat scratch fever” and is generally a nuisance but not dangerous for most people. But bartonellosis can cause serious problems in wildlife. Starting in 2006, for example, a die-off of sea otters in the Kenai Peninsula’s Kachemak Bay coincided with high rates of exposure to bartonella, as scientists explained in a study published in 2014.
 

A microscopic photograph taken in 2002 reveals numerous Francisella tularensis coccobacilli, the bacterium responsible for causing the disease, tularemia. (Photo by Larry Stauffer/Oregon State Public Health Laboratory/Provided by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.)
 

	When there is a health mystery with terrestrial animals, Ellis is often called upon to solve it. She works on contract for the Alaska Department of Fish and Game at the virology lab on the UAF campus. Veterinarians, scientists and even pet owners in the general public send samples for Ellis and her colleagues to analyze.
When unusual diseases emerge among marine mammals, the scientists called into action are generally from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, other government agencies, the Alaska SeaLife Center in Seward and Alaska Veterinary Pathology Services in Eagle River, which contracts with agencies like NOAA’s National Marine Fisheries Service.
One disease showing signals of growing presence among Alaska marine mammals is tularemia, a tick-borne disease sometimes called “rabbit fever.”
In Alaska, tularemia is generally considered a terrestrial disease associated with hares. However, polar bears — classified as marine mammals because their habitat is the Arctic Ocean and its sea ice — are showing increasing signs of exposure, according to blood tests that found the presence of antibodies. That trend, documented by the U.S. Geological Survey, comes as climate change has reduced sea ice extent over the long term, forcing polar bears to spend more time on land.
Tularemia has also shown up in marine mammals farther south — in the endangered population of Cook Inlet beluga whales, for example.
Tularemia was documented for the first time in that population after two pregnant belugas were found dead in the fall of 2023, according to research led by Alaska Veterinary Pathology Services. Tularemia was determined to be the cause of death for the belugas, with an environmental source suspected. The route of exposure, said the researchers’ report to the CDC, published in 2025, “was likely inhalation of contaminated water.”
 

A Cook Inlet beluga mother and calf are seen swimming in 2017. Tularemia, a tick-borne disease, was recently identified in two dead Cook Inlet belugas. (Photo by Hollis Europe and Jacob Barbaro/NOAA Fisheries)
 

	Tularemia can affect people too, though human cases are rare. There was one documented in 2023 in Anchorage, in the same Cook Inlet basin that is home to the infected belugas that were found dead that year. There was another documented Anchorage case in 2024 and one in Interior Alaska in 2025, according to state health officials.
For the doctors, veterinarians and scientists making discoveries about emerging zoonotic diseases, there are some mixed feelings.
Some findings can be worrisome, and inconclusive results can be frustrating, they say.
Still, putting together the puzzle pieces and gaining confirmation through lab tests at top scientific facilities can be satisfying.
That is the case for Werle, whose discovery of borealpox was an unexpected career turn.
“This is the kind of thing that you never expect is going to be a part of your medical practice as an individual community practitioner kind of in the front lines, in the trenches,” he said. “This is not something that you ever think you’re going to have a chance to be a part of, so I think it’s really been very rewarding for me to be a part of it.”
Jayne Ellis, assistant professor of veterinary medicine at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, stands on July 23, 2026, by a cabinet of animal samples at the Alaska state virology lab on the university campus. Ellis also works on contract for the Alaska Department of Fish and Game helping to track and analyze animal diseases. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: Mississippi Today
title: Sen.-elect Scott Colom holds first town hall in deep-red Itawamba County, where he lost
description: U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom answers questions at a town hall in Fulton, Miss., on Tuesday, Nov. 24.
text:
FULTON — U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom on Tuesday night answered questions at a town hall in northeastern Mississippi about rural health care, abortion rights, immigration, raising the minimum wage and how he plans to work with Republicans after he’s sworn into office. 
Colom chose Itawamba County, a deep-red conservative area that’s majority-white, for his first town hall since he won the Senate race because it’s the area where he drew the least amount of support on Election Day. 
His Republican opponent, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, won the county with over 81% of the vote, with Colom pulling in about 16%.
“We’re going to start at the place where I didn’t get the most votes because I represent the people in Itawamba County, just like I represent the people of every county,” Colom said. 
About 500 people filled the historic Fulton Grammar School auditorium. The event had to be moved from its original venue after it outgrew the space.
Kitchen-table issues
When he’s sworn into office in January, Colom said he would focus on “kitchen-table issues” affecting working families, starting with the cost of groceries.
Colom said the most immediate thing he could do to curb the rising price of groceries is to rein in President Donald Trump’s tariffs, calling them “a tax on everything” that has hurt Mississippi farmers who lost customers for their soybeans. 
He said he would not hand tariff authority “to a Republican president or a Democratic president.” When an attendee asked about the state’s grocery tax, Colom said that is a state issue and that Mississippians need a governor and Legislature who understand how it affects working families.
Colom also said he would work to raise the federal minimum wage, which has been $7.25 an hour since 2009 and is the default rate in Mississippi, which has no state minimum wage. 
Asked for specifics, Colom acknowledged that businesses have to be able to afford it. He said he would talk with business leaders and workers to “find some middle ground,” but added, “We’re going to raise the minimum wage.”
He said he supports banning members of Congress from trading stocks and wants to get a bill to the president’s desk “as soon as possible.” 
“If you are a public servant, you can’t be in it for profit,” Colom said.
Health care
Colom said health care was among his top three issues, and he warned that cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act put the state’s rural hospitals at risk of closing. He cited state Insurance Commissioner Mike Chaney, who said that about 400,000 Mississippians lack health insurance. 
“If they can’t pay, that means the hospital has less doctors, less nurses and less administrators,” he said.
He said he supports expanding Medicaid and exploring ways for people who can’t afford coverage to buy into the ACA or a similar program. 
Abortion
A local pastor asked Colom to clarify his stance on abortion. The soon-to-be senator said that he was personally pro-life, but, as a father of two daughters, he didn’t think a man should dictate women’s health care decisions for them. 
Colom also said he believed the issue was best left up to states and not the federal government. He specifically said the state Legislature should revive Mississippi’s ballot initiative process, which was invalidated in 2021 by the state Supreme Court over technicalities with Mississippi’s congressional districts. 
“That’s the democratic way to do it,” Colom said. “We really have to ask questions to our state legislators, our state senators, our state representatives. Why would they not bring the referendum power back?” 
Some lawmakers have attempted to restore the initiative process, but the Legislature for five years has failed to reach a consensus. 
Immigration, guns and hunger
Asked about border security, Colom said he supports a secure border and is “not going to allow open borders,” and that he thinks Trump “has done a good job on securing the borders.” 
He said he supports deporting people who commit violent crimes and that American workers should get priority for tech jobs, including those tied to H-1B visas.
On guns, Colom said he’s a “big believer in Second Amendment rights” and wants his wife to be able to protect herself and their daughters. He said that as a former prosecutor, he handled many gun violence cases, mostly involving handguns, and that good jobs and education are the best way to reduce it. 
When an attendee noted that one in four Mississippi children go to bed hungry, Colom said one step would be to reverse cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
Colom has pledged to do town halls throughout his time as senator, and challenged voters and reporters to hold Republican candidates in next year’s statewide elections accountable to do town halls in traditionally Democratic areas, such as Jackson and the Mississippi Delta. 
“Why am I doing town halls in Itawamba but they never do town halls in Jackson?” Colom asked. “When was the last time a Republican had a town hall in Jackson? It hasn’t happened in my lifetime.”

title: Those mourning overdose deaths need their neighbors most at the holidays
description:
When a death is from addiction, stigma often keeps friends and community at a distance.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Those mourning overdose deaths need their neighbors most at the holidays.
text:
This commentary is by Maxwell Crystal, a licensed independent clinical social worker in Vermont at Maxwell Crystal Therapy.
As the holiday season approaches, those grieving a death often feel its absence acutely: an empty seat at the Thanksgiving table, a family tradition that no longer feels the same, the house where everyone used to gather, perhaps now in someone else’s hands.
This grief is especially acute when the death is addiction related. Stories of recovery are becoming more normalized and celebrated, but stories of death are often swept under the rug.
A death from addiction can lead to disenfranchised grief for survivors. Disenfranchised grief occurs when a death is seen as socially unacceptable, which can lead to a withdrawal of support from community members or loved ones. Survivors holding disenfranchised grief often feel unrecognized, unvalidated or unsupported.
Luckily, overdose deaths from addiction are decreasing in Vermont. The Vermont Department of Health’s preliminary data show that in 2025 there were 170 drug-related overdose deaths, a 25% decrease from 2024. We can all be thankful that the harm reduction and recovery efforts have brought about this change.
However, death from addiction comes in many forms. It can be a slow process of liver failure or sudden and unexpected from an overdose. Whatever the circumstances, loved ones are often left to pick up the pieces. They often hesitate to tell people how their person died for fear of tarnishing the memory of their loved one. 

READ MORE

As a society, we often struggle to respond when someone dies. In an effort to protect ourselves, we withdraw from survivors, often when they need us most. This is particularly true when the death is from addiction. We fear saying the wrong thing to the bereaved, so instead we say nothing at all. 
This holiday season, I encourage you to check on your neighbors. Don’t be afraid to say the name of the person who died. Use the family’s words; if they say “overdose,” you can too. Don’t lead with “How did it happen?” Ask instead about their loved one. 
Simple actions, such as inviting them over for the holiday, bringing them a meal or shoveling their driveway, let the bereaved know they are not alone. We can go further by sitting down for a cup of tea and asking them how they are. 
This holiday season, I invite you to sit with your neighbors, loved ones and friends who are bereaved. Be a witness for them; join them in their experience. Be courageous, and be with them, even if it is uncomfortable for you.

title: The only Vermont band ever to perform at Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade? Drumroll, please…
description:
As the New York City march steps off for a 100th time, the Brattleboro Union High School band is marking the 45th anniversary of its nationally televised appearance in 1981.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The only Vermont band ever to perform at Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade? Drumroll, please….
text:
The Brattleboro Union High School band performs at the 1981 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, as pictured at the time on a television airing NBC coverage. Brattleboro Reformer photo

BRATTLEBORO — Ask Brattleboro Historical Society volunteers for popular posts on their Facebook page and they’ll point to the 1,000 or more views for recent remembrances of the 1891 visit of President Benjamin Harrison and the 1956 campaign stop of future Commander in Chief John Kennedy.
Then come the 64,000 clicks and counting for a video of the only Vermont band ever to perform at Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, set to mark its 100th march on Thursday.
Back in 1981, Brattleboro Union High School was one of 13 bands the sponsoring department store chose from 400 national applicants on the basis of musical and marching proficiency, appealing uniforms and awards such as top Vermont All State Music Festival parade honors for six of the previous seven years.
“There are not many bands that apply from New England,” a Macy’s producer told the local Reformer newspaper at the time. “But that is not why they were chosen. It was for their excellence.”

The Brattleboro Union High School band marches through New York City during the 1981 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Photo by Terry Sprague/Brattleboro Reformer

Once in New York City that Thanksgiving, the 102-student band practiced in Herald Square at 4 in the morning before performing on live television shortly after 10 a.m.
“Viewers included thousands of band fans in Brattleboro who had raised nearly $40,000 to bring the band to the parade,” the Reformer’s front page reported the next day. “For their family and friends waiting near Macy’s, there were goosebumps, fast-beating hearts and a sense of enormous pride as they caught the first glimpse of their band on Broadway.”
Finishing in front of the self-proclaimed “World’s Largest Store,” the band played the 1960s and 1970s hit “On Broadway” for NBC television cameras and tens of millions of viewers nationwide.
“I can’t believe that it is over,” one musician told the Reformer immediately after. “We will have our memories of this forever.”
That proved true for years. Students reunited in town annually in the 1980s and returned to New York in 1991 to watch the parade on the 10th anniversary of their appearance. Then time scattered members and socked away memories on now-obsolete VHS tapes.

The front page of the Nov. 27, 1981 Brattleboro Reformer reports on the Brattleboro Union High School band’s appearance at Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Enter social media. Family and friends shared the band’s performance and a resulting documentary upon the 21st century advent of YouTube. The historical society joined in two years ago, posting an initial Facebook video that racked up 21,000 views in a town of 12,184 residents.
“That brought tears of pride and homesickness to my eyes,” wrote one commenter.
“I get choked up,” said a second.
“Me too!” added a third.
When the historical society reposted the video last Thanksgiving, views rose by another 43,000.
“So glad you shared this!” wrote one commenter. “I remember watching it that day on TV looking for my cousin in the band.”
“And I was the kid in the middle with the 3 white drums!” said a second.
“No way!” replied the first. “I had no idea — now I’ll have to watch it again to look for you!”
The historical society expects another flurry of response when it reposts the video this week — and not simply because of the twin Macy’s and Brattleboro anniversaries.
“What gets the most hits,” says historical society volunteer Bob Cornellier, “are the things people remember.”

title: The Pilgrims would be proud: The midterms were a victory for religious freedom
description: This election offered another reason for gratitude in the same vein, with its wholehearted embrace of religious freedom – in response to some of the ugliest attacks on faith I have witnessed in American public life.
text:
AS WE APPROACH Thanksgiving, I have been reflecting on the meaning of the recent midterms and the message voters sent about the kind of country they want us to be. 
To be sure, voters were concerned about the economy and Donald Trump. But more than four centuries after the Pilgrims’ search for freedom of worship ended here in Massachusetts, this election offered another reason for gratitude in the same vein, with its wholehearted embrace of religious freedom – in response to some of the ugliest attacks on faith I have witnessed in American public life. 
In the runup to November 3, President Trump called Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a “jihadist,” joking that he would need to pass through a metal detector before entering the Senate. Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio said El-Sayed should be “nowhere near Washington, DC,” and questioned whether he understood “that Jesus came here for our salvation.” 
As a person of color and an observant Jewish woman, I have strongly disagreed with now-Sen.-elect El-Sayed’s positions on Israel. And I remain troubled by his association with influencer Hasan Piker. But we can challenge a candidate’s rhetoric, policies, and associations without treating their religion as evidence of disloyalty. 
We are not electing a priest, pope, rabbi, or imam. We are choosing public servants. Their characters, records and ideas belong in the debate. But using religious identity to declare them unfit crosses a line. 
In stark contrast to Trump and Moreno’s bigotry stood Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico. A Presbyterian seminarian, Talarico made his Christian faith central to his public service while opposing efforts to impose religious instruction and observance, such as requiring the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms. 
For Talarico, protecting religious freedom does not require us to leave our faith outside public life. Rather, it requires us to respect the freedom of those who believe differently.  It’s a line made clear in our Constitution, with Article VI barring religious tests for federal office, and the First Amendment protecting religious freedom. 
History reminds us how religious suspicion can be used to question someone’s belonging. President John F. Kennedy faced questions about whether his Catholic faith would make him loyal to the pope. Barack Obama was targeted with false claims about his religion and loyalties, often invoking his middle name, Hussein – and famously facing scrutiny over words spoken not by him but by his former pastor. Former Massachusetts governor Mitt Romney confronted suspicion about his Mormon faith. 
As JFK warned in his famous Houston speech to Protestant ministers, “For while this year it may be a Catholic against whom the finger of suspicion is pointed, in other years it has been, and may someday be again, a Jew—or a Quaker—or a Unitarian—or a Baptist.” Indeed, as JB Pritzker, Josh Shapiro, Jon Ossoff, and Rahm Emanuel are discussed as presidential candidates, suggestions of divided loyalty due to their Jewish faith are already entering the conversation. 
Of course, the complicated story of the Pilgrims is not the whole story of America.   
Twenty-five years ago, the American Jewish Committee (of which I am a board member) created America’s Table, a Thanksgiving reader that invited families to reflect on the many paths that brought people to this country. 
At a moment of grief in the wake of September 11, and fear for Arabs and Muslims, it offered a Jewish organization’s affirmation of our shared belonging: a reminder that standing against Muslim hate does not diminish our opposition to Jewish hate – but affirms that the freedom and dignity we seek for our own community belong to others as well.  
This Thanksgiving, let us give thanks for the freedoms that make our country stronger and that voters defended this year: the freedom to worship or not to worship, to vote, and to love whom we choose. 
But let us also remember that “giving thanks” for our freedoms is the easy part. Defending them for others and making room at our tables, and in our country, for one another takes not only character and courage. It takes work from all of us. 
Colette A.M. Phillips is president and CEO of Colette Phillips Communications, Inc., an inclusion-focused communications and consulting firm, and the founder of Get Konnected. She is the author of The Includers: The 7 Traits of Culturally Savvy Anti-Racist Leaders.

title: More CA seniors are working — only some of them want to
description: Happy Thanksgiving! We’re taking a break for the holiday and will return to your inboxes Monday, Nov. 30. Try to stay dry and be careful on the roads. More on that below.  Did you vote on Prop. 38, the ballot measure to pump $8.4 billion into medical research? A big chunk of that money likely […]
text:
Sue Bird helps a customer at the Big Valley Market in Bieber on Jan. 30, 2024. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




Happy Thanksgiving! We’re taking a break for the holiday and will return to your inboxes Monday, Nov. 30. Try to stay dry and be careful on the roads. More on that below. 
Did you vote on Prop. 38, the ballot measure to pump $8.4 billion into medical research? A big chunk of that money likely will go to one fledgling organization that has just three employees and no boss. 
We know many seniors are working these days, and new research shows they’ll make up an ever greater share of the labor force in the very near future. We hear there are some openings at that medical research center. 
California’s workforce is projected to get much older over the next decade.
By 2040, about 23% of Californians will be 65 or older, and the state’s labor force among those workers is projected to reach 1.8 million by then — an increase of roughly half a million people compared to 2024, according to an October report from the Public Policy Institute of California.
A look at years prior sheds light to this projection: The number of older workers has doubled in the last two decades. Between 2006 and 2024, the state’s labor force increased by 2.45 million workers, and of those workers, nearly a third, 31%, were workers aged 65 and older. Meanwhile, workers between 16 to 64 grew during that time period by only 10%.
PPIC’s data does not parse why people are working longer than in the past. For some, work can be personally gratifying and they continue to work because they’re healthy enough to do so.
For others, they work because they need to. And because of work, about 800,000 older Californians, mostly in the 65 to 69 age group, are not in poverty.

Hans Johnson, senior fellow at PPIC and demographer: “It’s more important, for example, than Social Security, at that age group in keeping people out of poverty.”

As the state’s labor force gets older, lawmakers and employers should consider policy issues that ensure work is available for older adults, said Johnson, such as providing training opportunities, guaranteeing accessible work conditions and protecting workers against age discrimination.
This is underscored by the fact that for workers younger than 50, about a quarter of those who lose their jobs do not find work three years later. But for workers around 70 years of age, half do not return to employment, according to Kara Segal, senior research manager at the California Policy Lab.

Segal, during a panel discussion about the PPIC report: “When older workers are laid off and their job is disrupted, the outcomes tend to be much, much worse.”




CalMatters Ideas Festival: 2027 Ideas Festival will expand to Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Francisco. One full day of candid conversations in each, with the leaders, innovators and changemakers shaping California’s future. Learn more.

Other Stories You Should Know


Here comes another big storm


Birds fly over a flooded road during high tides in Alameda on Nov. 24, 2026. Photo by Noah Berger, AP Photo




El Niño is expected to bring heavy rain, flooding and king tides through the Thanksgiving holiday. To make sure you’re ready, CalMatters’ Rachel Becker and Alejandra Reyes-Velarde go over what the state and local governments are doing to prepare for the downpour.
Dylan Flynn, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in the Bay Area, said breaking waves could hit 20 to 30 feet along the coast, and water levels could hit 2.5 to 3 feet above a normal high tide.
Flooding is also expected to disrupt travel, affecting an estimated 1,000 miles of roads statewide. Staying off roads is the best way to stay safe, but if you must travel, try to stick to high ground and avoid coastal roads that are near high tides, experts say.
To see if you’re in a high-risk area, Fraser Shilling, director of the UC Davis Road Ecology Center, published a report listing places vulnerable to coastal flooding in Central and Northern California, which includes areas like Highway 37 along the San Pablo Bay and parts of Highway 101 in Marin County. 
You can also check road conditions using this Caltrans map and sign up for local emergency alerts.
Read more.



Who’s in charge at newly flush research center?


An interior view of UCLA Research Park under construction in West Los Angeles on Aug. 19, 2024. Photo by Brian van der Brug, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images




A California institute that is the likely beneficiary of a voter-approved $4 billion bond to fund immunology research doesn’t have a chief executive, writes CalMatters’ Mikhail Zinshteyn.
Earlier this month voters passed Proposition 38, which sets aside $8.4 billion in bonds for immune system research. Specific language in the ballot measure points to a single unnamed institute that would receive half that money: The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, or CIII. The institute signed an affiliation deal with UCLA in 2024, and four top officials at UCLA sit on the board.
To date, it only has three employees. 
At a November University of California Board of Regents meeting, John C. Mazziotta, UCLA Health’s chief executive and a CIII board member, said the institute is “in the process of recruiting teams,” and has yet to find a CEO because prospective candidates are “very high-end people who have lots of other opportunities.”
The hiring lag is drawing criticism from Prop. 38 opponents.

David Panush, who co-led the No on Prop. 38 campaign: “Prop. 38 proponents promised voters that their institute would be ‘ready-to-go, competitive and world-class.’ But now we’re learning that CIII just has ‘initial thoughts’ and is still trying to find a CEO. When will we see a plan?”

Read more.



And lastly: Delay in report on murdered Indigenous people


A tipi with handprints by the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women movement commemorates the lives lost during a California Native American Day celebration at the state Capitol on Sept. 22, 2023. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




Homicide is one of the leading causes of death for Native American and Alaska Native people aged 44 and younger. But California has no statewide office dedicated to missing and murdered Indigenous people and no official count of cases. 
A 2020 state law intended to change that by requiring California’s justice department to conduct a report identifying barriers to investigating cases and recommending changes. Seven months after the report was due to the Legislature in 2025, however, there is still no report. Read more from CalMatters’ Melanie Henshaw. 






California Voices
California cannot wait for downtowns to revive on their own — it needs a deliberate, “high-road” economic strategy to protect thousands of security guards, cleaners and maintenance people, as well as the businesses that depend on them, writes Luis Sandoval, executive director of the Building Skills Partnership.

title: Kansas lawmaker accuses governor’s administration of stealing funds for I/DD waiver waitlist
description: TOPEKA — A Kansas lawmaker accused outgoing Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s administration of stealing money out from underneath Kansans with intellectual and developmental disabilities during a legislative hearing over the decision to shift $24 million from one disability services program to another. Another lawmaker said at the Monday hearing the administrat[...]
text:
Rep. Sean Tarwater, R-Stilwell, watches the action on the House floor on March 18, 2026, in Topeka. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A Kansas lawmaker accused outgoing Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s administration of stealing money out from underneath Kansans with intellectual and developmental disabilities during a legislative hearing over the decision to shift $24 million from one disability services program to another.
Another lawmaker said at the Monday hearing the administration disregarded legislative intent when funds were reappropriated from a program meant for Kansans with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
“What bothers me is that the Legislature, who our No. 1 responsibility is to produce a budget — that is constitutionally our role, and it was dismissed,” said Rep. Kristey Williams, an Augusta Republican and chair of the House government oversight committee.
Andrew Brown, the deputy secretary of programs at the agency that oversees the disability waiver program, maintained the $24 million transfer was allowed.
Williams and other lawmakers don’t see it that way.
“You knew the intent of the Legislature with any remaining money. It was specified,” Williams said.
She said the Legislature intended for the money to remain tied to the intellectual and developmental disability, or I/DD, waiver program in an effort to reduce its waitlist of more than 5,000 people. In the past two budgets, the Legislature added earmarks for I/DD waiver waitlist reductions. Brown said the funds were not initially appropriated to any particular waiver.
Williams told Brown the Legislature will now have to make its appropriations bill 100 pages longer to ensure there isn’t any further “misinterpretation.”
Rep. Sean Tarwater, a Stilwell Republican who recently lost reelection, said the Kelly administration “stole these funds.”
“She also — this governor — has never made them a priority,” he said.
He followed his claims with questions for Kelly:
“Why has this governor and this administration never once included these people in her budget?”
“What do you have against these individuals? What did they do to you?”
Keira Beatty, a spokesperson for the governor’s office, rejected Tarwater’s characterizations.
“Throughout her administration, Gov. Kelly has remained committed to meeting the needs of intellectually and/or developmentally disabled (I/DD) Kansans to ensure they can receive the care they need, when they need it, and within their communities,” Beatty said in a statement. “To suggest Gov. Kelly has not included investments in her budget proposals to address the I/DD waitlist is wholly inaccurate.”
In the two most recent fiscal years 2027, Kelly did not recommend in her budget proposals direct state funding allocations to the I/DD waiver, instead favoring funding for the community support waiver program, which acts as an alternative to the I/DD waiver meant for those who may not require the full swatch of services offered under the I/DD waiver. She did not recommend direct funding for the I/DD waiver program.
In fiscal year 2025, however, Kelly did recommend funding for 250 slots on the I/DD waiver. 
Monday’s hearing was the third time the $24 million has been brought up for discussion in the Statehouse since it was realized in August.
“We seem to be going over and over again,” said Rep. Barbara Ballard, a Lawrence Democrat. “The money is spent.”
Some say the transfer to another waiver program for frail and elderly individuals was authorized, and some say it wasn’t, Ballard said.
In August and September, two other legislative committees reviewed the appropriation and what can be done to prioritize reductions in wait times for people waiting for I/DD waivers.
Williams said the committee’s purpose Monday was to determine “whether state agencies are carrying out their duties with transparency, fidelity to legislative direction and careful stewardship of taxpayer resources.”
The waiver program, which resides within the Kansas Department for Aging and Disabilities and is funded through Medicaid, allows federal Medicaid eligibility requirements to be waived so Kansans who typically wouldn’t qualify for public health insurance can receive specific services for their conditions. The I/DD waiver program has been plagued by 10-year-long wait times and frustration with the agency that oversees the waitlist.
Steven Anderson, the state inspector general, presented preliminary audit findings to the committee that showed 92% of I/DD waiver cases contain insufficient information, including lacking proper forms and records of assessment.
The Legislature mandated the I/DD waitlist rise no higher than 4,000 people. It now sits at more than 5,300, as of October. Lawmakers argue that if the $24 million hadn’t been moved from the I/DD waitlist, it could have prevented such a continued rise.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Plane crash off Mississippi coast kills 6, including 2 children
description: Divers found their bodies in the fuselage after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island.
text:
A small plane crashed Tuesday off the coast of Mississippi, killing the six people, including two children, on board, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.
Divers found their bodies in the fuselage after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore. Four adults and two boys, ages 8 and 10, were on board, Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros said.
The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported about 3:45 p.m. that it lost contact with the aircraft, according to the Coast Guard. Responders searched for hours and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane’s cabin floating on the water, according to Ros.
The Cessna was en route from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.
Cmdr. Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard coordinator for search and rescue in the Mobile area, called the situation heartbreaking.
“While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families,” he said in a statement.
The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the crash.
Earlier this month, a Learjet 60 business jet nosedived into the ground in south Florida, killing all nine people on board. The terrifying crash was captured on video recorded by people inside their cars.
Associated Press reporter Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed to this report.

title: Montana Supreme Court sends Public Service Commissioner suspension back to district court
description: The Montana Supreme Court said Tuesday suspended Public Service Commissioner Brad Molnar needs a chance to fight his temporary removal from office. In July, Gov. Greg Gianforte suspended Molnar after an investigation into allegations of professional misconduct including sexual discrimination and retaliation. Molnar challenged the decision arguing in part he [...]
text:
Brad Molnar, left, and lawyer Matthew Monforton confer before a hearing about Molnar's suspension. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)The Montana Supreme Court said Tuesday suspended Public Service Commissioner Brad Molnar needs a chance to fight his temporary removal from office.
In July, Gov. Greg Gianforte suspended Molnar after an investigation into allegations of professional misconduct including sexual discrimination and retaliation.
Molnar challenged the decision arguing in part he had been denied due process, but he lost in district court.
In a unanimous decision, the justices agreed that Molnar doesn’t get to block the suspension right away, as the lower court decided.
But the justices sent the case back to district court to protect Molnar’s due process rights in the case he filed against three other commissioners and Gianforte.
A Lewis and Clark District Court judge said in August the suspension would stand because the public interest requires a Public Service Commission that’s free from sexual harassment and retaliation.
But Molnar’s lawyer, Matthew Monforton, said the decision meant an elected commissioner could be removed from office without ever having had the chance to test the evidence against him.
Molnar appealed, arguing in part he was denied due process.
The governor suspended him for one year without pay after the PSC voted 3-2 to request the suspension. The PSC regulates monopoly utilities in Montana.
In a unanimous decision, the justices found Molnar had been granted due process before the suspension decision, as the district court concluded, but not after it.
They said the Constitution doesn’t allow Molnar to be suspended without due process, and he must have the opportunity to challenge the suspension decision after the fact.
The justices said the defendants compared the case to other employee relationships, such as workers in grievance procedures, but Molnar had additional responsibilities as an elected official.
“Molnar has a substantial interest in exercising the duties voters entrusted to him during a finite term,” the justices said.
They agreed the government has an interest in protecting employees and ensuring a functional regulatory commission, but they weighed other considerations.
“Those interests do not reduce an elected commissioner to an employee whom agency managers may discipline under ordinary personnel authority,” the justices said.
They said a staff member reported that Molnar’s earlier demotion as PSC president reduced disruptions in the office, and the account weighed in his favor. That’s because he wanted to be an “ordinary” commissioner again, not president.
That meant he could perform commissioner duties remotely, without necessarily leading to the same disruptions in the office, the justices said.
Additionally, the justices said competing evidence supported Molnar’s argument he needed a chance to test the allegations against him.
Some of the information used to suspend him was disclosed late in the process, and the timing reinforced the need for a later proceeding where he could challenge the material too, the justices said.
They said the district court erred when it found Molnar had made his due process argument too late to be considered.
Tuesday, the justices sent the case back to district court to resolve the due process claim on an “expedited schedule,” partly because he has constituents who elected him.
“Molnar has a substantial interest in exercising the duties voters entrusted to him during a finite term,” they said.
They said the district court needs to address the unresolved post-suspension claim and grounds for continued suspension, and the procedures need to provide a meaningful hearing.
“A meaningful post-suspension hearing must allow Molnar to present evidence and challenge material adverse evidence before a decisionmaker who can resolve the contested grounds for continued deprivation,” the justices said.
The justices also said they were addressing the procedural question, not the disputed conduct.
Molnar’s suspension runs through July 8, 2027, and it requires he complete workplace training before reinstatement.
“Our decision upholds denial of the motion on the August 28 record,” the justice said of the decision to deny Molnar’s request to preliminarily block the suspension. “It does not authorize suspension through July 8, 2027, without the process the Constitution requires.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: How will data centers impact Michigan’s renewable energy goals? It’s complicated, new research says
description: As data center proposals pop up across Michigan, concerns about the amount of energy and water used by hyperscale facilities across the country has been at the forefront of arguments against the projects. With a facility under construction in Saline Township expected to use 1.4 gigawatts of electricity – roughly equivalent to the power usage […]
text:
DTE Monroe power plant (Photo by Susan J. Demas/Michigan Advance)As data center proposals pop up across Michigan, concerns about the amount of energy and water used by hyperscale facilities across the country has been at the forefront of arguments against the projects.
With a facility under construction in Saline Township expected to use 1.4 gigawatts of electricity – roughly equivalent to the power usage of 1.2 million Michigan homes – and another in Van Buren Township expected to demand 1 gigawatt from the grid, environmental advocates have raised concerns over how the electricity demand from facilities like these will impact Michigan’s clean energy goals.
In 2023, the Democratic-led Michigan Legislature passed a series of clean energy bills, including legislation requiring Michigan energy companies to supply power from a portfolio of 100% clean energy resources – which can include nuclear energy and natural gas facilities using 90% effective carbon capture and storage technology – by 2040.
Along with the clean energy standard, the law also requires energy companies to secure 60% of their power from renewable sources including solar, wind, geothermal energy and the movement of water by 2035.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While the law has benchmark requirements for energy providers to build up their portfolio of renewable energy resources, organizations such as the Michigan Environmental Council have argued that increased energy demand from data centers could extend the lifespan of fossil fuel plants, and incentivize companies to build additional gas plants.
In a recent research brief, the nonpartisan Citizens Research Council of Michigan examined how data centers could impact the state’s efforts to meet that 60% renewable energy standard within the next nine years.
Currently, only about 13% of Michigan’s electricity is generated from renewable energy sources, the report notes. 
The state is also facing separate challenges in building up its renewable resources, including ongoing legal challenges to the law around renewable energy siting, expiring tax credits from the federal Inflation Reduction Act, the growing cost of energy generation and the difficulties connecting energy resources to the grid.
The brief also noted that Michigan’s clean energy law was crafted in 2023, meaning policymakers hadn’t considered the possibility of rapid growth in electricity demand from hyperscale data centers when setting these goals. It also points to comments from the Data Center Coalition, an industry group, acknowledging that increased electricity demand from data centers “may challenge the utility’s ability to procure or develop sufficient clean energy sources, implicating statutory or regulatory clean energy and emissions reductions targets.”
Construction underway on Related Digital’s hyperscale data center in Saline Township, Michigan. June 20, 2026. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance
Data center tax breaks come with a clean energy requirement
When Michigan lawmakers penned the bills creating the sales and use tax exemption for data centers, they included requirements for data center developers to procure 90% clean energy. However the brief explains that the law does not specify how data centers would demonstrate this, leaving certification of the clean energy requirement to the Michigan Strategic Fund.
Under the fund’s guidelines, a data center can meet the clean energy requirement by contracting with an electric utility that is “actively pursuing compliance” with Michigan’s clean energy law. 
If the utility does not comply, the data center does not lose certification for the tax credit, the brief explains, noting that this effectively makes the 90% clean energy requirement a non-factor in meeting the requirements for a tax exemption. Considering the difficulty that new data center energy loads will impose on the utilities, the Citizens Research Council said that could prompt utilities to delay complying with the state’s clean and renewable energy requirements, through the law’s “off-ramp” provision.
Given that two utilities – DTE Energy and Consumers Energy – supply 90% of Michigan’s electricity, the Citizens Research Council examined each company’s plans for meeting the state’s renewable energy requirements.
Consumers Energy is already supplying power to a hyperscale data center, which the council defines as a facility using more than 100 megawatts at peak demand. Additional data center contracts are pending local approval.
In its most recent integrated resource plan, Consumers Energy acknowledged it must accommodate an additional 2,000 megawatts of electricity demand that it had not anticipated in its 2021 plan. It must do so while replacing 3,000 megawatts of fossil fuel generation as it retires the J.H. Campbell coal plant in Ottawa County and winds down operations at the Dan E. Karn Generating Plant in Bay County by 2031.
Consumers Energy has said closing the J.H. Campbell plant was expected to save Michigan ratepayers $600 million by 2040. (Photo/Sarah Leach)
To meet that demand, Consumers plans to add 3,000 megawatts of solar energy generation and 1,200 megawatts of wind by 2031, continuing at a similar pace through 2041. The company expects to bring 17,500 megawatts of renewable energy online over the next 15 years, which its analysts say will allow it to meet the state’s clean and renewable energy benchmarks.
DTE Energy, meanwhile, is contracted to provide power to both the Saline Township and Van Buren Township data centers. 
The Saline Township project includes an agreement for the data center to fund 1.4 gigawatts of 4-hour battery storage capacity, which would be owned by DTE. While battery storage is complementary to renewable energy use, the council notes that the batteries do not generate renewable energy.
In order to meet the state’s renewable energy portfolio standards while supplying power to the Saline Township data center, the council’s brief says Google will need to bring more renewable energy resources online than previously planned. 
As for the Van Buren Township project, Google, which is developing the data center, plans to ensure 40% of the power it receives will be generated by renewables. Google will also be funding 480 megawatts of energy storage and 1.6 gigawatts of renewable generation capacity, although the report said the renewable energy credits created by these sources will not be available to DTE. 
In order to serve the Google data center and maintain compliance with the state’s renewable portfolio requirements, DTE estimates that it will need to increase its long-term renewable energy target by 10.8%, which will be funded by a surcharge on Google’s bill. According to the company, the Google data center will be funding 40% more renewable energy than it uses
In its briefing, the council noted that funding for renewable energy and battery storage from these two data centers is critical to DTE’s recently proposed Integrated Resource Plan. 
While these agreements will help bring more renewables online, the Citizens Research Council said these data centers will also bring substantial, unanticipated energy load growth, creating a challenge for DTE to provide enough power for these energy loads while it works to retire 3 gigawatts of coal by 2032.
However, DTE expects to meet this challenge while complying with the state’s renewable portfolio requirements by building roughly 15 gigawatts of renewable generation, 4.5 gigawatts of battery storage, and two new natural gas plants for peak energy demand with a combined generation capacity of 2.1 gigawatts.
Wind turbine in mid-Michigan, Feb. 7, 2023 | Laina G. Stebbins
Data centers bring both opportunities and risks for renewable energy 
While the two utilities have provided plans to meet Michigan’s renewable energy requirements while supplying power to data centers, the Citizens Research Council does acknowledge concerns from environmental advocates that these companies would not need to develop a combined 3.5 gigawatts of new natural gas generation if they were not serving data centers.
Although it is theoretically possible to meet current and future energy demand with renewables alone, the council said that could prove difficult, and could be “unacceptably costly.” It notes that while fossil fuel energy  generation can be turned on and off to meet demand, renewable energy is contingent on climate and weather.
Power transmission could also present a challenge, the council said, as redistributing energy generation from a few large fossil fuel plants to several smaller renewable sites could require a substantial investment into transmission infrastructure that would ultimately be paid for by energy customers.
According to the council, if Consumers and DTE did not plan to build this additional natural gas generation, they would need to build at least 10 gigawatts of additional renewable energy alongside additional battery storage and transmission infrastructure to make that power available where it is needed.
“Michigan’s utilities are obligated to meet Michigan’s renewable goals, but they are also obligated to do so without impairing reliability or incurring excessive costs,” the council’s brief stated.
Although DTE and Consumers plans appear to meet their regulatory obligations, the council said these plans may not reflect real-world constraints. While together the utilities have planned to build more than 30 gigawatts of solar generation and substantial wind and battery storage, the addition of solar alone would require 150,000 acres of land, or 235 square miles, the brief explains.
Identifying suitable land and securing leases from landowners will be difficult, the council states. It also notes that utilities may struggle to obtain project approvals and secure labor and materials at the required pace.
While the council set out to determine whether data centers would make it more or less difficult for Michigan to meet its 60% renewable energy standard, its final conclusion is complicated.
In the short term, the additional electricity demand from data centers will make it more difficult for Michigan utilities to meet the state’s renewable energy requirements by 2035, the council found. The projects will require a rapid expansion of renewable generation, while potentially increasing the reliance on natural gas. 
Over the longer term, however, the data centers could help utilities meet those requirements by funding new renewable energy generation and battery storage. Contracts that allow data centers to reduce their electricity consumption during periods of high demand could also ease pressure on utilities. 
However, the council cautioned that utilities may nevertheless need to delay compliance with the state’s renewable energy targets.
