name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Republican Chad Westberg brings ag science expertise and business focus to state House
description: Republican Rep.-elect Chad Westberg has deep roots in his Elk River district dating back to the 1870s, when Minnesota was still a new state. He handily won deep-red House District 30B with 61% of the vote on a platform of lowering taxes, reducing regulations and combating fraud. He will replace Republican Rep. Paul Novotny, who […]
text:
Republican Rep.-elect Chad Westberg won an open seat for District 30B representing the Elk River area. (Courtesy photo)Republican Rep.-elect Chad Westberg has deep roots in his Elk River district dating back to the 1870s, when Minnesota was still a new state.
He handily won deep-red House District 30B with 61% of the vote on a platform of lowering taxes, reducing regulations and combating fraud. He will replace Republican Rep. Paul Novotny, who has represented the area since 2020 and did not seek reelection.
Westberg, 51, plans to bring a business-minded focus to the Legislature as well as his expertise in agricultural science. He worked in the ethanol industry and now runs a small business that develops agricultural solutions such as new delivery systems for fertilizers.
His hard science background comes through in his plainspoken delivery and no-frills campaign (he only has the one campaign photo).
“It’s facts or nothing,” Westberg said.
Westberg grew up in Rochester and moved to Iowa to study at Drake University, playing football and earning a degree in biology. He later earned a master’s degree in plant biology at the University of Minnesota. In 2007, he returned to his roots in Elk River, where he and his wife are raising three kids. For the past 15 years, he’s also coached high school football, which he calls his happy place.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity. It is part of a series of interviews with new state lawmakers, which you can find here. 
You have this interesting, purposeful career in science. Why take on the challenge of politics and run for office? 
I’ve been interested in politics since I was a kid, so it’s something that I’ve always been drawn to. I’ve been involved in our local BPOU (Basic Political Organizing Unit) for years. And, I’m a problem solver. That’s what I do, and I think I could help.
You’re in a pretty safe Republican district, but I still want to ask why you think you won. 
This year was a blue-wave type of election, right? The Democrats’ vote totals were pretty similar to 2024, but there were a lot of people who didn’t vote. Just because you’re in a strong Republican district doesn’t mean you can’t work.
There were things that we were communicating to our district: We want a strong and fair business climate; we don’t want unreasonable regulations and excessive taxes; we need predictable rules for our businesses. Across the state, we want to keep more money in the pockets of what families earn.
Affordability was a big issue, but ultimately, people who have families want to be left alone. They don’t want to have to deal with increased car tab fees. They don’t have to deal with increased taxes because that makes things more expensive for people.
The flip side to that question is, in this blue wave with Democrats coming back with a trifecta with an even greater margin than they had a few years ago, what do you think Republicans got wrong elsewhere?
I don’t think we got anything wrong specifically, especially in the state. We kind of got tied in with national politics, and I think sometimes people conflate the two. But there’s a lot of things in the state where national politics don’t really affect us, like car tab fees.
The biggest surprise to me was the fraud issue. Fraud is such a big deal, especially in my district and other districts. I’m surprised that it didn’t play more of a role in the election.
In terms of voters? Because it certainly played a role in the campaigns. 
Right. It’s a big deal, and I don’t know if the messaging wasn’t right or if we just got caught up in everything from the national level.
What are the top three issues you want to work on when you get to the Capitol?
I’d like a strong and fair business climate. I would like to lower taxes — I laugh because we’re in the minority. I don’t think that’s going to happen. And government accountability. Every dollar that’s stolen is stolen from someone who needed it.
I’m encouraged. Gov.-elect Amy Klobuchar said we’re not going to raise taxes. I can work with the governor with that. She also said she’s going to do a state audit and take care of this fraud issue. Hey, I’m all for that. I can work with the governor with that, too. I hope she’s serious about it.
Given your science and agriculture background, do you hope to serve on the agriculture committee?
I would like to serve on the ag committee. There’s probably a lot of people in our caucus that would like to serve on that committee. I’d like to serve on commerce. We’ll see what happens.
This could be a tough budget session ahead. I’m curious what’s an area of state government where you think the state could spend less, and maybe one where you think it should spend more.
That’s a good question. I think it could spend less on pretty much everything. I’m a fiscal conservative. As far as spending more, I’d have to research that. I can’t even come up with something right now, just off the top of my head, where we should spend more.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Longview senator plans bill to address fatal WA tank implosion
description: A Washington state senator is pitching reforms with the aim of preventing a catastrophe like the one that killed 11 people in his community from ever happening again.  Legislators will return to Olympia in January for a 105-day session, eight months after a tank rupture killed 11 workers at the Nippon Dynawave Packaging pulp mill […]
text:
Community members comfort each other during a vigil at R.A. Long Park following a fatal chemical storage tank failure on May 26, 2026 in Longview, Washington.  (Photo by Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images)A Washington state senator is pitching reforms with the aim of preventing a catastrophe like the one that killed 11 people in his community from ever happening again. 
Legislators will return to Olympia in January for a 105-day session, eight months after a tank rupture killed 11 workers at the Nippon Dynawave Packaging pulp mill in Longview, and spilled nearly a million gallons of caustic white liquor.
Lawmakers will consider proposed legislation from Sen. Jeff Wilson, R-Longview, that would regulate the tanks used for producing paper and cardboard. Contents include the white liquor in the Nippon tank, as well as green, red and black industrial liquors. 
Under current law, no state agency regulates the safety of the industry’s above-ground tanks, leaving the responsibility to mill owners. 
The bill, called the Pulping Liquors Safety Act, would give the state Department of Labor and Industries new authority to inspect and certify tanks that store chemicals at pulp and paper mills. The state agency would develop specific rules governing the tanks, such as operating standards, corrective actions and mandatory inspections.
Violations of the regulations would result in fines up to $5,000 per day. 
In an interview, Wilson said his bill, which he’s worked on for months, would “easily remedy the obvious gap in the place now where there is no or little regulation.”
“We put the value of people first, but we need the everyday course of business to help sustain that,” Wilson added. “This isn’t designed to put anybody out of business. It’s designed to add responsibility and absolutely fill that gap of where there hasn’t been anything before.”
Last week, the state fined Nippon a record-breaking $11 million, mainly for worker safety violations after an investigation found the company repeatedly ignored warning signs before the tank failure. The penalties came from Labor and Industries, as well as the Department of Ecology. 
“If you’ve got a leak on your ship, don’t put that leak off,” Wilson said. “This is going to be you fix the leak before you continue to sail on.”
State Sen. Jeff Wilson, R-Longview, pictured on the Senate floor in 2021, represents the 19th Legislative District in southwest Washington. (Legislative Support Services)
Labor and Industries cited Nippon for 75 violations, after reviewing more than 40,000 documents and interviewing over 70 witnesses, said Joel Sacks, the agency director. The case is being referred to prosecutors to consider criminal charges. Nippon is likely to appeal, and is fighting another $77,000 fine for unrelated violations.
Sacks agrees there should be a conversation about a new state law.
“There’s absolutely an opportunity as we reflect upon lessons learned and partner with legislators and ask whether putting something more explicit and specific in state law would be helpful moving forward,” Sacks said as he announced the Nippon fines last week. “That’s certainly a conversation we anticipate happening during this coming legislative session.”
Washington has two other kraft pulp and paper mills: another in Longview and one in Port Townsend. The Port Townsend facility has faced scrutiny over water permit violations and reportedly downplaying a spill of untreated wastewater into Puget Sound.
In light of the tank failure, Labor and Industries over the summer opened inspections at the two other mills.
A defunct mill sits in Cosmopolis, Grays Harbor County, where a U.K. businessman has tried to reopen it, but it faces numerous obstacles.
Industry groups, including the Northwest Pulp and Paper Association and the American Forest and Paper Association, are working with the mill workers’ union, the Association of Western Pulp and Paper Workers, on legislative solutions, but haven’t seen the text of Wilson’s bill. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“Workers should never have to wonder whether a serious safety warning was acted on,” union spokesperson Josh Estes said in a statement. “The people whose lives depend on these safeguards need to help shape them. We’re committed to closing the gaps that leave workers at risk and preventing another tragedy like Longview.”
Wilson worked at the Nippon mill as a contractor with his industrial cleaning company, including in and around the tank that imploded.
His proposal was in the state code reviser’s office this week, so Wilson declined to share a draft of the bill language. He expects it to get bipartisan support.
“This is the prime example of what Olympia needs to do: do its job,” he said. “And we’re going to plug those holes.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: This Mississippi man is out to prove there’s plenty to do in Jackson
description: Charlie Grant looks at his website, theresnothingtodohere.com, on his phone at Brent’s Drugs diner in Jackson on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026.
text:
Charlie Grant moved to Mississippi from Alabama 16 years ago. He used to be one of those people who thought there was nothing to do here. 
“I’ve said that before,” he said. “I believed it.” 
Since late August, though, Grant has worked to change minds as the man behind theresnothingtodohere.com — a list of hundreds of goings-on in the Jackson metropolitan area, which he collates with the help of AI and manually curates every day before publishing. 
Though the name is tongue-in-cheek — as is a live counter proclaiming there are “only” hundreds of events to do in the next month — its mission is earnest. Grant, 46, hopes to dispel stigma about Jackson and Mississippi at large.
A screenshot of theresnothingtodohere.com on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. The website offers multiple themes that users can select from a list or choose to randomize. That day, 325 events were listed for the next 30 days. 
It began this summer, when Grant went to see an “emo-punk-y” band play at the Urban Foxes coffee shop in Jackson. A couple of bars into the first song, he was hit with a feeling of home. It was the kind of music he used to play. 
“I need more of this,” he said he realized. 
Cody Cox, co-owner of Urban Foxes, said he had a long conversation with Grant after that show. The two have known each other for years. Grant told him that he hadn’t been that excited about music in forever, Cox said. 
But finding more shows wasn’t easy.
Several longtime Jackson residents — including Cox, 47, who moved to Jackson more than two decades ago — told Mississippi Today that they used to find out about events through print newspapers. “That’s all gone away, for the most part,” Cox said.
Social media didn’t fill the void, at least for Grant. While Urban Foxes and other venues advertise their events on Instagram, Grant isn’t a fan of the social media platform, saying its algorithm makes it hard to find events before they’ve already happened. 
A smattering of event posters on a wall at Urban Foxes coffee shop in the Belhaven Heights neighborhood of Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Credit: Julie Lee/Mississippi Today.
So, he made a website using AI, at first just for himself, to find more shows to attend. 
Then, something happened that he didn’t expect: “My weeks got full,” he said. “In a place where people say there’s nothing to do.”
But Grant didn’t just want to build something just for himself. He wanted others to have the same experience he did. And he knew what he wanted to call it.  
theresnothingtodohere.com went live at the end of August. 
The website gets an average of about 150 hits a day, and an Instagram account Grant created for the sole purpose of funneling people to the website had amassed more than 2,000 followers by mid-November. 
Grant is the sole maintainer of the website, working on it as a passion project alongside his year-round day job as an operations associate with the Mississippi Book Festival. He pays for the site’s upkeep himself and doesn’t make a profit. 
As per its origin story, the website lists plenty of music shows, but it’s also expanded to everything from book signings and yoga classes to pinball tournaments and martial arts classes. 
Christopher Kelly, left, and Kimar Cain share a light moment while chatting about the book they’re currently reading in the book club they started, Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, at Lemuria Book Store, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
The tool works by using AI to pull events from different sources around the internet, including Instagram accounts and other event calendars, such as Visit Jackson’s events page. As of mid-November, more than 200 sources fed into the website, Grant said. He manually reviews each addition before pushing it live, with a link to its original source. 
Yolanda Clay-Moore, director of external affairs, partnerships and alliances at Visit Jackson, sees the two websites as complementing each other, rather than being in competition. “We can’t do it alone,” she said. 
The website was designed to be an antidote to social media, but Grant knows people still congregate on Instagram, for the moment. So, in September, he made an Instagram account solely to shuttle people to his page. That’s how Sarah Caylor, 31, first found out about it.
For Caylor, it started with a breakup.
“I was just looking for community and things to do,” she said. The Instagram post caught her eye. Six weeks later, the Jackson resident and outdoor recreation enthusiast had filled her social calendar for the next six months.
Charlie Grant looks at his website, theresnothingtodohere.com, on his phone at Brent’s Drugs in Jackson on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. That day, the site listed 336 events in the following month.  Credit: Julie Lee/Mississippi Today
Caylor has lived in Central Mississippi since she was five, but she’s discovered new corners of Jackson through the website. “I’m coming into new neighborhoods, finding out (about) new businesses, new streets, new coffee shops,” she said. 
It’s also made planning dates less of a headache. Now, she just sends people the link. 
She loves that the website offers a medley of themes that users can select from or randomize, including themes with a vintage feel. When planning a weekend, she likes to select colors and fonts that match the vibe she’s going for. It’s made planning fun, she said, something she otherwise doesn’t enjoy. 
Grant made several themes for Halloween, including one with a spider crawling down the page and building a web as users scrolled. (Users can choose to turn off animations or switch themes). He expects he’ll make new themes for the end-of-year holidays, too. 
Besides the fun factor, he also hopes the themes inspire visitors to show the website to people around them. It’s one of several intentional design decisions he’s made, like the fact that the website started without a way to filter events.
“I want you to have to scroll past everything,” he said. “Just to dispel the myth.” 
Hayden Boyd, 35, is the manager of End of All Music JXN, an independent record store in the Fondren neighborhood of Jackson, pictured Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Charlie Grant, creator of theresnothingtodohere.com, is a regular at the store’s evening shows and Boyd says he uses Grant’s website himself.  Credit: Julie Lee/Mississippi Today
Jana Williams, 33, moved to Jackson from Texas 11 years ago to attend Tougaloo College. She uses the website all the time, she said. Coming from Texas, she gets a lot of visitors from out of state who expect her to know what to do. As a busy person, she doesn’t always have her finger on the pulse, so the website comes in handy. 
Williams thinks that the idea that there’s nothing to do in Jackson is a matter of perception, not reality.
“I truly think that Jackson doesn’t have a ‘there’s nothing to do here’ problem,” she said. “I think Jackson just needs more exposure.” 
Cox, the co-owner of Urban Foxes, felt similarly.
“If Mississippi is this misunderstood microcosm of the United States, I feel like Jackson is like a center part of this microcosm of misunderstanding in Mississippi,” he said, pointing to the stereotype of Jackson as the “big, scary city.” 
“I think a lot of people miss all the really positive parts of it because they’ve got all this misconception of the negative,” he added. 
Children dance as Chief Shaka Zulu performs during the 82nd National Folk Festival on Saturday, Nov. 8, 2025, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Williams and Cox drew parallels to the recent U.S. Senate race, in which Democrat Scott Colom prevailed over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state in more than four decades. (Colom celebrated the outcome at Tougaloo College, Williams’ alma mater.) The victory, not anticipated by most political pundits, forced many outsiders to re-evaluate their stereotypes about Mississippi. 
“People just need to see it, you know,” Williams said. “And the same for the website. I think everything kind of goes hand in hand. If more people saw it, they would have a different narrative of Jackson and Mississippi in general.”
Grant is still a frequent user of his own website, making it to around seven things a week, he said, often stringing together three or four events on Thursdays on his way home from work. In the process, he has gained, to his surprise, new friends and a sense of community. “I don’t feel so much out of place, even when I go to something new,” he said. 
While he generally prefers to stay in the shadows and has been described as “elusive,” Grant has gained unexpected attention due to the website. When friends introduce him to other people, he said, their faces light up when they learn he’s ‘the website guy.’ The newfound fame feels “odd” and, at times, uncomfortable. Still, he sees the publicity as important for his mission. 
“I just had a faith in this tool that I don’t have in much else,” he said. “I just keep having all these really wholesome and amazing experiences and I just want more people to have that.”
It’s only been a few months, but he seems to have succeeded.
“Everyone keeps thanking me,” Grant said. “That’s the thing I get the most. Thank you. Thank you for making this.”
Festivalgoers walk down Capitol Street during the 83rd National Folk Festival in Jackson on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today

name: Missouri Independent
title: Under Andrew Bailey, Missouri AG’s office backed electronic raffles for charities
description: Two years before Missouri’s attorney general struck a deal allowing a gambling company to temporarily keep its slot machines in nonprofits, her predecessor’s office offered a broad interpretation of state law that could complicate efforts to shut them down. In a 2024 letter, then-Attorney General Andrew Bailey’s chief of staff wrote that electronic raffle ma[...]
text:
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway speaks Nov. 16 during a news conference announcing an agreement with Torch Electronics to remove its games from most Missouri locations. Hanaway appeared with Greene County Sheriff Jason Johnson, back left, and Prosecutor Dan Patterson. (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent)Two years before Missouri’s attorney general struck a deal allowing a gambling company to temporarily keep its slot machines in nonprofits, her predecessor’s office offered a broad interpretation of state law that could complicate efforts to shut them down.
In a 2024 letter, then-Attorney General Andrew Bailey’s chief of staff wrote that electronic raffle machines were legal when operated for charitable purposes by religious and charitable organizations.
Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s office wouldn’t say Tuesday what role, if any, the letter played in recent negotiations with Torch Electronics. But a spokeswoman said the letter “does not apply to Torch machines.”
In the non-prosecution agreement announced Nov. 16, Hanaway agreed to allow Torch to operate its slot machine games at nonprofit locations until the end of May as long as they are in place by Jan. 1. 
Missouri AG agrees to let Torch Electronics keep slot machines in veterans, fraternal halls

The St. Louis Post-Dispatch reported that the next day, Torch machines were being delivered to a for-profit business location in Franklin County where the owner has a newly registered nonprofit. 
In a social media post, Hanaway said Torch “may have already breached the agreement. The operation of illegal machines in for-profit bars or convenience stores is in no way compliant with the agreement and is unacceptable.”
Torch’s attorney, Scott Rosenblum, did not respond to an email seeking comment.
But whether machines deemed illegal in convenience stores and bars can legally operate in nonprofits remains an unsettled question rooted in Missouri’s constitutional exemption for charitable raffles.
The Missouri Constitution says organizations “recognized as charitable or religious pursuant to federal law” can hold raffles and sweepstakes.
Lawmakers have never defined what constitutes a raffle. Criminal gambling statutes do not apply to “constitutionally authorized activities.”
In the 2024 letter, Jay Atkins, who signed it as first assistant attorney general, wrote that a raffle is the exchange of something of value for a chance to win a prize, whether it is conducted online, uses paper tickets or takes the form of an electronic game.
“We believe the use of e-raffle machines for a charitable purpose is lawful for religious and charitable organizations,” Atkins wrote.
During a news conference Nov. 16 in Springfield, Hanaway said her top goal in the agreement was to stop Torch from operating in most locations. Allowing the machines to remain temporarily in nonprofits, she said, would give those organizations time to find other ways to fund their programs.
“It’s tough to negotiate an agreement like this,” Hanaway said.
Atkins’ 2024 letter was addressed to attorneys representing a company that offered machines designated as e-raffle games. He wrote it about four months after a judge dismissed a lawsuit seeking protection from criminal prosecution.
Associate Circuit Judge William Devoy, upper right, conducts a preliminary hearing Feb. 25, 2021, in Linn County on whether an “electronic raffle” machine is an illegal gambling device. Arguing the case were Prosecuting Attorney Shiante McMahon, foreground, and defense attorney Nelson Mitten, left. (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent)
In that ruling, the judge wrote a jury would have to decide whether the Constitution shielded the games from criminal laws. The games were not like traditional raffles, the judge wrote, because each raffle had only one customer and the machine vendor received a share of the winnings.
Granting the exception for nonprofit locations is a prudent step, said Ben Trachtenberg, professor of law at the University of Missouri-Columbia. Giving them a date when the activity must end is also sensible, he said.
The letter from Atkins isn’t binding on the attorney general’s office, he said, but it provides a possible defense for any organization that relied on it.
“The fact that you say something on Tuesday doesn’t mean on Thursday you definitely have to believe the same thing,” Trachtenberg said. “If you punish someone on Thursday for doing on Wednesday what you told them on Tuesday was okay, that might seem unfair. But it’s very different to say: ‘Let it be known that going forward our position on this has changed.’”
Hanaway’s spokeswoman, Stephanie Whitaker, declined to offer any details of the talks with Torch.
“The office does not share the nuances of confidential settlement discussions,” she wrote.
 The agreement

Hanaway began pressuring Torch in February, after a federal jury ruled the company had improperly interfered with the business of a competitor that offered arcade games. A federal judge subsequently issued an opinion that Torch machines “meet the statutory definition of ‘gambling device’ and are therefore illegal…” and Torch agreed to turn off its machines in retail locations under threat of prosecution.
Customers play Torch slot machines April 10 at a Columbia convenience store (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
To avoid state charges, Torch will, under the agreement, pay the state $13.5 million over two years. 
Asked on Nov. 16 about the exception for nonprofits, Hanaway said those locations accounted for less than 1% of Torch’s business. 
Torch would “suspend, remove, or destroy all the gaming machines that they have in businesses,” she said.
The exception, the agreement states, covers “non-profit organizations, fraternal organizations, or any other similar types of entities or locations.”
Hanaway defined it this way: “They need to be existing not for profits. We have heard some rumors that people are sort of starting new not-for-profits or taping off areas in C-stores. None of that is in compliance with this agreement.”
State Rep. Betsy Fogle, a Springfield Democrat elected to the state Senate earlier this month, said in an interview with The Independent that she is puzzled by the exception.
“The attorney general has on record and repeatedly said that she views these machines to be illegal, and that her office is taking action against them,” Fogle said. “From the outside, it seems she has now created a golden ticket or a monopoly for Torch to operate their machines in nonprofits across the state.”
Fogle said she has asked the secretary of state’s office for a list of nonprofit organizations created in recent months. To qualify for the Constitution’s exemption, an organization needs to obtain tax-exempt status from the IRS. Registering as a nonprofit with the state does not automatically confer that status. 
“I would be surprised if the attorney general wasn’t aware that this settlement between her office and Torch was going to create an environment where businesses were going to open up a nonprofit arm to try to take advantage of the fact that the attorney general has now provided a framework of which that would be allowable,” Fogle said.
Trachtenberg said the agreement can probably be enforced based on Hanaway’s interpretation of its terms.
“It looks like some people are maneuvering through that gap to do what sort of looks like an ordinary gambling parlor,” Trachtenberg said. “It seems unlikely that this subterfuge will last forever.”
In a statement to The Independent, Hanaway said her office would investigate whether nonprofits are being created to undermine the agreement.
“The operation of gambling machines in for-profit bars, convenience stores, or similar establishments is illegal and not in any way compliant with our agreement with Torch,” Hanaway said. “If our review confirms these allegations, we will act swiftly to hold Torch accountable.”
 The politics

The pressure on Torch this year marked the company’s most substantial legal jeopardy since 2022, when a change in Linn County prosecutors following that year’s election led to the dismissal of the only felony charges ever filed against Torch.
Neither Bailey, nor his predecessor, Eric Schmitt, took any direct action against Torch or any other game vendor.
Lawmakers gave Schmitt $150,000 in the fiscal 2021 budget to spur action on the machines. In 2022, when he was running for the U.S. Senate, a rival accused him of “turning a blind eye” to the gambling.
Bailey, appointed to replace Schmitt, removed himself in 2023 from the defense of the Missouri State Highway Patrol in a lawsuit by Torch. His campaign committee and PAC took more than $40,000 in donations from PACs controlled by the lobbyist for Torch, which has the largest number of slot machine games in retail locations.
Gambling companies pour campaign money into fight over Missouri video lottery bill

The May 31 deadline for nonprofits to remove Torch machines gives lawmakers time to intervene. Among the possibilities contemplated in the agreement are legislation legalizing Torch’s machines or authorizing a state-regulated video lottery system.
Fogle opposes legalizing video lottery terminals. J&J Ventures of Effingham, Illinois, a company pushing lawmakers to authorize licensed video lottery terminals, spent almost $240,000 opposing her election.
Fogle said Springfield, which has an ordinance banning games that offer cash prizes, doesn’t want electronic gambling whether it is in nonprofits or convenience stores.
“People in Springfield don’t want predatory machines in our neighborhoods, in our gas stations, in our communities, profiting off of the backs of working families and people who are struggling to pay their bills,” Fogle said.
Andy Arnold, a lobbyist for J&J, said the agreement puts more pressure on lawmakers to pass video lottery. 
“We applaud anything that provides more money for education,” he said. “However, we are a little puzzled on whether allowing them to operate in not-for-profits through May 2027 makes the devices into raffle machines, or are the devices still considered an illegal gambling device.”
Fraternal organizations and veterans groups are groups no one wants to oppose, he said.
At her news conference, Hanaway said protecting those organizations was a priority in negotiating the exception.
“I didn’t want to hurt veterans,” she said. “I didn’t want to hurt these community organizations.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Kansas City’s World Cup fell short of its $35 million tax revenue projection
description: In July 2023, Kansas City’s City Council voted to give KC2026, the local World Cup organizing committee, $15 million over three years based in part on an estimate that, “the tax revenue generated for Kansas City from the World Cup will be approximately $35 million.” The matches are over and available tax data show revenue […]
text:
Kansas City is the smallest host city for the North American 2026  FIFA World Cup. A promotional sign appears on Jan. 13 outside the Kansas Statehouse in Topeka (Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector).In July 2023, Kansas City’s City Council voted to give KC2026, the local World Cup organizing committee, $15 million over three years based in part on an estimate that, “the tax revenue generated for Kansas City from the World Cup will be approximately $35 million.” The matches are over and available tax data show revenue fell far short of that projection.
This should be no surprise. As I’ve argued here, at the Show-Me Institute and in The Kansas City Star, mega-events rarely pay back the public money spent to host them. Records obtained from the city suggest an estimated $6.7 million in additional summer revenue across taxes affected by tourism, less than a fifth of what was promised.
The Council’s estimate of a $652.6 million economic impact came from the Kansas City Sports Commission, but the $35 million tax revenue claim has no identified author, methodology or report. It doesn’t appear in the city’s fiscal note, which instead promises, “an intangible positive fiscal impact that will allow the City to be stronger and more resilient”—a meaningless phrase if ever there were one. The omission raises questions about how much confidence city officials had in the $35 million estimate.
According to the Missouri Department of Revenue, sales tax collections associated with June and July 2026 sales were $8.1 million, or 13.5%, higher than during the same period in 2025. But sales from January through May, before any soccer match, were already running 6.8% ahead. Taking that into account, the World Cup produced only about $4 million in additional sales tax. In August, the first full month after the tournament, tax revenue was up just 2.6%.
Hotel taxes rose $1.7 million from  June through August compared with the same period in 2025, about $1.5 million above trend. But the gain came largely from prices, not guests. Hotels raised rates so sharply that occupancy fell below expected levels. The consulting firm HVS estimates Kansas City’s occupancy during match weeks fell 4.6 percentage points below what it otherwise would have been.
Restaurant taxes rose $1.4 million over the same months, about $1.1 million above trend. Restaurant tax collections fell 6.7% in September and October, suggesting some of the summer spending may have been shifted from other months rather than representing entirely new spending.
Other revenue sources barely moved. Short-term rental taxes earmarked to fund the city’s $15 million contribution brought in only about $60,000 more than in 2025. Earnings tax withholding showed no bump at all.
Even those numbers overstate the benefit to the city’s general budget. Nearly all of Kansas City’s sales taxes are dedicated to specific purposes such as capital improvements, transit, fire protection and parks. Convention and tourism taxes go to their own fund. The city’s July financial report does not mention the World Cup, and it shows convention and tourism taxes up just 0.8% for the fiscal year.
Dave Helling’s Kansas City Stack reached a similar conclusion in October, noting that June sales tax collections were up $2.1 million in the city’s monthly report. But June’s payment covered April sales, two months before the first match. The jump was there before the tournament began.
The organizers had little trouble securing funding, however. KC2026’s impact report lists $136.55 million in funding, about $101 million of it from taxpayers at the federal, state and local levels. We don’t know how all that money was spent, but KC2026’s 2024 tax return shows it paid $361,000 in lobbying expenses.
In May, when those projections faced scrutiny, Visit KC president Kathy Nelson told reporters, “We didn’t work 10 years for this to be a flop.” Unfortunately, if one uses the standard of tax revenue set by the City Council, the financial results are difficult to call a success.
Nelson’s colleagues claim success but won’t show their math without a fee. Visit KC, which is funded largely by the city’s hotel taxes, was asked for the report, spreadsheets and methodology behind its 680,000-visitor and $570 million estimates. It quoted 23 hours of staff time and $1,130.91, later cut to $920, explaining that the records “are not just ‘sitting around’ in a single file.” It won’t release anything, even the methodology, until paid. A public estimate that can’t be supported without three days’ work and a $920 invoice deserves caution.
World Cup supporters claim the real payoff is visibility, reputation and future events. KC2026’s impact report cites $2.4 billion in media exposure—which it admits does not reflect actual revenue—and four new corporate prospects. But the report does not establish how much additional tax revenue the tournament generated for Kansas City. The Council didn’t approve $15 million for visibility and media exposure; it expected a return of $35 million.
The World Cup was a financial flop for Kansas City taxpayers. Local and state leaders accepted projections without checking them and funded the organizations producing them. Media outlets repeated the claims, apparently without verification. Many of them got to go to the parties, and taxpayers were left with the tab.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ’s top court protects public access to waterfronts in permit spat
description: A Point Pleasant homeowners' association challenged New Jersey's requirement that it provide public access to riverfront site before building a bulkhead.
text:
People fish along the Manasquan Inlet on Sept. 18, 2022. (Photo by New Jersey Monitor)The New Jersey Supreme Court has sided with the fishing, boating, and beach-going public in a test of a 2019 law passed to prevent private property owners from hogging the shoreline and other waterfronts.
The law in question requires property owners who apply for permits to develop tidal lands to provide additional public access if development would change a structure’s existing footprint. Lawmakers meant for the law to clarify and expand the public trust doctrine, a concept rooted in an 1821 lawsuit over access to oyster beds in the Raritan River. The doctrine holds that the sea and its shores are common to mankind, and all people have a right to them.
Sea Point, a homeowners’ association in Point Pleasant Borough, challenged the law in court after it applied in 2020 for a permit to rebuild a deteriorated bulkhead on its property along Beaverdam Creek, and the Department of Environmental Protection conditioned approval on the submission of a public access plan, according to a state Supreme Court ruling released Tuesday.
The proposed project included extending the bulkhead two feet into the water and rebuilding piers and mooring piles that originally had been built without a permit, the ruling says.
Sea Point objected to the public access requirement, saying sufficient public access already existed elsewhere and offering to pay into a public access improvement project nearby, the decision says. The association characterized the law as unconstitutional, arguing it results in a taking of private property without just compensation.
The association took its fight to the Office of Administrative Law. That court sided with the state, the association appealed, and the appellate court upheld the decision.
Tuesday’s decision affirmed the lower courts’ rulings.
The association’s lawyers had argued that a 1984 court precedent requires officials to consider four factors, including the extent and availability of publicly owned sand nearby and the extent of public demand, when balancing public use with private property owners’ interests.
But Justice Douglas Fasciale, writing for a unanimous court, rejected that argument. That 1984 court precedent only applies to public use disputes outside of permit applications, while the 2019 law prevails in disputes where permitting is involved, Fasciale said.
“Sea Point’s proposed development triggers the statute’s public access requirements because the expansion of a bulkhead within the boat basin would change the structure’s existing footprint. Moreover, Sea Point seeks after-the-fact authorization for pre-existing finger piers and mooring piles, which were originally built without a permit. Because those structural additions must be authorized and must comply with the statute, they likewise constitute changes to the property’s footprint,” Fasciale wrote. “Therefore, Sea Point’s permit application falls squarely within the scope of activities that require additional onsite public access as a condition of permit approval.”
Justice Douglas Fasciale listens to arguments on April 28, 2025, at the Richard J. Hughes Justice Complex in Trenton. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)
The court declined to decide Sea Point’s constitutional claim, saying it was premature because state environmental officials had not yet determined what Sea Point’s public access obligation would be. The association can renew that claim in Superior Court if it objects to a final determination, Fasciale wrote.
Fasciale blamed state Department of Environmental Protection officials for driving Sea Point to sue by failing to pass rules and regulations, as legislators directed them to do within 18 months of the law’s enactment. That failure confuses permit applicants, he wrote.
“We cannot overlook the DEP’s disregard for its mandate to promulgate regulations the Legislature expressly directed it to adopt. Such inaction leaves affected parties uncertain of their obligations and imposes unnecessary costs on those forced to seek clarity through litigation,” he wrote. “Because the public is entitled to ‘sufficiently definite regulations and standards,’ as well as fair and predictable administrative decision-making, the DEP must fulfill its legislative directive.”
Caryn Shinske, a department spokeswoman, declined to comment.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma agency mum on number of districts allowed to switch meal options
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Almost two months after the Oklahoma State Department of Education abruptly ended a school supper program, the agency has declined to say how many districts it approved to convert to an alternative feeding option. About 68% of the 79 districts that served a third meal last school year have applied for an […]
text:
A student picks out a carton of milk in the cafeteria at Thelma R. Parks Elementary in Oklahoma City on Aug. 13, 2025. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Almost two months after the Oklahoma State Department of Education abruptly ended a school supper program, the agency has declined to say how many districts it approved to convert to an alternative feeding option.
About 68% of the 79 districts that served a third meal last school year have applied for an after-school food program, according to an Oklahoma Voice analysis of records the Education Department provided. But after encouraging districts to sign up for the after-school program, the agency has refused to say how many it approved to make the switch.
Two superintendents, meanwhile, said some or all of their students no longer have access to what was once a reliable meal. That’s despite previous assurances from state Superintendent Lindel Fields that “kids will not go hungry” because the after-school meal program would be available.
The agency drew the ire of state lawmakers and district leaders when it announced on Aug. 18, after the school year had begun, that on Sept. 30 it would discontinue the Expanded Learning Time Option. The federally funded program had allowed districts with extended school days to serve a third, late-afternoon meal before classes ended. School breakfasts and lunches were unaffected.
State Superintendent Lindel Fields speaks with news reporters after an Oklahoma State Board of Education meeting Oct. 23, 2025, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
While the agency said federal compliance concerns necessitated the change, school and state leaders argued the decision was needlessly abrupt and left little time to adjust. 
In all, 118 districts have submitted an application for after-school meal funding, 54 of which previously served food through Expanded Learning Time, state records show.
The state agency, though, said an application is no guarantee of approval or participation.
The Education Department’s child nutrition office declined repeated requests for data on how many Expanded Learning Time districts it has approved for the after-school program.
Jennifer Weber, the agency’s program director of child nutrition programs, told Oklahoma Voice on Oct. 19 that the application process was ongoing and the Education Department had no updated participation numbers to share. Weeks later, the agency gave a similar response through its communications office.
Applications for federal meal funds were arriving daily from schools, childcare centers, adult daycare centers, nonprofits, tribes and other organizations, creating “a particularly busy time” for staff overseeing the program, Weber wrote in an Oct. 19 email. The agency has 30 days after submission to review an application, request corrections or approve it.
“Some schools have pivoted and implemented qualifying afterschool programs, while others are still working toward implementation,” she wrote. “We also anticipated that some schools would not renew for other reasons, including changes to recess requirements or other local-level decisions.”
To qualify for after-school meal funding, a district would have to offer at least 30 minutes of structured activities or tutoring after the final school bell, the Education Department said. The agency also required districts to provide transportation home for students who stay for after-school programming.
Schools that didn’t already have such a program would have to create one in the middle of the school year and adjust bus schedules to accommodate it. 
Peggs Public Schools Superintendent John Cox said his district wasn’t able to do that once Expanded Learning Time ended. That means the third meal has gone away with nothing to replace it, though local churches are providing take-home snack packs on Fridays, he said.
Peggs Public Schools Superintendent John Cox attends a news conference Oct. 2, 2025, at Eisenhower International School in Tulsa. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
For years, the small, northeast Oklahoma district has kept classes in session for an hour and 10 minutes longer than the usual six-hour school day to better prepare students for state tests. Cox said it isn’t feasible to add an after-school program on top of an already lengthy instructional day.
State records show Peggs submitted an application for after-school meal funding, but Cox said he expects the state will deny the request for lack of an after-school program.
Last year, Peggs signed up for Expanded Learning Time to fit a third meal into the long school day. He said the extra meal made a “big impact” in a district where more than 80% of students come from low-income homes and qualify for free or reduced-price meals at school.
“I felt like for last year it was just as important to send our kids home with a full stomach as it was to learn more multiplication and division,” he said.
In Hartshorne Public Schools, Superintendent Jason Lindley said he put together an after-school program that was “the best we could offer under the circumstances.”
The southeast Oklahoma district is providing 30 minutes of academic remediation after school for students who ask for help. Lindley said he found teachers who were available to stay late in exchange for more pay and a bus that could circle back to pick up the students.
The new program, though, feeds fewer students than Expanded Learning Time did, he said. For example, none of Hartshorne’s student-athletes are able to participate because they have practice or games after school.
Lindley said he’d someday like to see a more robust after-school program with different activities available, but this year he had only 44 days to plan.
“You give me 44 days, it’s hard to put together a program that is going to meet all the needs of your stakeholders when you already have a bell schedule and you’ve already started your school year,” he said.

name: WyoFile
title: He once pumped gas at Yellowstone. Now he’s running the park.
description:
For Interim Superintendent Barclay Trimble, the new role “is like coming home.”
The post He once pumped gas at Yellowstone. Now he’s running the park. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
For three summers during college, Barclay Trimble traveled from his native Texas to Yellowstone National Park, where he worked pumping gas at the Old Faithful and Fishing Bridge service stations.
It represented his first meaningful encounter with America’s national park system. Trimble hiked and backpacked and explored on his time off hours and loved the experiences. And while today Trimble jokes that it’s “the one job that I never thought would show up on a resume,” he’s been reminded of that era during his first month in the role of Yellowstone’s acting superintendent. 
Trimble, a veteran National Park Service employee who has served in parks ranging from the Grand Canyon to Denali to Cape Hatteras National Seashore off the coast of North Carolina, filled the role that former superintendent Cam Sholly vacated in September.
At the helm of the country’s first national park, Trimble oversees 2.2 million acres of rugged landscapes, wildlife and geologic marvels that draw more than 4 million annual visitors — making it America’s third-most-visited park in 2025. 
Since he started in October, Trimble has been working to get up to speed and understand the dynamics, issues and relationships that are critical for Yellowstone, he said. 
“A lot of what I’m doing right now is still listening mode,” Trimble said. “I’m trying to learn from the park staff, I’m trying to learn from the state and federal partners, from the gateway communities and our tribal partners.” 
Lion Geyser eruption with a rainbow in Yellowstone National Park. (Jacob W. Frank/National Park Service)
And in the window of time he had before park sections began closing for the winter season, Trimble said, he got out to tour around, even visiting some of those old haunts from his gas station days.
“It’s good to come back and dust off the memory banks,” he said. “For me it really is kind of like coming home.”
Settling in 
Trimble brings a breadth of experience gained over 35 years in the agency. He served as acting superintendent of Grand Canyon National Park, worked in the Intermountain Region in Colorado and in Washington, D.C., and was the deputy regional director for the Southeast Region. Before coming to Yellowstone, he was the superintendent of Mammoth Caves National Park in Kentucky, which is home to the longest known cave system on Earth.
He’s happy to be back in the Mountain West, where he had spent about half of his career, he said. 
Sholly left the superintendent role after eight years to work at the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. He left a legacy of strengthening infrastructure, addressing worker housing and protecting the park’s wildlife and ecosystems. He also steered the park through crises like historic flooding and the COVID-19 pandemic, along with the more typical mishaps like bison gorings, visitor bottlenecks, tourists wandering off boardwalks and geothermal explosions. 
Trimble takes the reins on several ongoing projects, like rebuilding a new permanent North Entrance Road. After a catastrophic 2022 flood destroyed the former North Entrance Road, crews quickly constructed a temporary highway to connect the towns of Gardiner, Montana, and Mammoth Hot Springs. The new road will replace that with a highway engineered for longevity, according to the park. 

Gardner River floodwaters in 2022 obliterated many stretches of Yellowstone National Park’s North Entrance Road, which runs from Gardiner, Mont., to Mammoth Hot Springs, Wyo. (Kyle Stone/National Park Service)

“So all the planning and compliance is done on that, and we will be moving forward on going out to bid and trying to award a contract, and hopefully starting on that” in 2027, Trimble said. 
Work on a new Yellowstone River Bridge near Tower Junction finished in the last couple of weeks, and the park has projects ongoing to improve employee housing. 
Still, Yellowstone faces challenges in maintaining its inventory of buildings, roads, trails and campgrounds. The Park Service estimates $1.2 billion in deferred maintenance and repairs in Yellowstone. 
In October, the park announced the creation of a $105 million conservation and stewardship fund, the result of what it called the largest single private gift in the park’s history. Tallgrass, a Colorado company building an AI power hub near Cheyenne, seeded the donation. 
Among the projects the effort will fund is a $35 million visitor center at Norris Geyser Basin, which Trimble said will be a major undertaking. 
In general, Trimble’s philosophy when it comes to helming a national park is that “it’s not an island. It takes others for us to be successful,” he said. 
Gateway towns, state agencies and tribal partners are among the organizations crucial to Yellowstone, he said. 
A sow grizzly with a cub in Yellowstone National Park. (Frank van Manen/Interagency Grizzly Bear Study Team)
In that vein, he said, “one of my top priorities is really just kind of getting out, having those conversations, building that trust, and continuing whatever I can do to help strengthen those partner relations.”
Other leadership changes
Trimble isn’t the only new Yellowstone administrative face. Kristen Kosick became the park’s deputy superintendent in September, replacing Mike Tranel, who retired. 
Kosick previously worked as chief of Michigan State Parks. Before that, she spent 15 years working for the National Park Service — including five years in Yellowstone as the fee program manager and chief of staff.
The National Park Service has launched a process to name a permanent superintendent, meanwhile. 
Yellowstone is now downshifting operations in preparation for winter. Three of the four entrances have closed for the year, and park crews are preparing for the start of snowmobile and snowcoach travel, which begins Dec. 15. 
The park tallied 4.7 million visitors through October. The highest year on record was 2021, when the park reported 4.8 million visitors.

name: WyoFile
title: To Wyoming, with thanks
description:
Columnist Walt Gasson encourages readers to give thanks for home and family, but also for the intangible moments that make us grateful to be alive and in Wyoming.
The post To Wyoming, with thanks appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

I’ve always loved this time of year. The sun’s gone low in the south now, and that soft golden light in the late afternoon covers the slopes of Sheep Mountain like a warm blanket. The aspens are stark naked, and the wind whistles through them in tones like a red cedar flute. The horses are barefoot and a little shaggy. Hunting seasons are winding down, and unless you’re a hardcore brown trout angler, the fishing is moving into winter mode. Maybe this year there will be ice on the flat water and we can sit in a warm little ice fishing hut for hours and solve most of the world’s problems. It’s a good time for a little reflection. 
Seven decades and more into this life, my reflections sometimes turn to regret. But there will be more than enough time for that later. Now it’s time to remember and be grateful for the joys. Even in this time, and in these United States, there is so much joy to be celebrated. I have learned that when I can choose either regret for things that were not, or joy for things that are, I should always choose the latter. It’s always better to choose joy. 
It’s easy to find joy in the most tangible, most important things. I could speak from now until God calls me home about how much joy Kim brings to my life. We’ve been together for 56 years this month, and we have been side by side through more joy than we ever dreamed possible. Much of that joy has come from our four truly remarkable adult kids and their spouses, along with 15 even more remarkable grandkids. This family sustains us every day of our lives. They are our greatest joy and our greatest accomplishment. That’s top-shelf, tangible joy in our lives.
But it’s the intangible joys that are harder for me to clearly describe. Our experiences in other places taught us much about the simple joys of just living in Wyoming. Like the homegrown happiness of singing along with Ian Tyson to “The Old Double Diamond” when I’m headed down the county road at 4 a.m. Or how my heart swells when I’m again entranced by the way Charles Marion Russell captured on canvas the light of early morning in the sagebrush. Or that heart rush that comes when I gig the horse ever so lightly and feel his first steps between my knees. There is so much magic still in the ordinary things of life here in God’s own paradise when you allow your 21st century heart to be captured by the wild things and wild places of Wyoming. It is a hard and windy place, to be sure. But it can capture your soul like no other.
A dear friend told me a while back that I’m a “sense of place” writer. My favorite writer Wallace Stegner said that sense of place is about the knowledge that there is a place that we belong, a shared geography and shared values. God bless ol’ Wally. He was the real deal. But I think that in this hard place and this complicated time we need to talk about the simple things: The shared geography of all our home places, from the Bear River Divide to the Bear Lodge. The memories that are stored within us, like the smell of the coffee that my dad Gus poured from the Thermos in the eerie green light of the dashboard of his pickup as we headed off to hunt sage grouse in the desert in 1964. Or the feel of the horse’s back twitching when we’re brushing him down in the half-light of evening. We can speak of God and freedom and humility to the people we love in the solace of the places we love. That may be more important than ever now.   
Granted, conversations about faith and freedom and humility do not come by accident. Neither do I think they come from a book. They come the only way they have ever come — from the hearts of those we love, and by shared experience. None of us can fix the world. But I want our family and yours to know what is important. I want them to hear sandhill cranes passing overhead in a chorus of those bugle calls that Aldo Leopold said were the last reminders of the Pleistocene. I want them to be able to name the peaks and navigate the two-tracks and trails of their homeland. I want them to know the feel of a fish as it hammers their fly and to taste it fried crisp over a juniper fire. I want my family and yours to know Wyoming in their hearts and to love it to the depths of their being. For that is the only way we will keep it. 
More important than any of this, I want them to have a love for each other and for this hard country we call home. I want them to know it and respect it and to know what it has been and still could be here in the Big Empty, wherever they live. Maybe if we can help them keep their feet firmly planted on the ground, their eyes on the horizon, and their hearts in Wyoming, maybe that will be the best thing that we can do.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Why is Alabama’s K-12 enrollment down?
description: Alabama’s K-12 enrollment is down, and there isn’t one clear reason for the decline. Alabama State School Superintendent Eric Mackey said at a recent Alabama State Board of Education meeting that preliminary numbers show public schools in the state experienced a sharp decline in enrollment in the 2025-2026 school year. That year, Mackey said, there […]
text:
Students work in a classroom  in Salt Lake City in 2024. Alabama's public K-12 schools are experiencing an enrollment decline, but there isn't a clear reason for it. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Alabama’s K-12 enrollment is down, and there isn’t one clear reason for the decline.
Alabama State School Superintendent Eric Mackey said at a recent Alabama State Board of Education meeting that preliminary numbers show public schools in the state experienced a sharp decline in enrollment in the 2025-2026 school year.
That year, Mackey said, there were 702,000 students enrolled in Alabama public schools. That’s down roughly 12,000 students from the 2024-25 school year.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a statement last week, Mackey said he has “spent a great deal of time dissecting the data.”
“However, there is no one pattern that we have been able to identify. Of the decrease, several students moved out of state — that was the most consistent reason for the decrease. However, there were some transfers to private, home, or church school — a smaller, but significant number,” Mackey said. “I have decided that a much deeper, long-term analysis is needed. We have even reached out to some major research groups to possibly help analyze data trends. We are still working on it, but nothing imminent forthcoming.”
Jason Barnett, executive director of School Superintendents of Alabama, said in a statement Monday evening he also thought “the greatest contributor to the decline is a more transient population.”
“Families today are more mobile than ever, often relocating for employment opportunities, housing options, or other personal reasons,” Barnett said. “While Alabama has welcomed many students moving into the state, we have also experienced a larger number of students moving out of state. Based on my understanding of the matter, this population shift appears to account for nearly half of the overall enrollment decline.”
While the CHOOSE Act, Alabama’s school voucher program, played a part in the enrollment decline, Mackey told the State Board of Education members in October that “CHOOSE Act numbers that the Revenue Department has posted are not anything close to that.”
According to CHOOSE Act numbers released by the Alabama Department of Revenue, there were a total of 2,032 public school students who received CHOOSE Act funds to attend a participating private school. Of that number, 1,811 new students were awarded the funds.
The numbers also show that a total of 467 public school students received CHOOSE Act funds to enroll in homeschool programs. Of that number, 430 were new awards given to students.
Another potential reason for the decline is the national birth rate dropping. According to the U.S. Federal Reserve, In 2019, the national crude birth rate was 11.4 births per 1,000 people. The following year, the birth rate dropped to 10.9 births per 1,000 people. 
In 2021 and 2022, the birth rate increased to 11 births per 1,000 people and dropped to 10.6 births in 2024.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in 2020, Alabama’s birth rate was 60.6 per 1,000 people aged 15-44. By 2024, the birth rate in the state had decreased to 57.2 births. 
Barnett said that the declining birth rate contributed to the enrollment decline.
“For several years, our schools have graduated more seniors than we are bringing in through kindergarten enrollment. This demographic trend extends well beyond education and is being experienced in many states across the country,” Barnett said.
The enrollment decline could also lead to an estimated 800 teacher units lost.
Messages seeking comment were left with the Alabama Education Association Monday and Tuesday.
Barnett said it’s important to understand the decline didn’t happen all at once and that enrollment is “a fluid process that changes every day.”
“As a result, the roughly 12,000-student decline reflected in annual reporting did not occur at one moment in time but, rather, accumulated over the course of an entire year,” Barnett said. “Sometimes the annual figure can create the perception of a sudden or widespread departure of students when, in reality, it represents the net effect of enrollment changes occurring daily across our Alabama public schools.”
Enrollment in numbers released by the Alabama Department of Education last year showed that K-12 enrollment dropped by 5,800 students for the 2024-25 school year.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Commentary: Two education tax credits, two very different opportunities for Idaho families
description: On Jan. 1, Idaho families and students will gain access to one of the most exciting educational opportunities in a generation. Thanks to the new federal scholarship tax credit, Idaho taxpayers will be able to direct up to $1,700 of their federal income taxes toward supporting students and schools in their own communities. Money that […]
text:
The federal scholarship tax credit is fundamentally different from Idaho’s Parental Choice Tax Credit. While Idaho’s program exclusively benefits private school and homeschool families, the federal scholarship tax credit supports students in public, public charter and private schools, write guest columnists Terry Ryan and Duncan Robb. (Photo by Getty Images)On Jan. 1, Idaho families and students will gain access to one of the most exciting educational opportunities in a generation.
Thanks to the new federal scholarship tax credit, Idaho taxpayers will be able to direct up to $1,700 of their federal income taxes toward supporting students and schools in their own communities. Money that otherwise would go to Washington, D.C., stays in Idaho to support our schools and families.
This will unlock new resources for student learning, expand educational opportunities, and strengthen Idaho public schools — all at no net cost to participating taxpayers or the state, as we previously wrote, as seen in Idaho Education News.
The federal scholarship tax credit is fundamentally different from Idaho’s Parental Choice Tax Credit. While Idaho’s program exclusively benefits private school and homeschool families, the federal scholarship tax credit supports students in public, public charter and private schools.
Understandably, the two programs have caused some confusion, compounded by recent headlines surrounding an Idaho Tax Commission report on the state program. But the distinctions are significant: the programs differ in how they are funded, who benefits and how the funds can be used.
For starters, the federal scholarship tax credit applies to federal taxes, while Idaho’s Parental Choice Tax Credit applies to state taxes. Passed by the Idaho Legislature in 2024, the state credit took effect this year. The federal program, meanwhile, launches Jan. 1, when taxpayers can begin making qualifying donations and claim their credits when filing federal taxes in 2028 and beyond.
The funding mechanisms also differ significantly. Idaho’s tax credit is funded by a $50 million state appropriation, while the federal program relies entirely on individual and voluntary taxpayer donations to scholarship granting organizations.
Donors receive a federal tax credit for their contributions, and the total scholarship funding available to students depends on how many taxpayers choose to participate each year, effectively making individual Idaho taxpayers philanthropists for schools and students they want to support.
The federal tax credit can and will benefit public school students. In fact, public school is where the lion’s share of the impact will be because most Idaho students attend a public school.
Once donations are received and scholarships awarded, students can receive support without waiting for donors to claim their federal tax credits.
From speaking with our colleagues across the country, we know that Idaho and Bluum SGO are leaders in putting the federal scholarship tax credit to work for all students and school types. But we know that the recent proliferation of school choice programs nationwide and in Idaho make the landscape confusing for parents, taxpayers and educators in general.
To maximize the impact of the federal tax credit program for Idaho’s students, we will continue to clarify how the programs differ and show how public-school students benefit from this opportunity to empower taxpayers and families alike.
