name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: This Thanksgiving, Imagine A Hawaiʻi Without Hunger
description: What if we all approached ending hunger the same way?
text:
As the season of gratitude arrives, we look forward to gathering with family and friends amid the aromas of spiced pumpkin pie and roasting turkey, yet across our islands, too many empty tables tell a different story.
On Hawaiʻi island, 43% of households experience food insecurity, and an estimated 62% of keiki live in households where children experience food insecurity. These are not distant statistics; they are our neighbors, our coworkers, and the next generation whose future we share.
A challenge of this scale can feel overwhelming, but Hawaiʻi has long understood that our strength lies in what we can do together.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

We see this in the Hilo lei, where strands of tī leaf are twisted together. A single strand is delicate, but joined with others, it becomes part of something stronger. This lei is also the centerpiece of The Food Basket’s strategic plan, and I confess I love a plan guided not by metrics but by a lei.
What if all of Hawaiʻi approached ending hunger the same way?
For generations, Hawaiʻi sustained thriving communities through agriculture, fishing, stewardship, and sharing. Fields of kalo and ʻuala, groves of ʻulu, and coastal fisheries nourished our islands through aloha ʻāina and reciprocity, because our kūpuna understood that abundance requires knowledge, cooperation, and shared responsibility. That history reminds us of what is possible.
Too many tables in Hawaii go empty too often. Pictured is a food bank in Kalihi. (David Croxford/Civil Beat/2025) David Croxford/Civil Beat/2025
We saw that spirit again this year. When the Kona Low storms, a magnitude 6.0 earthquake, and Hurricane Lala upended lives, neighbors checked on neighbors, volunteers mobilized, businesses stepped forward, and farmers shared their harvests despite losses of their own.
Yet these disasters also deepened hardship as power outages spoiled refrigerated food, missed workdays meant lost wages, and repairs stretched tight budgets further. For families already struggling, the burden grew heavier; others faced new worries about putting food on the table.
Hunger is a quieter disaster, one that arrives without storm warnings or headlines. It unfolds in kitchens where parents skip meals so their children can eat, and in working households where grocery money runs out before the month ends.
What if we brought the same urgency, generosity, and determination to ending hunger every day, not only in moments of crisis? The possibilities are already taking shape.
Farmers are growing healthy food for island families, while volunteers gather surplus produce from donor farms and backyard gardens and share it through food banks, pantries, and soup kitchens. Healthcare providers recognize nutritious food as essential to good health, and businesses are buying locally, strengthening the livelihoods of those who grow what we eat.
Teachers and cultural practitioners are reconnecting young people with the ʻāina, and neighbors continue to do what neighbors have always done: share what they have with aloha.
Acts Of Caring
At The Food Basket, Hawaiʻi island’s Food Bank, we are privileged to be part of these connections. More than half the food we distribute, is sourced on Hawaiʻi island, a commitment that nourishes families, supports farmers, ranchers, fishers, and local businesses, and builds a more resilient food system and a strong island economy.
Each act of caring is a strand, and each partnership strengthens the weave, but the lei is not yet complete. You do not need farmland, wealth, or specialized expertise to help end hunger, only the recognition that what you have to offer matters.
It might be ripe citrus from your backyard tree, a morning packing food boxes, choosing island-grown produce at the market, or a donation that helps a family through a difficult month. Perhaps it is sharing a meal with a kūpuna living alone, teaching a child to plant a seed, or inviting your workplace or school to join in.
We must also weave together larger changes: affordable housing, living wages, strong local agriculture, and public policies that help families thrive. This November, Oʻahu voters approved a Food Security Fund dedicating a portion of annual property tax revenues to improving access to locally produced food, an example Hawaiʻi’s other counties may wish to examine as they seek lasting food security.
Your voice matters, too, whether you contact an elected representative, testify at a hearing, or help shape local solutions. What transforms an island is not the scale of one gesture, but our willingness to braid our efforts into something larger than ourselves.
We must also weave together larger changes.
Imagine the strength of a lei woven with strands of nourishment, opportunity, and abundance encircling every keiki, kūpuna, and family with dignity. We know how to come together when disaster strikes, so let’s bring that determination to ensuring no one in Hawaiʻi goes hungry.
This season of gratitude, bring your strand and weave it with others, knowing that every contribution matters and every strand makes us stronger. Together, we can weave a Hawaiʻi where abundance is shared, aloha guides our actions, and no one goes hungry.

name: National
title: Ahead of Thanksgiving, more Americans struggle to put food on the table
description: KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards. As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and […]
text:
Andreas Leal and his wife peruse the shelves at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas. Food banks and pantries across the country are experiencing surging demand amid declining federal food assistance and higher grocery prices. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards.
As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and the hodgepodge of donated items on the toiletry shelves. A 75-year-old retiree, Leal said every bit helps when trying to keep up with rising prices.
“It’s very expensive,” he said. “Everything is expensive right now.”
Leal said his monthly Social Security benefit can’t keep up with rising costs. While the federal program boosted benefits by 2.8% this year, he said he just received notice that his residential property tax bill will jump 30%, costing him some $600. The increases require constant trade-offs. For example, to save on gas, the couple forgoes trips to visit their son who lives about 45 minutes away.
Leaders of Cross-Lines Community Outreach say such stories are more and more common. Its Community Market, a food pantry resembling a grocery store, serves about 1,900 families per month — a 35% increase over last year.  
“Daily, we have to turn people away,” said Executive Director Susila Jones. 
The market previously aimed to provide a couple pounds of frozen ground beef each month to every family. But those costs are now too high, pushing Cross-Lines to buy ground turkey or chicken — if prices are low enough.
People shop at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas.(Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)
Cross-Lines serves people across Wyandotte County, one of the most populous counties in Kansas with a poverty rate that exceeds state and national averages. In recent years, the food pantry has become more lenient about its income requirements and welcomed people who seek aid from multiple organizations. 
“This is not what people want to do and so we really just let people come to us when they need to come to us,” she said. “Because we know even if you are working, if you’ve had steady income, just one paycheck can put you over the edge.”
Rising costs of groceries, housing and gas have pushed more people to seek emergency food assistance. At the same time, those charitable organizations are seeing a wave of Americans who have lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the nation’s largest food assistance program. 
About 5.5 million Americans have lost SNAP benefits since last July’s passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut taxes and federal safety net programs. The law changed SNAP eligibility rules, ended certain work requirement exemptions and shifted new costs to states that administer the federal program.
More people are expected to lose SNAP aid as the legislation is fully implemented in the coming years. And earlier this month, the Trump administration proposed enrollment rule changes that would cut eligibility for another 6.3 million people.
Without congressional action, few experts see much relief ahead, further stressing the nation’s patchwork of churches, food banks and nonprofits laboring to keep people fed.
“Unfortunately, it has become a big part of people’s lives because they keep cutting off SNAP benefits,” said Gina Plata-Nino, the SNAP director at the anti-hunger nonprofit Food Research and Action Center. “…And you have these volunteers at food banks trying to do their best, but they are suffering in terms of being able to keep up.”
‘A huge demand’
The line of cars waiting to pick up ingredients for a full Thanksgiving dinner stretched a mile long last week in Detroit’s East Side. 
The Capuchin Soup Kitchen had to close its line a few hours after opening when it became clear that the annual giveaway would quickly deplete its 500 turkey meal kits.
“If we had 750, we still would have to shut the line down,” said Brother Fred Cabras, director of social services at the nearly century-old Catholic nonprofit. “I imagine that whatever number we set, we will probably hit every time because there is a huge demand.”
Rising prices squeeze more Americans ahead of pivotal midterm elections

The organization serves about 1,000 hot meals each day across two locations and operates a food pantry for thousands of families. Food pantry visits have been surging in recent years. 
In 2022, the operation served about 15,000 families. Cabras expects that figure to reach 34,000 to 35,000 by the end of this year. 
“This is definitely worse than the pandemic,” he said. 
The surging demand — and food prices — mean the Capuchin Soup Kitchen spent about $20,000 more on the food it bought last month compared with September. But private donations have remained strong.
Cabras said the coronavirus pandemic and last year’s unprecedented disruption to SNAP benefits because of the federal government shutdown heightened the public’s awareness and compassion about growing hunger.
“People also realize it because they’re spending more money on groceries,” he said. “And they’re like, ‘Well if I have a decent job, and I’m struggling, I can’t even imagine for the folks who are not getting great wages how much they’re struggling.’”
Vegetables are available at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas.(Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)
While people tend to donate more generously around the holiday season, high prices have also squeezed the budgets of many regular donors to charitable food groups.
“Everybody’s struggling. People who were not struggling a year ago are in a different space, just because of the rising costs,” said Courtney Goff, associate director of United Crescent Hill Ministries in Louisville, Kentucky.
The nonprofit, supported by local churches, businesses and individuals, serves about 50 people per day at its food pantry. That’s quadruple the amount of people it served last year, Goff said. 
With federal cuts to food pantry aid and rising prices for consumers, Goff said her organization is purchasing more food on its own and increasingly asking the community for cash and food donations.
Still, the food disappears nearly as quickly as it’s stocked because so many people are struggling to afford the basics. 
“You have people who maybe they make enough money to pay their rent, but rent is so high that that means they don’t have money for groceries or they don’t have money for gas,” she said. “And so they’re picking what is the most vital in that moment, and then trying to scramble together for the rest of it.”
Food banks increase spending 
St. Mary’s Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, which calls itself the World’s First Food Bank, has had to dip into its savings this year to meet rising diesel and fuel costs.
“We bought more food than we ever have before,” said Jerry Brown, director of public relations. “And just like everybody else who goes to the grocery store, that food is costing more.” 
The food bank serves hundreds of communities across Arizona, which has experienced the nation’s sharpest decline in SNAP benefits. Between July 2025 and July 2026, about 450,000 Arizonans lost SNAP benefits — a decrease of more than 50%. 
St. Mary’s has seen an influx from those who lost SNAP, Brown said. But it’s also experienced more visits from retirees who are unable to keep up with rising prices.
More Americans lose SNAP as Congress weighs food stamps’ future

“They thought they had enough money to retire on, and then the price of everything skyrocketed, while the amount of money that they receive remains the same,” he said. 
In Texas, some food banks have had to ration food in the face of overwhelming demand.
While individuals have lost SNAP benefits, food banks have grappled with separate cuts to federal food assistance. 
Last year, the Trump administration cut hundreds of millions in funding from a local food program for food banks and school meals. The U.S. Department of Agriculture also slashed $500 million that had already been allocated to food aid nationwide through The Emergency Food Assistance Program.
That’s pushed more food banks to purchase more of the food their communities need, said Celia Cole, CEO of Feeding Texas, a statewide network of 20 food banks.
“And that’s a real concern because it’s not really sustainable,” she said.
While she foresees no immediate relief from high food prices, Cole said politicians are increasingly recognizing the growing threat of hunger across the country. She’s hopeful that Congress will make changes to last year’s federal legislation cutting SNAP benefits.
“I think everyone recognizes the importance of having a well-nourished population and sees how these changes to SNAP are leading to people losing access to what’s really the backbone defense against hunger in our country,” she said. “So I see a light at the end of the tunnel there because I think there is a lot of bipartisan concern.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: IndyStar reinvents the community forum
description: I have been interested in IndyStar’s opinion section ever since I learned from its editor, James Briggs, that it is one of the most-read sections of the paper and a reason people renew their subscriptions. This fascinated me because, historically, the opinions of columnists have made people cancel their subscriptions. And, opinions dominate our world. […]
text:
Since fall 2026, IndyStar added changes to its lineup of contributing columnists for its opinion section, one of the most read sections of the newspaper. (Tracey Compton/Poynter)
I have been interested in IndyStar’s opinion section ever since I learned from its editor, James Briggs, that it is one of the most-read sections of the paper and a reason people renew their subscriptions.
This fascinated me because, historically, the opinions of columnists have made people cancel their subscriptions. And, opinions dominate our world. Everyone has a hot take, from celebrities to 24-hour cable news pundits, to the influencer with a massive social media following. 
In other words, we’re bombarded with viewpoints. By contrast, we are bereft of local information. Could it be that local opinions, curated by an editor, can help bridge that gap?
First, a quick bit of newspaper history and terminology. 
Editorial pages were the section in the newspaper where the editorial board, made up of the paper’s leadership, voiced the official opinions of the paper and its publisher. They would endorse political candidates and advocate for policy changes. Opinion sections, commonly called “op-ed” because they ran on the page opposite the editorial section, featured columnists and points of view of people in the community. 
Over the past two decades, newspaper staff have dwindled, with economic turbulence leading to rounds and rounds of layoffs. Editorial boards and opinion columnists were some of the first to be cut. Also, many newspaper executives and owners have been less enthusiastic about taking heat for political endorsements in an increasingly polarized society.
Many veteran journalists bemoan the loss of editorial boards, citing them as the only real “weapons,” besides investigation teams, that papers had for effecting change in a community and holding those in power to account.

“In my view, the community wants leadership, wants an authoritative voice, and editorials are the best way to do that,” said Ken Paulson, a former editor-in-chief of USA Today.

As top editor of four major daily newspapers and as a former president of the American Society of Newspaper Editors, Paulson witnessed newspapers across the country scrap their editorial boards.

“I think they’re both beneficial,” he said of editorial boards and op-ed pages. “But too many newspapers have subbed the op-ed page for editorials and that, in my view, was a mistake.” 

Paulson’s preference leans toward editorials. Without editorials and investigative reporting, Paulson said newspapers risk becoming just another community blog.
(Courtesy banner)
Essentially, IndyStar has eliminated the official editorials of the paper, replacing them with opinion columnists and contributing voices from the community. Other newspapers have stumbled into this transition less gracefully. 

There was significant public backlash, when Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos infamously decided the newspaper would not endorse anyone in the 2024 presidential election. Although Bezos’ timing was suspect, he was not alone in arguing that political endorsements have outlived their usefulness.

IndyStar was less conspicuous than The Washington Post in adopting a new approach to its opinion section.

But Paulson argues that, when done well, authoritative editorials and endorsements help people work through their own thoughts on issues and candidates. 

“Great editorials never told people what to think,” said Paulson, head of the Free Speech Center at Middle Tennessee State University. “They told people what was important to the community and why they felt a certain issue had to be resolved in favor of the men and women of that town.” 

I did a Q&A with Indy Star’s opinion editor, James Briggs, so that we all can see how he curates the opinion section. 
Q: What do you think is the role of an opinion columnist/section at a daily newspaper today?
Much the same as it’s always been: to drive conversations. Columnists make sense of the news, introduce ideas and advocate on behalf of a particular worldview. One thing that has changed, I think, is good column writing often looks more like analysis than a pure expression of opinion. In other words, a columnist today should aspire to make people smarter even as they’re seeking to persuade. Columns also should make people feel something — joy, anger, sadness or hope. They should include humor. In an increasingly algorithmic world, columns should stimulate critical thinking and put people in touch with their humanity.
Q: What is your current vision for IndyStar’s opinion section? What did the former section lack and what did it get right that you would like to continue?
This is still evolving. I’m immensely proud of what we’ve accomplished so far. I started my job in January 2024 with no staff or contributors. It was just me sitting around writing as much as I could. We built the section up to over a half-dozen regular columnists between staff and contributors. We expanded the Sunday print section to make room for all the great columns we’ve been publishing online. IndyStar has been publishing the highest volume of Indiana-focused opinion columns since at least the early-2000s.
We’ve lost some of that momentum this year as columnists have moved onto other roles and opportunities. That has provided an opportunity for my colleague Jacob Stewart and me to expand our own voices in the section. We’ve been doing more writing lately, which I’ve enjoyed. We have a lot to talk about, especially after the midterm elections. We’re still working to find the right mix of contributor voices and also determine how to expand into video, which is a massive growth area in media.
Q: How did you choose the current mix of columnists? 
I’m looking for a few qualities in columnists. I mentioned before that analysis is important, so I’m looking for subject matter experts who can share insights on topics that people have shown us they care about, including education, urban planning and the economy. Economist Michael Hicks is the prototype. I’m also looking for compelling generalists. Rob Kendall, the radio host and podcaster, is a great example. Jeffery Tompkins fits into both buckets. Finally, I want engaging voices. People you’d actually want to talk to in real life, who enjoy lively discussions and don’t take themselves too seriously.
 
I’m pleased with the viewpoint diversity we’ve offered spanning center-left to center-right. We avoid the fringes. We try to publish columnists who agree on facts despite drawing different conclusions.
Q: You’ve written that you wanted “insightful writers who could offer rigorous good-faith analysis without fear of offending people.” Was there a trend or issue you observed that prompted this statement?
Opinion has to be provocative yet grounded in reality. That’s a difficult line to walk. Some people just want to say crazy things to get attention, and others just want to say smart things in a boring way. The latter instinct is especially common in Indiana, where there seems to be an aversion to causing offense. And I get it. There can be social and professional consequences to articulating sharp viewpoints on topics that people feel passionately about. But we need people to take those risks so we can grow as a society. People who are willing to embrace discomfort and earnestly work through disagreements in the public square are the people who counter bad-faith actors and move our city and state forward. I want IndyStar Opinion to be a platform for constructive debate.
Q: Gannett began eliminating editorial sections from its newspapers in 2022, but an opinion section prevailed at The Star. How did The Star manage to keep the section going, and why is that important? What purpose does the section serve in today’s media climate?
The company’s leadership has prioritized opinion in recent years. My hire in 2024 reflects that investment, as does our build-out. I couldn’t have grown this section if the company hadn’t committed to opinion. On top of the mission-driven case for opinion I’ve been making here, I’d say there’s also a business case for opinion. Strong opinion and analysis creates a special connection between us and our audience, which makes people want to join us as subscribers. I feel that connection from the people who reach out to share thoughts on what we’re doing.
Q: How do you distinguish the paper’s commentary and opinion columnists online when we are awash in online commentary from content creators and social media influencers?
We’re competing against every other way in which any person could be spending their time. That includes other news sites, Netflix or TikTok. Anything. We have to prove we’re worthy of attention by providing analysis and insights that don’t exist anywhere else. That can be Jacob sharing his first-hand expertise on how the Indiana Statehouse will move forward in the current political climate or me writing about Indianapolis’ education landscape based on my sourcing and experience as a parent.
Q: Do you think opinion columnists still resonate in spite of all of the sources of commentary online?
I know they do. Our audience shows me that every single day.



The Indy Public Editor is a grant-funded pilot project run by the Poynter Institute. This column is edited by Kelly McBride and copy edited by Lauren Klinger. The project is managed by Nicole Slaughter Graham with support from Amaris Castillo.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Biologists work to boost Louisiana’s striped bass numbers. They need help from anglers.
description: State biologists are trying to revitalize Louisiana’s population of striped bass, which they say aren’t adequately reproducing in the wild because of warming waters and shrinking habitat.
text:
Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries biologist Matthew Duplessis, left inserts a tag into a striped bass as  colleague Jonathan Winslow holds the fish. (Photo courtesy of LDWF)
State biologists are trying to revitalize Louisiana’s population of striped bass, which they say aren’t adequately reproducing in the wild because of warming waters and shrinking habitat.
A state Department of Wildlife and Fisheries program is tracking where striped bass find safe haven in Southeast Louisiana waters, but they can’t do it alone. Officials are asking anglers to help them collect samples of the fish and share where they’ve caught them to learn more about their domain and range.
“Ultimately, our goal is to use the best available science to help ensure the striped bass remains part of Louisiana’s fisheries for generations to come,” state fisheries biologist Jonathan Winslow said. “We have a great opportunity to learn more about striped bass in Louisiana, and we want the fishing public to be a big part of that effort.”
Striped bass can live in saltwater and freshwater, and they’re found in the rivers, streams and coastal waters of the Pontchartrain Basin that originates well into Mississippi. The fish eat just about anything they can find, from small crustaceans to other fish.
“They are fantastic fighting fish,” Winslow said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Winslow said the Gulf strain of striped bass has been on the decline for quite some time, though there has not been a dedicated assessment to quantify their numbers. Scientists and anglers generally agree and share anecdotal accounts of a significant decline spanning over decades. 
Researchers also point to temperature increases over time in the waters where the striped bass is found. The Gulf strain can withstand water temperatures up to 78 degrees, Winslow said, but warmer conditions can create significant stress, affecting its health and ability to survive.
Daily average air temperatures in Louisiana have increased 2.8 degrees Fahrenheit since 1970, according to data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. These hotter conditions strongly correlate with warmer water and other changes in the water cycle, including rainfall, flooding and drought, all of which can affect aquatic environments and the creatures living within them. 
“The biggest battle across the coast is finding where that cool water refuge is,” said Matthew Duplessis, a Wildlife and Fisheries biologist manager.  “(Striped bass) need access to cool water and in Louisiana, there’s not much cool water.” 
Striped bass also need access to uninterrupted stretches of fast-moving river water to reproduce. Human-engineered alterations, such as dredged channels, dams and other development, make it harder for the fish eggs to successfully hatch, according to scientists.
In order for eggs to survive once they have been fertilized, the flow of river water needs to be constant for uninterrupted lengths so eggs don’t fall to the bottom and get buried in sediment, Winslow said.
“With shortening the lengths of our rivers here, specifically the Pearl River and Bogue Chitto rivers … they can’t do that anymore,” he added. 
To find solutions, Louisiana officials and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service created the Striped Bass Collaborative Anglers Project. With input from sportsfishers, they can better track the species’ movement, its genetic makeup and more effectively restock the species in the Pontchartrain Basin to improve their numbers. 
The state has only three biologists assigned to the basin, making it hard for them to take enough striped bass samples, Winslow said. 
“Anglers are out on the water every day of the week, covering more ground, going to areas that we don’t get to,” he said.
Biologists can insert trackers into live striped bass and release them where they were caught, with hopes of learning where there are cold water havens where the fish frequent, Duplessis said. 
If anglers want to keep the striped bass they catch, they can still help scientists by clipping their fins for genetic research. Fin clip kits are available for free through Wildlife and Fisheries, and the department can pick up the samples. 
The department will also accept cleaned striped bass carcasses for testing, with arrangements made through the same online portal. Frozen samples should be placed in sealable plastic bags and labeled with the catch date, along with water body and general location where they were caught.
“The anglers are crucial for this project,” Winslow said. “Every sample we receive helps us get a better understanding of these fish, where they come from, where they’re going and how they’re contributing to the population.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: State responds to committee recommendations on addressing issues in NH’s disability system
description: In response to recommendations to improve the state’s disability care system, the New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services agreed to work with stakeholders on some points. However, officials also cautioned members of the ad-hoc System Review Committee that budgetary considerations might get in the way of the resource-intensive changes. Some memb[...]
text:
Members of the New Hampshire Developmental Services Quality Council consult during a Nov. 18, 2026, meeting in Concord. From left are Louis Esposito, executive director of ABLE NH; Gina Cannon, a member of the New Hampshire Autism Council; Howard Clark, a board member at Monadnock Developmental Services; Marissa Berg, executive director of the Community Support Network Inc.; and Stephanie Patrick, executive director of the Disability Rights Center. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)In response to recommendations to improve the state’s disability care system, the New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services agreed to work with stakeholders on some points. However, officials also cautioned members of the ad-hoc System Review Committee that budgetary considerations might get in the way of the resource-intensive changes. Some members called the state’s response insufficient.

System Review Letter On Recommendations for Change In Disability Care System
 

In September, the System Review Committee of the N.H. Developmental Services Quality Council sent DHHS and Gov. Kelly Ayotte a list of recommendations to fix issues within the system that are contributing to reports of abuse and neglect; DHHS responded earlier this month.
“The Quality Council’s recommendations are informed and made in a spirit of partnership and collaboration,” Health and Human Services Commissioner Lori Weaver wrote to the council. “They are worth consideration and broader stakeholder discussion. The Department’s ability to act on several of the Quality Council’s recommendations will ultimately be determined by the current fiscal environment in which we operate, given many of the recommendations will require additional resources.”
Ayotte’s office didn’t respond to the recommendations but told the Bulletin that DHHS’ response speaks for the state.
The System Review Committee was established immediately following a November 2025 Bulletin investigation into the system, which provides taxpayer-funded care to people with disabilities, such as autism or cerebral palsy. The Bulletin uncovered evidence of hundreds of instances of abuse and neglect within the system and told the stories of several disabled victims who were harmed at the hands of their caregiver or who died too soon. The Quality Council met Wednesday to review DHHS’ response.
Committee calls for changes to New Hampshire’s disability system

The committee’s recommendations require buy-in from stakeholders across state government, including multiple state agencies, the Legislature and the governor’s office. Some of the recommendations are:

The state should establish a new hotline with a 24/7 operator for people to report abuse, neglect or exploitation.
The state should create a centralized intake and triage system for abuse, neglect and exploitation complaints.
The state should implement unannounced visits and inspections to care facilities.
DHHS should report more data on abuse and neglect investigations publicly.
The state Legislature should better fund the system, so that care facilities can pay caregivers higher wages and attract higher quality talent and so that DHHS can hire more abuse and neglect investigators.
The state should do a better job encouraging reporting of abuse, neglect and exploitation.
Investigators should be able to deem an abuse or neglect report “inconclusive” if there’s not enough evidence for a guilty or innocent verdict.
The state should overhaul its paperwork and bureaucratic systems because they’re currently too onerous for the average family to understand and they create an unnecessary burden on staff that takes focus away from improving quality of care.

DHHS responded to each recommendation individually. On the hotline recommendation, DHHS said it already has multiple ways people can report abuse and neglect, though it acknowledged that none of them have a live person 24/7.

DHHS Responses to System Review Committe/Quality Council's Recommendations For Change
 

Among its top recommendations, the System Review Committee wants DHHS to establish one unified centralized intake and triage system with the hotline incorporated, as opposed to the several disparate agencies and procedures in place now. DHHS officials said they “support the concept” and “believe it would be useful.” However, “given our current resource limitations in personnel (the state has had a hiring freeze in place for nearly two years) and IT, the Department would like to work with the Council on the feasibility of this recommendation.”
On encouraging better reporting, DHHS pointed to ways it already encourages reporting as required by state laws and regulations. Council members were unsatisfied with that answer.
Stephanie Patrick, co-chair of the System Review Committee and executive director for the Disability Rights Center of New Hampshire, said the education methods DHHS is using are insufficient and “not happening in the level of detail that we would want.” Patrick suggested DHHS is focusing solely on “compliance” with the law rather than going further and focusing on the “quality” of the service they’re providing.
On the proposal to deem some abuse and neglect investigations “inconclusive,” DHHS said that would require a “legal review” to determine if state statute currently allows such a determination. It said it would consult with the New Hampshire Department of Justice.
However, due process concerns have also been raised about that suggestion.
“I understand our position,” Committee member Gina Cannon said, comparing it to a criminal process where no one is deemed guilty until the state has met the burden of proof. “But I also wonder whether we’re running afoul of due process for the person that’s alleged to have committed the infraction.”
“It’s not a criminal process,” Patrick countered, “but I do think that that is an important thing to think about.”
For many of the committee’s suggestions involved better educating the public about how the system operates, DHHS pointed the committee to its website. Cannon called that response “bordering on flippant.”
“The website is a mess,” she said. “It is a complete and total inaccessible mess.”
Other members agreed and said DHHS needs to do better about making the information understandable, accessible and in a user-friendly location.
A sign outside New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services offices in Concord on Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Howard Clark, one of the Quality Council members and a board member at Monadnock Developmental Services in Keene, said he sensed “a spirit of cooperation” and “an invitation to collaborate” in the response
“We and them need to meet and talk about this,” he said, “so I would want to make sure we take that invitation.”
Jake Leon, spokesperson for DHHS, said in a statement: “DHHS is committed to making services better for Granite Staters with developmental disabilities, and we have been working to implement recommendations from stakeholders and new laws signed this year that will improve oversight, accountability, and quality of care. We look forward to continuing this process with all stakeholders, providers, and most importantly, the individuals and families we serve to ensure those in the developmental services system receive safe, high-quality, and compassionate care.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Report: CT subsidizes bigger teacher pensions in wealthier school districts
description: Equable Institute found that retired teachers from CT's wealthiest districts get thousands more in pension payments from the state.
text:
There’s no shortage of discussion about inequity in Connecticut public education, but one aspect tends to fly under the radar: the teacher pension system.
The topic wasn’t addressed in the short list of policy ideas that came out of Gov. Ned Lamont’s Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability. But researchers at Equable Institute, a bipartisan think tank specializing in public retirement systems, contend it is a key part of how wealthy districts outperform their less affluent peers.
In latest iteration of its “Who Benefits?” study — slated to publish soon — Equable found the districts with the biggest state pension subsidies have less teacher attrition on average than those with the smallest subsidies. And in general, it’s the wealthiest districts getting the biggest subsidies.
“We hear that … the funding formula for education is intended to equitably distribute resources. But then we see that wealthier towns are getting thousands of dollars more — in effect, to pay for teachers — than lower-resource towns,” said Anthony Randazzo, Equable executive director and the author of the report.
Here’s how that happens.
In Connecticut, each district negotiates its own teacher salaries. If a district has more property wealth — and thus more property tax revenue to work with — there’s a good chance it will be able to offer bigger salaries to its teachers. When teachers retire, their retirement benefits are based in large part on those salaries.
But while the district pays their salaries, it doesn’t pay their retirement benefits. The state does. This is where critics say the problem lies. 
There’s a general principle baked into Connecticut’s overall school funding system that results in more state money being allocated to less affluent districts. A town like Greenwich can raise more money with comparatively lower property taxes than, say, Hartford. In order to support equal educational opportunity, the state seeks to make up some portion of the difference.
The teacher retirement system does the opposite, Equable researchers say.
According to Equable, the state pays just under $27,000 per teacher in pension subsidies to the highest-poverty quartile of districts, which includes Bridgeport and Hartford. It pays over $32,000 per teacher to the lowest-poverty quartile, which includes New Canaan and Westport.
(The report bases poverty level on free and reduced price lunch eligibility, a commonly used proxy. The highest-poverty quartile has 61.6% of the state’s FRPL students. The lowest-poverty quartile has 5.6%.)
Equable argues that Connecticut’s teacher pension system exacerbates a problem that financially-strapped districts — often with higher-need populations — are already dealing with: teacher attrition. Its latest report found the state’s highest-poverty districts have an average teacher attrition rate of 11.74%. In the lowest-poverty districts, it’s 8.82%.
This is the first time the Equable study has looked at pension subsidies on a per-teacher basis. Randazzo said researchers sought to highlight the damage to educational fairness the often-overlooked system can cause: Districts with the greatest need are getting $5,000 less per teacher in pension subsidies than those with the lowest need.
By way of solutions, Equable has suggested districts with the largest teacher compensation packages pay a portion of the normal cost of pensions — that is, how much to pay into the system to cover all benefits earned in a given year. Connecticut is among the minority of states that do not currently require local districts to pay into a teacher retirement system.
If Equable’s proposal were adopted, the state would continue covering all pension costs for lower-wealth districts and could potentially reinvest its savings into the Education Cost Sharing grant.
Despite the lack of public discussion this year, the problems with the teacher retirement system aren’t unknown to the state’s education leaders. 
Govs. Dannel Malloy and Ned Lamont both took a swing at changing the system without success. The topic came up a handful of times this year in the Blue Ribbon Commission — whose stated task is to reimagine education funding from the ground up — but was not included in a list of policy ideas to advance as the group deliberates on its final recommendations.
“I think the solution is rooted more in state funding for both education and municipal aid so that districts have more resources to raise teacher salaries,” said Rep. Jennifer Leeper, D-Fairfield, who co-chairs the legislature’s Education Committee and sits on the Blue Ribbon Commission.
Cathryn Vaulman, Lamont’s director of communications, noted the governor’s unsuccessful attempt to change teacher pensions in the past.
“His efforts faced opposition in the Legislature, but he remains open to conversations about addressing inequities in the system,” Vaulman said.
Michael Morton of the School and State Finance Project said part of the problem is that pensions are not an easy topic to grasp. “It is fairly in the weeds. It is not the sexiest topic by any stretch of the imagination,” he said.
But Morton agreed with Equable’s overall findings. “That [pension] system has been in place for quite some time, and I think that inequity has only grown,” he said.
Morton said his organization has spent 11 years educating people on the ECS grant, an issue that has gained traction among the public and in the statehouse. That work hasn’t happened yet for teacher pensions.
That’s “one of the reasons why I think you need something to continue after the life of this [Blue Ribbon] commission, to regularly take up issues like this,” Morton said.
Unlike ECS, the proposed solution to pension inequity — that some towns kick in a portion of their own money — is a political hazard.
“The biggest challenge is, again, you’re asking wealthier communities to pay more. This is like the basic problem with any tax conversation,” Morton said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Remembering an eagle-eyed editor and avid collector of books
description: One of the most bizarre crime stories ever to appear in a newspaper once ran in the Wichita Eagle. It involved an assault on a duck under the headline “Quack, quack, quack!” in ascending type sizes. An editor likely scrapped the headline and the story for the later editions, making this unusual story difficult to […]
text:
Columnist Carl Rowan’s book, “South of Freedom: The stirring personal report of an ace Negro journalist who returned to his native South to make a 6,000-mile tour and to ask dangerous questions,” was given to columnist Mark McCormick by Wichita Eagle editor Chuck Potter. (Photo by Mark McCormick for Kansas Reflector)One of the most bizarre crime stories ever to appear in a newspaper once ran in the Wichita Eagle.
It involved an assault on a duck under the headline “Quack, quack, quack!” in ascending type sizes. An editor likely scrapped the headline and the story for the later editions, making this unusual story difficult to find, and even more difficult to believe.
Years and maybe even decades later, a similar story surfaced and that story never made it past the editing desk before getting spiked, though the reporter and I thought we’d sufficiently toned down the subject matter. Newsrooms, in general, delight in such stories and in a brand of dark humor used as armor against the drumbeat of general awfulness reporters cover and editors manage.
As a few of us chuckled about the newer story, someone said the Eagle’s book editor, Chuck Potter, actually had a copy of the original story clipped from that early edition, and that he carried it around in his wallet.
Chuck didn’t disappoint. Always the editor, Chuck offered proof of the unbelievable story. At our alma mater, the University of Kansas, our journalism professors told us: “If you mother says she loves you, check it out.”
Chuck Potter
Those of us still connected to the newspaper’s former employees Facebook page learned that Chuck died Nov. 12 in Newton. The sometimes abrupt but eagle-eyed editor was 78.
Chuck could rub you wrong before you got to know him.
His white hair and white beard framed a face etched in annoyed urgency. He zipped around the newsroom in a simple shirt and jeans and did not seem to be held captive by etiquette. Like the Seinfeld character George Constanza, Chuck’s seeming annoyance made him seem incredibly busy. He brushed by me a couple of times and I wondered what I might have done to offend him.
One day, we started chatting about books, and the bibliophile just beneath the surface emerged like a sunny day revealed behind heavy curtains.
I learned about his love and investment in books and that he spent a lot of his time away from work on a hard-target search of every attic, basement, and estate sale within a drivable radius. He’d tell me about the gems he’d found here and there and seemed to appreciate my earnest interest. I came to consider him one of those rare and unusual personalities found only in their natural newsroom habitat.
He was born in Kansas City and attended schools there before studying journalism at KU. Before his time at the Eagle, he worked for the Salina Journal. Because we were both Jayhawks, we enjoyed talking KU basketball.
Chuck also had a thoughtful streak.
As I prepared to leave the Eagle after nearly 15 years, the last few as the metro columnist, he gave me one of the most thoughtful gifts I’d ever received — an original 1952 copy of trailblazing columnist Carl Rowan’s book, “South of Freedom: The stirring personal report of an ace Negro journalist who returned to his native South to make a 6,000-mile tour and to ask dangerous questions.”
Black columnists had proceeded Rowan, including Langston Hughes and Ida B. Wells, but Rowan was credited with being the first Black newspaper columnist whose syndicated column appeared regularly in major mainstream American newspapers.
It was signed, “To my good friend, Martin Perry, With best wishes, Carl T. Rowan.” An incredible gift for me, the departing columnist at a mainstream newspaper, more than 50 years later.
That book sits in a place of honor, next to some of my favorite books, on a shelf in my home.
I ran into him a couple of summers ago at, of all places, Wichita’s new downtown public library. He hadn’t changed much and seemed still very much in his element. His coworkers remember him as one of a kind.
Chuck was preceded in death by his parents and his sister, Charlotte Petersen. He is survived by his wife, Feryl, of Valley Center; daughters Laura (Chris) Wolf of Ogden, Kansas; and Jenny (Jimmy) Gee of San Diego, California; and three grandchildren.
I’m so grateful for the book, but I also kind of wish I had that story clipping from Chuck’s wallet.
People knew Chuck operated as a first-rate editor, and that despite an easily misread demeanor, they also knew he was a great guy.
But that duck headline? That’s another story.
Mark McCormick is a journalist and a nonprofit executive. He’s also the author of four books including “Barry Sanders: Now You See Him” (a New York Times bestseller), “Some Were Paupers. Some Were Kings: Dispatches from Kansas,” and his latest, “Kansas Matters: America’s Social Faultlines.” Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: NIPSCO internal review blames storm response on inconsistent operations
description: The Northern Indiana Public Service Company blames its lackluster response to widespread power outages in northwest Indiana last August on outdated systems and inconsistent regional restoration efforts. The conclusion came in a new internal review from the investor-owned utility. The company recorded more than 350,000 outages following an Aug. 11 derecho and[...]
text:
NIPSCO President Vince Parisi issued a memo to state senators outlining the findings of an internal review into the utility's response to widespread power outages last August. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Northern Indiana Public Service Company blames its lackluster response to widespread power outages in northwest Indiana last August on outdated systems and inconsistent regional restoration efforts.
The conclusion came in a new internal review from the investor-owned utility.
The company recorded more than 350,000 outages following an Aug. 11 derecho and subsequent storms, with winds reaching nearly 100 miles per hour in Lake County.
NIPSCO says it restored power to 100,000 customers within the first 48 hours. Those restoration efforts reached about 93% of customers by day 10, according to a letter from NIPSCO President Vince Parisi.
But some customers waited roughly two weeks for their power to be restored, prompting investigations into the company’s response.
Braun demands investigation into NIPSCO after prolonged northwest Indiana outages

NIPSCO submitted findings from an internal review of its storm response to the state Senate Interim Study Committee on Energy, Utilities and Telecommunications Tuesday. An independent review is also being conducted by Filsinger Energy Partners.
The internal report found NIPSCO’s local operating areas, or LOAs, acted independently rather than using a coordinated response, further complicated by manual paperwork and inconsistent storm damage assessments which “inhibited the flow of critical information and slowed our response” and strained communication with customers who lost power.
The memo cites the derecho’s “vast” and “unprecedented scale,” exacerbated by staffing gaps for key roles that strained the company’s ability to rotate crews and sustain around-the-clock operations.
The review also found NIPSCO’s decision to report information to the public as quickly as possible resulted in incomplete updates while assessments were still underway in places like Gary and Portage.
“We know excluding certain communities from some updates when assessments were ongoing confused and frustrated customers and community leaders,” Parisi wrote, “and we apologize and will work to do better.”
Rep. Randy Novak, D-Michigan City, said the memo paints a picture of a company “caught flat-footed.”
While the findings confirm many of Novak’s suspicions, he said it doesn’t go far enough to explain possible infrastructure and staffing issues, calling for a “truly independent” investigation into NIPSCO’s response.
“I think this goes way beyond NIPSCO, the company in Merrillville,” Novak said. “This is the pressure to turn a profit and the pressure to do things from higher-ups.”
Attorney General Todd Rokita told reporters Tuesday he offered to investigate the storm response, saying his office could stay impartial.
“The utilities are a very strong special interest at the Statehouse, particularly in the legislature,” he said, “and so we’ll see if we get any headway. But the offer still stands,” he said. “I’m happy to jump in and help the governor investigate NIPSCO, because I think they did the people of northwest Indiana raw, and I think they need to be held accountable.”
Parisi told senators the company is working to establish a coordinated emergency response and upgrade its technology for storm assessments following the internal review.
The utility will expand training, with an emphasis on core incident management teams and damage assessors.
And NIPSCO is working to expand electric storm response roles across the company, strengthen communications with the state’s emergency operations center and review options for union employees to take on more flexible storm response roles, according to the memo.
“The August storms were a stark reminder of the reality that weather patterns are changing and severe storms are becoming more common,” Parisi wrote to the committee. “Like other utilities across the region and the country, we will continue to harden our system so that customers have safe, reliable energy in the face of these growing challenges.”
“Preparing Indiana for the next major storm will require both strengthening our preparedness efforts and a broader, more concerted effort by all of us within the state to ensure our communities are ready.”
NIPSCO AAR Letter Nov 23 2026

name: Maryland Matters
title: Marylanders face nation’s lowest average cost for premiums on ACA marketplace, analysis shows
description: After two years of double-digit premium increases, Marylanders who purchase healthcare from the state’s insurance marketplace may take some solace from the fact that they will pay the lowest premiums in the nation in 2027, a new report shows.
text:
Marylanders looking to buy private insurance have until Dec. 31 to have coverage start in January. Those who miss that deadline have until Jan. 15 to sign up for coverage that starts in February. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)After two years of double-digit premium increases, Marylanders who purchase healthcare from the state’s insurance marketplace may take some solace from the fact that they will pay the lowest premiums in the nation in 2027, a new report shows.
A state-by-state analysis of plans by KFF, the healthcare research policy group, shows that for all three tiers of coverage — bronze, silver and gold — Marylanders will pay 33% to 45% below the national average for insurance purchased on the Maryland Health Connection, the state’s insurance marketplace part of the Obama-era Affordable Care Act.
State officials and healthcare advocates chalk the low rates up to statewide subsidies and other actions aimed at keeping more people enrolled in healthcare plans, even as prices skyrocketed over the last two years.
“I think we’ve made one of the strongest commitments of any state in the country towards affordability in the individual insurance market,” said Johanna Fabian-Marks, executive director for the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange which operates the state’s insurance marketplace.
Johanna Fabian-Marks, deputy executive director for the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange, during a meeting of the Maryland Health Insurance Coverage Protection Commission. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
“Although I am very proud that we have the lowest cost premiums in the country … I also want to acknowledge that most people don’t feel like their health insurance is as affordable as it could be,” she added.
The KFF data comes as families across the United States are weighing their healthcare options during the annual open enrollment period for insurance coverage offered through the Affordable Care Act.
Marylanders buying health plans on the state’s insurance marketplace face an average 14.6% premium rate increase this year, which follows a 13.4% rate hike last year.
But while the average premium in the U.S. for a bronze plan — the least expensive plans, but also the least comprehensive with high deductibles — is $511 a month, Marylanders will pay an average $293 per month, according to the KFF analysis. Idaho had the second-cheapest bronze plan premiums, at $369 a month.
A step up to silver plans finds the national average premium is $681 per month, while in Maryland it will be $459. New Hampshire was a close second for lowest-cost silver plans at $471 a month.
Gold plans provide greater coverage and lower deductibles, at higher monthly cost. The average gold plan in Maryland is $454 in monthly premiums, compared to a national average of $694. Iowa’s gold plans were second-lowest at $504.
Gov. Wes Moore said in a written statement that it’s “no accident” Maryland has the lowest premiums, as the administration and the Maryland General Assembly pushed legislation to counter recent federal decisions that increased healthcare costs nationwide.
“Where the Trump administration slashed health care and spiked costs on working families, Maryland will always protect our people,” Moore said in the Tuesday statement. “As prices nationwide continue to rise, we’ll keep fighting for affordable health care because no one should have to choose between lifesaving treatment, food for their family, or gas in their tank.”
Healthcare advocates and insurance representatives agree healthcare costs in Maryland would be higher for the individual insurance market if it weren’t for two policies in the state.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Matthew F. Celentano, executive director of the League of Life & Health Insurers of Maryland, points to the state’s long-standing “reinsurance” program that has kept premium costs lower in Maryland for several years.
“Marylanders should take comfort in the fact that the General Assembly has supported and implemented the reinsurance program which has direct correlation to affordability in the individual market – and has done so for many years now, consistently placing us as one of the most affordable states,” Celentano said in a written statement.
Vincent DeMarco, president of the Maryland Healthcare for All coalition, adds that state subsidies under the new Maryland Premium Assistance program have helped keep premiums down for those who would otherwise go without health insurance due to rising costs.
The subsidy was created to keep costs down for those who previously benefited from the federal enhanced premium tax credits that expired in December 2025 after Congress failed to renew them.
“One of the things that causes premiums to go up is when there are more people uninsured. And in other states, more people have become uninsured because of bad federal actions – in particular HR 1, hurting people, making it harder to stay on Medicaid, and the failure of Congress to extend the enhanced tax credits,” DeMarco said.
Healthcare panel endorses tax extension, prescription drug policy change

The Maryland Premium Assistance program is set to expire at the end of 2027, which would lead to increased out of pocket costs for those currently enrolled in the program unless the state can arrange a more sustainable source of funding for the subsidy.
Fabian-Marks note that for certain households, the Premium Assistance program kept monthly premiums stable, or in some cases lower, in the absence of the federal tax credits.
“In the state legislative session, we are expecting a conversation with all of our stakeholders around how we continue to support affordability and fund affordability in the individual market,” Fabian-Marks said.
Even with the lowest premiums in the nation, “it’s undeniable” that Marylanders may struggle to afford the options available on the marketplace and go without healthcare coverage, DeMarco said.
“It’s unfortunate that because of the bad actions of the federal government, Marylanders have seen their premiums go up more than they should have – it would have been a lot worse had not Gov. Wes Moore and the Maryland General Assembly mitigated these problems,” he said.
Marylanders have until Dec. 31 to shop the Maryland Health Connection and select a plan if they want coverage starting in January. For those who miss that deadline, they have until Jan. 15 to select coverage that starts in February.
“In every way possible, the Moore administration and our general assembly is working to protect Marylanders,” DeMarco said. “These numbers show that that work is succeeding.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Commentary: It’s time for Wisconsin to end wildlife killing contests
description: Wisconsin is known for its beautiful outdoors, abundant wildlife and proud hunting traditions. Generations of residents have grown up appreciating our natural resources and the importance of conservation. We pride ourselves on responsible wildlife management and passing our outdoor heritage on to future generations. So why does Wisconsin continue to allow or[...]
text:
Coyote (Wisconsin DNR photo)Wisconsin is known for its beautiful outdoors, abundant wildlife and proud hunting traditions. Generations of residents have grown up appreciating our natural resources and the importance of conservation. We pride ourselves on responsible wildlife management and passing our outdoor heritage on to future generations.
So why does Wisconsin continue to allow organized wildlife killing contests?
Wildlife killing contests are exactly what their name suggests. Participants compete to kill the most animals, the largest animals, or sometimes even the smallest animals within a designated period. Coyotes, foxes, bobcats, raccoons, rabbits, squirrels and other wildlife become targets in competitions where cash, firearms and other prizes are awarded.
Let’s be clear: This isn’t about banning hunting. It isn’t about taking away someone’s ability to protect livestock, manage legitimate wildlife conflicts or participate in lawful hunting.
It’s about drawing a line between responsible outdoor traditions and organized competitions that turn killing wildlife into entertainment.
What conservation value is there in rewarding someone for killing the most animals in a weekend?
Wildlife plays an important role in maintaining healthy ecosystems. Predators such as coyotes and foxes are an important part of Wisconsin’s natural landscape. Indiscriminate killing can have unintended ecological consequences and should not be confused with science-based wildlife management.
There is also a troubling ethical question. What message are we sending to the next generation when children are encouraged to participate in events where dead wildlife is lined up, counted, weighed, and awarded prizes? We should be teaching our children to appreciate wildlife, understand its importance, and respect the natural world — not celebrate how many animals can be killed.
Wisconsin is not alone in confronting this issue. Other states have already taken steps to prohibit or restrict wildlife killing contests, recognizing that conservation should be about protecting and responsibly managing natural resources, not creating competitions around animal deaths.
There is also growing momentum here at home. Wisconsin Conservation Congress resolutions have brought this issue before residents and wildlife policymakers. Support for ending these contests demonstrates that this is a conversation Wisconsin can no longer ignore.
And let’s recognize something important: Many responsible hunters do not support these contests. Ethical hunting and wildlife killing competitions are not synonymous. We can respect Wisconsin’s hunting heritage while opposing competitions that reward the largest number of dead animals.
Now that Democrats will have trifecta control of Wisconsin state government in January, there is an opportunity to finally make meaningful progress on ending wildlife killing contests across our state. With control of the governorship and both chambers of the Legislature, Democratic leadership will have an opportunity to turn growing public concern into meaningful action. I urge our newly empowered lawmakers to make ending wildlife killing contests a conservation priority. This is an opportunity to demonstrate that Wisconsin values its wildlife and that compassion, science and responsible stewardship matter.
Our lawmakers and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources should work toward a statewide prohibition on organized wildlife killing contests, including the organization, sponsorship, promotion and participation in competitions that reward killing wildlife.
As someone who has spent years advocating for wildlife, I believe we have a responsibility to speak for the animals that cannot speak for themselves.
Wildlife belongs to all of us. It is part of Wisconsin’s natural heritage, and its value cannot be measured by a cash prize or the number of carcasses at a weigh-in.
We should be a state that celebrates its wildlife, not one that rewards its destruction.
Wisconsin can do better. It’s time to end wildlife killing contests once and for all.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia food banks, families struggle to stretch aid this holiday season
description: Twice a month, people line up in cars and on foot at Enough to Share, a volunteer-run food pantry that operates out of the Atlanta Masjid of Al-Islam mosque in DeKalb County. When Enough to Share started in 2017, five volunteers pooled $20 each to buy groceries at a dollar store to provide food assistance […]
text:
Volunteers at the Enough to Share food pantry, which operates out of the Atlanta Masjid of Al-Islam mosque in DeKalb County, prepare for its bi-weekly food distribution event on Nov. 18, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder 
How to support local food pantries:

Donate to Enough to Share’s Giving Tuesday efforts here.
Support your local food pantry donating to Feeding Georgia here.
Plan to participate in the Hunger 5k Walk/Run in March 2027 that benefits Atlanta Community Food Bank and other local nonprofits.



Twice a month, people line up in cars and on foot at Enough to Share, a volunteer-run food pantry that operates out of the Atlanta Masjid of Al-Islam mosque in DeKalb County.
When Enough to Share started in 2017, five volunteers pooled $20 each to buy groceries at a dollar store to provide food assistance to about 30 families. Today, it serves about 240 families every two weeks.
“The demand has increased tremendously,” Nafeesah Madyun, a longtime volunteer, said as she prepared to check in “neighbors,” which is what the organization calls the people they serve, for their food distribution event a week ahead of Thanksgiving.
But at a time when grocery costs continue to climb, the bags that volunteers hand out are getting lighter. Organizers at Enough to Share say that a single bag once covered three to four meals per family. Now it stretches to about two, which forces those who need assistance to rely on multiple pantries and pop-up events during the holidays to piece together groceries.
Volunteers at the Enough to Share food pantry, which operates out of the Atlanta Masjid of Al-Islam mosque in DeKalb County, prepare to check in families at its food distribution event on Nov. 18, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Community pantries like Enough to Share purchase much of the food they distribute from food banks. Nafeesah Madyun’s husband Nassar, also a volunteer who manages the pantry’s order with the food bank, said that they get less than half the food they do now for the same price they did just as a few years back.
Whereas he used to buy 12,000 pounds of food for about $400, that same amount only gets the pantry about 5,000 pounds of food today. To fill that gap, he scours local greenhouses, partner groups and farmer markets for donations while the pantry dips into its own funds from fundraisers to buy groceries from supermarkets.
“Our primary source being the food bank, and when the food bank doesn’t have food, we don’t have food,” said Amina Ali, vice president of Enough to Share.
At the Atlanta Community Food Bank, which distributes food to hundreds of organizations across 29 metro Atlanta and North Georgia counties, interim president and CEO Jon West said that post-pandemic food inflation has largely eroded purchasing power for both households and nonprofits, which has a two-fold effect. It tightens families’ budgets, forcing many to rely on food banks – which increases demand – and it forces the food bank to get creative to fill the gap.
“Those dollars just aren’t going as far for us either,” West said. “As need goes up, resources are constrained and tight – and tight for us – we’re just not getting as much bang for our buck as we used to. There’s a lot of parallels between what’s happening at the household level and then what’s happening with us and our operations right now as well.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
West added that growing demand is coming from families who have no record of ever utilizing their food banks, saying that about 30% of visitors who got assistance over the last three months were first-time visitors.
The struggle is even sharper outside of metro Atlanta, West said, where there are fewer food banks and nonprofits providing food assistance and that requires residents to travel farther for help.
“Rates of food insecurity are actually higher in our rural areas than they are in our urban areas, and so there’s a variety of economic reasons behind that, but what that means also is that we have more hungry people in places that don’t have as many resources available to help them,” West said, pointing to Haralson County illustrate the issue.
“We just have fewer partners in that county because there are fewer organizations for us to connect with and partner with, and so you have to travel farther to get to resources, which takes more time, energy and fuel, and just makes it really harder to navigate,” he added.
Wesley Myrick, the executive director of the Georgia Interfaith Public Policy Center, said that because there is still significant demand in rural areas with fewer providers with less availability, they can get overwhelmed when they host a food distribution event.
“In our rural communities, you’ve got one, maybe two providers that service the whole county, and that one provider is bombarded as soon as they offer it,” Myrick said.
And at the same time, assistance from the federal level that low-income families rely on is shrinking. The Trump administration cut SNAP funding by about 20%, or about $187 billion, over the next decade through H.R.1 last year, which has already caused 5.5 million people to lose access to the food safety net program – representing a 13% drop, said Joseph Llobrera, senior director of research on food assistance at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
In Georgia, SNAP participation has declined by almost 10%, or roughly 150,000 people, overall and about 8% among households with children. Llobrera said that the decline in households with children is particularly alarming because households with children under 14 are exempt from the new law’s stricter work requirements.
“I think we are seeing historic, unprecedented changes to food assistance in this country,” Llobrera said.
Elaine Waxman, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute, said that as a result, state agencies are scrambling to avoid potential cuts to their SNAP federal funding. The new law could shift a share of the cost to administer SNAP benefits onto states if they fail to quickly lower their payment error rates, which measures administrative and paperwork mistakes rather than fraud, a focus of the current administration. As a result, states have demanded more frequent documentation, which has created a backlog that results in eligible families being knocked off the SNAP rolls.
“[State officials have] been so focused, understandably, on trying to reduce the risk of having to pay benefit costs that the scramble to do that has led to people falling through the cracks,” Waxman said.
Amina Ali, vice president of Enough to Share, and volunteer coordinator Brenda Rasheed pose for a photo as they prepare for the Enough to Share food distribution event at the Atlanta Masjid of Al-Islam mosque in DeKalb County on Nov. 18, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Back at the mosque where Enough to Share hosts their bi-weekly food distribution event, Brenda Rasheed, another longtime volunteer, said that despite slimmer bags due to the rising cost of food and less funding to address the gap, the mood in the drive-thru and walk-up lines has not changed.
“You see the gratitude on faces, the relief on faces,” Rasheed said. “People are grateful to have some support, some supplementing with their own foods that they’re able to secure.”
