name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio manufacturers urge federal regulators to ‘retool’ energy markets
description: The Ohio Manufacturers’ Association is urging federal regulators to “break the mold and retool” energy markets. A letter from the association sent earlier this month comes as regional grid operators like PJM Interconnection, state regulators, and lawmakers continue to wrestle with how to manage demand from data centers. The association’s critiques aren’t new[...]
text:
Work continues on a new data center. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for States Newsrooom)The Ohio Manufacturers’ Association is urging federal regulators to “break the mold and retool” energy markets.
A letter from the association sent earlier this month comes as regional grid operators like PJM Interconnection, state regulators, and lawmakers continue to wrestle with how to manage demand from data centers.
The association’s critiques aren’t new. The group contends regulators aren’t doing enough to scrutinize major transmission projects or data centers’ forecasts for their future demand. At the heart of the debate is the question of who pays for data centers’ development. In both cases, the association contends, ratepayers wind up covering the bill.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Industry groups like the Data Center Coalition have repeatedly insisted they’re ready to pay their own way. In a statement, the coalition’s Aaron Tinjum said coalition members “are committed to paying the full cost of infrastructure built to serve their facilities to ensure those costs aren’t shouldered by homes and other businesses.”
“When data centers pay their full cost of service, they share in existing fixed grid costs,” Tinjum went on. “Because those fixed costs would have otherwise been paid by existing customers, new data centers can help alleviate pressure on rates for other customers.”
The magnitude of the industry’s demand is vast — prompting utilities to invest in broader grid improvements and roiling the capacity marketplace PJM uses ensure reliability. Those indirect costs could eventually land on consumers’ bills if policymakers don’t step in to assign them differently.
State lawmakers drafted a data center bill this summer but failed to pass the measure before recess. Ohio House Speakers Matt Huffman told reporters that lawmakers are continuing to work on the bill.
The Ohio Manufacturers’ Association sees a more direct path. To make sure data centers cover their costs, the organization wants them to contract and pay for their infrastructure and power generation up front.
“Risky investment decisions of this magnitude should not be made by government or utility intermediaries who bear no risk,” Ohio Manufacturers’ Association President Ryan Augsburger wrote. “Competitive markets are the obvious solution.”
Augsburger is particularly critical of PJM’s capacity market, which uses an auction to ensure power is available to meet peak demand. Capacity prices have ballooned in recent years as a sharp increase in demand from data centers mixed with a logjam in PJM’s queue for new power plants.
Data centers go 0-for-21 in ballot initiatives around Ohio

Augsburger thinks the grid operator should lose its control over the capacity market. Under PJM’s leadership, he said, the market is “more political than functional” and “produc(es) economy-crushing electric costs with little to show.”
“To have a true market,” Augsburger went on, “multiple sellers need to compete for multiple buyers. To get politics and stalemates out of the capacity market, PJM’s sole-buyer role for capacity needs to go.”
What comes next?
For months, PJM officials have acknowledged their approach to the capacity market may no longer work, and the organization is publicly mulling what might replace it.
Following a 2024 auction that saw capacity prices climb more than 833%, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro sued PJM. As part of a court order, PJM capped capacity prices for several years.
“The capacity market’s done great,” PJM’s Asim Haque told Ohio lawmakers last May. “(It) did great during the shale revolution. It’s done its job for a particular period, but what we’ve done by putting this cap on the marketplace is we bought ourselves some time to potentially re-imagine what that marketplace should look like.”
In a recent white paper, PJM floated three different possibilities.
One would move to a longer-term model to ensure reliability instead of updating capacity prices through annual auctions.
Another would abandon the longstanding idea that all energy users should have the same standard of reliability.
Instead, PJM and its stakeholders would have to figure out ahead of time how to prioritize customers when demand peaks.
Third, PJM could move away from a capacity market — commitments to provide power on demand in the future — and instead structure its efforts around buying energy itself.
PJM doesn’t take a position on which approach is best. In a statement, spokesman Jeff Shields said, “PJM and its stakeholders expect to take action on evolving this market in the very near term.”
Will Ohio lawmakers pass data center legislation during lame duck?

Shields also noted two Ohio stakeholders have weighed in on how PJM should proceed.
The Ohio Energy Group, whose members include energy intensive companies like Cleveland Cliffs, Ford, and Intel, proposes drawing a line in the sand.
Data centers that haven’t come online by June of next year would be placed in a new category, responsible for the cost of building new power.
That new power should have no price caps, but OEG thinks with a few tweaks, legacy power plants could continue operating with the current capped capacity market.
The Public Utility Commission of Ohio said it “feels strongly” that PJM should continue running the capacity market and favors PJM’s first path which avoids volatility by moving to longer-term capacity purchases.
Unlike the Ohio Manufacturers’ Association’s call for a wide-open market, the commission sees efficiencies in PJM operating as the sole buyer.
“It is unclear why the benefits of centralized procurement should be discarded in favor of a less-efficient, balkanized model,” the commission stated.
From the Ohio Manufacturers’ Association’s perspective, however, PJM’s long-term approach just locks in risk.
“PJM’s auction design could commit regular customers to finance the riskiest bets made by the wealthiest of technology and energy companies,” Augsburger wrote. “This is the antithesis of customer protection.”
Shields dismissed the Ohio Manufacturers’ Association’s critiques, particularly when it comes to group’s skepticism about data center demand forecasts.
The organization’s “motivations for continuing to express that data center load growth is not real should be examined by its members and state government to ensure accountability for the organization,” Shields said.

title: Ohio Senate appoints new leadership. Ohio House will vote for speaker in January.
description: Ohio lawmakers have appointed new leadership for the next two-year General Assembly, which will start in January.  Ohio state Sen. Bill Reineke, R-Tiffin, will become the next Ohio Senate President.  “The beginning of each new General Assembly brings unique challenges, and I’m looking forward to working with our capable and experienced leadership team as wel[...]
text:
Ohio state Sen. Bill Reineke, R-Tiffin, in the Senate chamber. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)Ohio lawmakers have appointed new leadership for the next two-year General Assembly, which will start in January. 
Ohio state Sen. Bill Reineke, R-Tiffin, will become the next Ohio Senate President. 
“The beginning of each new General Assembly brings unique challenges, and I’m looking forward to working with our capable and experienced leadership team as well as across the aisle to continue making sure that Ohio is a great place to live, work, and raise a family,” Reineke said in a statement. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He has served in the Ohio Senate since 2021 and served in the Ohio House Of Representatives from 2015-2020. 
Reineke serves as business partner in Reineke Family Dealerships, a three-generation family business with locations in Northwest Ohio and Southeast Michigan. 
Current Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, R-Napoleon, said Reineke has earned the honor. 
“He’s a very measured individual who really takes the time to delve into these issues and get to know what the facts are behind the issues,” he said. 
“He’s somebody who loves the state. He’s somebody who loves his family. He’s somebody who wants to see Ohio’s best days in front of it.” 
McColley’s term ends Dec. 31. He ran on Vivek Ramaswamy’s ticket as lieutenant governor, but Democrat Amy Acton won the election. 
Ohio Senate Minority Leader Nickie Antonio, D-Lakewood, thinks Reineke will do a good job in his new role. 
“He will be someone who will be able to communicate with the new governor,” she said. 
“Reineke wants what’s best for the people of Ohio. Sometimes we disagree about what that is, but I don’t ever doubt his genuine concern for the people of Ohio.”
Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman, R-Lima, also had positive things to say about Reineke. 
“He is a very thoughtful guy. Intellectually, very capable,” he said. 
“But I think in addition to that, he has a real ability to make decisions and cut to the quick when he has to.” 
The Ohio House will have a floor vote for speaker in January after the new General Assembly begins. 
The Ohio House Republicans recently voted for Huffman for speaker behind closed doors. 
Ohio House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn, D-Cincinnati, was reelected as minority leader.
“With a broken supermajority and Governor-elect Amy Acton, this caucus will continue to fight for an Ohio we can all afford,” he said in a statement. 
COLUMBUS, OH — MAY 08: State Rep. Beth Liston, D-Dublin, speaks during the Ohio House session, May 8, 2024, at the Statehouse in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal)
Isaacsohn said he hopes to build a deeper relationship with Reineke. 
“There’s certainly a lot we need to do when it comes to healthcare, education, housing, energy, infrastructure, childcare,” Isaacsohn said. 
“There’s so much we have to do in the next General Assembly, and so we’re going to need good relationships across the aisle to get some of those things done.”
Ohio state Sen. Beth Liston, D-Dublin, was elected the next Ohio Senate Minority Leader. 
“I am excited for the incoming leadership team and our growing caucus to accomplish great things for the people of Ohio this year,” Liston said in a statement. 
Liston has served in the Ohio Senate since 2025 and was in the Ohio House of Representatives from 2019-2024. She is also a medical doctor. 
Current Senate Minority Leader Nickie Antonio’s term ends on Dec. 31 and she did not run for reelection.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida SNAP error rates are on the rise
description: An effort by the Florida Legislature to lower errors in a food security program appears to have had the opposite effect — a trend that could reverberate in the near future. Preliminary error rates in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — SNAP — have been on the rise, recent reports obtained by the Phoenix show. […]
text:
Florida makes too many eligibility errors in a key food-security program.
(Photo by Christine Sexton/Florida Phoenix)An effort by the Florida Legislature to lower errors in a food security program appears to have had the opposite effect — a trend that could reverberate in the near future.
Preliminary error rates in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — SNAP — have been on the rise, recent reports obtained by the Phoenix show.
To help lower the state’s SNAP error rate, the Legislature in 2026 agreed to direct $4 million to the Department of Children and Families (DCF) to hire a vendor and use AI to ferret out fraud.

The Legislature also required the state to submit monthly reports to the House and Senate disclosing the latest error rates.

The September DCF document shows the unofficial error rate through March 2026 was an average 14.49%.
The October DCF report shows the error rate through April climbed to 14.52%.
And the November report shows the error rate through May climbed to 14.61%

DCF is the state agency charged with determining eligibility for programs such as SNAP, Medicaid, and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families.
DCF was directed by Sept. 1 to hire a vendor “capable of providing large-scale analyses of eligibility determinations using machine learning, identifying and correcting erroneous determinations, identifying root causes of erroneous determinations, and recommending operational improvements to avoid future errors.” 
The Phoenix asked DCF whether it had hired a contractor but the agency did not respond. But, according to the October DCF report the agency inked a deal with Executive Information Solutions on Sept. 11.
Payment error rates measure the accuracy of each state’s eligibility and benefit determinations and include overpayments as well as underpayments.

Snapshot of SNAP
SNAP is the nation’s largest nutrition assistance program, accounting for about 69% of federal nutrition assistance spending in fiscal year (FY) 2025.
There were 2,219,639 Florida residents on SNAP in July 2026, a near 6% drop from June enrollment, while July enrollment fell by 22% from July 2025, when 2,849,239 residents received food benefits.
The data, updated last month, show 1,256,484 households received SNAP benefits, down more than 7% from June and nearly 22% from July 2025.
Gov.-elect Byron Donalds says the state is doing the work necessary to get waste and fraud out of that system, a mandate under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) he supported in Congress.
That is the “prudent, common-sense thing that not just Florida but every state in the nation should be doing,” Donalds told reporters in South Florida earlier this month.
Donalds said his mother received food assistance for a time when he was a child. “It was the old food coupons, not the card that you have today. We want to make sure that people who do need those benefits get them.” 
Eliminating fraud, he said, will help make sure that “people who do need resources get those resources and they get them efficiently and in the time that they need them.”
OBBBA changes
OBBBA, President Donald Trump’s signature tax reduction bill, reduced federal funding for Medicaid, the safety net health care program for the poor and disabled, by about $1 trillion over the next decade. It reduced SNAP by about $187 billion.
The SNAP reduction is accomplished by requiring states to pay more administrative costs, to 75%. The increased commitment means a $50 million annual increase in costs to the state.
The Legislature included $38 million in recurring general revenue in the current-year budget that covered the costs from Oct. 1 — the start of the federal fiscal year — through June 30, 2027, the end of the state’s fiscal year.
DCF has included a request for an additional $12.6 million in its legislative budget request for state fiscal year 2027-28 to cover the administrative costs.
Federal cost reductions also are accomplished by putting states with high SNAP error rates, such as Florida, on the hook for costs of the food benefit beginning October 2027. That means any funding for the costs of the food would need to be included in the budget the Legislature works on next year when it meets in regular session.
Specifically, under the OBBBA, states with error rates below 6% won’t have to contribute to the costs of the food. Cost sharing is required for higher error rates:

States with error rates between 6% and 8% will be required to contribute 5% of the costs.
States with between 8% and 10% error rates would be required to cover 10% of the costs.
States with error rates above 10% have to contribute between 15% and 25% of the costs of the food.

Preliminary error rates are calculated monthly but aren’t finalized until June.
States can use 2025 or 2026 error SNAP error rates when determining their cost share requirements. Florida’s official error rate for 2025 was 12.97%, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). The error rate is so high that, under the federal law, Florida could be on the tab for 15% of the costs of the food.
Based on previous spending, that could be up to $1 billion.
DCF’s FY 27-28 legislative budget request touches on the potential of having to cover the costs of food and includes a nominal $1 placeholder.
Sky Beard, Florida director of No Kid Hungry. (Photo via No Kid Hungry
OBBBA does, though, temporarily delay cost-sharing for states with error rates greater than 13.3%.
If Florida’s final error rate for 2026 exceeds 13.3%, the state wouldn’t be required to contribute to the costs of food until fiscal year 2030, something the state’s most recent Long Term Financial Outlook notes.
In the just-completed organizational session of the Legislature, there was no talk from legislative leaders about the potential financial obligation.
“This is something we’re going to have to continually talk about,” Sky Beard, Florida director of No Kid Hungry, told the Phoenix. “If we do not qualify for the delayed implementation, it is a this-coming session, this-coming budget, issue.” 
More time 
Florida may have been tossed a lifeline.
The USDA on Friday issued guidance that allows states to recalculate their SNAP error rates, a move that may help states with high SNAP error rates, such as Florida, lower their potential financial contributions for the program going forward.
The revised guidance came after a federal court ruled in September that states weren’t given enough time to comply with the changes the federal law made to the SNAP program.
The ruling did not undo the changes Congress made to the program in its 2025 tax and spending law, H.R. 1, including a provision requiring states with higher payment error rates to cover part of the cost of benefits beginning Oct. 1, 2027, or the start of federal fiscal year 2028.
The case centered around a 120-day grace period intended to give states time to put new SNAP rules in place without mistakes counting against their payment error rates, according to the Virginia Mercury.
Federal judge strikes down SNAP deadline that put Virginia at risk of added costs

 The USDA treated that period as beginning July 4, 2025, the day the law was enacted. However, according to the ruling, the agency did not issue its first implementation guidance until Aug. 29, 2025. It waited another two months to tell states how to handle changes to noncitizen eligibility.
That left states one day under USDA’s timeline to make those eligibility changes. A subsequent memo, issued Nov. 14, told states the grace period had already expired, the Virginia Mercury reported.
U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai opined that states could not reasonably be expected to implement federal changes before the government told them how to do it. In his ruling, the judge vacated the deadline in USDA’s guidance and ordered the agency to give states 120 days after issuing an implementation memo, along with adequate notice of when changes must be made.
This story includes reporting from the Virginia Mercury, which is part of States Newsroom.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: More foxes in CT’s hen house will not save the chickens
description: CT's majority party has held power for decades and is largely responsible for what makes our lives worse.
text:
I read with interest the recent opinion piece, “CT voters gave us a mandate. Let’s meet the moment.” In it Comptroller Sean Scanlon lists what the majority Democrats should do to “make our lives better.” What his out-of-touch opinion fails to point out is that his majority party has held power in our state for decades and is largely responsible for what makes our lives worse. 
Let’s look at his four issues from different perspective.
Healthcare:  Connecticut Democrats keep well hidden the fact that they use the word “residents” in the same context as “citizens.” There is a difference, and if more Connecticut taxpayers realized this they might think differently about who is benefiting from taxpayer-funded healthcare.
Biden era healthcare subsidies were put in place during Covid to help Americans who lost employer sponsored healthcare plans because governors like Ned Lamont declared their jobs “non-essential” and they could not work. Democrats tried to make those subsidies permanent but the subsidies were designed to sunset, and they did.
The trouble is subsidies do not make healthcare more affordable. They just support something that is foundationally unaffordable. Instead of directly addressing affordability, politicians tax the providers and wrap the system up in government and insurance red tape. Then they redistribute the money they took to help people pay for what their policies made more expensive.
This erects walls between doctors and patients and diverts money that should go to patient care to government, administration and compliance. That’s what needs to be fixed. And health insurance companies should be banned from contributing to political campaigns.
Also, unemployed able-bodied adult “citizens” should do something for the benefits they receive. Whether it’s part-time work, education, job training or community service, they should contribute something. But Democrats will never encourage self-reliance over dependence. It could jeopardize their loyal voting base.
Property taxes: This should be a simple one for someone in Scanlon’s position. The never-ending stream of un-funded and under-funded mandates state lawmakers keep placing on cities and towns is driving high property taxes. Many are associated with schools and education, but the latest one on low-income housing is sure to be a problem for many small communities.
The state must be required by law to fully fund any and all new spending mandates they have or will impose on our communities. And if they don’t, compliance by the cities and towns should be optional. That would pretty much fix it. But because Democrats never cede power unless they are forced to, and they are in power, it will not change.
Artificial intelligence and data centers: Not many people I know can define Artificial Intelligence (AI). They know what it does, but not what it is. Simply stated, it’s better algorithms. The problem lies with who created these algorithms, and what they are used for. AI can be used for nefarious reasons, the same computer viruses and mal-ware that can mess up your PC or phone. But it’s already here, it’s being used every day and it’s not going away.
If we don’t pursue this technology other players will, and we will be victims of what they do with it. If government gets involved, what will its role be? Government cyber-security agencies are focused on protecting the government. How often does government prosecute someone for infecting our computers with a virus or distributing malware or ransom-ware? My guess is no matter how this shakes out, you and I are on our own and tech companies will capitalize on selling us AI protection.
As for data centers, the average American carries an electronic device everywhere they go. Most businesses use computing devices in one form or another. Do you use all these wonderful things at your fingertips that 30-40 years ago were just imagined? But people take for granted what goes on behind the scenes that allows this communication and data technology to be possible. Most people use it, and they want more.
Think about your Facebook page, Instagram, X account or other on-line activities. Every picture you put on Facebook requires data storage. No new data centers means no new storage. Will the “not in my backyard” mentality change when storage is used up and you have to erase what you have in order to post more social media? And despite the political chest thumping that’s going on, like always all politicians really want is to somehow control and tax all of it.
Stocks and predictive markets: This is the one that really made me laugh. Every Democrat member the U.S. Senate voted against “The Stop Insider Trading Act,” introduced by Nebraska Republican Pete Ricketts. Every single one. Yet, Scanlon believes after electing more Democrats to vote against a bill they all voted against, will get it passed.
How gullible would you have to be to believe that letting more foxes into the hen house will save the chickens? But even more baffling is why he believes passing this particular legislation will make Connecticut a more affordable place to live. If he truly believes that, I have a bridge in Brooklyn that our Comptroller might be interested in buying.
Bob Brzozowski lives in East Haddam.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT erased 170,000 criminal records. Most of those people don’t know it.
description: A law that clears your criminal record without telling you is only half done.
text:
Somewhere in Connecticut today, a person will check “yes” on a job application that asks about past convictions. They will be wrong, and they won’t know it, because the state erased that conviction and never told them.
Connecticut’s Clean Slate law, signed in 2021, automatically erases most misdemeanors after seven years and lower-level felonies after ten, once a person has finished the sentence and stayed out of trouble. After years of delay, the state says it has caught up. As of July, all 170,000 eligible people have had their records erased, covering nearly 350,000 cases. New erasures now happen on a rolling basis as people become eligible.
That is a real achievement. Erasures were supposed to begin in early 2023, but as of April 2025 only about 13,000 people had been cleared. The state’s public safety commissioner once called the project likely the most complex IT project Connecticut has ever taken on. The Department of Emergency Services and Public Protection finished it, and it deserves credit.
But a law that clears your record without telling you is only half done.
Connecticut has no system to notify people that their convictions were erased. In March, state officials said they were still working out how to reach the people they had cleared. In July, the department said it hoped to launch a free online portal by the end of this year. That deadline is now about five weeks away.
The cost of the gap is easy to predict. People who qualify keep disclosing convictions they no longer have to. They pass on jobs that require a background check. They assume an old case still blocks them from an apartment or a license, and they never apply. Erasure only helps the people who know about it.
Until the state fills that gap, here is what anyone who thinks they might qualify should know.
The rules. Misdemeanors are eligible seven years after your most recent conviction. Class D and E felonies, unclassified felonies with a possible sentence under five years, and drunk-driving convictions are eligible after ten. You must have finished every part of every sentence, including probation and parole, with no new conviction during the waiting period.
The exceptions. Family violence offenses, sex offenses and a list of other crimes, including several assault and weapons charges, are never erased under Clean Slate. A drunk-driving conviction followed by another within ten years doesn’t qualify. Offenses committed before 2000 are not erased automatically; you have to petition the court.
How to check. You can search your name in the Judicial Branch’s online criminal case lookup, or request your criminal history from the State Police Bureau of Identification. If a conviction from 2000 or later should have been erased and still appears, the state’s Clean Slate website explains how to ask the department for a hearing.
What erasure means. An erased record isn’t destroyed, but it is sealed, and Connecticut law treats the person as never having been arrested on that charge. They may say so under oath. Employers may not require anyone to disclose an erased record, and any job application that asks about criminal history must say so in plain terms.
None of this should depend on people stumbling onto an op-ed or hiring a lawyer. The state already knows exactly whose records it erased. Officials have said Connecticut’s notice problem is similar to other states’, and that is fair. But after finishing one of the hardest technology projects in state history, a letter is the easy part.
So, two asks. First, launch the free portal by year’s end, as promised, and build it so a person can use it on a phone without a lawyer. Second, starting in 2027, send a plain-English letter to every person whose record is erased, saying what was cleared and what it means for them.
The legislature did its part in 2021. The department did the hard part this year. Telling people is the last step, and the cheapest one.
Nate Baber of Vernon is a Connecticut attorney. He writes plain-English guides to the state’s criminal courts at ChargedCT.com.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The people who answer the call need a community of their own
description: A town's most engaged volunteers are the essential, beating heart of any community, a treasure worth preserving and supporting.
text:
For 13 years I have been a volunteer EMT with Weston Volunteer EMS . When a 911 call comes in, my neighbors and I leave our dinner table or warm bed and drive toward someone else’s worst moment. 
The work is physically, emotionally and technically challenging, and yet it is the most rewarding work I’ve ever done. It has taught me that a town’s most engaged volunteers are the essential, beating heart of any community, a treasure worth preserving and supporting.
Across Connecticut, engaged volunteerism is shrinking. A 2025 census by Comptroller Sean Scanlon’s office found that the state’s volunteer firefighter ranks had fallen 62.7% since 2017 , and some volunteer ambulance services have closed outright.  
Yet Connecticut is generous: in 2023, 37.4% of residents volunteered through an organization, the seventh-highest rate in the nation. Clearly, people care. The problem is that so much of our civic life rests on a very small number of people who shoulder an oversized burden, often unconnected and alone. Moreover, our 169 towns and cities are proudly independent, which is a virtue —until a good idea in Hamden never reaches Torrington, and vice versa.
That’s why Gerry Goldberg, Andrew Ferguson, and I founded The Neighborhood, a peer network and grant program for our state’s most active volunteers and civic leaders. We built our offering after listening across the state this Spring, through 15 focus groups with 149 volunteers and leaders in 13 communities, from Stonington to Stamford and New Haven to Simsbury.  People serve, we heard, because they love their home. Nearly all were drawn in by a personal ask from someone they trusted.  And beneath remarkable records of service ran a quieter theme: the loneliness of leading. 
This month, The Neighborhood named its first ten Catalyst Awardees, chosen by an independent committee from 122 nominees in 49 communities across all eight counties. Each receives $15,000 to advance their civic work, as well as an invitation to join a community of practice designed specifically for them, customized to their interests and goals, and the needs of their town or city. It offers them resources and, most importantly of all, the opportunity to share with and learn from their peers: active volunteers and civic leaders who lead similar work throughout the state.
 Who are these Catalysts?  Here are four. In Bridgeport, Al Ramirez, a union carpenter, founded Build Bridgeport From Within, whose neighborhood cleanups have grown to about 200 volunteers. At Success Village this summer,   his crew spent much of the day helping elderly and disabled residents   haul out belongings they could not move on their own. Through Al’s Helping Hands, he also repairs homes for neighbors who cannot afford it, at no cost. 
 In Hamden, Allison Batson saw families going hungry and started   Dinner for a Dollar   at her church 15 years ago. It now runs several nights a week and serves 100 to 200 meals a night, prepared by volunteers she recruits and trains. As she once   put it  , “It’s not us giving to them. It’s we together.” 
 In Branford, Bob Imperato, the town’s tax collector, helped build the   Branford Microfund  , which makes interest-free loans of up to $3,000 to neighbors facing an emergency who cannot turn to a bank.
 And in East Haddam, Theresa Govert’s all-volunteer effort has distributed roughly 280,000 diapers, menstrual products and other basics to families across the lower Connecticut River Valley since 2020. 
 These Catalysts work on different problems in very different places. Yet each has figured out something the others need: how to make the personal ask, how to keep volunteers coming back, how to turn a good idea into something that lasts.
 Why now? Because the cost of disconnection has never been plainer. In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General warned of an   epidemic of loneliness and isolation  , reporting that about half of American adults experience loneliness, and named stronger social infrastructure in local communities as the first pillar of a national response. Service is among the best remedies we have, but the people who make service possible for everyone else are aging out, burning out and too often working without support. 
 The Neighborhood is our answer: a statewide peer community where the people who hold our towns together can learn from and lean on one another. We are excited to expand The Neighborhood in the years to come, and hope our efforts and investment will help show our state’s most engaged volunteers how much we appreciate and value their work. Truly, they are Connecticut’s living treasures. 
 On an ambulance, no one answers a call alone. Connecticut’s most dedicated volunteers should not have to either. 
 Don Kendall lives in Weston, and is a co-founder of The Neighborhood. He is a volunteer EMT with Weston Volunteer EMS, a social entrepreneur and a philanthropist.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Green Demands Rapid Notice Of Oil Spills After ‘Outrageous’ Delays
description: He again expressed outrage over the delayed reporting of the H-power incident, which he described as “immoral.”
text:
Gov. Josh Green on Tuesday announced actions intended to speed up responses to future fuel spills and assess groundwater contamination from the H-Power plant in O’ahu.
A draft report on what exactly led to the leakage of more than 400,000 gallons of diesel fuel  — and why it took so long to be made public — is expected on the Hawaiʻi governor’s desk within 30 days.
The report, to be conducted by Department of Transportation Director Ed Sniffen and finalized no later than 60 days from now, is intended to “strengthen” the reporting of oil “of any volume” to the state Department of Health, Green said at a media conference.
As part of a new executive order, the report will also address whether additional groundwater monitoring wells around the H-Power plant are needed and make recommendations on how to improve future responses to such spills.
Although the leak, which was underground near Honolulu’s trash-burning facility in Kapolei, occurred from January through May of this year, Mayor Rick Blangiardi said he only learned the scope of the spill on Nov. 17.
Green said Blangiardi informed him the very next day of what happened while the governor was on business in Utah. The public was told Nov. 19.
“Everyone is wondering why we didn’t have this information earlier,” Green said at a press conference at the Capitol. “We’re going to get to the bottom of that.”
“I may have used the F-word because it’s outrageous,” Green said of his conversation with Blangiardi. “It’s outrageous that neither he nor I knew about this or were told about this for several months. We should have all been informed, in my opinion, on May 4 when there was 6,500 gallons of diesel that was released. At that point, sharing that would have at least helped.”
Green said an unidentified branch manager failed to report the spill to upper level DOH personnel, something he described as immoral. 
“My opinion is they should have escalated that information to the environmental health director so that she could have immediately asked for more support, a lot more personnel, a lot more demands on Reworld and so on,” said Green. “That’s why the chain of command is so important.”
The governor said his understanding was that Reworld, the company running H-Power, would pay for all expenses to clean up the spill.
“I’m going to leave it to him to make ultimate decisions about his contractors,” Green said referring to the mayor. As for Reworld, “I think they’re in deep shit, to tell you the truth, because they did not give us the whole picture, and that’s not okay.”
From left: Department of Transportation Director Ed Sniffen, Department of Health Director Kenny Fink, and Gov. Josh Green answer questions at the Capitol from the news media about the H-Power diesel spill. 
It’s unclear how long remediation work, which is being coordinated by the state Department of Health, will take. The scope of the plume, said DOH Director Kenneth Fink, is in the process of being identified.
Fink said it would take “years” to clean things up. He declined to specify how many years it could take. 
For now, Fink and Green reiterated that Oʻahu’s drinking water is safe. The state is also working with U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 9 officials to respond to the fuel spill. The EPA will then present its own inspection report.
Green also said also reconvened the state’s water committee, to be led by Department of Land and Natural Resources Director Ryan Kanakaʻole or his designee. It will coordinate oversight of the response and cleanup along with the help of the state departments of Health, Land and Natural Resources, the Attorney General and Transportation, along with the Honolulu Board of Water Supply and the city’s Department of Environmental Services.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Voter turnout set record for midterm elections, officials say
description: A record number of Maryland voters cast ballots in this year's midterms, with relatively few problems despite fears of possible federal inteference, election officials said Tuesday. It was, in other words, a "smooth and boring" election, just the way officials like it.
text:
Dozens of Prince George's County voters stand in line and cast their ballots on the last day of early voting Thursday inside the Upper Marlboro Community Center. Despite record turnout for a gubernatorial election, Maryland election officials reported few problems this year. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)A record number of Maryland voters cast ballots in this year’s midterm elections, and relatively few problems were reported despite fears going in of possible federal inteference, election officials said Tuesday.
It was, in other words, a “smooth and boring” election, just the way Maryland State Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis likes it.
“Marylanders had a heightened awareness of this election,” DeMarinis said Tuesday, just days after the final votes from the Nov. 3 election were counted. “I’m ecstatic, and I want to have everyone make their voices heard and be a part of the process in how we want to take Maryland forward.”
As of Saturday, all Maryland precincts had finished their canvassing for the general election, with the returns to be officially certified Dec. 1. About 53.2% of Maryland’s eligible voters participated in this year’s election, while the 2022 midterm elections – which saw the two candidates running for governor – garnered participation from nearly 49.3% of the state’s registered voters.
Incoming Democratic Congress fuels hope of more federal dollars for elections

In all, 2,284,985 ballots were cast this year, 253,800 more that the 2,031,185 cast in 2022, according to board of elections data. The most votes were cast in the governor’s race, where the 2,254,987 ballots were divided between Gov. Wes Moore (D) with 65% of the vote to 30% for Republican challenger Dan Cox. Green Party nominee Andy Ellis and Working Class Party nominee Cathy White each got about 2% of the vote.
Of the statewide ballot issues, Question 3, to lift restrictions on congressional redistricting, drew the most votes, with 2,171,366. Of those, 68% voted for passage and 32% opposed the measure.
Turnout during the Oct. 22-29 early voting period reached 604,396 this year, compared to just to 381,972 four years ago. The state elections board had also counted 507,357 mail-in ballots of the 645,962 that were mailed out to voters this year.
Alysoun McLaughlin, director of the University of Maryland’s Election Resilience Lab, said in late October there has been an uptick in voters who prefer to use mail-in ballots since the pandemic, though the rate may be remaining steady as the quarantine time period gets further away.
“We’ve kind of returned to a trend that’s more similar to what we were seeing before the pandemic,” she said. “We’re sort of through the blip. We’ve had a policy change where permanent voting by mail is now available. Voters have some experience with that now, so they’re doing it.”
McLaughlin, who has previously worked as a Montgomery County election official, noted less than a week before Election Day that voters shouldn’t be worried about the security of mail-in ballots. The U.S. Postal Service works with election officials to ensure proper ballot tracking and is in constant communication with directors in the event something goes wrong.
“It’s a dynamic that you manage, a dynamic that you watch. But you know, I do recognize that voters are going to have their own desires, and I’m not really going to argue with them if they’re more comfortable,” McLaughlin said. “That’s why we have choices.”
She said the biggest pressure on election officials this year would be the “scrutiny” driven by voter narratives. It’s easy for people to worry about the credibility of an election when looking at localized incidents on social media or when seeing candidates mobilize voters based on these fears, McLaughlin said.
These concerns shouldn’t deter people from voting, she added. McLaughlin urged voters to trust that officials were set to do their jobs and handle or alert the community if rules weren’t being followed.
“In the course of voting, know that the people who are sitting there, the election judges … who are working hard that day … to make sure that every voter gets one, and only one, opportunity to cast their ballot are people, too,” she said in late October.
SecureTheVoteMD, an organization striving to promote secure and accountable elections, held a news conference in front of the Maryland State Board of Elections office in Annapolis Tuesday to highlight its concerns surrounding election transparency and to call for DeMarinis’ resignation for what they say was a mishandling of the election.
Among other issues, they pointed to the board’s decision earlier this year to mail out 565,000 replacement mail-in ballots for the primary election, after an error by the state’s printing vendor resulted in some voters receiving a ballot for the wrong party. In Maryland, primary elections are limited to voters registered with the Democratic or Republican party.
DeMarinis said Tuesday there was “no reality” to the claims they made about election security and lost ballots.
“Elections have been transparent. This activity out here is designed to do one thing, and that’s to sow distrust,” he said of the group’s gathering.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Ellsworth takes official misconduct fight to Montana Supreme Court
description: State Sen. Jason Ellsworth is taking the fight over whether he abused his authority as Montana Senate president in late 2024 to the state Supreme Court, according to his lawyer. Ellsworth, a Hamilton Republican, pleaded no contest Tuesday to official misconduct for exceeding his lawful authority as Senate president by steering $170,000 in state contracts […]
text:
Sen. Jason Ellsworth, R-Hamilton, sits during closing arguments of his trial on Tuesday, July 21, 2026, in Lewis Clark District Court in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)State Sen. Jason Ellsworth is taking the fight over whether he abused his authority as Montana Senate president in late 2024 to the state Supreme Court, according to his lawyer.
Ellsworth, a Hamilton Republican, pleaded no contest Tuesday to official misconduct for exceeding his lawful authority as Senate president by steering $170,000 in state contracts to a close business associate.
His lawyer, Joan Mell, said Lewis and Clark District Court approved a plea agreement in the misdemeanor case, and Ellsworth will appeal it. The final agreement was unavailable at press time from the court.
According to the Montana Free Press, a prosecutor with the Department of Justice said in court Tuesday the appeal came as a surprise, and the idea for the agreement was to have “finality.”
In a statement, Ellsworth said the move saves money for him and for taxpayers.
He said he believes the time spent on his misdemeanor has been “unprecedented in Montana if not nationwide.”
“Continuing to burn through Montana taxpayers’ money over a misdemeanor is unconscionable, and stepping off this path is the righteous thing to do for the people footing the bill,” Ellsworth said.
In the case, Ellsworth is accused of circumventing the state procurement process to secure a pair of contracts, later merged into one, for a friend to track judicial bills in the Legislature.
A jury found Ellsworth guilty of the misdemeanor in July, but the court vacated the verdict after a court error meant the jury received documents it should not have had.
Mell said Ellsworth signed the plea agreement because he doesn’t want to be in front of a court that already miscommunicated to the jury.
Mell said the plea agreement allows him to ask the state Supreme Court to decide the legal issues, and there are many in this case.
In a statement provided by a legislative staff member, Ellsworth said he is not admitting guilt, but he is choosing not to fight “in this courtroom.”
“A second trial in the same courtroom made me uncomfortable even though the judge insisted he and his staff would be fair,” Ellsworth said.
The contracts were terminated in early 2025 but ethical implications of the case dominated the 2025 Montana Legislature.
The Montana Senate censured Ellsworth in April 2025 after its own ethics inquiry.
During the session, Ellsworth denied wrongdoing, and he did so again in a statement Tuesday.
He said he hired “a trusted company,” the Department of Administration wrote the final agreement, and the Governor’s Office approved the funding.
At trial this summer, the Department of the Administration director described the final contracts as “putting lipstick on a pig,” and the governor’s budget director said it had no input on the documents.
Mell said Tuesday the plea agreement has been “stayed,” or suspended, pending the appeal, so no penalty is imposed at this time.
Department of Justice spokespeople did not respond to a request for comment late Tuesday.
The DOJ filed charges after the Legislative Auditor, responding to a fraud, waste and abuse hotline tip, found Ellsworth abused his power and wasted state resources, and the auditor submitted a referral to the DOJ.
In the statement provided to media, Ellsworth outlined conditions of the plea agreement as follows:

No jail time, or 180 days fully suspended;
Six months of law-abiding behavior;
A $500 fine and $85 statutory surcharge;
Right to appeal is intact; and
Forfeiture of office, although his term ends on Jan. 6, 2027.

In his statement, Ellsworth said the case had cost “countless nights of frustration,” but it had been an honor to represent his constituents.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Lt. Gov. announces end to contentious voter roll agreement with U.S. Department of Justice
description: Alaska Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom announced Monday the state is terminating its agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice to share uncensored voter information with the federal government, effective immediately.  The announcement came just hours after the Alaska Division of Elections, headed by Dahlstrom, had certified the results of the 2026 elections on [...]
text:
Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom and Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher listen to testimony at a July 27, 2026 hearing in Anchorage on Ballot Measure 2. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Alaska Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom announced Monday the state is terminating its agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice to share uncensored voter information with the federal government, effective immediately. 
The announcement came just hours after the Alaska Division of Elections, headed by Dahlstrom, had certified the results of the 2026 elections on Monday. 
The agreement had drawn public criticism, an investigatory hearing by the Alaska State Legislature and a lawsuit challenging the state’s sharing of the voter rolls as a violation of Alaskans’ constitutional right to privacy. The rolls contain sensitive personal information — including partial social security numbers, addresses and drivers license numbers.
As part of the agreement, the Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher signed a memorandum of understanding that stated that the division would remove voters from the rolls within 45 days of a request from the DOJ if it deemed them ineligible. 
In a statement with the announcement on Monday, Dahlstrom said the agreement is “no longer operative” and cannot be used to share voter information in the future.
“The Division entered the agreement in good faith to cooperate with our federal law enforcement partners as permitted under Alaska law,” Dahlstrom said in the statement. 
“The circumstances have now changed, the election has concluded, and the agreement no longer serves a continuing purpose,” she said. “Alaska has strong list-maintenance procedures and will continue to protect both the accuracy of its voter rolls and the rights of eligible Alaska voters.”
The division provided the confidential voter list to the DOJ in December 2025, but the agency did not flag anyone to be removed, according to the statement.
“Since that time, the DOJ has not identified any potentially ineligible voters or raised concerns regarding Alaska’s voter registration records. No voters were removed from Alaska’s voter rolls as a result of the agreement,” the statement said. 
However, the division removed over 3,000 Alaska voters from the rolls in July, saying they could be eligible if they provided additional proof of U.S. citizenship. Some of those voters were removed erroneously, according to reporting by the Alaska Beacon. 
The division said it had directed the DOJ to destroy Alaska’s confidential voter information in accordance with the agreement. 
The division’s Monday announcement also acknowledged that a U.S. District Court had vacated the DOJ’s voter removal program in October, saying the DOJ did not have the authority to obtain and review state voter lists. 
But the division said termination does not constitute an acknowledgement of any wrongdoing.
“Alaska entered the agreement in good faith under state law, before any court had ruled that the DOJ’s program was unlawful,” the statement said. “Following a review of the changed circumstances, the Division determined that Alaska’s interests are best served by terminating the agreement and continuing to rely on its established voter list-maintenance procedures.”
“Alaska will continue to consider credible information, apply the law, and make its own decisions,” Dahlstrom said.
The lawsuit challenging the division’s agreement, brought by the League of Women Voters, Alaska Black Caucus and the Alaska Public Interest Research Group, is still open in Anchorage Superior Court.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Division of Elections certifies 2026 election results
description: The Alaska Division of Elections certified the results of the 2026 general election on Monday. While the results settle Alaska’s closely watched statewide elections, there will be at least one recount to determine the winner of an Alaska House race.  On Tuesday, incumbent Republican Rep. Kevin McCabe had filed for a recount of votes in […]
text:
Voters line up to cast their ballots at the Midtown Mall polling site on Oct. 21, 2026. The mall site is among several in the state open for early voting in the general election. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Division of Elections certified the results of the 2026 general election on Monday. While the results settle Alaska’s closely watched statewide elections, there will be at least one recount to determine the winner of an Alaska House race. 
On Tuesday, incumbent Republican Rep. Kevin McCabe had filed for a recount of votes in House District 30 after he lost to Republican Doug Massie after ranked choice tabulation by three votes.  
Recounts can be requested by losing candidates or ten eligible voters if the margin is less than 20 votes or .5% of votes cast. Recounts must be requested by a division deadline of Saturday, or by Friday for the governor’s race. 
The Alaska Division of Elections announced the general election results were certified on Monday, two days ahead of schedule. Officials with the division did not respond to a request for comment on why it was early.      

Mary Peltola greets supporters on election night, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at a Mary Peltola watch party in downtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks at an Oct. 5, 2026, campaign rally in Fairbanks. The headliner at the rallly was Vice President JD Vance, who traveled to Alaska with Sullivan on Air Force 2. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

In Alaska’s U.S. Senate race, voters elected Democrat Mary Peltola who will become the first Alaska Native woman elected to the Senate. She defeated Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, who has held the seat since 2015. She won 50.14% of the vote, 12,500 more votes than Sullivan who had 45.78%. 
Outgoing Sen. Sullivan conceded the race on Tuesday. In an emailed statement, he thanked Alaskans and acknowledged the results, but he did not name Peltola directly. 
“As I’ve always said I would, and out of respect for the people of Alaska and our democratic process, I accept the results certified by the Division of Elections. Alaskans deserve confidence in the integrity of their elections, and I trust that the ongoing federal and state investigations will provide answers to the questions that remain,” he said. 
Outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and President Donald Trump launched state and federal criminal investigations into a report from the New York Times that said the Peltola campaign recruited spoiler candidates to the race, including a candidate with the same name as the incumbent Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg. The Alaska Beacon has not independently verified the Times’ reporting. Sullivan, Peltola and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have all denied the allegations.
On Tuesday, a spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Public Safety said by email the state investigation is ongoing.
“The Alaska Bureau of Investigation continues to investigate allegations related to the Alaska US Senate election. To protect the integrity of the ongoing investigation, we are unable to provide additional details at this time,” said Austin McDaniel.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Alaska did not respond to a request for information on a federal criminal investigation into groups affiliated with the Peltola campaign. A spokesperson told the Anchorage Daily News the investigation was still active last week. 
A lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice against the Division of Elections seeking to block the certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan lost re-election was dismissed by a U.S. District Court judge, and the federal government dropped its appeal last week. 
In the U.S. House race, Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III won re-election to represent Alaska’s sole seat in the 435-member House. He garnered 47.52% of the vote, ahead of independent challenger Bill Hill who had 41.77%, a margin of 16,503 votes. There was nearly 48% voter turnout in the race. Democrat Eric Hafner — a perennial candidate in federal races, who is serving a federal criminal sentence in New York — got 7.92% or more than 22,700 first-choice votes.
Alaska elected its youngest governor and first Democrat since 1998, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, along with running mate and independent, Zac Johnson. The pair won with 51.09% of the vote, ahead of three Republican challengers, with 48% of voters casting ballots.
Kreiss-Tomkins is set to be sworn in on Dec. 7.
Alaskans keep open primaries and ranked choice voting 
Alaskans voted down a ballot measure that would have overhauled the state’s election system by repealing the open primary system, ranked choice votings, and some campaign finance laws.
Voters rejected the measure, opting to keep the current system, enacted in 2020.
‘No’ votes outweighed ‘yes’ votes in the first round of results on election night. By the final count the margins widened to 52.83% of voters voting no, and 46.18% voting yes.
A similar ballot measure was rejected in 2024. 
Voters overwhelmingly approved Ballot Measure 3, a small language change for voter eligibility in existing state law to clarify that “only” U.S. citizens are permitted to vote. The measure does not change state law. Voters approved the ballot measure with 68.23% of the vote, with 31.77% voting no. 
New and former representatives in the Alaska State Legislature 
There were 50 seats up for election this year, including ten in the Alaska Senate and 40 seats in the Alaska House.
Former House Speaker Rep. Bryce Edgmon, an independent from Dillingham, was elected to the Senate representing Western Alaska and the Aleutian Islands in Senate District S, formerly held by Sen. Lyman Hoffman who retired this year. 
Republican Rep. Louise Stutes of Kodiak was elected to the Senate District C, replacing Sen. Gary Stevens who also retired this year. Republican Rep. Frank Tomaszewski of Fairbanks was elected to represent Senate District Q, after former Sen. Robb Myers stepped down after three terms.     

Rep. Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla, talks with Rep. Zack Fields, D-Anchorage (left) and Rep. Justin Ruffridge, R-Soldotna (right) shortly before election as Speaker of the House on Wednesday, Jan. 18, 2023, at the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau, Alaska. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)
 

In a shakeup in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, incumbent Sen. Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla, lost her re-election bid after ranked choice tabulation to Republican Ryan Berry by 467 votes. 
Tilton has served in the Alaska House since 2015 and was appointed to the Senate by Dunleavy in 2025 to replace Mike Shower who resigned to run for lieutenant governor. This year, Tilton was accused by Mat-Su residents of having a predatory relationship with a teenager starting in the 1990s, as reported by the Anchorage Daily News. She has denied any criminal wrongdoing.
The 20-member Senate is expected to govern by a bipartisan majority coalition of 11 members. The nine members of the minority caucus are all Republicans.
In the Alaska House, four Republican seats were flipped to Democrats and independents, widening the margin for the multipartisan House Majority coalition. The coalition is expected to hold 25 seats, with the Republican-led minority caucus making up 15 members.  
A handful of races were decided by razor-thin margins, and at least one race will be subject to a recount. 
On the Kenai Peninsula, Incumbent Republican Rep. Sarah Vance of Homer lost her re-election to independent Brent Johnson by 59 votes. Vance conceded the election to Johnson last week.
In House District 30, which spans the western part of the Matanuska Susitna Borough and Denali Borough, Republican incumbent Rep. Kevin McCabe lost to Republican Doug Massie after ranked choice tabulations by 3 votes.
 

Rep. Kevin McCabe is seen speaking on the House floor during debate on the operating budget on Apr. 13, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

	McCabe said in an interview Tuesday he’s filed to request a recount, and believes there are “anomalies” that should be reviewed. Those included absentee and questioned ballots that he said could have been improperly thrown out.
“The cast vote record exports identified 223 House District 30 contest records coded “invalid contest,” including 109 absentee records and 114 questioned records,” he said. 
“The exported markings and status code leave unresolved whether any properly cast votes were omitted or whether any rankings were incorrectly recorded or treated in tabulation. So there’s some significant anomalies there,” he said. “And I want to know why.”
McCabe said he expects the recount to be completed early next week. 
In nearby House District 29, incumbent Republican Rep. Garret Nelson won re-election by 4 votes, narrowly beating out Republican challenger Steve Menard.
Menard did not respond to a request for comment on whether he planned to file a request for a recount on Tuesday. 
Judge’s retention elections
Alaska voters in the Third Judicial District rejected two judges standing for retention elections.
Of 21 judges standing for retention, they were the only two that the non-partisan Alaska Judicial Council recommended not be retained ahead of the election. The council is charged with vetting, nominating and evaluating judges’ performance on the bench.
Voters rejected Kenai Superior Court Judge Kelly Lawson with 58.88% voting ‘no’ on retention, and 41.12% voting ‘yes.’ 
Voters also rejected District Court Judge Martin Fallon’s retention with 59.92% voting ‘no,’ and 40.08% voting ‘yes.’ 
Voter turnout in both instances was 48.65%. 
Both judges are scheduled to step down in late February, 90 days after the results are certified. Their cases will be transferred to retired judges, called pro tem judges, who will fill in while the seats are vacant. The council will interview and nominate candidates for the two judicial vacancies, at its next meeting in May. The nominees will then advance to Gov.-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins to make appointments.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: H-Power Spill Calls For Transparency, Accountability And Prevention
description: Hawaiʻi needs an independent investigation, accessible testing results and an enforceable prevention standard.
text:
Hawaiʻi has endured too many environmental failures followed by delayed disclosure and promises of accountability. The estimated 403,000-gallon fuel spill at Oʻahu’s H-Power waste-to-energy facility raises an urgent question: Have we learned the lessons of Red Hill?
According to Reworld, H-Power’s operator, No. 2 fuel oil leaked from an underground pipeline between late January and early May 2026. The company initially reported approximately 6,500 gallons to the Hawaiʻi Department of Health in May.
By July, the department had been told the release might total 200,000 to 400,000 gallons. Honolulu’s Department of Environmental Services learned of the larger estimate in September. The public was not informed until November.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

The state has not independently verified the final volume. Nevertheless, a release of this magnitude demands prompt disclosure and a thorough explanation of the communication failures.
Public Health Requires Evidence, Not Assurances Alone
Petroleum-related chemicals can cause headaches, nausea, respiratory irritation and other health effects, depending on the exposure. But detecting fuel underground does not prove that residents have been exposed.
The Honolulu Board of Water Supply says its drinking-water wells are safe. Officials explain that the affected groundwater is saline, not used for drinking, and separated from the nearest drinking-water well by distance and elevation. Those distinctions matter. So does the need for independent, publicly available testing.
Mayor Rick Blangiardi held a press conference Thursday morning to announce roughly 400,000 gallons of fuel oil was spilled at the city’s H-Power waste-to-energy plant earlier this year.  (Ben Angarone/Civil Beat/2026)
Reworld reports that fuel has migrated beyond its property to the west and south. The extent of contamination remains under investigation. Monitoring should address potential movement toward coastal waters and any implications for marine ecosystems.
For Native Hawaiian communities, protecting the ʻāina and ocean is also protecting cultural practices, traditional gathering and future generations. Environmental justice means involving affected communities before decisions are finalized, not merely notifying them afterward.
Federal Financing Deserves Scrutiny, Without Speculation
On Oct. 16, the Environmental Protection Agency announced a $109 million loan for the Kalaeloa seawater desalination project. The announcement came months after government agencies first learned of the H-Power spill.
That sequence warrants questions, not accusations. When did EPA officials learn of the release? Were relevant environmental assessments reviewed? Does the contamination pose any credible risk to the proposed seawater intake or other project infrastructure? Proximity alone cannot answer these questions, and no evidence presently establishes financing fraud.
Red Hill Should Have Changed Our Expectations
The 2021 Red Hill fuel contamination crisis demonstrated the human cost of failures in prevention and communication. H-Power involves different geology and exposure pathways, but the obligation to detect leaks early and notify the public promptly is the same.
A 2015 Honolulu City Auditor’s report identified inadequate oversight resources and contract provisions that constrained the city’s ability to monitor H-Power’s operator. City officials have not yet provided a complete accounting of the recommendations implemented. That accounting is overdue.
Reworld says it replaced the damaged underground line with aboveground piping, installed 22 monitoring wells and recovered approximately 5,000 gallons of fuel. These steps matter, but cleanup may take years. The cause of the pipeline hole remains undetermined.
Accountability Requires Action
Hawaiʻi needs an independent investigation, a public disclosure timeline, accessible testing results, clear cleanup milestones and enforceable prevention standards. Officials should explain what EPA knew and when. Legally responsible parties should bear appropriate cleanup costs.
Transparency is not optional after an environmental emergency. It is the foundation of public trust — and it must begin when contamination is discovered, not months later.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: Blue wins and bipartisanship in red Alaska
description: A year ago, most Alaskans would be hard pressed to believe our next governor would be a Democrat and the youngest to hold that office in any state. Or that an Alaskan would be the last of 56 Democrats to flip the U.S. Senate. We’d be more likely to witness the return of glacial ice […]
text:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democratic former state House member, won the state's gubernatorial primary last month. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)A year ago, most Alaskans would be hard pressed to believe our next governor would be a Democrat and the youngest to hold that office in any state. Or that an Alaskan would be the last of 56 Democrats to flip the U.S. Senate.
We’d be more likely to witness the return of glacial ice lost to climate change.
After all, two thirds of Alaska’s three-member congressional delegation had all but relinquished its power to the President — along with a Republican majority Congress — diminishing any hope of them opposing the dismantling of democracy, dehumanization of immigrants and destruction of public lands.
Since we moved to the capital in the early 1990s, Juneau’s been a blue pocket of this red state. Back then the Legislative Speaker of the House was a steely Republican woman named Ramona Barnes. Then there was the Democratic Representative who voted Republican. Richard Foster spent House floor sessions leaning back in his chair with his feet on the desk, thumbing through gun magazines.
But here we are, awash with hope by a blue tsunami. An Alaska Native woman from Bethel is replacing an establishment Republican incumbent from Fairbanks. An Alaska Native fisherman might have kept the Republican incumbent from retaining the lone House seat, had he received the votes that went to a perennial sham candidate and convicted felon.
Since statehood the majority of Alaskans voted Republican. Only 11.6%of last frontier voters are registered Democrats. So how did we get here?
The short answer is more of us are just as fed up with the rising cost of living as the rest of America. But there is more to it.
Alaskans know that divisive politics hinder progress. And with about 737,000 people inhabiting 665,384 square miles, or a population density of just over one resident per square mile, we must team up to survive.
Alaska legislators routinely band together in a bipartisan caucus. It’s how they passed much needed funding for education, only to be repeatedly vetoed by outgoing Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy.
In her first interview as senator-elect with the Anchorage Daily News, Mary Peltola said, “Those who want to engage in partisan rhetoric and stagnate while we’re just engaged in partisan mudslinging — those folks have been sidelined, and I would love to see that happen on a federal level.” The headline: Peltola calls for bipartisanship after winning U.S. Senate race: ‘Alaska has so much to teach the rest of the nation.’
Governor-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, aka JKT, is one of 30 Democratic governors elected nationwide. Crossing the aisle to get things done was his M.O. during the decade he spent as a state legislator in his 20s and 30s. “Republican, Democrat or Independent; majority caucus or minority caucus; rural or urban; we will work with anyone and everyone who wants to solve problems and move Alaska forward,” he said in a victory statement earlier this month. He’s also seeking solutions from fellow Alaskans. His transition team consists of a Democrat, a Republican and an Independent. 
Kreiss-Tomkins’ proclivity for bipartisan cooperation earned an endorsement from Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski, who as a moderate in a divided Congress could equally tick off both Republicans and Democrats.
But that’s Alaska. Just ask Mary Peltola. As a member of the House of Representatives in 2023 Peltola was one of only two Democrats who voted to defund a White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention.
Years ago the Permanent Fund replaced oil as the main source of revenue for the state of Alaska. To this day few Alaska lawmakers oppose drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. Peltola’s a defender of the oil and gas industry and in favor of expanding fossil fuel development in the Arctic.
On Nov. 3 a record number of women were elected to public office, and will now represent just over a third of Congress. Alaska is now one of a handful of states with both Senate seats held by women. A Democrat and a Republican. Peltola expects them to “work hand in hand together.”
But bipartisanship requires compromise, which requires trade-offs. The term can be used as a cover for regressive legislation. Case in point: the troublesome Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act aka BAAJA, en route to the House after passing the Senate by just one vote. It would fast track energy and infrastructure projects, including data centers, while cutting environmental and historical protections and ignoring laws for public and tribal input. Compromised is a healthy planet and climate for the next generations.
The longer answer to how the blue wave hit Alaska is a sweeping generational turnover in American politics, led by young leaders like the mayor of New York and the new mayor of Los Angeles. A record number of millennials were just elected to Congress. Two-thirds of college educated Alaskan voters aged 30-45 went with Peltola.
The President of the United States is exhibit A for aging boomer politicians hellbent on ruining things for everyone but themselves.
I do some substitute teaching at the elementary school down the street. Each morning, we recite class promises reinforcing that kindness, respect, compassion, listening and honesty are required to work with and get along with each other.
How a bully who would have been expelled the first day of school conned enough voters to win the presidency twice is beyond me.
On Dec. 7 a positive young guy willing to work with lawmakers regardless of party becomes our new Governor.
Alaska and the rest of the country just might be growing up.
