name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Feds have added mitigation strategies, local aid ahead of lead azide detonation
description: What started as a plan to detonate nearly 5 tons of degraded explosive material in Iowa, with coordination between the U.S. Army and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, has since triggered multiple state emergency responses and an “unprecedented” coordination of federal agencies.  The detonation is scheduled for Wednesday about 9 a.m. at the U.S. Army’[...]
text:
Col. Aaron Teller, an Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal commander, speaks alongside federal officials from many agencies Nov. 24, 2026 during a press conference at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. (Photo via U.S. Army on Youtube)What started as a plan to detonate nearly 5 tons of degraded explosive material in Iowa, with coordination between the U.S. Army and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, has since triggered multiple state emergency responses and an “unprecedented” coordination of federal agencies. 
The detonation is scheduled for Wednesday about 9 a.m. at the U.S. Army’s ammunition plant in Middletown in southeast Iowa. The scheduled time follows numerous delays over the past week from the Army, a lawsuit, intervention from the president, and widespread public concern of the health and environmental effects associated with detonating a lead-based explosive. 
Lead deposition maps released by the Army Tuesday morning show lead released by the detonation could be dispersed in the air as far as 100 miles southwest of Middletown and cross into Missouri. An additional map shows there is a potential for lead surface dust to settle as far as 50 miles southwest of the detonation site. 
The Army has recommended, and FEMA is supporting, the evacuation of Iowans in Middletown and the immediate area – a 5-mile cone to the southwest of the detonation site – during the detonation period. 
Soldiers, environmental teams and other federal officials are in the area helping to sample soils and alert residents of the detonation plans. The Army will be releasing maps, adjusted for the latest weather conditions, six hours ahead of detonation and every hour leading up to detonation. 
A slew of federal officials from the Army, the EPA, Department of Health and Human Services, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, Department of Agriculture and more gathered at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant Tuesday for a press conference and shared new information with the public about the response. 
Relocation assistance
When the detonation was originally announced, the Army recommended individuals in a select neighborhood of Middletown evacuate during the detonation, due to concerns that the blast could cause some windows to shatter. 
After nearly a week of nationwide, public outcry and calls from politicians for greater protections of the surrounding area, additional efforts are in place to mitigate the amount of lead dust that is emitted, and the government is working to help Iowans in the area. 
Speaking at the press conference Tuesday, Sean Kaufman with HHS said the highest risk is for pregnant individuals, children, or people with chronic illnesses who live or plan to be in the areas the Army forecasts will be impacted.


FEMA has a hotline available, 1-800-621-3362, and has sent out emergency alerts to cellphones in the area about the planned detonation. Additional assistance can be found online.


“You definitely want to be out of that area,” Kaufman said of the at-risk groups. “I would evacuate that area that’s signaled in the model.” 
A press release from the Lee County Sheriff’s Office said Tuesday that U.S. Army soldiers would begin going door to door to “notify residents” of recommended evacuations. 
FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton said at the news conference that the White House has made it “very very clear that we are to spare no expense to ensure that Americans are kept safe.” 
Hamilton said it has been “made clear” to communities southwest of the detonation site that “if they choose to relocate, we will offer services.” He said FEMA is offering transportation, food and relocation assistance to those in the impacted areas. The Army release said short-term lodging will be provided to eligible Iowans through Friday, Nov. 27. 
Hamilton noted that the maps shared by the Army represent “some of the worst case scenarios” of the lead dispersion. 
“We care deeply about the American people,” Hamilton said. “What you see here is not red, not blue, it’s red, white, and blue. This is the very best of the American’s team.” 
State response 
Gov. Kim Reynolds issued a disaster proclamation Tuesday for Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren counties for the planned detonation, activating the response plans for the counties and state agencies.
According to a news release from the governor, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services is working with federal partners, as well as other state agencies, and evaluating potential public impacts. The department is also providing precautionary guidance to communities and informing local public health partners. 
The Iowa Department of Natural Resources is assessing Army, EPA and other federal plans for pre- and post-detonation monitoring of air, land and water quality and the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship has published new guidance for livestock producers within 20 miles of Middletown based on most recent weather information. 
As many as 100 Iowa National Guard soldiers will be available to aid local, state and federal agencies in their public safety plans, the release stated. They will also help provide guidance and assistance to around 150 households with a temporary evacuation. 
“Today’s briefing by the U.S. Army highlighted the responsible planning and coordination that have gone into the upcoming detonation. I greatly appreciate their due diligence, responsible approach, and focus on the public health and safety of Iowans in nearby communities,” Reynolds said in the release. “Iowa agencies are actively engaged alongside our federal and local partners, and we remain focused on ensuring communities have the information and resources they need before, during, and after the operation.” 
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe has also launched a state emergency center and Illinois Governor J.B Pritzker said he has put state agencies on alert, though the plume models don’t currently show the state will be impacted.
“While risk to Missourians remains minimal, our State Emergency Operations Center is activated and our state agencies continue to be in constant contact with federal partners to take the necessary actions to protect the health and safety of our citizens, livestock, and environment,” Kehoe said in a statement.
These models predict the areas where lead concentrations have the possibility to exceed the EPA clearance levels for lead dust when cleaning up lead-based paints. (Maps courtesy of U.S. Army)New maps will be released 6 hours prior to detonation. (Maps courtesy of U.S. Army)
Feds have ‘continuously added’ mitigation protocol
Politicians, Iowans and environmental groups have repeatedly called for more transparency from the Army and associated federal partners since the original plans for the detonation were released.
Sen.-elect Josh Turek of Iowa called the Tuesday news conference “long-overdue.”
“I’ve repeatedly reiterated that Iowans’ health and safety must be the number one priority in the execution of this operation, and that transparency and clear communication – both of which have been sorely lacking up to this point – are paramount,” Turek said in a statement Tuesday.
At the news conference, acting Secretary of the Army Hon. Adam Telle emphasized that the government’s priority was the “health and safety of the citizens of this region.” 
Telle said those involved have sought advice from “every expert” in and outside of the federal government and have considered all viable options and data before reaching the conclusion to proceed with detonation. 
“There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, is far preferable to an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation of that substance,” Telle said. 
‘Not a time for panic’: Governor says Missouri is prepared for possible lead fallout from Iowa blast

Some of those mitigations include: sand around the structure holding the barrels; two walls of four, 16,000-gallon water tanks, a plan to “flood” the exterior of the storage area with aqueous foam to help absorb particulate matter from the blast and modeling to forecast impacted areas based on weather conditions. 
The “water walls,” as Telle called them, and the foam were not part of the Army’s originally released detonation plans.
Telle said federal agencies have been working “24 hours a day” the past several days on the situation in Middletown and have “continuously added” mitigation measures.
“There has been unprecedented collaboration across the federal government,” Telle said. “Unprecedented.” 
He also emphasized that “every reliable bit of information” the government has over the next 24 hours is “going to be made available to the public.” 
Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commander of the Army Sustainment Command, said there has been “multi-agency” work on the situation since the degraded lead azide was discovered in March. 
“This is not simply an Army problem set, nor will it be an Army solution. It is a whole of government response,” Shirley said. 
What is lead azide?
U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives director Rob Cekada said lead azide is a “sensitive” primary explosive that has been phased out by the government for around 15 years. 
Cekada said in 2009 the “nation’s stockpile” of lead azide — nearly 10,000 pounds of the material, some of which he said was “already 60 plus years old” — was moved to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. 
Information filed by the government in a legal case about the issue said that the barrels were visually checked monthly and annually refilled with a solution of water and ethanol. The crystallization that the Army noticed in March meant that this year the mixture couldn’t be administered, for fear of setting the explosives off. Cekada said this means there is less liquid in the barrels, making them more susceptible to the approaching freezing temperatures. 
Cekada said the stockpile was intended to be kept at IAAAP in the event that the U.S. military needed to deploy lead azide as a primary explosive again. 
Col. Aaron Teller, the Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal commander executing the detonation, said the last major disposal of lead azide was in 1977 in Colorado. He said that detonation had “zero mitigation” in place and only 25% of lead material from that detonation was released into the atmosphere. 
“So we believe we can significantly reduce that last 25% with the mitigation strategy that we have in place,” Teller said. 
EPA on site sampling
Thomas Croci, with the EPA’s Office of National Security and Operations Coordination, said the agency had a “blanket” of sampling teams out in the region collecting before-detonation samples and preparing to collect samples following the detonation. 

EPA sampling requests should be directed to 1-833-649-9624. More information can be found on the EPA response site.

“No one should feel like they will not get a sample,” Croci said. “If you want your home sampled, your property sampled, your school sampled, you will get that sample and the EPA will assist with that sampling.” 
Croci said there are “more than 150 teams” sampling areas in three states, and have four mobile laboratories deployed to test air toxins and “anything that comes off the combustion.” 
Agricultural concerns 
Richard Fordyce, an under secretary at USDA, said the department estimates 350 farms in Iowa and Missouri will be potentially impacted by the detonation. 
The USDA posted on X that it was working with Iowa and Missouri officials to “protect livestock, support producers and safeguard our food supply.” The department recommended farmers shelter or move their livestock from the region and contact veterinarians if they suspect animals were exposed to lead. 
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig told reporters Tuesday in Ames that it’s “unfortunate” that the situation in Middletown has reached the point where detonation is the only option, and he thinks questions will need to be answered after the detonation as to how things got to this point and where communication broke down. 
“I think that obviously the late notice to the state has caused a lot of work now over a short number of days, so I think that could have been handled differently,” Naig said. “But here we are, and we need to get through this, and we need to make sure that Iowans have their questions answered, and that our farmers, at least in my lane here, we want to make sure that our farmers are supported through the process.”
With harvests essentially complete for the year, Naig said the Iowa Department of Agriculture is focusing on helping livestock producers prepare for the detonation and record what they can before and after for testing and compensation if necessary. 
“There’s a lot of things that’ll have to be determined after we see the impact and what kind of levels we see. And there’s all kinds of monitoring that’ll be going on in the area,” Naig said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Essence Festival departs New Orleans amid frigid conditions between city, state leaders
description: New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno and the Essence Festival of Culture have signaled an end to the city’s host role for the annual event that has attracted millions of visitors for more than three decades.  Their relationship has come to an apparent end as state support for one of the nation’s largest Black tourism draws […]
text:
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno speaks at a news conference  Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, for the Bayou Classic at Caesar's Superdome. (Photo courtesy of New Orleans Mayor's Office)New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno and the Essence Festival of Culture have signaled an end to the city’s host role for the annual event that has attracted millions of visitors for more than three decades. 
Their relationship has come to an apparent end as state support for one of the nation’s largest Black tourism draws has dwindled and dialogue between state and city leaders turned icy.   
The mayor and Sundial Media Group, the festival’s parent company, said discussions have dissolved over their inability to reach a long-term deal to keep the event in New Orleans. 
At a news conference Tuesday morning for the Bayou Classic, Moreno said negotiations to keep Essence Festival in the city have been fruitless. The event has been held each Fourth of July weekend in New Orleans since 1995. The only exceptions were a temporary relocation to Houston in 2006 after Hurricane Katrina, and the move to a virtual event for the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021.
“It’s time for potentially Sundial and the city to come out with some kind of mutual statement on going our separate ways,” Moreno said. “Obviously, we wish them the very best with what they are determined to do.”
Sundial followed with its own statement, confirming that it would not be back in New Orleans for 2027. The company said it had repeatedly asked to meet with city officials to discuss a multiyear contract but received no response, adding that New Orleans “this summer signaled it never intended to offer Essence a multiyear agreement.”

Moreno said Tuesday she is working with city tourism leaders to create another Black cultural event to fill the void in the calendar left by Essence. Lt. Gov. Billy Nungesser, the state’s top tourism official, confirmed there are plans underway that will involve New Orleans-based talent, and he is supportive of those efforts. The mayor said in a social media post that she will share more details about the “new, world-class Fourth of July festival.” on Dec. 9   
“It’s important for tourism to fill those hotels that weekend,” Nungesser said in an interview. “Whatever that takes — advertising, funding — we need to make that happen.”
Hotel occupancy rates in the city typically peak around 80% during Essence weekend, according to New Orleans & Co., the industry-backed tourism promotion agency. Businesses in the hospitality sector have relied on the festival to provide a revenue boost during the slow summer season for visitors.
Essence organizers have said as many as 500,000 people converge in New Orleans each year for the nightly Superdome concerts as well as its extensive slate of speakers, seminars and vendors at the Morial Convention Center. Atlanta and Houston are among other cities that Sundial has said it will consider relocating the festival.
The Essence Festival’s departure coincides with declining financial support from the state of Louisiana. After having received as much as $2 million from a state special events fund for the Essence Festival, the state offered no financial incentives to event organizers this year. 
Meanwhile, the Landry administration has used the fund to bring other events to New Orleans. 
It’s allocated $2 million for this year’s first-time stop from the Hondo Rodeo Fest and has promised the same amount next year.
The state also pledged $7 million in 2025 for a LIV Golf tournament at City Park scheduled for this past June, including $2 million for upgrades to the host course. But the league canceled its New Orleans plans once it lost the backing of the sovereign wealth fund controversial Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman manages. The state had paid $1.2 million to LIV Golf by the time it declared bankruptcy in September.
Moreno, whose office did not respond immediately when asked for comment, has not said state officials or a lack of state involvement had anything to do with the inability to reach terms with the Essence Festival. But in its statement, Sundial referenced an ongoing dialogue between New Orleans and state leaders.
“We are at a larger inflection point and we don’t want to get caught in the political discourse between the city and state of Louisiana,” the statement reads.
There has been no public comment yet from Gov. Jeff Landry on the festival’s exit. 
Until a near catastrophe in the city earlier this month, Landry, a Republican, and Moreno, a Democrat, had not interacted publicly since the spring. Their standoff started once GOP legislators, with the governor’s support, approved laws to shrink the New Orleans court system and eliminate one of the city’s two elected court clerks. Attorney General Liz Murrill, a Republican and close Landry ally, threatened to arrest Moreno and other city officials if they carried out plans to subvert the new law.
Tensions boiled over in July when a New Orleans judge issued an indictment against Murrill in response to her threats. Although the charges were eventually dropped, Landry and Murrill ordered a criminal investigation from Louisiana State Police into who was responsible for the indictment. The governor said he would not personally talk with the mayor until that probe was complete.
Tensions between the two eased earlier this month after a tanker in the Mississippi River rammed into a riverboat docked at the Port of New Orleans’ headquarters. Landry raced to the mayor’s side Nov. 13 to offer state support as more than 100 passengers and crew were rescued from the sinking riverboat.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Abrego Garcia flies to Spain, ending 20-month deportation battle with Trump administration
description: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland resident who became the face of the Trump administration’s heavy-handed deportation efforts, reportedly self-deported Tuesday to Spain. The move would end 20 months of legal wrangling between the administration and immigration advocates fighting on behalf of Abrego Garcia, an immigrant from El Salvador who was picked up by [...]
text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia stands outside U.S. District Court in Greenbelt in December 2025 beside his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, left, and Lydia Walther-Rodriguez with CASA, after a federal judge ruled he was allowed to remain free. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland resident who became the face of the Trump administration’s heavy-handed deportation efforts, reportedly self-deported Tuesday to Spain.
The move would end 20 months of legal wrangling between the administration and immigration advocates fighting on behalf of Abrego Garcia, an immigrant from El Salvador who was picked up by immigration agents March 15, 2025, and erroneously deported to his native country.
Neither his attorneys nor the Department of Homeland Security immediately responded to requests for comment Tuesday from States Newsroom.
The immigration advocacy group We Are CASA declined to comment Tuesday night, except to say, “Our priority continues to be keeping the family safe.”
The deportation attracted international attention to the administration’s immigration crackdown, early in Trump’s second term, and brought attention to the notorious CECOT prison in El Salvador where U.S. deportees were housed.
Top ICE official elaborates on plan to send Kilmar Abrego Garcia to Liberia

Legal challenges were immediately filed to the detention and deportation. The case reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which unanimously ordered the administration to “facilitate” the return of Abrego Garcia.
It also brought a visit from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. who traveled to El Salvador and demanded to meet with Abrego Garcia, who had been kept largely incommunicado since he was detained. In a statement Tuesday evening, Van Hollen confirmed that Abrego Garcia was leaving the U.S.
“A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag,” Van Hollen’s statement said. “Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity.”
While Van Hollen did not specify Abrego Garcia’s destination, news reports Tuesday said he was seen getting on a plane to Spain.
The apparent self-deportation also ends a monthslong fight with the Department of Homeland Security, which had proposed deporting Abrego Garcia to Liberia, Eswatini or other third countries where his safety and his future would have been in doubt.
A 2019 immigration court order barred the government from sending Abrego Garcia back to his native El Salvador, for fear of his safety there, but not from sending him to a third country – an increasingly popular deportation tactic of the administration.
Abrego Garcia had offered to self-deport to Costa Rica, but the administration opposed that move.
It is not clear when or how the European deportation plan was agreed to. But Van Hollen’s statement said that as Homeland Security had been “trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation.”
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” the statement said.

name: WyoFile
title: $6M Boys’ School verdict sparks call for more juvenile justice reforms
description:
The state says “sweeping reforms” are underway. Advocates say internal policy changes alone won't prevent future abuse. 
The post $6M Boys’ School verdict sparks call for more juvenile justice reforms appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In the wake of a $6 million jury verdict in favor of a former Wyoming Boys’ School resident whose constitutional rights were violated, the state-run facility for delinquent boys ages 12 to 21 announced Monday that “sweeping reforms” are underway. 
Juvenile justice reform advocates and a state lawmaker warn, however, that internal policy changes won’t be enough to prevent future abuse and mistreatment. They say increased oversight and transparency are needed. 
Jurors in the U.S. District Court in Casper came to a unanimous decision last week that boys’ school staff subjected Blaise Chivers-King to punitive isolation in the state-run facility’s 7-by-10-foot cinderblock detention rooms and denied him due process to challenge his confinement. The jury, however, did not rule in favor of Chivers-King’s claim of excessive force.
The state is still facing five more lawsuits from former residents who allege they suffered civil rights abuses ranging from punitive use of a restraint chair to indifference to medical needs. The six former residents initially sued together, but the court separated them into different trials after a request from the state’s attorneys described the case as “deeply complex and full of fact-intensive claims involving multiple plaintiffs and defendants over a four-year time span.” 
The Wyoming Department of Family Services, which oversees the 38-acre residential facility near Worland, released a statement Monday that it “cannot comment on the recent jury verdict in the U.S. District Court for the District of Wyoming, as litigation is ongoing,” but noted that Chivers-King’s experiences at the boys’ school in 2021 “do not reflect current practices.”
“Current WBS Superintendent Dale Weber instituted sweeping reforms that address the issues raised in the trial,” according to the DFS statement. “These reforms include eliminating detention rooms and detention status except under extreme circumstances, implementing nonviolent crisis intervention training, and prohibiting the use of the restraint chair.” 
The DFS statement also said that Weber — who was one of the defendants in Chivers-King’s lawsuit — eliminated the mandatory head-shaving policy and brought the detention facility’s practices into alignment with nationally recognized best practices. 
DFS did not immediately respond to WyoFile’s request Monday for the specific best practices or the dates these changes took place. A DFS spokesperson estimated it would take a week to provide more detailed information. 
In response to questions from WyoFile about actions the state should take in light of the verdict, Gov. Mark Gordon also declined to comment, citing the ongoing litigation.  
Juvenile justice reform advocates, including Laramie Democratic Rep. Karlee Provenza, hope the verdict spurs much-needed change.
An opaque system
For decades, Wyoming has recorded the highest juvenile confinement rates in the country. Research shows that locking kids up doesn’t reduce delinquent behavior and often creates a new set of problems by exacerbating the mental health challenges that led to criminal activity in the first place, according to a report issued by the Sentencing Project. In response, many states have been moving toward community-based models that focus on providing struggling kids with support and tools, and using incarceration only when necessary. 
In 2021, state lawmakers set out to study why Wyoming relies so heavily on locked facilities like the Boys’ School and Girls’ School, but hit a wall accessing information. 
The state can’t easily track why young people get in trouble, what local law enforcement does in response or the outcomes of efforts to address delinquent behavior, a Wyoming Community Foundation report found. Because each of Wyoming’s 23 counties handles juvenile cases differently, a child in one community might land in a community-based program while somewhere else a judge might send a kid to a juvenile facility for similar behavior. 
This decentralized approach makes it hard for the state to track what’s happening to young people in the juvenile justice system, like whether they graduate from high school or reoffend as teens or adults. Those outcomes matter because they concern the well-being of children and the spending of public dollars. 
Responding to the data gap, the Wyoming Legislature’s Joint Judiciary Committee sponsored a bill in 2022 to strengthen information sharing about state-supervised youth, including those in the juvenile justice system. The measure has yet to pass because many Freedom Caucus members opposed it on privacy grounds. But Provenza, who helped craft the original bill, plans to bring it back during the legislative session that begins in January. She hopes the recent verdict will motivate her colleagues to take a closer look at juvenile justice. 
“My intention is to create the processes that allow for us to examine if what we are doing is working or not,” Provenza said. “Particularly as I start trying to push for more investment in the things that keep kids out of detention facilities.” 
Korin Schmidt, director of the Wyoming Department of Family Services, addresses the House Judiciary Committee on issues surrounding juvenile justice on Feb. 16, 2022 in the Wyoming Capitol in Cheyenne. (Lauren Miller/Casper Star-Tribune)
Back in 2021, when the data limitations were identified, Provenza also started to hear concerns about the climate at the Boys’ School. During a presentation by DFS Director Korin Schmidt and Superintendent Weber to the Joint Judiciary Committee, Provenza asked about allegations of abuse or mistreatment and was told that records or other information about the number, nature or resolution of incidents were not made public. 
Schmidt explained to the committee that because abuse allegations at the state-run facility are handled as Child Protective Services cases, they are “confidential under the statute.” CPS is a component of DFS, meaning the agency investigates the allegations itself, without any external oversight or transparency.
While the Joint Judiciary Committee was in the midst of its off-season study of juvenile justice in 2021, Chivers-King was at the boys’ school. 
Four years later, during an eight-day jury trial, the details of what the then-teenager experienced saw the light of day. (Whether he formally complained at the time wouldn’t have changed whether the allegations became public back in 2021. That’s because the state’s existing laws barred the release of such records.) 
Attorneys showed jurors images of the school’s detention facilities throughout the trial, where at one point Chivers-King was held for 15 days. The white cinderblock rooms are barren besides a toilet and a mattress that staff provided at night. The rooms don’t have windows that look outside, and staff at times covered the window in the door with a magnet.
Chivers-King testified during the trial that his confinement felt arbitrary. He described feeling confused when staff kept him isolated even after he had become calm. He was also on occasion locked in a detention room for a predetermined amount of time. “Even when he did what he was supposed to do, they kept him in there,” Ciara Boerman, one of his attorneys, told jurors during closing arguments. 
Images and video footage presented to the jury showed Chivers-King self harming while in detention, including banging his head against the wall and at multiple points trying to strangle himself. “The vast majority of that time he spent with his own thoughts, thinking about how to end his life,” Boerman said during closing arguments. 
“I hope this sends a message that legislation needs to be enacted in Wyoming to address solitary confinement,” Allison Mahoney, another one of Chivers-King’s attorneys, said after the jury delivered its verdicts.
Opening the black box
In addition to better tracking how young people move through Wyoming’s juvenile justice system, Provenza wants the Legislature to clearly define what solitary confinement is, “so that everybody has the same definition, and creating some strict guardrails around when it can be used, that basically keeps it from ever being used, except for very short stints that protect the safety of the child.” 
Provenza also wants the state’s use of confinement to be reported publicly, first and foremost to parents of incarcerated kids. 
“I think that’s an important component of this because parents are the best advocates for their children,” Provenza said. “What happens in the boys’ school feels like a black box to, I think, parents, but also to the state.”
“Why would we give taxpayer-funded agencies the chance to just take their word for it, and to say, ‘Trust me.’ Like, why on Earth would we do that?”Josh Rovner
There’s a connection between the public’s lack of information about Wyoming’s juvenile justice system and the abuse Chivers-King experienced at the boys’ school, according to Josh Rovner, a senior research analyst with the Sentencing Project, who recently published a report on widespread abuse in juvenile detention facilities nationally. “We count things we care about in this country.
“We know how many hogs were slaughtered last quarter. We know how many bushels of corn were exported. We know how much a gallon of gasoline costs down to the nearest milli-cent, right?” he said. If Wyoming cares about how it treats kids in detention facilities, it should make juvenile justice information public with that same level of detail. “There are plenty of states that are able to monitor, track, report, and publish what is happening with solitary confinement in their facilities.”
The Department of Family Services has fulfilled WyoFile’s multiple records requests for data on the boys’ school’s use of detention rooms and restraints, but does not automatically make the information available to the public. 
The state makes public education data easily accessible so communities understand how their public schools perform without jeopardizing student privacy, which Rovner said is an apt comparison for what’s possible with juvenile justice data. 
“Why would we give taxpayer-funded agencies the chance to just take their word for it, and to say, ‘Trust me,'” Rovner said. “Like, why on Earth would we do that?”
Provenza would also like the Legislature to play a stronger oversight role than it has in the past.
“Like at some point, someone has to say ‘the buck stops with us,’ and so I think we have to keep trying. I also know … we’ve got a bunch of freshmen coming in, but we have to deal with this,” she said, referring to newly elected lawmakers. Pointing to the Joint Judiciary Committee’s 2021 study of juvenile justice, which has yet to result in any reforms, Provenza realizes some might be skeptical about lawmakers considering the issue again. 
Rep. Art Washut, chair of the House Judiciary Committee, did not respond to WyoFile’s questions about whether he plans to do anything in response to the verdict against the Boys’ School. 
“I understand the sentiment, and part of me also has some fear that the legislative branch is not going to do the best job of overseeing what needs to happen,” Provenza said. “But I also know that we have to start somewhere, and this is our job. We fund these facilities. We write laws that impact them. We write the laws that send kids into these facilities, and so we have to take responsibility for the impact that they have and actually fix them.”
WyoFile reporter Maya Shimizu Harris contributed to this story.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Judge orders Fulton County to turn over 2020 election records to State Election Board
description: A Fulton County judge has ordered the county’s Board of Registration and Elections to turn over a complete, unredacted copy of the 2020 election records to Georgia’s State Election Board. FBI raids Fulton County elections warehouse seeking 2020 ballots The records, which included all ballot images from the 2020 election in Fulton County and Fulton […]
text:
Federal Bureau of Investigation agents seized 700 boxes of 2020 election records during a raid at the Fulton County Election Hub and Operation Center in January. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderA Fulton County judge has ordered the county’s Board of Registration and Elections to turn over a complete, unredacted copy of the 2020 election records to Georgia’s State Election Board.
FBI raids Fulton County elections warehouse seeking 2020 ballots

The records, which included all ballot images from the 2020 election in Fulton County and Fulton County’s 2020 voter rolls, were seized by FBI agents during a January raid on the Fulton County elections warehouse. In her Tuesday order, Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe ordered the documents to be delivered to the board on a flash drive by 5 p.m. Wednesday.
Attorneys for Fulton County have filed an appeal in the case, meaning a hearing will likely be held Wednesday. A spokesperson for the county declined to comment, citing pending litigation.
Fulton County, a Democratic stronghold that is home to much of the city of Atlanta, has been one of the places at the center of President Donald Trump’s unfounded claims that the 2020 election was stolen in Georgia and other swing states. Two recounts, including a hand recount, affirmed former President Joe Biden’s narrow victory in Georgia. Previous investigations into the 2020 election found no merit to claims of widespread voting fraud or intentional misconduct by Fulton election workers and leaders.
In February, the Republican-dominated State Election Board, which is responsible for investigating cases about alleged election violations, passed a measure seeking access to the Fulton County election records upon their return from the U.S. Department of Justice’s custody. In May, a federal judge ruled against the county’s lawsuit seeking to force the return of the records.
State Election Board member Salleigh Grubbs, a top Georgia GOP official who was appointed to the board last year, speaks during a February board meeting held in Barrow County. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Salleigh Grubbs, a top Georgia GOP official who was appointed to the board last year, said Tuesday that she was relieved that the judge chose to side with the board’s request.
“I think it’s about time,” she said. “The State Election Board has the statutory duty to investigate cases, and we have quite a few cases that were never able to be properly investigated because we didn’t have all the information.”
But State Rep. Saira Draper, an Atlanta Democrat and election attorney, said she wasn’t sure what new information could come from the data. In July, the FBI redirected hundreds of analysts to assist with the ongoing investigation of Fulton’s 2020 election records, but no criminal charges have come from those efforts.
“The idea that members of the State Election Board who don’t have the resources of the federal government, who don’t have the investigative experience, who don’t have the elections experience, that they would somehow acquire this data and could find something that the FBI hasn’t found, it does not make sense,” Draper said.
The order also allows members of the board to share the records “on an as-needed basis to witnesses, prospective witnesses, or persons requested by counsel to furnish technical or other expert services” as long as the person in question signs a protective order.
Georgia state Rep. Saira Draper, D-Atlanta speaks during a press conference at the Georgia State Capitol on Wednesday, Feb. 11, 2026. (Matthew Pearson/WABE)
Draper also said she worries about the potential for voters’ private information to be accessed by bad actors.
“Even though this is a protective order that obliges people that have this data to keep it private, there is a lot of leeway within this protective order for them to share it with outside consultants,” she said. “These are not actors that I would personally trust with any kind of voter information or personal information or election worker information.”

title: Christmas tree arrives at Kansas governor’s mansion as lieutenant governor opines on economic work
description: TOPEKA — On a chilly Tuesday morning celebrating the launch of the holiday season with the arrival of a Kansas-grown Christmas tree at the governor’s mansion, Lt. Gov. David Toland took a minute to talk politics. Toland, who also serves as secretary of commerce, said he’s excited to see new ideas and energy coming into […]
text:
Santa Claus hitches a ride on the buggy that delivered a live Christmas tree to the Kansas governor's mansion on Nov. 24, 2026, in Topeka.  Riding in the carriage were friends and family of tree farmers and others involved in organizing the event. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — On a chilly Tuesday morning celebrating the launch of the holiday season with the arrival of a Kansas-grown Christmas tree at the governor’s mansion, Lt. Gov. David Toland took a minute to talk politics.
Toland, who also serves as secretary of commerce, said he’s excited to see new ideas and energy coming into state government with the new administration and leadership of Gov.-elect Cindy Holscher.
“On one hand, I wish I could have 50 more years to try to finish everything that’s been started and to start the next chapters of the work, but I also believe that public service should not be something that you do forever,” he said. “I need to go back to the private sector, and we need fresh ideas and fresh legs coming into the Commerce Department to take the agency to the next level. 
“So it’s the right time to leave. There’s always more that I wish I could do, and I think it’ll be OK that we didn’t get everything done. I did all I could.”
Toland told reporters at the annual event, where a horse-drawn carriage delivers a fresh pine tree to the governor’s mansion, that his personal pride in what happened while he was at the Commerce Department focuses less on big projects — like the Chiefs stadium and the Panasonic battery plant — and more on differences made in small towns. 
“The things that I have enjoyed the most as a professional and as a human being have been when we do a mural on the side of a building in small-town Kansas, when we are able to take an old building which was dilapidated that’s on a main street somewhere and do a (Historic Economic Asset Lifeline) grant to bring it back to life,” he said. “We’ve been able to push economic development into places that hadn’t seen it in far too long.”
Toland, who filled in for Gov. Laura Kelly, who was unable to attend, spoke briefly after the festivities that included a Santa Claus visit for children, highlighting the importance of supporting Kansas tree farms and the forestry industry, and introduction of the Trees for Troops program.  
 

Charlotte Cooper, granddaughter of Dave Bruton, center, presented a wooden wreath she handpainted to Lt. Gov. David Toland on Nov. 24, 2026, after she rode in the carriage that delivered a Christmas tree to the governor’s mansion. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)

Kansas forests
Dave Bruton, with the Kansas Forest Service, organizes the tree delivery and told those in attendance that people don’t always understand Kansas does have a logging industry. 
In fact, people in his division take a lot of joking at conferences when people ask them how the “one tree” in Kansas is doing. 
“A lot of people think we don’t have an industry here in Kansas, and of course we do,” he said. “Black walnut is, of course, our most valuable timber species. We have logs that are exported around the globe.”
Kansas has about 2.2 million acres of rural forestland, according to the Forest Service, and 95% of it is privately owned. 
Growing Christmas trees
Vickie Andrews and daughter-in-law Cynthia Andrews are learning first-hand about growing trees in Kansas. They launched Sibleyville Farms in Lawrence this year, planting 500 pine seedlings that will one day decorate someone’s home at Christmas. 
As they wait for the trees to grow, they’re going to begin by selling pre-cut trees to start to get their name known in the community, Cynthia Andrews said. This year, they donated a large wreath for the front door of the governor’s mansion. 
Christmas tree farms are part of holiday traditions for many families, the two women said. 
“I think people want traditions, they want to make memories, they want to be together,” Cynthia Andrews said. “That’s what we’re going to offer is that time to connect, that time to slow down for a few minutes. Enjoy bonfires and s’mores and have some hot cocoa and take some pictures and just remember the reason we’re having this season is to be together and enjoy each other’s company.”
This year’s Christmas tree, a nine-year-old Scotch pine, was donated by Chris’ Tree Lodge in Abilene.
Harry Peckham, left, Kansas coordinator for Tres for Troops, talks with Lt. Gov. David Toland about the program that donates live trees to soldieres and their families. They were part of Nov. 24, 2026, festitivies at the governor’s mansion in Topeka. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Trees for Troops
Harry Peckham, a Christmas tree grower near Ottawa, attended the event to share the importance of Trees for Troops, which donates live Christmas trees to soldiers and their families across the country.
Last year, the organization set a record by donating 21,000 Christmas trees, he said. About 125 trees were donated from Kansas farms. Fort Riley participates in the program, Peckham said, and the organization expects to send trees to 100 bases nationwide this year. 
Peckham is the Kansas coordinator for the program and said Trees for Troops sells teddy bears, which he wore in the front of his hoodie, to raise funds for the program.
 
Cynthia Andrews, left, and Vickie Andrews deliver a large wreath for the front door of the Kansas governor's mansion, part of festivities Nov. 24, 2026, that ushered in the holidays. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)A Scotch pine, grown by Chris' Tree Lodge, Abilene, was delivered to the Kansas governor's mansion on Nov. 24, 2026. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)One of the horses that pulled a carriage to deliver a live Christmas tree to the Kansas governor's mansion on Nov. 24, 2026. name: Daily Montanan
title: Commentary: Permitting bill poses threats to our public lands, wildlife
description: As the holidays approach, the first snows are blanketing the flanks of the Yellowstone ecosystem. With them the migrating snow geese have come to Montana, moving south from the Arctic. White-bodied with black wingtips, they pass over by the hundreds in great, wavering skeins, chattering eagerly with each other as I shovel the driveway of […]
text:
Near the summit of the Beartooth Pass, south of Red Lodge, Montana (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan). As the holidays approach, the first snows are blanketing the flanks of the Yellowstone ecosystem. With them the migrating snow geese have come to Montana, moving south from the Arctic. White-bodied with black wingtips, they pass over by the hundreds in great, wavering skeins, chattering eagerly with each other as I shovel the driveway of my Gallatin Valley home. Their flyover brightens this mundane task with a moment of wonder.
Especially since the pandemic, many of us have reconnected with the ways in which such natural encounters enrich our lives. Both national park visits and participation in wildlife-focused activities such as birdwatching surged after the COVID lockdown, and for many, the respite from our tech-focused lives that comes from “touching grass” now involves grass along a hiking or birding trail. Montana’s public lands, offering open access to all, are essential for these activities.
Yet even as our “last child in the woods” culture seeks to renew its relationship with the natural world, the permitting bill now under consideration by the lame duck Congress would roll back many of the core legal protections that for 50 years have made these kinds of experiences possible. Alongside this legislative threat, the Trump administration recently announced plans to sell off public lands, an alarming move that could happen quickly following passage of this bill. The House of Representatives will vote on the bill as early as next week.
This legislation’s proponents contend that the payoff for this sacrifice will be streamlined permitting for clean-energy projects to fight climate change. However, the bill’s changes would also clear the way for many other projects—including logging, drilling, mining, and data centers on our public lands—that will no doubt look much more attractive to the Trump administration officials who will administer any new permitting authority.
The bill’s backers claim this bulldozer approach is needed to cut back on administrative processes that don’t allow America to build what it needs. That critique might legitimately justify a thoughtful review of our bedrock environmental laws by lawmakers who would take care to pluck the baby from the discarded bathwater.
However, the permitting bill reflects no such surgical approach. For one thing, the bill would ultimately make it harder for the public to learn about, or stop, the sale of public lands. Interior’s land sell-off plan has already sparked opposition from conservation groups and even Montana’s congressional delegation– but they and all Montanans would have reduced power to block or reverse land sales if this bill passes, given changes the bill would make to the National Environmental Policy Act.
Beyond this, the bill is loaded with measures that demolish some of the most fundamental protections of our bedrock environmental laws, including the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Historic Preservation Act. These are the laws that cleaned up the Great Lakes, saved the bald eagle from extinction, injected tribal perspectives into management of sacred cultural spaces, and provided a host of other benefits that Americans have long taken for granted.
Weakening these protections now, in the midst of the most environmentally hostile presidential administration in history, threatens hugely harmful and unpopular consequences. One of the bill’s Republican sponsors, Utah Sen. Mike Lee, in 2025 pushed for legislation to sell 3 million acres of our public forests, mountains, and deserts—our national patrimony of lands held in common for all Americans to enjoy without needing to ask permission from a billionaire land baron. His proposal drowned under a tsunami of opposition from a broad cross-section of the American people. Is it any wonder that Lee is now proposing to gut the laws that enable public opposition to federal environmental decisionmaking at just the moment when the Trump administration is resurrecting his public land disposal idea in the form an Interior Department work plan?
Many of us have lived most of our lives under the shelter of the environmental legal framework that arose from a 1960s-’70s political consensus about the kind of greener world our nation wanted. The architects of that framework lived with burning rivers, oil-soaked coastlines, and expiring wildlife species. By and large, we don’t. Instead, we can fish from our waters, hike through intact public forests, and draw inspiration from the spark of wildness that comes with the passing of snow geese after an early snowfall.
Let’s keep it that way.
Timothy Preso is Managing Attorney for Earthjustice’s Biodiversity Defense Program, based in Montana.

name: VTDigger
title: A three-alarm fire in Montpelier leaves one teenager unaccounted for
description:
First responders from several neighboring towns aided the Montpelier Fire Department Tuesday afternoon.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A three-alarm fire in Montpelier leaves one teenager unaccounted for.
text:
First responders from several nearby towns aided Montpelier Fire Department in managing a fire at 23 Cummings St. on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. Photo by Tierney Flavin/VTDigger

MONTPELIER — A teenager appeared to be unaccounted for Tuesday evening as firefighters tried to contain an apartment fire in Montpelier. 
The three-alarm fire at 23 Cummings St. started with an explosion at approximately 2:30 p.m. Fire departments from surrounding towns, including Barre City, Barre Town, East Montpelier, Middlesex, Northfield and Williamston, aided Montpelier Fire Department. 
First responders were still working to contain the fire at 5 p.m. Seven people independently told VTDigger that a 14-year-old who lived in the building was missing, but officials on the scene were not available to confirm that. 
Reached by phone Tuesday evening, Montpelier police would not address the status of a missing person since the investigation is ongoing. Vermont State Police Public Information Officer Adam Silverman could not be reached for comment by the time of publication.
Amanda Grandfield, a resident of a neighboring unit, was sitting in her living room when the explosion happened.
“It felt like a big tree fell on the house,” Grandfield told VTDigger. She also saw fire in the woods outside her home, she said.
Grandfield lived in the building with her 10-year-old child, two teenage sons, her 21-year-old daughter and granddaughter. All were either away from home or accounted for, she said. The unit’s roof was entirely charred and demolished.
Ashes fell on the scene as firefighters sprayed the roofs of the city-managed apartment complex from a truck’s fire ladder. 
The fire appeared to badly damage three adjoining units in the 20-unit complex. All three roofs had caved in, and flames could be seen through the afternoon. Unit two, where residents say the fire began, was blackened from the flames with several windows missing. 
Hoses lined Elm Street and Cummings Street as the fire departments worked to transport water from a fire hydrant about a half mile away on Elm Street. 
Julie Griffin, a resident of one of the burned units, said she heard a big boom, as if something had fallen through the floor.
“I looked out my back window, and I saw all the flames like in the woods,” Griffin, who said the fire spread to her unit, told VTDigger. 
Griffin was able to rescue her dog from the fire, but lost her possessions after the fire spread from the first apartment to hers, she said.
This story will be updated.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Third person dies as Wisconsin’s measles outbreak approaches 1,000 cases
description: A third person in Wisconsin has died from measles this year — the first adult in the state to succumb to the once-eliminated viral illness that has reemerged in the U.S. over the last couple of years. In the outbreaks across Wisconsin, more than 900 people have been infected, according to the state Department of […]
text:
A child's stomach shows a red rash from measles. Wisconsin measles outbreaks have sickened more than 900 people in 2026, state health officials say, and led to three deaths. (Getty Images)A third person in Wisconsin has died from measles this year — the first adult in the state to succumb to the once-eliminated viral illness that has reemerged in the U.S. over the last couple of years.
In the outbreaks across Wisconsin, more than 900 people have been infected, according to the state Department of Health Services.
DHS did not release demographic details about the Lafayette County adult whose death was reported Tuesday, citing the privacy of the individual and their family. DHS reported that 920 people have been diagnosed with measles in Wisconsin in 2026.
Since August, when the initial outbreaks were reported in southwestern Wisconsin, measles has spread to 24 Wisconsin counties, Dr. Stephanie Schauer, the Wisconsin immunization program manager at DHS, said Tuesday. She said 20 people have been hospitalized, including people who have since been discharged.
Public health officials have so far this year reported that 14 people in Wisconsin have been diagnosed with measles while pregnant, Schauer said. One infant has been born with measles contracted before birth, she said.
Dr. Ryan Westergaard, the state epidemiologist and chief medical officer in the DHS bureau of communicable diseases, said Tuesday that a team from the federal Centers for Disease Control will be helping state health officials with case investigation, public communication and managing data from the outbreaks.
“We decided to do this now, several months into the outbreak, when it became clear that the outbreak was growing rather than shrinking, and we needed to make sure that the additional counties where they’re dealing with local local measles transmission have all the resources that they need,” Westergaard said.
Westergaard said understanding whether one has immunity from the measles is “the most important thing for people to do” as outbreaks continue across the state.
The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccination rate in kids has been falling from 88% in 2013 to just under 80% as of 2025, according to DHS. 
Public health experts have said vaccination rates should be 95% of the population to ensure widespread immunity and promote safety, especially for people who cannot be vaccinated because they have a compromised immune system or because they’re infants under a year old.
With holiday travel on the horizon, Westergaard noted that a number of measles outbreaks in Wisconsin this year have been traced to travel outside the state.
“Definitely the best tool that we have for stopping transmission and keeping people safe while traveling is the MMR vaccine,” he said. “And it’s available everywhere where people can get vaccines — pharmacies, doctors’ offices, and health departments.”
He recommended that before traveling people pay attention to whether measles is circulating where they’re going, and to be mindful of people in their circle who are immunocompromised or infants too young to be vaccinated.
“One of the things that’s made this outbreak challenging is because it is not a single chain,” Westergaard said. “It’s multiple introductions of measles from different parts of the country, and that’s been challenging for multiple states that are dealing with measles outbreaks right now.”
The MMR vaccine is given in two doses to children age 1 and older, and the two-shot regimen has been in place since 1989.
While the standard two doses provide the best protection today, Westergaard said adults now who were vaccinated before 1989 and only got one shot are probably adequately protected. For people who don’t know if they’ve had two doses, “it’s safe to get another one,” he said.
Schauer said the Vaccines for Children program provides vaccines free to children who are uninsured, underinsured, on Medicaid or BadgerCare, or are Alaska natives or American Indian.
“They’re available at a healthcare provider where they’re already seeking care, as well as at local health departments,” Schauer said. “No child should be going without an MMR dose because of concern of cost.”
DHS issued guidance earlier this autumn for parents with infants 6 to 11 months old who might be at additional risk from measles to give an earlier vaccination against the virus. Schauer said the health department has given out 55,000 MMR doses across the state since Aug. 1, including for infants under a year old as well as for children enrolled in the Vaccines for Children program.
People not sure about their immunity who are exposed to measles can also get the MMR vaccine within 72 hours of being exposed, which can help prevent an infection, Schauer said. In addition, people with health conditions that prevent them from being vaccinated can get immunoglobulin up to six days after being exposed to the virus.
“So it’s really important if you are exposed to contact your healthcare provider and see if you need to take any of these immediate steps,” Schauer said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC voting rights advocates warn against lame-duck election changes as state certifies results
description: Voting rights groups gathered outside the North Carolina State Board of Elections Tuesday, urging lawmakers to avoid making changes to election laws during the final weeks of Republican control of the legislature.  The rally at Halifax Mall, organized by the Our Future Our Vote NC coalition, came as lawmakers are preparing to return to Raleigh […]
text:
Voting rights advocates gathered on Halifax Mall in Raleigh as state elections officials met nearby to certify the midterm results. (Photo by Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)Voting rights groups gathered outside the North Carolina State Board of Elections Tuesday, urging lawmakers to avoid making changes to election laws during the final weeks of Republican control of the legislature. 
The rally at Halifax Mall, organized by the Our Future Our Vote NC coalition, came as lawmakers are preparing to return to Raleigh as soon as next week for another lame-duck session. 
Democrats will take control of the state House of Representatives in January, while Republicans will keep control of the Senate. 
During the 2024 lame-duck session, Republican lawmakers transferred appointment power over the state elections board from the governor to the state auditor. The change gave Republican state Auditor Dave Boliek authority to appoint members of the state and county election boards. 
In the upcoming lame-duck session, Republican lawmakers could revisit a bill that would shorten early voting in primary and special elections. Gov. Josh Stein vetoed the bill in August, but that veto could be overridden with enough votes. 
Sailor Jones, state director of Common Cause North Carolina, said advocates want lawmakers to understand that voters are paying attention to what happens during the remaining weeks of the session. 
Just because the election is over, he said, that doesn’t mean it’s safe for voters to stop paying attention. “We want to make sure the General Assembly understands that we’re watching.” 
Earlier this year, Republicans on the state elections board voted to reject Sunday early voting hours in many counties. They also rejected proposals to add early voting sites at UNC Greensboro and N.C A&T State University. 
Denied a campus early voting site, NC A&T students again march to the polls

Olu Rouse, a senior at N.C. A&T, said at Tuesday’s rally that even though students’ efforts to secure an on-campus early voting site were unsuccessful, they turned out anyway.
“We marched over 40 minutes to the polls to show that a roadblock was never enough to stop us,” he said. 
The concerns extended beyond college campuses. Jones said advocates saw problems this year involving voting access, poll workers and early voting around the state. 
The rally coincided with the state BOE’s canvass meeting to certify most results from the midterm elections. During the meeting, members of the board sparred over the board’s handling of concerns about voting site access. 
Jeff Carmon, a Democratic board member, criticized the board’s response to student advocates.
“You can move early voting sites. You can eliminate college polling sites. You can disregard thousands of public comments, but what you can’t do is silence voters,” Carmon said. “And you can’t ignore the results.” 
GOP board member Stacy “Four’” Eggers IV accused Carmon of “echoing talking points from advocacy groups,” which he said is “inappropriate.” 
“The purpose of this board is to run safe, secure and accessible elections,” Eggers said. “I think that’s what we’re all here to do.” 
The board voted unanimously to certify most contests under its jurisdiction, excluding two races awaiting a partial hand-eye recount. 
State elections staff reported that more than 4.2 million ballots were cast statewide in the Nov. 3 election, and turnout was 53.8% of registered voters in North Carolina.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: State accuses doctor of illegal abortions, restricts his practice
description: The Department of Health took emergency steps Tuesday to restrict a South Florida physician from providing abortions, as Attorney General James Uthmeier said the doctor may have provided “at least”149 illegal abortions over two years, “possibly including late-term abortions.” The emergency suspension order filed against Dr. Sylvester Braithwaite and signed b[...]
text:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier speaking at the Cuban Club in Ybor City on April 17, 2026. (Photo by Don Kruse for the Florida Phoenix)The Department of Health took emergency steps Tuesday to restrict a South Florida physician from providing abortions, as Attorney General James Uthmeier said the doctor may have provided “at least”149 illegal abortions over two years, “possibly including late-term abortions.”
The emergency suspension order filed against Dr. Sylvester Braithwaite and signed by Department of Health Secretary Joseph Ladapo alleges the number of illegal abortions performed between June 2024 and September 2026 at Women and Teens Healthcare in North Miami Beach at “more than 50.”
Uthmeier cited “initial reports from state health officials” for the higher number he referenced on social media.
The emergency suspension order doesn’t mention late term abortions. The order prevents Braithwaite from performing any elective pregnancy terminations or nonemergency medical abortions. It does not restrict his ability to provide other healthcare while the allegations are being investigated.
“As a licensed medical doctor, Dr. Braithwaite is mandated to comply with the laws and rules which govern pregnancy termination. Dr. Braithwaite’s termination of more than 50 pregnancies outside of the boundaries permitted by law demonstrates his indifference towards the laws and rules governing the practice of medicine,” the order reads.
“Therefore, Dr. Braithwaite’s continued practice of medicine constitutes an immediate, serious danger to the health, safety, and welfare of the public.”
An attempt to get in touch with Braithwaite at the clinic where he serves as medical director were unsuccessful.

I am calling on the Florida Board of Medicine to revoke Dr. Sylvester Braithwaite’s medical license. Initial reports from state health officials indicate he performed at least 149 illegal abortions in North Miami Beach between June 2024 and Sept 2026, including late term abortions. My office is investigating and will prosecute violations of law.
— Attorney General James Uthmeier (@AGJamesUthmeier) November 24, 2026

“Florida is a pro-life state. Our Heartbeat Protection Act protects unborn children once a fetal heartbeat is detected. It is not a suggestion, it is the law and physicians must follow it,” Uthmeier said on X. “Each of these abortions violated Florida law. Each is a third-degree felony. My office is investigating this conduct and we will follow the facts wherever they lead and we will prosecute doctors who ignore our laws.”
Florida’s six-week abortion ban took effect May 1, 2024. A proposed constitutional amendment to overturn the ban fell short of voter approval in November 2024.
Dated Nov. 24, the emergency order contains some details but not many. For instance, it alleges abortions were performed between June 2024 and September 2026. But the order doesn’t include any information about the terminations, why the documentation indicates they were performed outside the six-week window, or how far into pregnancy they were conducted.
“It’s light on facts, but it may not need a lot of facts because if you set the premise that performing these abortions outside the limits of the law creates an imminent danger to the public, then you don’t need a lot of facts,” Julie Gallagher, a longtime healthcare attorney who routinely defends physicians before the Florida Board of Medicine, told the Phoenix Tuesday afternoon. She’s not involved in Braithwaite’s case.
The order also doesn’t include any information about “late term” abortions, a term that the American College of  Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) says “has no clinical or medical significance.” Abortions performed later in pregnancy are those occurring after 21 weeks gestational age.  KFF reports abortions occurring after that time frame are “rare.”
Uthmeier said in the video that some of the procedures were “possibly” late-term abortions. But he wrote in his post that the procedures did include late term abortions.

Uthmeier’s involvement in the allegations against Braithwaite comes early in the process.
The emergency order is the first step in the physician disciplinary process, according to Gallagher.
The allegations spelled out in the emergency suspension order must be considered by a probable cause panel of the Florida Board of Medicine. If the panel agrees there’s probable cause to beleive a violation occurred, it can file an administrative complaint.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Two-thirds of Idaho voters turned out for 2026 general election, final results show
description: About two-thirds of Idaho’s more than 1 million registered voters cast ballots in the midterm election held earlier this month, according to finalized state election data. The turnout didn’t eclipse rates from 2018, when the governor seat was open without an incumbent, but this year’s election still turned out to be the state’s largest midterm […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at the Calvary Baptist Church in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)About two-thirds of Idaho’s more than 1 million registered voters cast ballots in the midterm election held earlier this month, according to finalized state election data.
The turnout didn’t eclipse rates from 2018, when the governor seat was open without an incumbent, but this year’s election still turned out to be the state’s largest midterm election, with about 734,000 voters showing up, Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane said Tuesday. McGrane, the state’s top election official, attributes that last metric to the state’s years as one of the nation’s fastest growing states. 
Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican, attends a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“It really was a successful election,” McGrane said. “When you think about 734,000 people going through and doing the same thing. That’s a huge Herculean effort.”
Weeks after the Nov. 3 general election, the Idaho State Board of Canvassers on Tuesday certified the results of the election as official. At the board’s meeting at the Idaho State Capitol, officials delved into the results of audits of counties’ election results — including in two counties that underreported votes — and reflected on lessons learned from the election.
The final results showed that no races in Idaho were close enough to warrant a free recount, McGrane said. But he said there still might be a recount in a county assessor race in Shoshone County. 
Here’s a few snapshots about how voters turned out to vote earlier this month:

About 40% of voters didn’t cast ballots at the polls on Election Day. About half of those votes were early in person, for a total of roughly 146,000, and the other half were by absentee ballot, for a total of roughly 145,000. Both of those voting types are becoming more popular, McGrane said. 
Overall, the rate of voters who turned out this year was close to matching the 2018 election, which saw the highest turnout of a midterm election in recent years when nearly 67% of registered voters cast ballots. But this year’s turnout still pales in comparison to years when the president is on the ballot, when an average of nearly 76% of voters show up. 
About 56,000 Idahoans registered to vote on Election Day. McGrane said that might’ve contributed to lines at polling places in some areas. Registering to vote typically takes longer than checking in at the polls. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Idaho’s top election official addressed issues in three counties

In North Idaho’s Latah County, where officials announced 2,300 unreported ballots almost a week after the election, McGrane attributed the issue to human error. The ballots had been counted on a machine, he said, but that machine’s memory device was mistakenly not uploaded to a computer that can share votes to the state’s election results. 
Idaho voters turned out at high rates to vote in midterm election. Some waited hours to vote.

When his team flew up the day after the unreported ballots were announced to oversee a full recount, he said the room started out packed with observers. By the end of the day, the crowd had winnowed, he said. A week later, when McGrane’s team flew up again to randomly audit batches of votes in the county, he said no one showed up.
“… I think we satisfied the concerns and addressed the questions on the first go around,” McGrane said. “But we will be working with them both in terms of training, and I think there’s a lot of lessons learned from their team from this, to say the least.”
In eastern Idaho’s Bannock County, local election officials found 333 uncounted ballots a week after the election. McGrane said officials discovered it while rounding up election supplies. McGrane called the mistake unusual, and said his office is working to prevent a similar issue from recurring.
“I will say there were safeguards in place, some of which, for lack of better (term), had been ignored on Election Day,” McGrane said. “They’re now aware, and we’re reviewing what we could do, or and even some of our maybe software changes in terms of updates to see if we can’t flag or catch that much sooner in the process.”
Vote tallies ran late into the night for Bannock County on Election Day.
One issue there that delayed vote counting, he said, is that some absentee ballots had been apparently folded by hand, instead of by machine, which caused delays in machine counting votes, he said. Officials spent four hours reproducing those ballots, McGrane said, because a barcode that scans the ballots identity had been folded. 
“I think one of the contributing factors for them was fatigue,” he said. 
And in southern Idaho’s Canyon County, the state’s second most populated, some voters waited in lines for four hours to cast their ballot. The last voter there cast their ballot into the next day — at 12:20 a.m. the day after Election Day, McGrane said. He said the county needs more polling locations and equipment.
But McGrane said other counties also saw long lines — partly driven by the length of the ballot, which sometimes spanned three or four pages. 
 What Idaho election auditors found in counties

Idaho Secretary of State’s Office Voting System Specialist Dan Lee overviewed how state election officials came to different counts on handfuls of votes across eight counties they audited.
Several of those came down to how voters expressed their vote. 
Instead of filling in the bubbles to the left of candidate names, some voters filled in candidates’ political party affiliation abbreviation, which is marked between parenthetical marks that somewhat resemble a bubble. 
An example of a mismarked ballot in the 2026 Idaho general election, as shown in a slideshow by the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office on Nov. 24, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
The discrepancy wasn’t enough to swing the races that the secretary of state slated for audits. 
In Adams County, for instance, state officials said they would’ve counted 11 votes in the attorney general’s races that local election officials tossed. Four of those would’ve gone to Democrat Lori Hickman, and seven would’ve gone to Republican incumbent Raúl Labrador, who won reelection. 
But the audits don’t change the results of the races, McGrane said, so those changes won’t show up in the election results. 
Still, he said, the audits highlighted an issue for his office to address.
“Overwhelmingly, every election voters follow the instructions and fill out the … box appropriately, including in these audits,” McGrane said.  “… But there’s enough of these, and when you look at the instructions, I think there’s more clarity that we can provide in the instructions to help drive the voters to make the mark where they’re supposed to.”
In Benewah County, a rural county that hand tallies election results and was the last to finish reporting election results the morning after the election, state officials flagged a number of issues related to the handling, tallying and documentation of election results. 
In that county, state officials audited the results of a nonbinding statewide vote to endorse a state gun.
McGrane, who chooses which races are audited in each county, pointed out how few voters weighed in on that question.
“More people skipped it than voted for the first choice,” McGrane said, referencing the winning gun, the Winchester Model 1873. 
“And it was titled ‘Gun that Won the West,” Lee soon added.
“That also helps,” McGrane said.
