name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Rep. Gaskey going to court to halt certification of election results
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: Gaskey is trailing Democratic challenger Sarah Hewins by 60 votes following recounts in Wareham and Carver.
text:
REPUBLICAN REP. JOHN GASKEY says he’s heading to court to try to halt the certification of November’s election results, a move that could in turn hit pause on a districtwide recount in the 2nd Plymouth House district that he also sought. 
Gaskey is trailing Democratic challenger Sarah Hewins by 60 votes following recounts in Wareham and Carver. That margin is less than half a percentage point of the total vote count, or 94 votes, according to Secretary of State William Galvin’s office. As a result, the race appears to be eligible for a districtwide recount, pending certification by Gov. Maura Healey and the Governor’s Council, Galvin spokesperson Deb O’Malley said. That recount, which Gaskey previously filed for, would occur in Middleborough — the only precinct in the district whose votes have not yet been recounted. 
But Gaskey’s attorney Michael Walsh told the News Service he plans to seek a temporary restraining order in Plymouth Superior Court to halt election certification and seek a preliminary injunction in connection with concerns about voting.
“We’re filing a court case that is going to seek to appeal some of the decisions of the registrars and secretary, arguing that the race is too close to call due to some clerical errors and some legal errors. There’s a voter registration issue, there’ve been some challenged ballots, there are some open questions of law,” Walsh said. “He’s asking for a judge to look over that data and to call a new special election.”
“If we can get the certification delayed, then a judge will be a little bit more willing to make decisions about the ballots in either direction,” Walsh said.
Asked about what data they have proving their claims, Walsh said that a volunteer put together spreadsheets that show hundreds of errors, based on things like voter registration, in Carver and Wareham. Their data comparisons of Carver showed five people “who voted in Carver who probably shouldn’t have,” Walsh said. Around 3:40 p.m. on Tuesday, Walsh said they received Wareham data and were going over it. 
“We need to find enough errors about the counting or who was entitled to vote to eat the margin of victory,” Walsh said. “In terms of determining whether or not there’s a real or viable case, we need to confirm that it makes enough of a legitimate difference to go before a judge.”
Walsh said they plan to file in court on Wednesday morning. 
Vote totals provided by Galvin’s office show that Gaskey won his hometown of Carver and precincts in Middleborough, while Hewins won Wareham. Updated figures following a recount in Wareham on November 20 show that Gaskey received 4,580 votes compared to Hewins’s 5,266. Hewins lost 66 votes and Gaskey lost 17 votes in the recount compared to initial numbers, per Galvin’s office.
A recount in Carver on November 23 reported that Gaskey received 2,822 votes to Hewins’s 2,617. In Middleborough, Gaskey received 1,897 votes to Hewins’s 1,476. 
“As far as my feelings go, it’s pins and needles. Whatever happens, happens. I’m looking forward to resolution of this, but with regards to the recount, I think this is an important democratic process that we really need to undertake,” Gaskey told the News Service. Asked if he believes he won the race, and for his perspective on the tight margin, Gaskey said, “Yes, there’s a belief that potentially — I really don’t know what to believe at this point.”
“Inside, I’m like, there’s no way. I won,” he said. “Sitting down and looking at the reality on the ground, the clerical errors that were happening in Wareham through this whole thing really brought a lot of questions about how the ballots were handled, about who was actually voting and the procedure all the way around. That’s really where we’re focused right now. Are there people voting in this race that were not supposed to be voting in it?” 
The council and Healey plan to certify the 2026 election results on Tuesday, December 1 at 12:30 p.m., according to O’Malley. Once they’re certified, Galvin will look at the results and determine whether the difference between candidates in the 2nd Plymouth race is within a half of a percent. If that’s the case, he’d order a recount in whatever precinct hasn’t yet been recounted, which is Middleborough.
“If the Wareham data comes back and they don’t have enough to make the margin, then we have no margin and we’re flat-out,” Walsh said. “I told Gaskey at the very start that this was a long shot.”
Since Galvin can only order a districtwide recount if the election results are certified, what happens in Middleborough depends on what Gaskey files and what the court decides, O’Malley said, adding, “We intend to certify, unless ordered otherwise, next Tuesday.”
Hewins is aware of the potential for a Middleborough recount, but had no additional comments when informed about Gaskey’s legal plans.
“My understanding is we’re still 60 votes ahead. Whatever comes next, I can’t wait to be the district’s next representative and get things done,” she said. “That’s really important. I’m eager to get in there and start getting things done regardless of how long it takes.”

title: Idaho state employees receive additional paid day off Friday following Thanksgiving

text:
The Idaho State Capitol is reflected in the Joe R. Williams building on March 21, 2021. (File photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho state employees will receive an additional paid day of leave from work on Friday following the Thanksgiving holiday, Gov. Brad Little announced Monday.

(Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)A new report from one of the lead advocates for opening New Mexico’s primary elections to independent voters credited its outreach strategy for a significant turnout boost in the June 2 election. The primary marked the state’s first-ever foray into allowing independent and “decline to state voters” to cast ballots for one of the state’s two major parties. Previously, those voters would have to either sit out the primaries or register as a Democrat or Republican before or on election day to participate. 
However, voters registered with third parties still had to change their registrations to either “decline to state,” or to one of the major parties in order to participate, which makes New Mexico’s primary “semi” versus fully open. States with fully open primaries allow any registered voter to vote in any party’s primary without being a member of that party. Twenty states hold fully open primaries, according to the Independent Voter Project.  
In the months leading up to the primary, Let Us Vote New Mexico, the local chapter of the national Open Primaries Organization, tried to reach as many independent voters as possible. They procured voter lists and devised media campaigns that aimed to inform the state’s roughly 410,000 independent voters about their new right. 
In the end, 11% of independent voters — about 47,000 people — cast ballots in the primary, according to the report. That’s far higher than the 5% turnout Open Primaries President John Opdycke told Source NM he was expecting. 
“I was hoping we could move the needle by a couple percentage points,” Opdycke said in an interview Monday. “I mean, we’re up against a culture in America where even in states that have had open primaries for decades, most people don’t vote in the primaries.” 
Opdycke credits his organization’s phone outreach to a little more than 125,000 voters as one reason independents cast ballots. 
By the #s: New Mexico’s growing independent voter base

According to the report from his organization, independent voters Let Us Vote New Mexico contacted turned out at a rate of 23.8%, compared with 16.5% of those the organization did not contact. Both groups of independents had voted in the 2024 election.
While Opdycke and other report authors stressed that their study is not based on a randomized sample and therefore is not scientific, the difference in turnout represents the “strongest comparison available and a meaningful one” and serves as a baseline to compare future elections against. 
He also said the 11% turnout was surprising given the lack of buy-in from county clerks across the state. With just days before early voting started, 20 of 33 county clerk websites did not prominently mention the change. 
“I don’t know the county clerks and how underfunded they are. I’m sure there’s good reasons,” he said. “But it just was disappointing to see how something so simple became so hard.”
But overall, the state’s first-ever semi-open primary was a success, he said, and marked the beginning of a change in the way campaigns are run in the state and what kinds of candidates are successful. 
“It’s going to change how candidates talk about themselves, how candidates market themselves, and who they reach out to,” he said. “Independents are now part of the equation.”

name: VTDigger
title: A wreath to remember veterans lost
description:
As December grows nearer, Wreaths Across America still needs sponsors to help it cover every veteran’s grave in Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A wreath to remember veterans lost.
text:
Green Mount Cemetery in Montpelier in January 2021. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

When Susan Sweetser first came to lay a wreath on her daughter’s grave, the graves outnumbered the wreaths that she and fellow volunteers planned to lay throughout the cemetery.
So Sweetser took out her phone and began to record the scene: snowflakes tumbling from a dark gray sky, a tiny gathering of people by the many headstones surrounding them.
“I think that video helped, like, get people to feel what it felt like being there with so few people, so few wreaths,” said Sweetser, who posted the video on social media to raise awareness. “And every year since then, we’ve had more and more wreaths sponsored.”
Since her first time participating in the ceremony, Sweetser founded the Vermont Veteran Moms group for Wreaths Across America, a nationwide organization that aims to lay a wreath on every veteran’s grave in the country in a ceremony before Christmas each year.  The nationwide ceremony began in 2008, and every year since, Congress proclaims one Saturday each December as National Wreaths Across America Day. This year, the date is Dec. 19.
The ceremony is a chance for the larger community to band together and honor the people who fought for the country.
Last year, the group reached a major milestone, covering every headstone at participating cemeteries across Vermont. Vermont is 1,840 wreaths away from its goal — just over 10,000 wreaths — as of Tuesday, according to Sweetser.
Since Sweetser’s first year involved in the organization, she’s seen more people get involved. It’s typical of Vermonters to participate in things like this, she said.
“We’re a community of people,” Sweetser said. “We have our differences, but at the end of the day, it’s like fighting with your sister.”
The participating cemeteries are Bennington’s Vermont Veterans Home, Randolph’s Vermont Veterans Memorial Cemetery, St. Albans Cemetery, Fort Ethan Allen Cemetery, Norwich University Cemetery and cemeteries in Stamford, Cornwall and in the Townshend area, according to a press release from Nov. 8. St. Albans is the cemetery that she worries most about covering this year, according to Sweetser. Each wreath costs $17, and the deadline for sponsoring wreaths is Tuesday, Dec. 1.
Organizers need additional wreaths this year because more cemeteries are taking part, Sweetser said. 
For her, the initiative is a way to turn her grief into purpose. She lost her daughter, Virginia “Ginny” Sweetser, to suicide in 2020. Ginny Sweetser was a veteran of the Iraq war, deployed there while serving in the Army Reserves. She drove heavy equipment transporters in Iraq and transferred to the Vermont Army National Guard upon her return.
“When she came home, she was just changed,” Sweetser said. “She was changed, and she struggled with PTSD for 15 years.”
Ginny Sweetser tried to transform her struggles with PTSD into a way to help others, Sweetser said, by becoming a licensed clinical social worker. But while helping her own clients, she still searched for help for years. And the Covid-19 pandemic was a difficult time for her.
“She saved lots of other people’s lives,” Sweetser said. “But she couldn’t save her own.”
Getting involved in Wreaths Across America didn’t take away Sweetser’s grief. But it was something to focus on, a place to turn that pain into action. And Sweetser and her fellow volunteers have become a powerful organizing force, according to Robert Burke, director of the Vermont Office of Veterans Affairs.
“They get out there and they spread the word,” Burke said. “You know, they do radio, they do print, they do, you know, everything and anything.”
Although Wreaths Across America has been around for years, the ceremony became more popular in Vermont around five years ago, according to Collin Johnson, the cemetery operational administrator at the Vermont Veterans Memorial Cemetery in Randolph Center. Covid-19 may also have played a role in increasing support, he said.
“It was something that people could go and do outside in the community,” Johnson said. “They felt like they were part of something bigger, and you know, it was during a time where nobody was really getting out and socializing.”
Returning volunteers have found creative ways to handle wreaths, Johnson added.
“They never used to do this,” Johnson said, “but now people bring like big sleds to carry the boxes and the wreaths on, or they’ll bring like kitchen brooms to put the wreaths on the stick to carry them around. You know, people will bring plastic-edged shovels to clear the flat stones off.”
Sweetser is touched by all the community members who may not have personally known the veterans they come to honor. For one brief instant, she sees politics and differences fall away, replaced by simple remembrance.
“Everybody is there together as one big, beautiful community to say thank you for your service.”
If you are in crisis or need help for someone else, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline) or text VT to 741741 for the Crisis Text Line.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: 2 refugees who settled in Providence join nationwide legal challenge to Medicaid cuts for immigrants
description: Two men who fled from Africa to Providence to escape war in their respective homelands of Congo and Sudan are among five lawfully present immigrants suing the Trump administration over their recent loss of Medicaid coverage resulting from changes under H.R. 1. The proposed nationwide class action lawsuit filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court for […]
text:
A Brown University Medicaid fellow holds informational materials detailing federal changes to Medicaid during community outreach in Providence on Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Two men who fled from Africa to Providence to escape war in their respective homelands of Congo and Sudan are among five lawfully present immigrants suing the Trump administration over their recent loss of Medicaid coverage resulting from changes under H.R. 1.
The proposed nationwide class action lawsuit filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island centers around restrictions on some noncitizens’ Medicaid coverage that took effect Oct. 1. 
The 37-page complaint — filed by a team of lawyers from the National Health Law Program, the ACLU of Rhode Island and the Lawyers’ Committee for Rhode Island — argues that these restrictions were placed into law without removing a stipulation meant to protect coverage for Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients. 
The five plaintiffs — including one plaintiff each in Illinois, South Carolina and Missouri — are all lawfully present in the United States and receive SSI payments monthly. The means-tested federal program limits eligibility to older adults and people with disabilities who have smaller incomes and resources. Monthly payments are up to $994 for an individual and $1,491 for a couple. Federal maximum rates are set to rise to $1,029 for an individual and $1,544 for a couple in January. 
One Rhode Island plaintiff, identified as A.W.M., is a 69-year-old man living with his wife and two minor children. According to the complaint, A.W.M. fled Sudan because of the ongoing civil war, and stopped in Chad and Cameroon before arriving in the U.S. in February 2024. 
His green card application is pending, and he began qualifying for SSI payments in August 2024. He and his wife have a combined monthly income of less than $2,400. They pay $1,500 in rent. 
Before his Medicaid coverage ended on Oct. 1, he relied on the benefits for management of issues including knee pain, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and prostate and stomach pain. 
According to the complaint, A.W.M. missed a doctor’s appointment last week because it would have cost $985.65 without insurance — a bill that would have essentially consumed his entire $987 monthly SSI payment. 
“He is scared of what will happen when he is no longer able to afford his medications because, if left untreated or unmedicated, he could get very sick or die,” the suit reads.
The other Rhode Island plaintiff is a 77-year-old refugee from the Republic of Congo, identified as G.M., who fled war in his country with his family. G.M. arrived with his wife and son in the U.S. in April 2024, and his only income source is a monthly SSI check under $500.
“Their monthly income covers their rent and utilities, but they already rely on food pantries for food, as they do not have enough money for food, let alone for medical care,” the complaint writes of G.M. and his family.
G.M., according to the filing, now takes his daily blood pressure medication only two or three times a week, less than the prescribed once-per-day. He has also had to forfeit his regular visits to an optometrist for vision issues, including an Oct. 14 appointment he canceled because he could not pay the $150. 
“If his vision problems remain undiagnosed and untreated, he could go completely blind,” the complaint states. 
The complaint names as its defendants the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, and the agencies’ respective leaders, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Mehmet Oz. 
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday. 
Brown students take to the streets to help Rhode Islanders navigate Medicaid changes

H.R. 1, the sweeping federal tax and spending law which became law in July 2025, narrowed eligibility for federally funded Medicaid benefits based on immigration status. But H.R. 1 did not actually repeal or amend a separate federal provision which protects SSI recipients’ Medicaid. The law dates back to 1997 and requires states to extend Medicaid eligibility to noncitizens who receive SSI benefits, as long as these noncitizens are subject to the same terms as citizen SSI recipients. 
Fewer than 2,000 Rhode Islanders were deemed ineligible for Medicaid coverage under the Oct. 1 restrictions on noncitizens, Kerri White, a spokesperson for the Rhode Island Executive Office of Health and Human Services, said in an email Tuesday. How many of these individuals also receive SSI was not immediately available.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) issued guidance on April 8 that H.R. 1 did not amend this SSI safeguard. But the agency stated it would no longer supply matching funds for Medicaid for certain noncitizen SSI recipients — a distinction important in the government’s view, because joint funding between states and the federal government is part of what constitutes Medicaid. 
H.R. 1 “did not clearly and unambiguously alter the fundamental structure of the Medicaid program, whose ‘cornerstone’ is ‘financial contribution by both the Federal Government and the participating State,’” the CMS guidance reads, quoting an earlier court precedent. “[W]e would not consider health coverage that a state opts to continue to provide with 100 percent state-only funds to be Medicaid.”
The CMS guidance also argues there was nothing in the provision’s legislative history suggesting “a clear Congressional intent to require that states provide full Medicaid benefits to qualified noncitizens without receiving federal matching funds for that coverage.”
The lawsuit seeks to temporarily and permanently block the disputed policy nationwide. It follows on the heels of a similar legal challenge in Washington state that resulted in a Sept. 30 preliminary injunction protecting Medicaid coverage for more than 800 residents of that state.
The court also needs to certify the suit’s proposed class before the case can proceed as a class action.
The complaint adds that the Department of U.S. Health and Human Services “is in sole possession of the information regarding the total number of potential class members across the country.”
The case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge Mary S. McElroy.

title: Human rights groups sue ICE alleging detention of pregnant, nursing immigrants
description: The Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and several other groups filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement alleging that the agency is illegally detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants against its own policies. The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the[...]
text:
Federal immigration officers are shown at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in March. A lawsuit filed by advocacy organizations alleges the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is violating a 2021 directive by detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing women. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)The Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and several other groups filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement alleging that the agency is illegally detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants against its own policies.
The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, cites a 2021 ICE directive, which states that agents “should not detain, arrest, or take into custody for an administrative violation” anyone who is known to be pregnant, postpartum or nursing.
According to the complaint, ICE has stopped tracking the number of women who are pregnant, postpartum or nursing and being held in detention under the Trump administration. But one of the plaintiff organizations — the Women’s Refugee Commission — obtained data through a Freedom of Information Act request. Those documents showed an increase of pregnant women in ICE detention between January 2025 and March 2026 from nine to 128, or a 1,320% increase, the complaint states.
The length of detention for pregnant women has also increased substantially, according to the complaint.
“Since 2025, ICE detained more than 557 pregnant women for an average of 43 days,” the complaint reads. “Nearly 14% of these women were detained for 90 days or longer, with one woman detained for 219 days, almost seven months of her pregnancy.”
ICE did not immediately respond to a Stateline request for comment.
Mayors describe ICE presence in their cities

The complaint details the experience of one woman detained in Kentucky, who asked for emergency assistance because she was pregnant and had been bleeding for more than a day. She eventually miscarried while shackled to a hospital bed, according to the document. Another woman who was detained in her third trimester of a high-risk pregnancy was told by ICE officers they would “take her baby away forever” after she gave birth, and she waived her right to see an immigration judge out of fear and was quickly deported, the lawsuit said. Others who are nursing have been separated from their infants and denied breast pumps, the complaint says.
The 2021 directive also prohibited the use of GPS ankle monitors on this population of women if they were granted supervised release, but the complaint says women are being forced to wear them anyway, which one woman said is making her high blood pressure worse. Another, who was nursing an infant at the time, said she couldn’t receive treatment for a painful hernia while the ankle monitor was attached because of burn risks in the operating room.
A hearing in the case will likely be scheduled in the coming weeks. The plaintiffs are asking the court to declare that the 2021 directive is still effective and order the agencies to comply with the policy.
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: New SC senator taps former governor, GOP state senator and Dem Party chairs to help transition
description: U.S. Sen.-elect Annie Andrews announced a transition team that includes a former GOP state senator and South Carolina's last Democratic governor.
text:
Dr. Annie Andrews celebrated with supporters in downtown Charleston Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, as the Associated Press declared her the winner of South Carolina's U.S. Senate Race. Behind Andrews is Jaime Harrison, the former chair of the Democratic National Committee. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)The people advising U.S. Sen.-elect Annie Andrews ahead of her taking office include a former GOP state senator, South Carolina’s last Democratic governor, Columbia’s former mayor, and current and former state party leaders.
Andrews announced her seven-person transition committee Tuesday. They will help Andrews recruit her staff and prepare for her Jan. 3 swearing in, when she’ll become the first Democrat in 22 years to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate. 
South Carolina voters elected Andrews earlier this month over Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed in July following the death of her brother Sen. Lindsey Graham.
Andrews flipped the seat with 51% of the vote, according to certified election data.
Her transition team includes former state Sen. Katrina Shealy, R-Lexington, who has been sidelined by her party since losing her re-election bid in 2024. The Senate’s only chairwoman was among three GOP female senators ousted after voting against the state’s 2023 law banning most abortions past six weeks gestation and helping to block a ban from conception.

Sen. Katrina Shealy, R-Lexington, holds up Wednesday, June 26, 2024, with white gloves the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award given in fall 2023 to the five bipartisan “sister senators” who helped block a near-total abortion ban. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

Saying she still has “a lot to give,” the former chairwoman of the Lexington County GOP brought bipartisan support to campaigns this year. 
On July 30, she introduced Rep. Jermaine Johnson, Democrats’ nominee for governor, as he announced his pick for a running mate. She didn’t officially endorse him until Oct. 23.   
That same week, she endorsed Andrews over Graham for U.S. Senate.  
“I’m grateful to this bipartisan group of South Carolina leaders for coming together as we work to build the strongest, most effective Senate office our state has ever seen,” Andrews said in Tuesday’s release. 
Andrews flipped the seat with the help of independents and Republicans splitting their ticket. She was the only Democrat to win statewide office and the first to do so in 20 years. Her margin of victory — at 4.5 percentage points — was the same as Gov.-elect Alan Wilson, according to election results. 
Andrews intentionally reached out to Republicans during her campaign. Her efforts included a TV ad released in mid-September with her dad, a Republican. During her only debate with Graham, she emphasized growing up in a Republican household. 

Former Democratic National Committee and state Democratic Party Chair Jaime Harrison takes the stage at the Annie Andrews watch party at the Charleston Marriott on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

Since her win three weeks ago, Andrews said she’s met with Wilson, Graham, and South Carolina’s senior U.S. senator, Tim Scott.
Democrats on the committee
Democrats make up the other six members of Andrews’ transition team.
They include former Gov. Jim Hodges, the last Democrat to win the governor’s office in South Carolina. 
In a TV ad released a week before Election Day, Hodges and the Republican he ousted in 1998, Gov. David Beasley, appeared together to endorse Andrews. 
Two state Democratic Party chairs are on the team: Current Chair Christale Spain and Jaime Harrison, the former chair who in 2020 lost his bid to oust Lindsey Graham. 
Harrison then became chairman of the Democratic National Committee from 2021 to 2025. 

State Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain talks to other supporters of Annie Andrews at her election night watch party at the Charleston Marriott in downtown Charleston on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

The other former elected officeholder on the team is Columbia Mayor Steve Benjamin, who decided in 2021 not to seek a fourth term. In 2023, President Joe Biden made Benjamin his senior adviser. 
Two political strategists who worked on Andrews’ campaign will continue helping in the transition: Senior adviser Antjuan Seawright, CEO of Blueprint Strategy whose previous clients include Hillary Clinton and the state Senate Democratic Caucus; and AJ Lenar, co-founder of Declaration Media.
Transition website and resume request
Andrews also announced Tuesday the launch of a website about the transition process.
On the website is a portal for people to upload their resumes if they are interested in a job with the senator-elect’s office. Job descriptions will be posted at a later time, the website reads.

title: Republican lawmaker files bill to replace Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion program
description: Arkansas lawmakers may consider replacing the state’s Medicaid expansion program with traditional Medicaid during the legislative session that starts in January. Senate Bill 9, which Green Forest Republican Sen. Bryan King filed Friday, proposes ending the expansion program known as Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me, or ARHOME, at the end of 2027.  ARHO[...]
text:
Arkansas lawmakers may consider replacing the state’s Medicaid expansion program with traditional Medicaid during the legislative session that starts in January.  (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas lawmakers may consider replacing the state’s Medicaid expansion program with traditional Medicaid during the legislative session that starts in January.
Senate Bill 9, which Green Forest Republican Sen. Bryan King filed Friday, proposes ending the expansion program known as Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me, or ARHOME, at the end of 2027. 
ARHOME uses Medicaid money to purchase private insurance for the program. King’s bill would move expansion individuals to fee-for-service coverage, meaning the state pays healthcare providers directly for their services. 
SB 9 is the first bill filed for the 2027 session that addresses the future of Medicaid expansion in Arkansas. The program has been up in the air since July, when the federal government rejected the state’s request to extend ARHOME for another five years starting in January.
Arkansas will bolster services for kids with disabilities after public outcry over long waitlist

Last year’s federal tax and spending cut legislation known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act requires special Medicaid programs, such as ARHOME, not to cost the federal government more than would be projected without them.
King said in a phone call Tuesday that he has long supported a fee-for-service model, which he said is less expensive than the state’s Medicaid expansion program. 
“With it being more expensive, it crowds out other things in Medicaid that could be funded, like the CES waiver,” he said. 
The Community and Employment Services Medicaid waiver offers community-based services to people with disabilities, according to the Arkansas Department of Human Services. The state announced in September that it would bolster services for kids with disabilities after facing a public outcry over a long waitlist of more than 2,400 families. 
More than 800,000 low-income and disabled Arkansans receive some form of Medicaid coverage. As of Nov. 1, nearly 209,000 receive expansion coverage.
Arkansas officials asked the Trump administration to extend the expansion program for two years while the state formulates a new Medicaid model. The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced this month that the program will remain active until June 30, 2027.
Six months is not long enough to transfer all Medicaid expansion enrollees to either managed care or fee-for-service Medicaid, state Division of Medical Services Director Elizabeth Pitman told lawmakers Nov. 10.
Arkansas still set to enforce Medicaid work requirements Jan. 1 despite option of 6 extra months

Arkansas’ first-of-its-kind expansion model uses Medicaid money to purchase private insurance for beneficiaries. In 2013, Arkansas adopted the hybrid model as an alternative to expanding Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act.
The compromise passed the Republican-led Legislature and was signed into law by then-Gov. Mike Beebe, a Democrat, making Arkansas the first southern state to expand Medicaid.
Republicans won the governor’s office and expanded their majorities in 2014 with several lawmakers, including King, running on a promise to kill Medicaid expansion.
The program has remained in place, and Arkansas was the first state to impose work requirements on Medicaid expansion. More than 18,000 Arkansans lost coverage before a federal judge blocked the policy in 2019. The state launched ARHOME without work requirements on Jan. 1, 2022.
The federal government is implementing work requirements for Medicaid enrollees next year. Arkansas plans to enforce work requirements starting Jan. 1, despite the federal government allowing states six more months to put the mandate in place.
Deputy Editor Antoinette Grajeda contributed to this report.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Hoeven touts permitting reform bill for lowering housing costs
description: U.S. Sen. John Hoeven says a bipartisan permitting reform bill that recently passed the Senate will help lower costs and ease inflation for homebuyers and builders. The bill is meant to address “massive quality of life issues,” said Hoeven, R-N.D. A key issue is helping young people afford their first house, build equity and work […]
text:
U.S. Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., discusses permitting reform in a news conference Nov. 24, 2026, at a home under remodel in Bismarck. North Dakota Petroleum Council President Ron Ness, left, and Boulder Homes owner Joe Hillerson, right, listen. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)U.S. Sen. John Hoeven says a bipartisan permitting reform bill that recently passed the Senate will help lower costs and ease inflation for homebuyers and builders.
The bill is meant to address “massive quality of life issues,” said Hoeven, R-N.D. A key issue is helping young people afford their first house, build equity and work up to their dream home, he said at a press conference held in a home being remodeled in north Bismarck.
“This is one of the biggest issues we face, is we’ve got to find ways to produce more homes and make them more affordable,” the senator said.
The bill is called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The Senate passed the bill on Thursday in a 62-33 vote, sending it to the House in the lame-duck period of Congress before Democrats take control in January.
Bill to reduce regulations on building energy infrastructure passes US Senate

Permitting has delayed $1.1 trillion of projects around the U.S., Hoeven said. Government regulations make up about 25% of the costs for building single-family homes and 40% for apartments, he said. Timelines and approvals drive up the costs, he said. The legislation aims to reduce those burdens, such as reducing the time periods for environmental reviews, he said. 
Opponents say the bill will weaken the National Environmental Policy Act and hurt Native American tribes in the consultation process. 
The bill also includes legislation by Hoeven to streamline permitting of oil and gas on lands where the federal government owns no surface acres and less than half the mineral acres, leaving the state to permit wells, he said. The state permits an oil well in about 40 days, while the feds take more than nine months, Hoeven said.
Another piece by Hoeven enables and expedites permitting of geothermal wells for heating, he said. 
Those provisions are estimated to save 3.5% to 7% on energy costs, Hoeven said.
The bill also requires data centers to cover the cost of electricity they use and building of transmission infrastructure, meant as protections for neighborhoods and ratepayers, Hoeven said.
Joe Hillerson, owner of Boulder Homes in Bismarck-Mandan, said he hopes the bill is the beginning of a framework for easier development. 
“This addresses developing, land development, getting more lots online for cheaper, quicker, so I’m hoping that is what ends up happening,” Hillerson said. “We’d love to see the cost of our home come down. It seems like affordability is at an all-time low, even for rent.” 
The timeline for when consumers could see benefits, should the bill become law, is hard to predict, Hoeven said. He said relief could be felt immediately or in the near term of months, similar to how diesel and gasoline prices have dropped since the Nov. 3 election.
“My point is you can’t always specify the timing,” he said. “What you’ve got to do is put the right policies in place and then pursue them relentlessly, and it will happen.”
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Jury acquits former state DCF worker of sexually assaulting a minor
description:
A trial in the case took place last week with jurors returning the not guilty verdicts on all charges on Friday.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Jury acquits former state DCF worker of sexually assaulting a minor.
text:
The Chittenden County Superior criminal court in Burlington on Tuesday, July 25, 2023. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

A former state Department for Children and Families employee accused of sexually assaulting a youth has been acquitted of all charges.
Sonja Herman, 33, of Swanton, had faced charges of sexual assault on a minor entrusted in her care and sexual exploitation of a minor, according to court records. 
Herman was arraigned in the case in 2024 following an investigation that spanned several months after authorities received in 2023 the report of an alleged sexual relationship between Herman and the youth.  
The Chittenden Unit for Special Investigations stated it was referred a case from the Vermont Department for Children and Families regarding the alleged sexual abuse of a minor that began when he was in DCF custody.
A trial took place last week in Chittenden Superior criminal court with the jury returning not guilty verdicts on the charges Friday.
“You never know really what convinces a jury but I think it was a reflection of the relative weakness of the state’s evidence,” Robert Kaplan, Herman’s attorney, said Tuesday. “The jury reached the verdict that we hoped and expected they would.”
Kaplan said his client did not testify during the trial. He said the jury deliberated about 90 minutes over parts of two days.
“Sonja Herman is very relieved to put these allegations behind her and be able to move on with her life,” Kaplan said.  
Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George, whose office prosecuted the case, stated in an email Tuesday that she appreciated the time and energy the jurors put into the trial.
“It was an emotionally exhausting case but they maintained incredible attention to the details and took care with the evidence,” George said. 
“These cases are very complicated, and the State’s burden is incredibly high,” George added. “Being the triers of fact is a very difficult task, and although it was not the outcome we hoped for, we absolutely respect it.”
Investigators had alleged that Herman had a sexual relationship that spanned several years with a youth in DCF custody.  
According to charging documents, Herman, who had worked as a DCF family services worker at the time, did not directly supervise the youth she was charged with assaulting.
However, the documents alleged that Herman was involved in his care plan and available as an emergency care social worker when his social worker wasn’t available.
VTDigger attempted to reach officials with DCF for comment about Herman’s past employment there but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hinds DA candidate has history of not filing campaign finance reports
description: Campaign sign for attorney Darla Palmer, located at the intersection of Northside Drive and California Avenue, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in Jackson. Palmer is running for Hinds County District Attorney along with four other candidates.
text:
Darla Palmer, who topped a crowded slate of candidates vying to become Hinds County’s next district attorney, could be blocked from taking office if she wins Tuesday’s runoff unless she files long-overdue state-mandated financial reports showing how much money she spent and received during a previous campaign for the post. 
Palmer, a defense attorney, led the five-candidate field during the Nov. 3 special election, receiving roughly 3,000 more votes than her closest rival, Gwen Agho. Both are competing to finish out the term of former Hinds DA Jody Owens, who resigned over the summer after pleading guilty to a federal corruption charge.
Palmer has previously run for Hinds DA in 2019 and 2023, losing to Owens in both attempts. Since she first ran, Mississippi Today found that Palmer did not file or was late in filing the majority of the required reports under the state’s campaign finance laws. 
“My biggest thing is my stuff is an oversight,” she said in an interview. “It has nothing to do with holding out so that people won’t know who is giving me money, ‘cause I just don’t have a lot of donors.”
Darla Palmer, a private attorney running to be Hinds County District Attorney, in her office on County Line Road on Nov. 19, 2026. Credit: Molly Minta/Mississippi Today
Her failure to file timely reports has resulted in the Mississippi Ethics Commission fining Palmer nine times since she first ran for office, for a total of $3,700 in penalties. 
The Ethics Commission could not find any records showing how much, if any, of those fines were paid. 
Under state law, candidates who do not file campaign disclosure reports within 10 days of the deadline can be fined $50 a day for up to ten days, yielding a maximum fine of $500. 
State law bars candidates who have not submitted all their required reports from taking office. If a candidate has not filed all their required reports within the past five years, they could be prevented from appearing on the ballot. 
But the Secretary of State’s Office did not check to see whether Palmer had any outstanding reports before she was certified to run in the special election because it was not part of the office’s protocol, spokesperson Liz Jonson wrote in an email. 
“In order to prevent this from occurring again in the future, this office has added campaign finance checks to the internal checklist for all future candidates,” Jonson wrote. 
Mississippi’s confusing and poorly enforced election laws are ill-equipped to address a case like Palmer’s, according to three election law experts who spoke to Mississippi Today. 
Sam Begley, a Jackson-based attorney who has advised candidates on their campaign reports, called Palmer’s repeated failure to file “egregious.”
“Most candidates, particularly when you get high up on the food chain like this, tend to be more fastidious,” he said. 
Tom Hood, the Ethics Commission’s executive director, said it’s not unusual for candidates to file late reports or ignore commission fines. He said the lax enforcement of Mississippi’s campaign laws persists because no single agency is responsible for it. 
While his agency is responsible for levying fines against campaign finance violators, the Ethics Commission depends on the Secretary of State’s Office, which collects campaign finance reports, to tell them who has violated the law. 
Hinds DA candidate Gwen Agho is vying in a Dec. 1 runoff election. Credit: Courtesy of Gwen Agho campaign
“The whole thing is a mess,” Hood said. “The law is a mess. The system between us and the Secretary of State’s Office – it’s a mess.”
Hood doesn’t point fingers at the Secretary of State’s Office.
“You just can’t have two agencies doing the same thing at the same time,” he said. “You’re just asking for confusion. The whole thing is very frustrating.” 
The Mississippi Attorney General’s Office is supposed to pursue the fines from Palmer, but a spokesperson said the office could not find any record of the Ethics Commission reporting the outstanding fines to them. 
Palmer told Mississippi Today she didn’t know she had unpaid fines. 
“You’re kidding,” she said. 
Another fine is pending. Prior to the Nov. 3 election, Palmer was the only candidate among the five candidates on the ballot who failed to file the mandated preelection report by the deadline, resulting in the Secretary of State’s Office recommending the Ethics Commission levy a $500 fine. 
Palmer filed the report, as well as a Nov. 24 report required ahead of the Dec. 1 runoff, after Mississippi Today asked her about it. She said she was working to pay the Ethics Commission fines and file her outstanding reports from 2023. 
“I’m usually always a little behind,” she said. 
In her 2019 campaign, records show Palmer filed her first report 19 days late, prompting state elections officials to recommend a $500 fine. Palmer said she contested the fine because her father had recently died, but the Ethics Commission’s records do not show that she sought a waiver. 
Palmer then filed two periodic reports and a preelection report on time, before failing to file three subsequent reports. 
In January 2023, Palmer filed an annual report for her 2019 campaign – three years late. 
Palmer would file three more periodic reports – two of which she submitted late – for her 2023 campaign. To date, Palmer has not filed four of the required reports from that election and an annual report that was due in 2025. 
The Ethics Commission will rule on Palmer’s latest fine at its Dec. 4 meeting. 
Should she become district attorney, Palmer would be responsible for prosecuting election law violators at the county and city levels, said Pete Perry, who has certified candidates in his former role as the chair of the Hinds County Republican Party’s executive committee. 
“There’s an irony,” he said.
The deadline for Palmer’s opponents to challenge her qualification on the ballot has passed. But Perry said anyone could challenge Palmer’s election if she wins. 
None of Palmer’s four opponents in the Nov. 3 special election contested her appearance on the ballot before it was approved by the State Board of Election Commissioners. 
Agho said she was unaware of Palmer’s history of campaign finance violations and that she didn’t know she could challenge her opponent’s qualifications.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ residents embrace some vaccines, but not universally, new Rutgers poll shows
description: Most New Jerseyans are confident in the MMR and flu vaccines, but less so when it comes to COVID-19 shots, a new Rutgers poll found.
text:
Most New Jerseyans are confident in the MMR and flu vaccines, but less so when it comes to COVID-19 shots, a new Rutgers poll found. (Photo Illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
New Jerseyans have strong faith in several decades-old vaccines, but less when it comes to the COVID-19 shot — and politics seems to impact their feelings, according to a new poll from Rutgers University.


Some 86% of residents said they were confident in the safety of the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps, and rubella, and 77% felt the same way about influenza immunization, Rutgers found. But only 57% of respondents said they were very or somewhat sure COVID-19 shots were safe, while 20% voiced concerns about it, poll results say.


Commissioned by the Center for Health Equity and Wellbeing, New Jersey’s newly formed public health institute, the poll also showed Democrats are far more confident about vaccine safety than Republicans or independents. People with more education and higher incomes also were more likely to embrace immunization, it found.


“Confidence in long-standing vaccines like MMR and, to some extent, the flu is strong, but the COVID-19 vaccine remains a significant partisan flashpoint nearly six years after its rollout,” Ashley Koning, an assistant professor and director of the Rutgers’ Eagleton Center for Public Interest Polling, said in a press release.


The poll surveyed just over 1,000 adults over several days in late September.


The data was released a week after global health authorities announced that measles was officially endemic again in the United States, following a year of continuous outbreaks around the country, including in Pennsylvania and New York. New Jersey has had several reports of possible measles exposure and two reported cases, but no measles-related deaths in 2026.


Denise Anderson, executive director of the health equity center, said the loss of measles elimination status underscores the need to address misinformation around vaccines. Immunization rates have ebbed in New Jersey and nationwide, prompting concerns for healthcare leaders.


“Public health agencies, health care providers, and community partners must work together to build trust in science. That starts with listening to people’s questions and sharing clear, accurate information in ways that reach them, through channels they use and messengers they trust,” Anderson said in the release.


According to the poll, most New Jerseyans get vaccine information from their doctor or another healthcare expert, while some talk to a pharmacist. Half trust advice from family and friends, while half avoid talking about immunization with these sources.


Residents are also split fairly evenly on whether they trust the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, long considered the leading source of guidance on communicable disease, until President Trump tapped vaccine-skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to lead the health agency that oversees it.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Citing legal concerns, Whitmer orders EGLE to halt Line 5 tunnel permit activity
description: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer announced Tuesday she was putting environmental permit considerations for the Enbridge’s Line 5 tunnel project on ice, until the state can resolve legal questions raised by the state Supreme Court over the summer. The 645-mile pipeline running from northwest Wisconsin to southwest Ontario includes a 4.5 mile dual segment restin[...]
text:
"Shut Down Line 5 - No Tunnel" sign on the grounds of the Michigan Capitol. | Laina G. StebbinsMichigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer announced Tuesday she was putting environmental permit considerations for the Enbridge’s Line 5 tunnel project on ice, until the state can resolve legal questions raised by the state Supreme Court over the summer.
The 645-mile pipeline running from northwest Wisconsin to southwest Ontario includes a 4.5 mile dual segment resting on the bed of the Straits of Mackinac, where Lake Michigan and Lake Huron meet.
At the end of July, the Michigan Supreme Court ordered the Michigan Public Service Commission to revisit its decision to issue a permit for the controversial project. The court ruled that the commission, which regulates Michigan’s energy and utility companies, had not properly considered the environmental harms that could arise from extending the lifespan of the oil pipeline.
In September, the governor directed the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy to examine how the Supreme Court ruling affects its permitting decisions.
This map shows the proposed tunnel and the existing dual pipelines crossing the Straits of Mackinac. | Screenshot from the MPSC Line 5 Issue Brief
Following Whitmer’s announcement, pipeline opponents filed two separate requests for a contested case on a set of permits EGLE approved in July, arguing that the tunnel project posed a serious threat to the environment and the lifeways and cultural resources of Native American tribes in the region.
EGLE has yet to issue a decision on a National Pollution Discharge Elimination System permit, which would allow Enbridge to release up to 6 million gallons of wastewater created during construction into the Great Lakes, after treating it at one of two sites on opposing ends of the Straits of Mackinac.
“Protecting the Great Lakes and the people who depend on them has been a top priority of mine since day one,” Whitmer said in a statement on Tuesday. “I have always said my ultimate goal is to get Line 5 out of the water. Just one spill threatens irreparable damage to our water, our economy, and our way of life. Given what is at stake, and the Michigan Supreme Court’s recent decision, I have directed EGLE to suspend further action on its Line 5 Tunnel Project permits at this time. Michigan will continue to put the protection of our water, environment, public health, and communities first.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
EGLE Strategic Communications Advisor Scott Dean confirmed the department was suspending further permitting action until the legal questions are resolved.
“Taking a step back until we have greater clarity is the right thing to do for the Great Lakes, our natural resources, and the communities whose livelihoods depend on them,” the department said in a statement.
Enbridge spokesperson Ryan Duffy said the Michigan Supreme Court’s decision to revoke the permit from the public service commission had introduced new uncertainty as the company aims to secure the permits needed to move forward with the tunnel, “even as the permitting record remains strong.”
“The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy issued permits in July 2026 and previously in 2021. Both permitting rounds included detailed technical reviews, public meetings, hearings, and consideration of thousands of public comments,” Duffy said in a statement. “They also involved extensive interaction between Michigan’s tribal leaders and state agencies.”
Photo by Laina G. Stebbins
The fight against Line 5 has stretched on for years, with tribal nations and environmental advocates calling for the pipeline to be shut down.
“This decision is not the finish line,” Whitney Gravelle, president of the Bay Mills Indian Community said. “Our responsibility to protect the Great Lakes does not end with a pause in permitting. Tribal Nations have been here since time immemorial, and we will be here long after any corporation has come and gone. We must keep fighting for our waters, demand that our voices are heard, and ensure that decisions affecting our homelands respect our rights and responsibilities. The future of the Great Lakes must be shaped by those who have care for these waters, not by the interests of corporations seeking to profit from them. We have a responsibility to future generations, and we will not stop speaking up or standing up for the Great Lakes.”
In response to concerns that the pipeline may rupture, spilling crude oil into the Great Lakes, Enbridge agreed to replace the dual pipelines with a new segment, housed within a utility tunnel buried beneath the lakebed.
In her 2018 campaign for governor, Whitmer promised to take action against the pipeline, later revoking and terminating Enbridge’s easement to operate the pipeline within the Great Lakes.
Enbridge has since taken legal action against Whitmer and the director of the Michigan Department of Natural Resources, arguing that federal regulations and a 1977 treaty between the United States and Canada bar the state from terminating the easement. 
While Judge Robert Jonker of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan deemed Whitmer’s move to revoke the easement unenforceable, the governor and DNR Director Scott Bowen appealed the case to U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit. Arguments in the case are scheduled for Dec. 15.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Some law enforcers say Utah’s emergency radio system – their ‘lifeline’ – is unreliable
description: Several Utah police agencies say the state’s public safety radio system is unreliable, driving up risk for officers in dangerous situations.
text:
A Salt Lake City police officer and Draper police officer wear body cameras at the scene of a shooting at a No Kings protest in Salt Lake City on Saturday, June 14, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Several Utah law enforcement agencies say the state’s public safety radio system is unreliable and at times prevents their officers from calling for backup or communicating with 911 dispatchers — issues they warn can drive up the risk for officers in already dangerous situations and delay emergency response.
“What’s at stake is our officer safety,” said Brad Bishop, chief of the rural Payson City Police Department about an hour’s drive south of Salt Lake City. “If we have a situation where an officer is in need of help quickly and they can’t get out on the radio, that’s their lifeline.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bishop, also the president of the Utah Chiefs of Police Association, told state legislators on a law enforcement panel last week that the topic dominates his discussions with other police chiefs. 
He’s worried police calls for urgent medical help or to fire departments also aren’t getting through. And he said he’s observed communication gaps firsthand. A few weeks ago, he and some of his officers were having lunch at a diner when a dispatch call came in. 
“Two of the officers get the transmission; the other three don’t get the transmission,” Bishop told the Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice Interim Committee on Wednesday. “This happens frequently.” 
He surveyed police and sheriff’s departments about the radio system that’s been in place for two years and shared responses from 15 agencies ranging from St. George in southern Utah to Brigham City to the north. While a handful of those law enforcement agencies are satisfied with the system, others reported frustrations with issues such as garbled audio and missed or clipped transmissions.
Brad Bishop, Payson police chief, speaks to the Utah Legislature’s Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice Interim Committee on Wednesday, Nov. 18 as Spencer Turley, deputy commissioner for the Utah Department of Corrections, looks on. (Utah Legislature video feed)
It’s a concern for the state’s prison and parole system, too. 
Spencer Turley, deputy commissioner for the Utah Department of Corrections, sat next to Bishop last week at the Capitol. Turley told members of the committee there’s been “marked improvement” as crews have worked on a radio tower near the prison’s Salt Lake City site. 
But until recently, he said it took officers four or five tries to make a call, with some carrying two radios at a time to make sure their message went through. 
“Some of them resorted to using hand signals because they couldn’t get their radio call to go through, and the problem just perpetuated,” Turley said. “Officers are saying, ‘I’m not safe to come to work because I can’t get my radio to go through if I need help.’”
He said to the credit of the Utah Communications Authority, which oversees the system,“they are responding and we are seeing an improved difference at the prison, but there’s still concerns.” 
The Utah State Correctional Facility is pictured from a “free speech zone” set up about two miles from the facility in Salt Lake City on Wednesday, Aug. 7, 2024 as the state prepared to execute death row inmate Taberon Honie just after midnight. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
It wasn’t the first time lawmakers have heard about the safety concerns. Rep. Ryan Wilcox, an Ogden Republican who chairs the committee, recalled one police chief telling him that the department now sends out two officers to respond to calls instead of one. 
“He has to double up on every call because they can’t have – they don’t have – reliable service, which means we’re cutting law enforcement in half,” Wilcox said during last week’s meeting at the Capitol. 
He noted an audit of the communications authority’s performance is underway but hopes the Legislature won’t wait for it to wrap up to start addressing issues with the system. 
“I’m concerned there’s some underlying network issues with network design and how we’ve done some of this, let alone the rollout,” Wilcox said. 
Rep. Ryan Wilcox, R-Ogden, speaks during a news conference announcing an online dashboard for domestic violence lethality assessment data at Veterans Memorial Park in West Jordan on Thursday, Aug. 21, 2025. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)
The Utah Communications Authority, an independent state agency, oversees the system that transitioned from Motorola to L3Harris Technologies in late 2024 and early 2025 under a $51 million contract.  
L3Harris Technologies did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Tina Mathieu, the authority’s executive director, told Utah News Dispatch a reliable public safety radio system requires a joint effort between the authority and the agencies using it. 
“UCA’s job is to build, maintain, and keep improving the statewide network, and we are dedicated to this mission,” Mathieu said in an email.  
She went on to say the “agencies’ part is making sure the radios in their officers’ and firefighters’ hands are up to date, in good working order, and running current firmware. The network can only perform as well as the equipment connected to it. When both sides do their part, first responders get a system they can count on, and that’s the goal we all share.”
Mathieu said the authority relies heavily on feedback from police, fire, emergency medical services, and dispatch centers, and that her agency works to find the root cause of problems and determine the right solution. 
A Payson Police Department cruiser is pictured on Monday, May 13, 2024. (Kyle Dunphey/Utah News Dispatch)
She told members of the law enforcement committee last week that many radios in the state run on outdated firmware that can drop or mangle transmissions – some with versions released as early as 2014. And while some issues can appear to stem from the network, they’re actually tied to the radios themselves, which departments are responsible for.
Another factor: signal boosters called bi-directional amplifiers that are used to eliminate dead zones in buildings. When the system changed over two years ago, those amplifiers needed reconfiguration to work properly, according to Mathieu.
Mathieu said a poorly installed or badly maintained bi-directional amplifier can take down radio coverage not just for that building, but beyond it. 
Bishop, the Payson police chief, said his department has updated radios and antennas, but is still having issues. 
“We’re not necessarily saying we want a new system,” Bishop said. “We just want the system we have to work correctly.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Charitable giving in North Carolina fell by one-sixth last year, says Secretary of State Marshall
description: The last fiscal year has been a tough one for charities in North Carolina. That’s according to the latest annual charitable solicitations report from the office of state Secretary of State Elaine Marshall. This year’s report finds that charities licensed by the state collected $39.6 million for the 2025-26 fiscal year. That represents an 18% […]
text:
Inter-Faith Food Shuttle President Ron Pringle, left, joins N.C. Secretary of State Elaine Marshall and her team as they discuss a decline in charitable donations in 2025-26. (Photo by Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)The last fiscal year has been a tough one for charities in North Carolina. That’s according to the latest annual charitable solicitations report from the office of state Secretary of State Elaine Marshall.
This year’s report finds that charities licensed by the state collected $39.6 million for the 2025-26 fiscal year. That represents an 18% decline from the $48.1 million in overall giving collected the previous year.
The aggregate percentage of donations that went to charities’ programs this year also declined, falling 6 percentage points from around 75% in 2024-25 level to 69% in 2025-26.
Inflation and a challenging economy have contributed to the falling donations, she said.
Marshall said paid professional solicitors can also have a big impact on the bottom line of North Carolina charities, but professional fundraising campaigns saw an even bigger decline this year than charitable giving overall.
The Charitable Solicitation Licensing (CSL) Division reported charities netted $27.1 million from reported fundraising campaigns, a more than 24% decrease from the amount netted from campaigns by charities in last year’s report.
“This report is a great resource for North Carolina’s giving public,” said Marshall. “You can see how much of each dollar donated in campaigns using professional fundraisers went to the charity’s programs versus how much went to fundraising and administrative overhead.”
“We want the public to give generously, but also we want them to give wisely,” Marshall said.
The staff at the Secretary of State’s office held a food drive for the food shuttle and presented the donation of over over 2,000 items on Tuesday. (Photo by Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
Marshall says North Carolinians should take the time to investigate how much of the money they give to a charity is supporting the actual program, versus paying for fundraising services.
“I always advise people to look at two or three years’ worth of activity for those donations,” said Marshall. “The bottom line is this: if you look at the annual report and you see low numbers that disturb you, check into it. Ask questions.”
Her office offers a downloadable donor’s checklist of questions to ask when a solicitor calls and asks for a year-end donation.
Marshall presented the report Tuesday during a press conference held at Raleigh’s Inter-Faith Food Shuttle, where 94 cents of every dollar collected goes to hunger-relief programs.
Marshall said the Raleigh nonprofit represented “a good guy charity” maximizing its resources to meet community needs.
Ron Pringle, president and CEO of the Food Shuttle, noted that one in six children in the seven-county region they serve is food-insecure. The cost of the nonprofit’s “Backpack Buddies” and grocery bags for seniors programs has grown by 15% in the last five years. Their fuel costs for transporting food have increased by 25% in just the last year.
“There are thousands of nonprofit organizations that are struggling right now,” said Pringle.
Pringle said he has been moved by the number of small $5 and $10 donations they’ve received, and he’s hopeful those who can afford to give more will do so to support the Food Shuttle’s programs targeting children.
“I challenge you to challenge yourselves to say, ‘Am I giving my best? Am I supporting what is important to me?'” Pringle said.
NC food pantries see a surge in demand as inflation, federal cuts hit household budgets

Marshall said it was “outstanding” that the Food Shuttle could pour more than 90% of what it raised back into its programs. In prior years, the Secretary of State’s office has found organizations where only 20% of what was raised went to the charitable cause.
“If 50% or more goes to the fundraisers, there’s another charity that serves those in need here in North Carolina that does better with your dollars,” said Marshall.
In this season of giving, Marshall says people should be skeptical of solicitations that come via text message. Rather than immediately clicking on the link, she recommends researching the organization, finding out where it’s located, and checking with the Secretary of State’s office to see if it’s  legitimate.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Some New Mexico distance learning schools not meeting state, federal requirements, report says
description: New Mexico regulations governing distance learning have not kept up with the growing number of students using such programs, according to a new Legislative Education Study Committee report, and in some cases the programs and schools lack compliance with state and federal rules.
text:
New Mexico Legislative Education Study Committee analysts, in a report presented to lawmakers on Nov. 19, 2026, say the state’s regulatory framework for K-12 distance learning has “failed to keep pace” with the current environment. (Photo via Getty Images)New Mexico regulations governing distance learning have not kept up with the growing number of students using such programs, according to a new Legislative Education Study Committee report, and in some cases the programs and schools lack compliance with state and federal rules. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The report, presented to state lawmakers on Nov. 19, responds to a law passed earlier this year requiring a comprehensive study of K-12 distance learning in the state. It includes numerous recommendations for the state to create a more comprehensive framework for distance learning, which Senate Education Committee Chair William “Bill” Soules told Source NM will be “one of the highest priorities” the committee addresses in the session starting Jan. 19.
According to the report, 9,700 students in New Mexico attended a full-time distance learning program or school in the 2025-2026 school year. Because “the state’s regulatory framework has failed to keep pace with the rapidly evolving programmatic landscape of distance learning,” the report says, some of these programs have a variety of concerns, including class sizes that exceed statutory requirements; different ways of calculating instructional hours; and lack of financial and program oversight, among other issues.
The report recommends several legislative actions, including authorizing the Public Education Department to approve and revoke distance learning programs; prohibiting the programs from being included in the public education funding formula; and prohibiting class size waivers for full-time distance learning programs and charter schools.
The report also examines alleged problems tied to third-party distance learning companies, including Chama Valley Independent Schools and Santa Rosa Consolidated Schools’ contract with for-profit virtual learning company Stride Inc., which operates the K12 online school program.
According to the report, neither school district provides adequate oversight for how Stride uses funds in its full-time distance learning program. The contract also requires the districts to pay Stride 95% of funds received through a public education funding formula known as the State Equalization Guarantee, as well as federal funding through the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. Federal regulations require that the funds be used for special education and assistive technology services.
LESC’s report contends both districts may have relinquished control of their IDEA funding to Stride “without specific guardrails or requirements” that would ensure Stride uses the federal funds in accordance with regulations.
The report further highlights oversight concerns by noting Chama Valley paid $1.6 million for a fraudulent invoice sent by a fake email address pretending to be a representative of Stride K-12. The district was unable to recover the funds. LESC staff added that the district could not produce data on the number of teachers employed in the program, their licensure and residency. 
Soules told Source NM that addressing the issues the report identifies with third-party contractors will be a focus in the session. 
“It’s about getting control so that distance learning is really a part of the New Mexico education system,” Soules said, “not handing over all of education to some company where we have no input, control or accountability oversight.”
Stride Vice President of Student Services Katrina Mohamed told Source NM that she was “shocked” by the LESC report. She added that all classrooms at DCA meet mandated classroom ratios with state-certified teachers, though they might not live in New Mexico, and that federal IDEA funding is used appropriately. 
“We welcome accountability. We welcome transparency,” Mohamed said and pointed to the report’s own note that Santa Rosa used funds to hire an individual to provide oversight on the program. “We are hoping that now that this report is completed, it opens the opportunity for us to have more conversations with legislators.”
Cadie Carrillo, Santa Rosa Consolidated Schools administrator, told Source NM in an emailed statement that the district “will provide an in-depth response to the LESC’s report” and that they remain “committed to responding to areas requiring clarification and working collaboratively with PED and other state leaders to ensure ongoing compliance and accountability.”
Chama Valley administrative assistant Shauna Jones-Martinez told Source NM in an email that the district’s partnership with Stride “operates under multiple layers of oversight, including the district, PED and annual audits, and it complies with state and federal law. We disagree with the report’s suggestion otherwise.”
Stride Inc., headquartered in Virginia, is not new to the state. Last year, Gallup-McKinley County Schools sued the company, accusing it of “intentionally and knowingly” boosting its profit margins by cutting back on the number of teachers and staff members it employed. 
Although the parties settled the lawsuit in February, the incident led to a $35 million education budget shortfall because Gallup-McKinley school district continued to receive funds for students who had left after the district terminated its contract with Stride. In January, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed Senate Bill 19 into law, giving education officials time to determine whether the district was overpaid and to develop a plan to recoup funds.
Rep. Andrés Romero (D-Albuquerque), House Education Committee Chair, echoed Soules’ call to address the issue next session. 
“We’re going to be looking at what the quality of education is for these online programs,” he said in a call with Source. “And whether we should have for-profit companies running these online schools at all in the state.”

name: VTDigger
title: Burlington airport adds first international commercial flight in years
description:
Travelers will be able to take a nonstop trip to and from Bermuda starting in May. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Burlington airport adds first international commercial flight in years.
text:
Director of Aviation Nic Longo announces new direct  flights to Bermuda from Leahy Burlington International Airport at a press conference in South Burlington on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
SOUTH BURLINGTON — Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport is once again living up to its name.
Airport leaders announced on Tuesday that, for the first time in nearly a decade, travelers will be able to book a commercial flight to and from Vermont’s largest airport and an international destination: Bermuda.
The nonstop route, operated by BermudAir, will make its first trip on May 8, 2027 and run through September. It will fly only on Saturdays in May, then on Mondays and Fridays in June and July before returning to a Saturday-only schedule into the fall, airport officials said at a press conference.
Since 2018, when BTV discontinued flights to and from Toronto, the only international service at the airport has been on private or charter jets. The airline that flew to Canada, Porter Airlines, nixed that route amid low passenger counts and a struggle to find staff.
Airport leaders hope Bermuda, a tropical archipelago in the western Atlantic Ocean, will be an appealing vacation destination — even as the new flight there is set to operate largely during the summer months, when Vermont is already warm. 
The trip will take about two hours and connect to Bermuda’s sole airport in the town of St. George’s. There will be one flight a day each to and from Bermuda. 
“It gives (Vermonters) that direct trip to one of the most beautiful places in the world, and it opens the door for Bermuda travelers to enjoy Vermont,” Nic Longo, the airport’s director of aviation, said at the press conference Tuesday. 
He was clad in sunglasses and a pink shirt, a nod to the famous color of the sand on the country’s beaches. 

Director of Aviation Nic Longo announces new direct  flights to Bermuda from Leahy Burlington International Airport at a press conference in South Burlington on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Longo said he hopes traveler demand will make it feasible for the flight to operate year-round in the future so Vermonters can have a new wintertime travel option, too. He described the five-month service as essentially a test-run, since there has never been a flight between Vermont and Bermuda before. 
BermudAir chose to start a flight out of Burlington to ease pressure on a busy route it already operates out of Boston Logan International Airport, he said, roughly a 3-hour drive away.
At the same time, Burlington officials liked the idea because Bermuda’s airport has a facility where U.S.-bound passengers can go through U.S. customs before boarding their flight, a process known as “preclearance.” When passengers land in Burlington, they’ll be able to walk directly out of the airport just like they would from a domestic flight.
That means BTV does not need to build a new passport control facility, Longo explained, or direct passengers to its existing U.S. customs facility used by private passengers, which is small and located across the tarmac from the main terminal building. 
BermudAir will be the sixth airline operating out of BTV. Airport officials said Tuesday that one of their next goals is to convince United Airlines to make its existing flight from Burlington directly to Denver International Airport year-round. Currently, only indirect flights to Denver are available during certain parts of the year.
The announcement also comes as Burlington saw its highest-ever monthly passenger count last month, Longo told reporters Tuesday. It served 82,000 outbound passengers and roughly the same number inbound, for a total of about 160,000 trips.
BermudAir, which launched in 2023, also announced summertime flights to and from several other U.S. cities on Tuesday including Portland, Maine; New Haven, Conn.; Nashville, Tenn., as well as New Orleans and San Antonio.
The airline is seeing “tremendous interest” around New England, Adam Scott, its founder and CEO told Travel + Leisure magazine.
