name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa pardons two turkeys on Iowa State University campus ahead of Thanksgiving
description: AMES — More than three years into an avian flu epidemic and after a year of hardships for Iowa’s agriculture industry, state, university and agriculture officials gathered to celebrate resiliency and pardon two turkeys. Turkeys named Early and Bird were pardoned on the Iowa State University campus Thursday by Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig. […]
text:
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig read a proclamation from Gov. Kim Reynolds pardoning Early and Bird. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)AMES — More than three years into an avian flu epidemic and after a year of hardships for Iowa’s agriculture industry, state, university and agriculture officials gathered to celebrate resiliency and pardon two turkeys.
Turkeys named Early and Bird were pardoned on the Iowa State University campus Thursday by Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig. He read a proclamation by Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds and gave his own comments about how Iowans should take a moment this holiday to give thanks for those who produce the “food, fuel and fiber” to keep things running.
“This gives us a chance to recognize that food security starts on productive farms, productive farmers, and healthy livestock, and we can certainly celebrate that today,” Naig said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the proclamation Naig read, Iowa farmers care for close to 12 million turkeys annually, ranking Iowa  seventh in the nation for turkey production. The turkey industry employs more than 38,000 Iowans, with a total economic impact of $10.6 billion.
“This longstanding tradition during Thanksgiving week recognizes the commitment from poultry producers across our state to provide holiday turkeys for Iowa families,” Reynolds said in a news release after signing the proclamation. “Iowa is home to nearly 130 turkey farms, many of which are operated by generational farm families.”
Reynolds and past governors have normally personally pardoned turkeys at Thanksgiving, but this year Reynolds canceled her event scheduled for Tuesday at Terrace Hill, the governor’s mansion, amid preparations for a planned detonation of lead-based explosives by the U.S. Army at its ammunitions plant in Middletown.
Iowa Turkey Federation President Josh Berg and his family provided Early and Bird for the pardoning. The Sac County farmers have raised turkeys for just over 10 years.
“It definitely has its challenges with diseases and, I guess, economic issues, but it looks like we always persevere,” Berg said. “So I know bird flu has been a topic amongst the past few years, but we are kind of looking for brighter days ahead, and we are eager to, I guess, keep our industry going strong.”
Reynolds issued a disaster proclamation for Sac County in October after a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza was found in a commercial 44,000-turkey flock, the first case of the influenza found in an Iowa commercial flock in nearly a year. Iowa tops the nation for most birds infected by the avian influenza since the outbreak began in February 2022.
Yuko Sato, an associate professor of vet diagnostic and production animal medicine, said the “longstanding outbreak” has been joined by avian metapneumovirus, another disease that has “been devastating” the turkey industry.
“Both diseases have caused catastrophic effects to the turkey industry, and the turkey farmers have been holding vigilant and trying to fight in keeping the turkeys healthy,” Sato said.
Producers have focused on what they can control when trying to mitigate the spread of disease, Sato said, like biosecurity practices. While they don’t have a “magic 8-ball” to tell the future, she hopes these efforts will help to keep reducing the outbreak’s severity.
ISU College of Veterinary Medicine Dean Dan Grooms said the university has a “long and well-established working relationship” with Iowa’s turkey farmers as the oldest land grant college of veterinary medicine in the U.S.
Other challenges Naig said Iowa farmers are facing include policy uncertainty, high input prices, pressures on profitability and markets not looking the way they’d want, but he emphasized that Iowans shouldn’t take for granted the markets and opportunities that may not exist in other countries.
“All of those pieces are contributing to where we are. But it’s always true, we get to this time of year, and I think there’s lots of reasons you’ve got to pause and be thankful,” Naig said. “I do truly mean that and hope that Iowans will just take a moment to understand and to think about what it takes to make sure we’ve got the food and the fuel and the fiber that we need in this country, and we are blessed.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota’s investments hit milestone of underperformance, but managers see silver lining
description: South Dakota’s state government investment portfolio tends to bring in less money from the stock market at times when other portfolios are making more.  That’s by design, according to the portfolio’s managers. The “contrarian” approach includes putting a smaller share of money in stocks when prices are high, and snatching up more stocks when prices […]
text:
Members of the South Dakota Investment Council on April 4, 2024, in Sioux Falls. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s state government investment portfolio tends to bring in less money from the stock market at times when other portfolios are making more. 
That’s by design, according to the portfolio’s managers.
The “contrarian” approach includes putting a smaller share of money in stocks when prices are high, and snatching up more stocks when prices dip.
During the most recently completed fiscal year, that meant even though the state made money on the stocks it has, the returns weren’t enough to cancel out losses or lower returns from other investments, namely in private equity and real estate.
As a result, the South Dakota Retirement System fund made less money than its benchmark target on a 20-year time scale for the first time in the system’s 53-year history. 
“It’s been really good more often than really bad,” State Investment Officer Matt Clark said of the state’s investment returns. “But the really bad’s been clustered in the last three years.”
Clark and other members of the state’s investing team spoke to South Dakota Searchlight last week about the public release of an annual report that documented the 20-year milestone of lackluster performance, as well as news about positive early earnings for fiscal year 2027.
“We’re hoping for a comeback,” Clark said.


Retirement system falls behind
The South Dakota Investment Council reviewed the annual report during a meeting Nov. 17. The council oversees the retirement system’s money managers, who also manage investments for various other funds that benefit schools, healthcare and the state budget.
Between the retirement system and the trust funds, the Investment Council oversees more than $21 billion, with the retirement system representing about $16.4 billion.
The retirement system has about 107,000 members, including state workers, teachers, police officers and other public employees. They pay at least 6% of their salaries into the retirement fund, matched by the state, in return for a guaranteed pension in retirement. Retirees get a cost-of-living adjustment each year, but that adjustment’s been less than inflation since 2021.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The retirement system still makes money — it grew year-over-year by about 11% in fiscal year 2026 — just not as much as the benchmark the Investment Council is measured against. 
In April, three members of the Legislature’s Executive Board voted against approving a raise and incentive-based bonus for Clark. 
One of the board’s members, Spearfish Republican Rep. Scott Odenbach, said lawmakers are bound to get questions from retirees who’ll want to know “are you doing your job to make sure we’re getting the returns?”
Clark’s team told Searchlight that the long-term strategy is designed as a buffer for the retirement system against the worst impacts of an economic downturn, and his team has pointed to stability as positive overall for retirees.
In June, the South Dakota Retirement System board learned that state pensioners would again see a cost-of-living adjustment lower than inflation, but the news was presented alongside figures showing that the average adjustment for South Dakotans still outpaces what state government retirees see in neighboring states.
Bulwark against potential losses
According to an analysis shared with the Investment Council privately and later with Searchlight, the state’s retirement system would remain 95% funded if an economic downturn as serious as the one in 2008 were to take place today. 
If the system invested in stocks the way its benchmark fund does, that figure would fall to 85%, prompting not only the loss of a cost-of-living adjustment for retirees, Clark said, but potentially spurring talk of benefit cuts.
“The goal is to keep it 100% funded,” Clark said.
Lawmakers approve pay and bonus package for investment manager, despite concerns about returns

Clark’s team also points to past results as proof that the long-term strategy can pay off.
Not long after the 2008 crisis, South Dakota was able to give retirees cost-of-living adjustments near or higher than the rate of inflation, according to figures shared with the retirement board. In 2014, 2015 and 2016, those adjustments hit the then-maximum rate of 3.5%. Inflation during those years was 1.6%, 0.1% and 1.3%, respectively.
Jarrod Edelen, a portfolio manager for the state, said many public retirement systems didn’t fare so well after 2008. Some states took out loans to shore up underfunded pension plans or increased state and employee contributions to their retirement plans.
A report from the Pew Charitable Trusts in 2021 estimated that state retirement systems as a whole were 80% funded “for the first time since 2008.”
“That dynamic that occurred, with other states being underfunded, began in 2008 in spades when the market fell and their funded status declined significantly,” Edelen said. “They were stuck with that lack of recovery, but we got an enormous recovery.”
Other factors contribute to underperformance
The retirement system’s underperformance — its returns were 11% in fiscal year 2026 while the benchmark’s were 18% — is mirrored across the other funds managed by the Investment Council, including the School and Public Lands Trust and the South Dakota Cement Plant Trust.
The amount of money transferred to the state general fund for fiscal year 2026 was $136.8 million, down from $150.6 million the year before.
New voter-backed trust fund could become South Dakota’s largest, state treasurer says

That the state missed its 20-year benchmark in 2026 but outperformed it in 2008 is partially reflective of a current problem with part of the state’s portfolio that wasn’t present 18 years ago.
Back in the 2008-2009 financial crisis era, the state lost money when the stock market took a dive, but was buoyed by the returns delivered by its real estate investments just before it started.
Some of those real estate partners, Clark said, sold off real estate assets just before the crisis, then bought distressed assets afterward at a discount. That enabled those partners — and the state by extension — to lose less and bounce back more quickly.
During the 2026 fiscal year, real estate investments were under water. The Investment Council doesn’t buy real estate directly, but invests in firms that do. South Dakota lost more on those real estate partnerships in 2026 than it has in years.
There’s been a “slow-motion unraveling” in the real estate market, Clark said, because investors “thought interest rates would stay low forever.”
Because the state’s real estate partnerships are 10- and 15-year arrangements, Clark said, “it’s hard to sell and get out.”
The state’s private equity investments also faltered, not losing money but returning less than the state had hoped.
“We’ve never had them all do bad at the same time before,” Clark said.
A bad year, but hopeful signs
Shortly after accepting the annual report, members of the Investment Council heard the state’s retirement system returns were 1.27% in the first few months of fiscal year 2027, which began July 1. The benchmark’s returns in that time frame were -0.75%.
“But again,” portfolio manager Darci Haug told the council, “just note that this is only four-and-a-half months into the fiscal year.”
Even so, Clark told the council he sees some evidence that the strategy that’s kept the state from collecting on the stock market’s historic gains in recent years may finally be paying off. 
“I guess it shows that contrarian strategies can eventually work out if you’re patient enough,” Clark told the council. “But you have to be very patient. Fortunately, I think you know that’s something we can do.”
He went on to say that South Dakota’s trading team is competing with “the best of the best” in the investment industry. 
In that respect, Clark told the council, patience “may ultimately be our only competitive advantage.”



South Dakota trust funds
South Dakota’s trust funds benefit schools, healthcare and the state budget. Their value and year-over-year investment returns for fiscal year 2026 are listed below. The returns for all four trailed the 16.2% growth of the state’s benchmark fund.

School and Public Lands Trust: $487 million value, 9% growth
Dakota Cement Plant Trust: $392.3 million value, 8.2% growth
Education Enhancement Trust: $842.5 million value, 8.7% growth
Health Care Trust: $241 million value, 9.3% growth

title: Maine’s projected $1 billion budget gap shrinks after latest update
description: Maine is expecting $515 million more in revenue over the next three years, shrinking the earlier projected $1 billion budget gap. On Tuesday, the Revenue Forecasting Committee updated the predictions on which Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree will base her forthcoming two-year budget proposal due to lawmakers in February.  Earlier this fall, the Maine Department of [...]
text:
The Maine State House in Augusta. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/Maine Morning Star)Maine is expecting $515 million more in revenue over the next three years, shrinking the earlier projected $1 billion budget gap.
On Tuesday, the Revenue Forecasting Committee updated the predictions on which Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree will base her forthcoming two-year budget proposal due to lawmakers in February. 
Earlier this fall, the Maine Department of Administrative and Financial Services’ Bureau of the Budget had projected a $1 billion structural gap in the general fund for the 2028-2029 biennium, which was based on revenue predictions in March. However, that gap has narrowed with the latest update. 
“I think a big part of the increase this time was simply more data,” said committee member Luke Lazure, who is the director of the legislature’s nonpartisan Office of Fiscal and Program Review. 
When the committee put out its projections in March, there were more unknowns regarding expected tax revenue. Since then, the state decided how to conform with federal tax changes and added a new state-level millionaire’s tax. 
Now, in fiscal year 2027 and 2028, the state is expecting about $6.1 billion in general fund revenue each year, up from the previously anticipated roughly $5.9 billion each year. In fiscal year 2029, the state is expected to take in even more, $6.3 billion, up from $6.1 billion. 
That $515 million total could all go toward closing the gap, though the increased revenue for fiscal year 2027 could be used earlier for emergency legislation.
“That is why any deficit is always a bit of a moving target,” Lazure said. 
The differences in the latest projections are based on the same key revenue generators that typically cause projection changes year over year: sales and use tax, individual income, corporate income.
“Those three lines accounted for the vast majority of all of the increase in all three years,” Lazure said.
The updated projections come after the state ended fiscal year 2026 in June with $119 million more in revenue than anticipated. The forecasting committee has underestimated revenues over the past several years.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: 8 weeks before budget deadline, Foulkes takes ‘getting up to speed’ tour of RI Community Food Bank
description: Pallets of canned corn, peaches, peanut butter jars and other staples lined the aisles of the Rhode Island Community Food Bank’s Providence warehouse Tuesday as Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes toured the facility ahead of Thanksgiving. “Food is at the heart of so many issues from a societal perspective,” Foulkes, a Democrat, told reporters after the […]
text:
Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes, left, speaks with Rhode Island Community Food Bank CEO Melissa Cherney, right, during a visit to the food bank's Providence warehouse on Nov. 24, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) Pallets of canned corn, peaches, peanut butter jars and other staples lined the aisles of the Rhode Island Community Food Bank’s Providence warehouse Tuesday as Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes toured the facility ahead of Thanksgiving.
“Food is at the heart of so many issues from a societal perspective,” Foulkes, a Democrat, told reporters after the 30-minute tour. “Unfortunately, the need is more intense than it has ever been.”
Foulkes made a brief stop at the food bank to encourage Rhode Islanders to donate, noting that monetary contributions allow the nonprofit to buy food in bulk and stretch each dollar further. The visit came before she kicked off a four-part listening tour across the state at 5 p.m. Tuesday at the Elmwood Community Center in Providence.
Nearly 94,000 Rhode Islanders visited a food pantry in October alone, the food bank’s CEO, Melissa Cherney, said as she introduced the governor-elect. Rising costs are straining household budgets and driving up the food bank’s own expenses to purchase and distribute food, putting pressure on a network already struggling to keep up with demand.
“The new normal is crisis,” Cherney said in an interview after the governor-elect left.
Food pantry use reached record levels in Rhode Island last year. More than 102,000 Rhode Islanders visited food pantries in November 2025, when a federal government shutdown disrupted food assistance benefits. The food bank’s annual hunger report, released in January, also found that one in three Rhode Island households experienced food insecurity throughout the last year.
Both Cherney and Foulkes said changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) under President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act added to the pressure on Rhode Island families and the local pantries trying to feed them.
The GOP-led legislation signed by the president last July imposed work requirements on adult SNAP recipients who are capable of working and are younger than 64 and without dependents younger than 14. Previously, those with dependents 18 or younger and those older than 54 were not subject to SNAP work requirements. The new rules also removed exemptions for people experiencing homelessness, veterans and former foster youth under the age of 25.
Another provision of the law could pose an especially steep cost for Rhode Island, Cherney said. She was referring to a requirement that states with high SNAP payment error rates cover a share of the program’s benefit costs.
Why Rhode Island can‘t afford to lose the race to reduce its SNAP error rate

Rhode Island’s payment error rate was 12.42% in federal fiscal 2024, well above the 6% threshold.
Beginning Oct. 1, 2027, states with payment error rates above the federal limit — based on benefits distributed in fiscal 2025 or 2026 — will have to cover a portion of SNAP benefit costs. 
The share will depend on the state’s error rate and could reach up to $100 million annually, based on projections from the Rhode Island’s Executive Office of Health and Human Services.
“We’d have to be able to sustain it,” Cherney said. “And there’s not really any good options at this point.”
Cherney said she hopes Congress or the Trump administration will delay the shift of SNAP benefit costs to states. Even a one or two-year delay in shifting costs to states would give Rhode Island and others time to get their payment error rates under control and plan for how to pay their share, she said.
Canned corn stacked on pallets at the Rhode Island Community Food Bank’s Providence warehouse during Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes’ visit on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Foulkes said she wants to better coordinate the state’s response to hunger, as families struggle with the rising cost of living — including those who earn too much to qualify for food assistance but still have trouble putting food on the table.
The food bank too is facing higher operating costs. Cherney said prices for food, fuel and even cardboard used in packaging are squeezing the nonprofit’s budget.
“It’s impacting us hard,” she said. “When we’re spending money on things like fuel and cardboard costs, we’re not spending it on food.”
Gov. Dan McKee in January called for doubling the state’s $1 million allocation to the food bank to $2 million in his proposed fiscal 2027 budget. The General Assembly increased the total allocation to $3 million, but it was designated as one-time funding.
Under state law, Foulkes must submit her first proposed budget by the third Thursday in January. She did not commit to a specific figure on Tuesday, noting she was “getting up to speed” on the food bank’s issues. She told reporters she expects the state will need to help fill gaps in food assistance left by changes at the federal level.
“We have to make sure that we’re taking care of our most vulnerable populations,” she said.

text:
The Rev. Calvin Robinson speaking on the Command Media podcast. (Screenshot)U.S. officials are said to be reviewing the visa held by the Rev. Calvin Robinson — a controversial right-wing British Anglican pastor who has switched his Christian denomination several times over the past decade — following comments on a podcast in which he called for American Jews to be driven out of the country.
Robinson is the current congregation leader of St. Paul’s Church in Grand Rapids.
The Telegraph newspaper, based in the United Kingdom, on Tuesday reported that Robinson’s visa that allows him to live and preach in the U.S. was under review by U.S. Department of State officials, with the newspaper noting that the review fell in line with President Donald Trump’s 2025 executive order calling on the nation to either prosecute or remove visa holders who engage in antisemitic behavior or harassment.
The newspaper also reported that the review was jumpstarted by one of Trump’s personal attorneys, Robert Garson, who is also the current president of the American Association of Jewish Lawyers and Jurists. Garson is reported to have reached out to Trump’s special envoy to battle antisemitism on American soil, Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun.
In a statement to Michigan Advance via email, Robinson said “Christian countries should be governed by a Christian moral compass.”

“I like to think the Founding Fathers would agree,” Robinson told the Advance. “I am unsure why my words were so controversial, but I am thankful that I live in a country with a strong belief in free speech. Thank God for the First Amendment. God bless America — the only country in the world where people are truly free to express themselves without persecution.”
Robinson’s new issues with his visa came after he appeared on a podcast earlier this month co-hosted by Robinson and his associate, Joe Enders, who had claimed that a “Jewish oligarchy” controlled America and called some of their core beliefs heretical to Christian teachings. Enders had then asked Robinson how that “heresy”  could be prevented from spreading or “permeating” into various levels of the federal government.
Robinson’s answer was to drive Jews out of the country.
“There are more Jews in America than there are in any other country, including Israel,” Robinson said on the podcast. “They are disproportionately represented in all the key areas that are subverting our culture, from Hollywood to music, and that needs to end.”
On X, last Friday, Robinson also called Jews a protected class, and claimed that anyone who criticizes American Jews is also seen as someone who wants to do them harm.
“We must never ever upset a Jew, because if you upset a Jew you clearly want to fire up the gas chamber and put them all in it. We do not need to burn them. We can just deport them,” Robinson wrote on Nov. 20.
Robinson has used his X account since the controversy began to double down on his commentary, claiming he was not an antisemite, but rather just a Christian.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: New voter-backed trust fund could become South Dakota’s largest, state treasurer says
description: A trust fund endorsed by voters on Election Day could grow to become South Dakota’s largest, according to State Treasurer Josh Haeder. Haeder made his comments during a recent meeting of the South Dakota Investment Council, which manages the state retirement system and trust funds that benefit schools, healthcare and the state budget. The state […]
text:
South Dakota State Treasurer Josh Haeder speaks with lawmakers at the Capitol in Pierre on Jan. 15, 2025. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)A trust fund endorsed by voters on Election Day could grow to become South Dakota’s largest, according to State Treasurer Josh Haeder.
Haeder made his comments during a recent meeting of the South Dakota Investment Council, which manages the state retirement system and trust funds that benefit schools, healthcare and the state budget. The state treasurer is a permanent member of the council, and last week’s meeting was Haeder’s last in the role. Republican Melissa Hull was elected to succeed fellow Republican Haeder, who is term-limited.
Voters endorsed Constitutional Amendment K to allow management of the state’s Unclaimed Property Trust Fund by the Investment Council, which will generate investment earnings to help fund state government.
Unclaimed property typically takes the form of unclaimed money from sources including bank accounts, stocks, life insurance payouts, uncashed checks and the contents of safe deposit boxes. If the entities holding the funds can’t find the owners within three years, the money can be transferred to the state. Anyone can claim their funds at any time, so the property is a perpetual liability for the state, but most unclaimed funds go uncollected.
Voters say yes to South Dakota Investment Council management of unclaimed property money

Haeder told the Investment Council on Nov. 17 that unclaimed property receipts for 2026 stood at $294 million. He’s proud, he said, to have pushed for a managed trust fund during his last year in office.
“That has the potential to become the largest trust fund in the state of South Dakota,” Haeder said.
The council manages four other trust funds: the Cement Plant Trust Fund, School and Public Lands Trust Fund, Education Enhancement Trust Fund, and Health Care Trust Fund. The largest by dollar amount is the Education Enhancement Trust Fund, seeded largely by money from a 1998 multi-state tobacco lawsuit settlement. That fund ended state fiscal year 2026 with a value of $842.5 million.
In a call with South Dakota Searchlight, Haeder said the reason the Unclaimed Property Trust Fund could grow to be the state’s largest is a matter of “simple math.”
More money comes in as unclaimed property every year, sometimes more than $200 million. Even after paying for marketing campaigns to convince people to collect their money and paying claims, the amount that would be transferred is likely to be significant.
In 2025, the state received $357 million in unclaimed property, according to the State Treasurer’s Annual Report, and paid out $49.6 million to claimants. That year was an unprecedented surge, but Haeder said annual receipts of $100 million or more are commonplace. That’s largely due to favorable laws and regulations that have attracted some national banks to place their headquarters in the state.
Within 10 years or so, Haeder said, the new trust fund could surpass $1 billion through annual allocations.
“It’s not a fund where we’re transferring a one-time dollar amount,” Haeder told Searchlight.
The idea behind creating the trust fund is that investing the money will do more for the state budget than gains from a small interest rate. 
The investment council will use some of the money to buy stocks and bonds and make other investments, pushing returns — and the resulting amount transferred to the state general fund — to a higher level.
The other four trust funds earned year-over-year returns between 8.2% and 9.3% in fiscal year 2026, according to the Investment Council’s latest annual report. 
Lawmakers passed a bill earlier this year sponsored by Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, to put unclaimed property into a trust fund, but needed the recently approved state constitutional amendment to allow the Investment Council to put some of the money into stocks.

title: Ada County Democrats back Van Hollen over Schumer as US Senate leader
description: Ada County Democrats are calling for a change in U.S. Senate party leadership. The county party committee passed a resolution Monday to call on U.S. Senate Democrats to back U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland over New York’s U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer as majority leader.  A spokesperson for the statewide Idaho Democratic Party could not […]
text:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer addresses reporters on Tuesday, Dec. 16, 2025, after a closed-door briefing on U.S. military strikes on alleged drug smuggling boats near the coast of Venezuela. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, is among four senators who say a stopgap spending bill must cut off funding for the Iran war. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Ada County Democrats are calling for a change in U.S. Senate party leadership. The county party committee passed a resolution Monday to call on U.S. Senate Democrats to back U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland over New York’s U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer as majority leader. 
A spokesperson for the statewide Idaho Democratic Party could not immediately be reached. 
Schumer has been in the Senate since 1998 and was first selected as majority leader in 2021. Van Hollen was first elected in 2016, and announced on Nov. 12 he was challenging Schumer for the leadership position. 
“This is the first contested race for a Democratic leader in decades, and it’s an opportunity to show the country a new direction,” Ada County Democratic Party Chair Jared DeLoof said in a press release. “The leadership of the past has not been adequate to meet the challenges working families are facing. We are in a crisis. The middle class is disappearing, the wealthy hoard money at the top while the rest of us scrape by. Artificial intelligence threatens the jobs we all depend on, all while corruption goes unchecked in Washington. We need major action now on AI, health care, inflation and jobs, and Senator Van Hollen has shown he will fight for it.”
During the Nov. 3 general election, Democrats flipped nine seats in the U.S. Senate and will have a 56-44 majority when the new Congress begins in January. 
Members of the party that controls the chamber select their majority leader, who sets the schedule for floor business each day and serves as a spokesperson for their party’s interests. 
The Ada County Democrats’ resolution was sent to Schumer, Van Hollen and members of the U.S. Senate Democratic Caucus. Both of Idaho’s senators are Republican and will not be selecting the majority leader.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Game on? Braun, Rokita trade barbs over potential 2028 Indiana gubernatorial matchup
description: Indiana’s 2028 gubernatorial primary might be 18 months away, but Republican Gov. Mike Braun and Attorney General Todd Rokita are already trading jabs over a potential rematch. Braun on Monday declared “game on” at the prospect of a primary challenge from Rokita. The attorney general fired back Tuesday, though, saying governing Indiana is “not a […]
text:
Attorney General Todd Rokita, left, and Gov. Mike Braun in 2026 Statehouse press conferences. 
(Photos by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz and Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana’s 2028 gubernatorial primary might be 18 months away, but Republican Gov. Mike Braun and Attorney General Todd Rokita are already trading jabs over a potential rematch.
Braun on Monday declared “game on” at the prospect of a primary challenge from Rokita. The attorney general fired back Tuesday, though, saying governing Indiana is “not a game” — and declining to rule out a run against his GOP counterpart.
The exchanges came during back-to-back Statehouse news conferences focused on storm recovery and just days after Braun launched his reelection bid.
“A wise man told me once, ‘Never say what you’ll never do.’ So, it’s not going to be a no. It’s not going to be a never. It’s not going to be anything like that,” Rokita said when asked if he was considering challenging Braun. “My plan is to be — and do the job of — attorney general. That’s what the people elected me to do.”
Both Republicans emphasized that they continue to work together despite their public disagreements. Rokita noted that he and Braun had spoken just before Tuesday’s news conference.
Rokita presses governor over Charlie Kirk posts after no Indiana educator licenses revoked

“I consider the governor a partner. I want he, and especially his team, to be better,” Rokita said.
Braun shared a similar sentiment Monday: “We share almost all the same principles, different styles, and all I can tell you is I embrace competition.”
The governor pointed to his experience in previous statewide campaigns and said applying for the governor’s job was harder than doing it.
“Nobody will outwork me,” Braun said.
Rokita didn’t see it that way, however.
“To the extent the game is on, I would say this is not a game. This is about the state of Indiana,” the attorney general said. ““It’s anything but easy to govern, and I think that speaks volumes to the mindset of where that administration is at, and I don’t want it to be.”
“Governing should be challenging. Governing should be hard,” Rokita continued. “These agencies, I represent them in court. This government deserves full attention. It deserves a lot of proactivity.”
It’s not the first time the two have been at odds.
Rokita has most recently publicly criticized the administration’s handling of Indiana educators who made controversial social media posts following the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.
No Indiana educator licenses have been revoked in connection with those posts. Braun has repeatedly pointed to the state education department’s internal review process and First Amendment considerations.
Rokita reiterated Tuesday that the educators’ licenses should be subject to formal review. He said his office spent two months working with the Braun administration under the impression that it would be allowed to investigate the cases itself, only for that effort to go nowhere.
“When we have other disagreements, I will also be speaking out again,” Rokita said.



Quotation







To the extent the game is on, I would say this is not a game. This is about the state of Indiana.


– Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita


The attorney general outlined several other disagreements Tuesday.
Rokita said his office’s ongoing IEDC investigation is focused primarily on allegations that companies that donated to the corporation’s foundation subsequently benefited from grants or other transactions. He did not have a timeline for its completion.
The attorney general additionally accused Braun’s administration of ignoring his offer to investigate NIPSCO’s response to summer storms and questioned the progress of the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission’s own probe into the utility’s storm preparedness and prolonged power outages.
Braun and Rokita have met in the campaign arena before when Braun defeated him in a bid for U.S. Senate in 2018.
Rokita said he made a promise to himself and his family when he returned to the Statehouse in 2021 that he wouldn’t hold back.
“I am going to put forward thoughts, ideas, call out behavior,” he said. “I promised myself that I wouldn’t leave anything unsaid when I look back at this time in my life, years from now.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Giant Hole In Ground Gapes For Years Amid Sustained Fingerpointing
description: As neighbors walk and drive by, the city and a private company each say the other is responsible for closing up a giant hole along the side of a residential road.
text:
Nobody is clamoring to fix the longstanding hole in the ground in lower Kamehameha Heights.
Measuring several feet long and at least two feet wide – large enough to eat a moped – it lies in wait along Alani Street near its intersection with Aupuni Street, an area with no sidewalks just down the hill from Kamehameha Schools Kapālama. Rusty rebar twists out of it and what appears to be a manhole cover sits inside tilted with grass on top.
“What it needs is a big sheet of metal that can’t be moved,” neighbor Carole Kaapu said. 
It’s unclear exactly how long the gaping hole has been in this condition. Kaapu said she remembers first encountering it while walking past it four years ago.
“What the heck is that?” she remembers thinking to herself. 
Since then, she said, she has been pounding the drum on this issue, including to Honolulu City Council member Tyler Dos Santos-Tam.
“Everybody who lives within several hundred feet of this knows about it,” he said in an interview. “It’s pretty obvious.” 
He said he has heard complaints about it for years. The problem, however, is that the hole resides on a private road owned by the McInerny Foundation, a nonprofit foundation started in 1937 by the McInerny family, who launched a clothing company in Honolulu – and the McInerny Foundation no longer exists in its original form. 
The family put their foundation under Bishop Trust Company, and the company that held that trust was acquired by Bank of Hawaiʻi in the 1990s.
“This giant hole that’s in the drainage infrastructure is not the city’s,” Dos Santos-Tam said. 
Dos Santos-Tam blamed the McInerny Foundation’s successor trustee Bank of Hawaiʻi. So did Department of Facility Maintenance Director Gene Albano, who said as much in a letter about the hole he sent to Bank of Hawaiʻi this January.
“As the landowner, it is your responsibility to mitigate hazards originating from your property that affect public safety,” Albano’s letter says, “such as pedestrians injuring themselves by stepping into or falling into the open catch basin.”
A manhole cover appears to be hiding under grass that fell into the giant hole.  Ben Angarone/Civil Beat/2026
Bank of Hawaiʻi disputes that. Melissa Torres-Laing, its senior vice president for corporate communications, said in an emailed statement that the kuleana lies with adjacent lot owners and the City and County of Honolulu.
“Bank of Hawaiʻi is aware of the issue and the concerns raised,” she said. She shared a copy of a quitclaim document from 1991 that she said absolves the McInerny Foundation from management of the hole. 
In a 2024 letter to Bank of Hawaiʻi, Dos Santos-Tam said it appears the foundation is still the fee owner of the roadway despite the quitclaim from 1991, meaning the city is not liable – an argument Kaapu said she’s heard.
“The reality is, it doesn’t matter,” she said. “If somebody gets hurt, the city’s going to be involved …  Somebody has to take responsibility for it.” 
Who’s Responsible? 
That’s in dispute between Bank of Hawaiʻi (808-643-3888) and the Honolulu Department of Facility Maintenance (808-768-3343).
Fixed It!
Another recent hole – this one in Waikīkī ​​– was promptly fixed after we reported on it in September, months after a resident reported it to the city and heard crickets in response. 
In addition, those pesky steel plates along Kalākaua Avenue heading into Waikīkī are finally gone after rattling drivers since 2019.
A difference in sidewalk colors is all that remains of the hole that for months sat across the street from a Denny’s. Ben Angarone/Civil Beat/2026
Got A Tip For Fix It!?
Tell us where the problem is, as specifically as possible. A cell phone photo would be helpful. Here are ways to get in touch:  
You can submit in minutes using this form. 
You can send us an email at news@civilbeat.org. Put “Fix It” in the subject line so it doesn’t get lost among the many other news tips we receive.
You can send a letter to the newsroom at P.O. Box 10857, Honolulu, HI 96816.
We won’t use your name without your permission but, if we pursue your fix, we will get back to you with what we find.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: As temps fall, United Way reactivates homelessness fund
description: The organization reactivated its Rapid Response Fund on Monday — a flexible, cold-weather initiative designed to pay bills for people.
text:
As homelessness increases for the fifth consecutive year, a regional United Way that serves 56 communities in Connecticut has reactivated its Rapid Response Fund, a flexible, cold-weather initiative designed to pay bills for people that could mean the difference between being housed or on the street.
“We work with our local municipalities, our other community partners, to provide this direct cash assistance to individuals and families who are at risk of homelessness,” Eric Harrison, the president of the United Way of Central and Northeastern Connecticut, said Tuesday.
The program’s resources, while nearly doubling from last year, are relatively modest: United Way is upping its spending on Rapid Response from $100,000 to $190,000. 
It gives municipal social workers and others access to grants of up to $1,000 to buy heating oil, repair a car or stave off an eviction.
“One of the greatest benefits of these funds is they are unrestricted, allowing recipients to use the assistance where it is needed most, while also providing our social service departments greater flexibility and ease in distributing funds quickly and efficiently,” said Christina Morra-Tiu, a social worker employed by Wetherfield.
In other words, there is no red tape. 
“Traditional systems take a lengthy amount of time to get support. This is quick. This is easy. This gives families more autonomy in what they need, which is something that we’re definitely missing,” said Kelly Murphy, the manager of the city of New Britain’s community services office.
Being able to afford a car repair might be the difference between keeping or losing a job. Providing a security deposit could keep a family off the streets. Murphy said grants filling those needs not are only vital for the recipients, but they ultimately are cost effective.
“This also reduces long-term costs when you’re thinking about how the city will support residents,” Murphy said. “When residents are financially stable, parents maintain employment, there’s less housing interruption, children have housing stability, and there’s more neighborhood connection.”
Last year, 216 households across what United Way calls the “860 region” received rapid assistance totaling $120,618 — an average grant of less than $560. United Way budgeted $100,000, then continued to raise money — as it is doing this year.
“We have helped individuals and families purchase heating oil while waiting for heating assistance, pay rent to prevent evictions, and cover utility bills to avoid shut-off,” Morra-Tiu said. “We have also provided temporary motel accommodations for several individuals and families experiencing homelessness, giving them a safe place to stay while awaiting placement in a shelter.”
A wealthy state falls short
The United Way, with Gov. Ned Lamont and Rep. Kate Farrar, D-West Hartford, announced the the reactivation Tuesday at a press conference at the Legislative Office Building. The funds became available Monday.
Lamont is an enthusiastic supporter of the philanthropic initiatives combatting hunger and homelessness. Last week, he highlighted the 27th annual campaign by Connecticut Foodshare, with financial backing by Bank of America, to provide 40,000 Thanksgiving meals.
Such events are double-edged, underscoring the inability of the administration to fully address housing and food insecurity in Connecticut, a wealthy state with a problem named ALICE. 
That is an acronym for “Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed,” an annual United Way research initiative focused on the vulnerability of the working poor. This year, it found 39% of households have income below what is needed to afford basic necessities such as housing, food, child care, health care, technology and transportation.
It calculated that in Connecticut the “ALICE Household Survival Budget” is $40,140 for a single adult and $116,304 for a family of four with two adults, an infant and a preschooler. By comparison, the federal poverty level is $15,060 for a single adult and $31,200 for a family of four. 
“Look, the state does a lot,” Lamont said. “The need is more. But I also love the spirit of giving.”
Gov. Ned Lamont donates a turkey last week at Connecticut Foodshare. Credit: mark pazniokas / CT Mirror
Jason Jakubowski, the chief executive officer of the nonprofit Connecticut Foodshare, said last week that federal agencies have cut their contributions of food to places like Foodshare by 50% or more. 
“There’s at least one family in each of the 169 towns in Connecticut that don’t know where their next meal is coming from,” he said. “It ends up being 536,000 Connecticut residents — one in every seven individuals, one in every five kids here in the state of Connecticut.”
The federal cuts have both increased demand — nearly 63,000 people have lost SNAP benefits — and availability of food that Foodshare distributes to food pantries and at mobile distribution sites. 
The Lamont administration and General Assembly have been responsive, he said.
“You’ve got Democrats and Republicans, came together and said it’s unacceptable the cuts that we have gotten from the federal government,” Jakubowski said. “This year, between appropriations and between emergency funds, Connecticut Foodshare is getting $17 million from the state government.”
Every penny must go to the purchase of food and cannot be used for overhead or other administrative purposes, he said.

name: Nevada Current
title: Cortez Masto eager to grill Huang over Nvidia, Trump
description: U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto says she’s looking forward to questioning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang next week and “the opportunity to push for the answers the American people deserve.” Cortez Masto, a Nevada Democrat, is a member of the Senate Banking Committee, which has a hearing scheduled Dec. 3 for Huang to testify about export […]
text:
NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang delivers remarks as President Donald Trump looks on during an “Investing in America” event in April 2025. (Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian)U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto says she’s looking forward to questioning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang next week and “the opportunity to push for the answers the American people deserve.”
Cortez Masto, a Nevada Democrat, is a member of the Senate Banking Committee, which has a hearing scheduled Dec. 3 for Huang to testify about export controls on advanced artificial intelligence chips, whether American chips were diverted to China, and his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive with the Chinese firm Megaspeed.
Huang, an unabashed enthusiast of unregulated AI, resigned last week after news of his affair with Alice Huang surfaced, raising concerns about possible espionage and chip smuggling. 
On Sunday, Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated Huang after urging from President Donald Trump. The president told CNBC that he “made the deal” for Huang to return.  
Trump said Monday that U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Huang has been “exonerated” regarding chip diversion to China. Huang has not faced criminal charges.
Financial disclosure forms reveal Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of 2025. The stock plunged following Huang’s resignation and rebounded Monday after he was reinstated. The stock was down slightly Tuesday.
“Once again, President Trump put his financial interests ahead of our national security,” Cortez Masto said in a statement. “This corruption puts all of us at risk, and we need to get to the bottom of it.”
A spokesperson for Cortez Masto says she’s “long been pushing to ensure America’s national security is preserved in the development of cutting-edge technologies.” 
The senator’s FIGHT China Act, revised as the COINS Act, is awaiting implementation by the Treasury Dept. and will prohibit U.S. investment in high end chips and AI in China. 
She is a co-sponsor of the BLADE Act which is intended “to deter our foreign adversaries from stealing the proprietary capabilities of America’s frontier AI companies,” according to her spokesperson.

name: WyoFile
title: Man killed in I-80 deputy shooting didn’t have gun but went into ‘shooting stance,’ Laramie County Sheriff’s Office says
description:
The Laramie County Sheriff’s Office released body and dash camera footage of pursuit along Interstate 80 that resulted in Nov. 11 shooting. 
The post Man killed in I-80 deputy shooting didn’t have gun but went into ‘shooting stance,’ Laramie County Sheriff’s Office says appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Do you have questions about this story? Or information to share? Reach out to Maya Shimizu Harris at maya@wyofile.com.
A man that Laramie County Sheriff’s deputies shot and killed after a car chase didn’t have a firearm on him at the time of the incident, according to a video released by the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office on Tuesday. The sheriff’s office says the man went into a shooting stance during a foot chase, prompting officers to fire their weapons at him.
The released video combines body and dash camera footage taken from a Nov. 11 pursuit along Interstate 80 east of Cheyenne. The department acknowledged the shooting a few hours after the altercation, but Tuesday’s video release offered the first description of what happened before and during the incident.


On Nov. 11, two deputies, who aren’t named in the video, spotted a white flatbed Ford truck that had been reported stolen. They tried to stop the truck on an Interstate 80 service road. The truck initially pulled over, but as the deputies began to exit their vehicle, the driver, identified by Cowboy State Daily as 27-year-old Anthoney Bryant, sped away and got onto the interstate heading back toward Cheyenne. 
Dash camera footage shows the ensuing car chase. The deputies activated their emergency sirens and pursued the truck. Bryant made two U-turns through the center median of the interstate, cut across a grassy area to an exit and drove through a stop sign on the service road. 
A Laramie County sheriff’s deputy pursues a fleeing truck along Interstate 80 on Nov. 11, 2026. (Laramie County Sheriff’s Office YouTube screenshot)
Bryant continued on the service road then drove through a fence and back toward the interstate. By the interstate, Bryant got out of the truck and ran across one side of the expressway and the median. He fell, then got up again and continued running. Body camera footage shows him appearing to reach with his right hand to his pocket after he fell. 
The deputies stopped in the median, got out of the vehicle and ran after Bryant. “Get on the fucking ground!” one yelled as they pursued him. The deputies crested a small rise and drew their weapons. 
The body camera footage is pixelated and unclear, but appears to show Bryant facing the deputies as they approach him. Brandon Warner, the public information officer for the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office, described Bryant turning toward the deputies, pulling his right hand from his pocket, bringing his left hand up to meet his right hand and assuming “an aggressive shooting stance.” 
Two Laramie County sheriff’s deputies run toward a fleeing man after a car chase on Nov. 11, 2026. Authorities say the man took a shooting stance shortly afterward, and then at least one of the deputies shot and killed him. (Laramie County Sheriff’s Office YouTube screenshot)
Body camera footage shows one of the deputies ducking his head “as he believes the suspect is shooting at him,” Warner says in the video. The other deputy fired his weapon at Bryant. Four shots are heard in the video footage. WyoFile was unable to verify by publishing time whether one or both deputies fired at Bryant. 
The deputies gave Bryant medical aid until medics arrived. He was pronounced deceased at the scene. 
The Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation is reviewing the incident.
“An objective of the investigation is to determine what actions each deputy took, in addition to what the deputies believed and when they believed it,” Ryan Cox, the division’s commander, said in an email to WyoFile, adding that “making any statements at this time would be premature.” 
Cox said officer-involved shooting investigations “vary on multiple factors,” but expected the review to take four to six months.
This story was updated on Nov. 24 at 2:38 p.m. with comments from the Division of Criminal Investigation.

name: National
title: Turkey production bounces back but prices still rise
description: Turkey production for Thanksgiving has increased this year for the first time since avian diseases reduced supplies for years, but prices still rose as labor shortages created bottlenecks, according to federal reports. Turkey farmers, like other livestock producers, say they need more foreign workers as immigration crackdowns and the ending of protected stat[...]
text:
Turkeys gather for feeding at Whiffletree Farm in Virginia in September. Turkey production is up this year after two years of decline but prices rose because of strong demand and a shortage of whole birds. (Photo courtesy of Whiffletree Farm)Turkey production for Thanksgiving has increased this year for the first time since avian diseases reduced supplies for years, but prices still rose as labor shortages created bottlenecks, according to federal reports.
Turkey farmers, like other livestock producers, say they need more foreign workers as immigration crackdowns and the ending of protected status for many immigrants take a toll on their workforce. Many producers support proposed bipartisan federal legislation to give them more access to visas for temporary workers. 
Disruptions to Temporary Protected Status for some immigrants “could create significant operational challenges and further tighten an already constrained labor market,” Leslee Oden, CEO of the National Turkey Federation, wrote in an October op-ed supporting the federal visa legislation.

Top state turkey production, 2025

Minnesota – 33.5 million birds
North Carolina – 28.0 million birds
Arkansas – 21.5 million birds
Indiana – 20.0 million birds
Virginia – 15.3 million birds
Missouri – 14.7 million birds
Iowa – 10.8 million birds
Pennsylvania – 7.6 million birds



“This is a good first step to help packers and processors keep the rural economy moving and to ensure American consumers have access to affordable food,” Meat Institute CEO Julie Anna Potts said in a statement earlier this year. 
Minnesota, North Carolina and Arkansas last year had the highest turkey production numbers, and millions of turkeys were also produced in Indiana, Iowa, Missouri, Pennsylvania and Virginia, according to a U.S. Department of Agriculture report. 
Wholesale prices shot up to a projected $1.76 a pound for whole hen turkeys this year from $1.36 last year and just 94 cents in 2024, according to the USDA, a 30% one-year increase. But a Farm Bureau report found retail prices for turkey up only about 10% from last year as retailers used turkey promotions to draw customers – some reported prices as low as 69 cents per pound. 
Production increased this year to 5.1 billion pounds, after dropping two years in a row to as low as 4.8 billion pounds last year, but it’s still well below 2020’s 5.7 billion, according to the USDA report.  
“They’ve had a lot of disease pressure over the years, so they’re still building up production numbers. That being said, grocery stores love to offer turkey deals,” said Farm Bureau Deputy Chief Economist Faith Parum in a November podcast. 
New bird flu cases appear in dairy herds as state ag, vet officials seek vaccine urgency

Jesse Straight, who sells about 1,000 turkeys a year directly to customers at his Whiffletree Farm in Warrenton, Virginia, said he hasn’t been as affected by labor and disease issues as other, larger operations. His birds live outside on pastures with more fresh air than factory farms, and he pays a small staff fair wages, he said. 
“We get people coming to our farm from all over the country because they believe in our mission,” Straight said. “Our mission is to heal the land and give the animals a life that fits their nature, and heal our customers through good food.”
Nationwide, higher prices in most areas do not translate into more money for farmers, Farm Bureau Associate Economist Cameron Castillo told Stateline.
“Significantly higher costs are prohibiting farmers from capturing any economic benefit this year,” he said.   
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC anglers get another month to catch red snapper
description: After choppy waters led to fewer fish caught in October, a federal agency agreed to extend the state's snapper season.
text:
South Carolina anglers will have an additional month to catch red snapper. (Photo courtesy of Claire Filaski, SC Department of Natural Resources)COLUMBIA — Anglers who missed their chance to catch red snapper last month will have another opportunity this year.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration agreed to allow recreational anglers to continue capturing the fish off South Carolina’s coast throughout the month of December, the state Department of Natural Resources announced Tuesday.
Choppy waters led to fewer fish captured during the two-week window in October than anticipated, according to the agency. Anglers didn’t hit the cap approved in the state’s request for a longer season.
Anglers had 2 days to catch red snapper off SC’s coast this year. They want a much longer season.

The decision followed months of back and forth over how much time anglers should have to capture the fish, which many consider fun to catch and delicious to eat.
In past years, seasons have lasted only a day or two, which anglers and state officials said led to people taking more risks to catch the fish or skipping the season altogether.
The federal agency overseeing fishing permits initially approved the state’s request for a two-month season, but a federal lawsuit put the decision on pause. The agency ultimately approved a two-week season that lasted Oct. 9-22.
The rules for the December season are the same as the one in October. Anglers who don’t already have a permit can get one for free through the Department of Natural Resources. Anyone who goes fishing for red snapper must report their trips and any of the fish they catch.
Correct data reporting is crucial to getting longer seasons in the future, the state agency said in a news release. The longer season is part of a pilot program meant to determine how many of the fish are actually swimming off the Atlantic coast.
The federal government shortened seasons significantly because of a dwindling population of red snappers. But in recent years, anglers have reported seeing increased numbers of fish, suggesting the population may be healthier than previously believed, the state agency has said.
The South Carolina-based Coastal Conservation League, which focuses on preserving resources along the coast, is on board with the idea as a way of better managing the population of fish.
The Southeastern Fisheries Association, which represents nearly 300 southeastern businesses, and the Ocean Conservancy, a national nonprofit, are against expanding the seasons.
The two sued the U.S. Department of Commerce, which oversees the permit process, over the approval of expanded seasons in South Carolina, Florida, Georgia and North Carolina. The organizations said in court filings the federal government failed to consider the possibility of overfishing in violation of a 1976 conservation law.
That case is ongoing.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi to receive over $51M in FEMA disaster response funds
description: Corinth resident Shana Bates captured a photo of damage to a home caused by Winter Storm Fern in Corinth, Miss.
text:
Toward the end of a year in which Mississippi saw three federally declared disasters, the state is set to receive over $51 million in recently approved federal recovery funds.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency announced the approvals Monday. The grants include $10.3 million for Tallahatchie County to assist with debris removal following Winter Storm Fern in January. The announcement also listed the following awards:

Nearly $4.5 million to Tishomingo County Electric Power Association to repair and restore fiber-optic cables.
More than $4.2 million to Alcorn County Electric Power Association to repair and restore fiber-optic cables.
More than $3.9 million to Northeast Mississippi Power Association to repair and restore armored fiber-optic cables.
More than $2.2 million to Tishomingo County for debris removal.
More than $1.5 million to Montgomery County for debris removal.

In total, federal officials have obligated over $318 million in Public Assistance Program grants to assist Mississippi’s recovery from Fern, FEMA records show. Of that money, over $222 million is for debris removal. The state initially reported $416 million in damages from the storm.
Public Assistance funds, which go toward costs incurred by local and state governments in disaster recovery, include a 75% contribution from the federal government. State and local governments have to pay the remaining 25%.
In October, the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency told lawmakers it was struggling to stay afloat as it pays the state match for FEMA grants. In addition to Fern, one of the costliest disasters in state history, Mississippi received federal declarations for Tropical Storm Arthur and the May tornadoes. 
FEMA’s recent grant approvals include $378,000 through the agency’s Hazard Mitigation Grant Program and $375,000 through the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program. Both pots of money are intended to reduce the risks of future natural disasters through efforts like buying out flood prone homes or building safe rooms.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Mecklenburg County DA dismisses charge against Rep.-elect Womack of NC-14
description: LaKesha Womack ousted one of the state’s most powerful politicians when she defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Tim Moore in a surprise upset earlier this month.
text:
LaKesha Womack at a campaign event. (Photo: Womack campaign)The Mecklenburg County District Attorney’s office has cleared a felony charge against LaKesha Womack, representative-elect to North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District. 
Womack, a Democratic political newcomer, ousted one of the state’s most powerful politicians when she defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Tim Moore in a surprise upset earlier this month.
Moore served as speaker of the North Carolina House for a decade and oversaw the redistricting that carved out the 14th District for himself. He easily won the seat in 2024, but lost to Womack in 2026 by more than 6,000 votes, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. 
Womack’s victory is part of a blue wave that helped Democrats flip seven U.S. House seats in North Carolina. The Tar Heel State will send 11 Democrats and three Republicans to Washington in January. 
After moving to North Carolina in 2016, Womack and her young son became unhoused when a medical emergency left her hospitalized in intensive care. In 2020, she received a criminal summons for failing to return a rental car on time in 2019.
Unlikely political newcomer unseats NC powerhouse despite big challenges

Womack wasn’t served with the warrant until last month during a campaign event. 
Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer Merriweather dismissed the charge on Tuesday.
Merriweather said his office was informed of an agreement between Womack and the rental car dealer early last week.
“In the days that followed, we were able to confirm that the victim rental corporation received a sum of money from the Defendant equal to an assessed rental cost from the day the vehicle was deemed overdue until the day it came back into the possession of the victim corporation,” Merriweather said in a statement. 
“In a subsequent phone call with a prosecutor, representatives for the victim rental corporation said explicitly that the corporation did not wish to proceed further with prosecution and considered the matter resolved,” Merriweather continued. 
The district attorney’s office dismissed the charge, and with the matter closed, will provide no further comment, the statement said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Shreveport man arrested for threatening AG Murrill over prediction markets lawsuit
description: A Shreveport man was arrested Monday for allegedly making threats to kill Attorney General Liz Murrill over her lawsuit that temporarily halted prediction markets from operating in Louisiana, her office said in a news release.
text:
A Shreveport man was arrested after he allegedly threatened to kill Attorney General Liz Murrill. He was reportedly upset she had sued Kalshi and other prediction markets over their operations in Louisiana. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A Shreveport man was arrested Monday for allegedly making threats to kill Attorney General Liz Murrill over her lawsuit that temporarily halted prediction markets from operating in Louisiana, her office said in a news release.

Murrill announced Tuesday the Louisiana Bureau of Investigation, which she oversees, arrested Demarion Zyclaiborne Crowell with the help of the Shreveport Police Department. He has been charged with intimidation of a public officer and illegal telephone communications that involve improper language and harassment, according to the attorney general’s office. 

“I take the threat on my life and on the lives of the hundreds of employees at the Louisiana Department of Justice seriously. No one should have to live in fear for doing their public duty,” Murrill said in a written statement. 

Crowell allegedly called the Louisiana Department of Justice multiple times Nov. 13 and made threatening statements to a receptionist. He specifically mentioned being upset about a lawsuit Murrill had filed against Kalshi, Polymarket and other prediction markets, according to the attorney general’s office. 
Last week, a Tangipahoa Parish judge ruled in favor of Murrill and temporarily stopped those companies from operating in Louisiana. The threatening phone calls were reportedly made the day after that court order. 
The attorney general’s office said Crowell allegedly told the receptionist the attorney general needed to “quit f—ing with the market before she gets hurt. This will cause someone to get hurt because she is messing with people’s money.” 
In another call, Crowell allegedly said the agency needed to make a change “before I kill her and all you mother f—ers up there.”
Kalshi, Polymarket and similar companies take bets on the outcome of events, everything from the winner of an election to the effects of a natural disaster. Several people use the platforms to buy “event contracts” on the results of sports competitions, including specific plays that happen within games. 
In her lawsuit, Murrill alleges these activities amount to gambling operations that should be subject to Louisiana gambling laws. The prediction market companies and Trump administration officials disagree. 
The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission has countersued Louisiana and Murrill, arguing only the federal government, not states, have the authority to regulate the industry. 
Louisiana is one of several states — including Utah and Arkansas — engaged in legal battles over whether their gambling laws apply to prediction market operators. 

Crowell was expected to be transferred from Shreveport to the East Baton Rouge Parish jail, according to the attorney general’s office.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania considers whether to delay enforcing Medicaid work requirements
description: The state has until Dec. 11 to reach a decision, and the hold harmless period would last until the end of June. Otherwise, the work requirements — or volunteer hours — begin in January.
text:
Economic assistance application for the South Dakota Department of Social Services. (Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Earlier this month, states learned that they could delay enforcing work requirements for their residents on Medicaid. But Pennsylvania is “reviewing” guidance from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) “to determine next steps” before a December deadline.
“It is important to understand that this option is not a full delay of Medicaid work requirements or any other change to Medicaid required by (the law),” said a DHS spokesperson. “Taking advantage of this hold harmless option would only delay eligibility determinations and disenrollments made based on compliance with the new rules, it does not suspend the need for individuals to complete their Medicaid renewal.”
Pa. grapples with implementing Medicaid work requirements 

According to health policy researchers at KFF, 16 states have said they will delay, while another three said they would “likely” adopt the “hold harmless” option. Pennsylvania is one of 18 states that has yet to decide.
Amy Lowenstein, the director of policy with the Pennsylvania Health Law Project, noted that the commonwealth will still need to check if someone complies during that time, but won’t have to terminate anyone’s coverage.
“They’ll still go through the actions, but if someone turns out to be non-compliant, then they’re not supposed to take negative action,” Lowenstein said in a recent webinar. 
The state has until Dec. 11 to reach a decision, and the hold harmless period would last until the end of June. Otherwise, the work requirements — or volunteer hours — begin in January. 
The new rules are a priority for the Trump administration and only impact a select number of enrollees. There are exemptions for caregivers, students and others, but advocates warn that documenting these exemptions and tracking new requirements will be a barrier for people in need of health coverage.
“While this is an important option that all states should pursue, merely delaying the harm of a horrible law is not a sustainable solution,” said the Legal Action Center in a recent release, adding that participants may be confused by several rule changes.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“For people with substance use disorders and people leaving incarceration, such confusion could lead them to delay or stop seeking treatment and other care they need. That’s an enormous harm in itself, and yet another reason that Congress must repeal the rules once and for all,” the statement continued.
The organization pointed to newly imposed work requirements for food benefits. The state Department of Human Services estimates that 98,000 Pennsylvanians no longer receive food benefits due to those rules. The Legal Action Center appealed to the incoming Democratic majority in Congress, urging them to repeal requirements for both programs “to prevent further coverage losses and restore the vital food assistance many families have already lost.”
U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic nominee for House speaker, said that the Medicaid cuts included in the bill “should’ be reversed, but the process could be lengthy.
 Some states move ahead with work requirements amid confusion

A few states have pushed their work requirements out ahead of the planned rollout, some more smoothly than others. In Nebraska, for example, the vast majority of recently denied applicants simply failed to provide the proper documentation, meaning they could still qualify.
Stakeholders told States Newsroom that one of the biggest challenges was communicating various exemptions. Requirements can be met through work, by volunteering or going to school. But people with a documented substance use disorder, recently released prisoners and parents of young children are also exempt.
Previously, states redetermined someone’s eligibility annually — but now, those must happen, at a minimum, twice a year. An estimated 63% of Medicaid enrollees work 80 hours a month or attend school, and another 15% were exempt because they qualified as caregivers or had a disability. Of the remainder, some are retired or may be unable to find work for other reasons.

Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



A state DHS spokesperson said the agency had hired more than 700 caseworkers between November 2025 and October 2026, the staff who would be responsible for verifying if Pennsylvanians meet work requirements.
“It does take up to a year for a new caseworker to complete comprehensive training and master the skills needed to take on full caseload processing, which is what will make an impact on priorities like Medicaid redeterminations,” the spokesperson continued.
An early point of contention were rules around medical frailty, a category that Lowenstein said was “difficult to judge.” 
“DHS is going to do its best to try to figure out who falls into this exemption using information it already has,” Lowenstein said. “Hopefully, if that works, that means people will not have to do a lot to demonstrate this.” 
The law passed by Congress carved out an exemption for someone who is medically frail, such as someone with an HIV diagnosis or a disability like blindness. But the administration added a new rule over the summer that someone’s ability to work must be “significantly” impaired to qualify.
Pennsylvania joined onto a multi-state lawsuit to overturn the rule, and a judge ruled in favor of the states in late October.
