name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico joins lawsuit against Dollar General, alleges company overprices customers at checkout
description: The New Mexico Department of Justice on Monday announced the state had joined the Federal Trade Commission and a 30-state coalition in a lawsuit against discount retailer Dollar General, alleging the company violated federal and state consumer protection laws by overcharging consumers.
text:
The New Mexico Department of Justice announced Nov. 23, 2026, that it joined a lawsuit, along with the Federal Trade Commission and 30 other states, against discount retailer Dollar General, alleging the company has overcharged consumers at checkout. (Photo by Greg Childress/NC Newsline)The New Mexico Department of Justice on Monday announced the state had joined the Federal Trade Commission and a 30-state coalition in a lawsuit against discount retailer Dollar General, alleging the company violated federal and state consumer protection laws by overcharging consumers. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Dollar General, headquartered in Tennessee, is a chain of discount stores with more than 20,000 locations nationwide. In a recent lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, the FTC and 30 states allege that the company has systematically charged consumers more at checkout than the prices advertised. 
The lawsuit cites that Dollar General received at least 29,265 complaints categorized as “Did Not Honor Marked Price” between Jan. 1, 2023 to March 31, 2026, in all states where it operates. The complaints “demonstrate widespread consumer harm and confirm that customers nationwide have been charged more than the advertised price,” and that the company has not implemented safeguards to correct the issue, the lawsuit added.
The lawsuit also details that on several occasions earlier this year, undercover FTC agents made purchases at Dollar General locations in Ohio, Missouri, Pennsylvania and Maryland that resulted in overcharges to advertised prices. 
According to an NMDOJ news release, New Mexico state regulators also conducted 73 pricing inspections at Dollar General stores statewide from January to April. Of those inspections, 53% resulted in failures, with one store in Clovis failing three consecutive inspections.
“Families across our state, particularly those in rural communities who rely on Dollar General for affordable groceries and everyday necessities, should not have to worry about being overcharged when they check out,” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement. 
Dollar General disagreed with the lawsuit’s allegation that it “willfully disregarded the affordability needs of our customers” in a statement.
“Nothing could be further from the truth,” the statement continued. “Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store.”
The plaintiffs asked the court to order Dollar General to stop and prevent the practices alleged in the complaint, provide restitution to affected consumers and pay civil penalties. NMDOJ brings the lawsuit under the state’s Unfair Practices Act, a consumer protection law the state has used against vape retailers and social media behemoth Meta, which the First Judicial District Court ordered to pay $25 billion in October. 
“Pricing transparency is a basic responsibility of every retailer,” Torrez added in a statement. “Consumers should not be forced to spend additional time checking receipts, challenging incorrect charges or returning to stores to recover money they should never have been charged in the first place.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado to seek 6-month grace period for new Medicaid work requirements
description: Colorado will seek a six-month delay on enforcement of new Medicaid work requirements as officials build capacity to fully review enrollees’ eligibility. That means recipients of Medicaid, the health insurance program for low-income people, will not lose coverage until July if they can’t prove to the state that they work a required number of hours […]
text:
(Getty Images)Colorado will seek a six-month delay on enforcement of new Medicaid work requirements as officials build capacity to fully review enrollees’ eligibility.
That means recipients of Medicaid, the health insurance program for low-income people, will not lose coverage until July if they can’t prove to the state that they work a required number of hours every month or are otherwise exempted.
“Colorado is grateful to take the ‘hold harmless’ option so that we can prevent members from losing coverage due to the new federal work requirements for the first six months of 2027,” Adela Flores-Brennan, the Colorado Medicaid director, said in a Monday statement. “We will use this time to help our members understand how to meet the new requirement, work out operational concerns, offer additional training for eligibility staff and get additional guidance from” the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
CMS announced on Nov. 13 that it would delay enforcement of the new Medicaid work requirements for states that opt in. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act from 2025 requires that adults covered under Medicaid through the Affordable Care Act expansion earn $580 or complete at least 80 hours per month of work, volunteering or other qualifying activities. About 377,000 of the 1.2 million Coloradans on Medicaid are in that expansion population, according to Colorado’s Department of Health Care Policy and Financing.
“We have heard directly from states about their implementation timelines, impediments to successful launches at scale, policy updates, operations, and overall readiness,” Daniel Brillman, the CMS director of Medicaid, wrote in the letter announcing the “hold harmless” option. “We are aware that leading up to January 1, 2027, and continuing thereafter, states are and will be actively identifying and addressing deficiencies, such as updating eligibility determination logics and system-generated notices, and mitigating challenges to maintain compliance with timely eligibility operations.”
He wrote that states should use reliable existing data and automation as much as possible to determine if Medicaid enrollees satisfy work requirements. Colorado is already planning to do that, officials said during an October briefing with reporters. People will be able to self-attest to their work activities during 2027, but Colorado will have to start verifying work hours in 2028.
Health First Colorado launched an online self-screener tool for Coloradans on Medicaid to determine if they are subject to the new requirements.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Federal retiree clears hurdle with $8,200 refund claim against Kansas Department of Revenue
description: A Manhattan resident moves step closer to $8,200 reimbursement for overpayment of state income taxes paid in 2017 despite a 3-year statute of limitations.
text:
Ellen Goeckler testifies Nov. 10, 2026, before the Joint Committee on Claims Against the State to seek reimbursement of overpaid income taxes from 2017. (Kansas Reflector screen capture from Kansas Legislature video)TOPEKA — The Kansas Department of Revenue confirms Ellen Goeckler overpaid state income tax during four consecutive years on distributions from a federal retirement plan.
The state agency agreed to refunds for Goeckler covering three years of improper tax assessed on payouts from a Thrift Savings Plan, but declined reimbursement for 2017 because of a three-year statute of limitations. Goeckler lost an administrative appeal, and complained to the governor’s office and to state legislators. Eventually, she sought relief from the Kansas Legislature’s Joint Committee on Claims Against the State.
Goeckler, of Manhattan, anchored her argument for the $8,232 reimbursement to an allegation the Department of Revenue conspired to limit public awareness of the agency’s 2013 policy change ending assessment of state income tax on withdrawals from federal 401(k)-style TSP plans. She asserted the agency’s leadership avoided proper transparency because of fear it could cost the state treasury $6 million per year in refund demands.
“In this case,” she said, “the executive branch failed the public, creating a situation where it was functionally impossible for an ordinary citizen to know they were overpaying their taxes. As a result, the state spent years quietly accepting overpayments from retirees like me who were relying on the state’s public-facing instructions.”
Ted Smith, the current chief counsel at the Department of Revenue, said there was no factual dispute about whether Goeckler overpaid on her state income taxes. He said there was no “purposeful intent” by the state agency to bury the administrative policy change on taxation of the federal retirement accounts, but otherwise accepted as accurate Goeckler’s explanation of what transpired in her case.
Smith urged the committee to reject Goeckler’s request for reimbursement on her 2017 assessment. He told legislators that waiving the statute of limitations on tax appeals would set bad precedent.
“The question for you is how granular does the Department of Revenue have to get with regard to everybody’s tax circumstance?” Smith said. “We would respectfully ask the committee not to approve the request.”
The committee left unresolved debate about a conspiracy of silence but approved a recommendation that the full Legislature mandate payment of $8,232 to Goeckler for the fourth year of overpayment on her state taxes. To do so, the committee agreed to waive its internal Rule 6(a) to sidestep a three-year cap on claims.
“Three years did get repaid,” said Rep. Susan Humphries, a Wichita Republican and an attorney serving on the claims committee. “Are we not going to repay one more year just because of a rule?”
Rep. Ken Rahjes, R-Agro, said the committee was a place where Kansans who lacked alternative legal recourse and believed they were treated unfairly by state government could be heard.
“I was trying to look at it from a non-attorney standpoint,” Rahjes said. “It seems like this is the court of last resort, if you will, and the state messed up. To me, when it comes to a matter of taxes, a partial payment doesn’t seem right.”
Goeckler, of Manhattan, said a statute of limitations on tax reimbursements made since if the state demonstrated it was operating on a level playing field.
“It assumes the state of Kansas acts with transparency,” she said. “I did not overpay my taxes because I made a mistake. I overpaid my state income taxes because the state chose to change their interpretation … and not tell anyone.”
Before 2013, the Department of Revenue applied state income tax to federal Thrift Savings Plan withdrawals. During the 2012 legislative session, revenue secretary Nick Jordan signed testimony endorsing House Bill 2480 to affirm TSP distributions as taxable income in Kansas. Jordan said at that time the department was fighting an administrative appeal related to TSP taxes that could grow into a court case and, if the state lost, impose a “potential negative fiscal impact” of $6 million per fiscal year. That bill wasn’t approved by the Legislature.
Goeckler said that in 2013 the Department of Revenue reversed course and relied on administrative authority to make TSP distributions exempt from Kansas income tax.
“But the Department of Revenue did not publish a formal administrative regulation,” Goeckler said. “They did not issue a broad public notice. They did not change the plain language in the annual tax booklets used by everyday citizens. Instead, they chose to roll out this massive statutory shift quietly, through internal administrative channels.”
On this point, Smith said the Department of Revenue wouldn’t deceive taxpayers to claim a $6 million benefit to the state’s bottom line.
“In scope of how much money we collect,” Smith said, “you know $5 or $6 million is not something that you’re going to say, ‘OK, let’s carve out a little exception. Let’s keep this secret.’ ”
Rep. Bob Lewis, an attorney and Garden City Republican on the claims committee, argued the Legislature should take into account the legal concept of “laches.” The doctrine allowed a court to deny relief to a plaintiff who unreasonably delayed assertion of a claim and caused prejudice against a defendant.
“In this situation we need to think about the equities,” Lewis said. “I don’t think the department was intentionally obfuscating or hiding this from taxpayers. At most it was maybe, perhaps, negligence.”
Sen. Brenda Dietrich, a Topeka Republican who chairs the claims committee, said it was noteworthy a tax refund claim for the 2017 tax year was being heard by the committee in 2026. If approved by the full Legislature, the resolution would take place a decade after the fact in 2027.
“If it was that urgent I would have hoped it would have gotten here sooner,” she said.
Goeckler said the statute of limitations was a vital legal tool that could be used to address questions of liability when taxpayers sat on their rights when the rules were clearly defined. In this instance, she said, the Department of Revenue didn’t publish sufficient clarifying information on the tax exemption for TSP accounts until 2021.
“It is not intended to shield the state from returning money it wrongfully collected because it kept a policy clarification secret,” she said. “I did not miss a deadline due to negligence. I missed it because of administrative concealment.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont: CT’s savings habits pay big dividends in next budget
description: Gov. Ned Lamont touted the nearly $11.5 billion in surplus funds CT has contributed toward pension payments since 2020.
text:
Connecticut must spend almost $3.4 billion next fiscal year to fund pensions promised to state employees and municipal teachers.
But while that burden likely will consume a healthy share of the next state budget, about 12% according to analysts, it would be almost $1 billion greater if Connecticut hadn’t reformed its savings habits, Gov. Ned Lamont announced Tuesday.
“Paying down our pension debt is one of the smartest investments we can make for Connecticut taxpayers,” the governor said, referring to nearly $11.5 billion in surplus the state has poured into its two pension programs since 2020.
Connecticut must contribute a minimum amount yearly that’s based not only on the thousands of retirees drawing benefits, but also on the assets those pension funds hold. And for decades prior to 2011, governors and legislatures found legal loopholes to short-change those required payments.
But by voluntarily depositing surplus funds — in addition to making the full, required payment — state officials have stopped those mandatory contributions from growing exponentially and stealing resources from other vital programs, Lamont said.
“That’s money we can put toward the services Connecticut families rely on instead of old debt,” he added, “and it keeps retirement secure for the teachers and public employees who earned it.”
“Connecticut continues to demonstrate what disciplined fiscal management and thoughtful, long-term planning can accomplish,” said state Treasurer Erick Russell, who joined Lamont and Comptroller Sean Scanlon in announcing the pension savings Tuesday in the State Office Building. “We will continue to build on this momentum to ensure the retirement security of teachers and public servants for generations to come.”
But Lamont and the General Assembly will be hard-pressed to continue to dedicate as much surplus to pensions in future fiscal years as they did over the past seven.
Many of the governor’s fellow Democrats in the legislature’s majority say the budget caps that forced surpluses averaging $1.9 billion yearly over the past decade — representing 8% to 9% of the General Fund — were too aggressive. Those caps stripped more dollars from education, healthcare, social services, municipal aid and other vital programs than surging, mandatory pension contributions would have, some have argued.
But it was easy for officials to compromise most of those years because Connecticut received more than $4 billion in emergency federal COVID grants through the American Rescue Planning Act and the Coronavirus Relief Fund. And Lamont and lawmakers could use huge chunks of those dollars annually to backfill traditional state revenues stripped from the General Fund by budget caps.
That pandemic relief now has been exhausted and Democratic legislative leaders are calling for Lamont to modify savings efforts somewhat. They argue Connecticut still can enjoy budget surpluses, albeit smaller ones, while devoting more resources to core programs.
Lamont, a fiscal moderate, said Tuesday he was cautious about making any major changes to budget caps. Despite having enough assets in each pension fund to cover more than 65% of long-term costs, the state still carries nearly $29 billion in unfunded obligations, according to the governor’s budget office.
And Lamont likely will have some support from minority Republicans, who also have warned against significant adjustments.
“The challenge now is protecting the system that made it possible, one built through good bipartisan reforms in 2017,” said Rep. Joe Polletta of Watertown, ranking House Republican on the Finance, Revenue and Bonding Committee. “The threat will come from Democrats in the legislature, members of the governor’s own party, who are willing to not only cut pension payments so they can spend one-time, volatile revenue, but also change the rules to put even more of it into government programs instead of tax relief.”
Scanlon, who has said he believes the budget caps need some adjustments to allow investments in important programs such as municipal aid, said Connecticut nonetheless has been very successful with its savings efforts in recent years.
“Connecticut’s finances have seen a complete turnaround in the last eight years, and we should be really proud of that as a state,” the comptroller said Tuesday. “Our mission now is to continue that progress and combine it with sustained economic growth and an aggressive effort to lower the costs businesses and families are dealing with.”
Scanlon and Lamont said much of their focus over the next few years will be to contain surging healthcare costs, both for the state as well as Connecticut families and businesses.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: USDA suspends license of a major Iowa puppy mill
description: Federal regulators have suspended, for 21 days, the license of one of Iowa’s largest puppy mill operations. The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service has taken the action against Christine A. Snakenberg, the licensed operator of a large-scale breeding facility in West Point, Iowa. The kennel was formerly licensed to Stev[...]
text:
This kennel in West Point, Iowa, has been repeatedly cited for failure to provide adequate veterinary care. The USDA suspended the owner's license in 2023, and in November 2026 suspended the license of the current operator, Christine Snakenberg. The dog pictured here is one of those that federal inspectors alleged was in need of veterinary care in 2022. (Aerial photo courtesy of Bailing Out Benji. Inset photo taken by USDA inspector, courtesy of Bailing Out Benji)Federal regulators have suspended, for 21 days, the license of one of Iowa’s largest puppy mill operations.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service has taken the action against Christine A. Snakenberg, the licensed operator of a large-scale breeding facility in West Point, Iowa. The kennel was formerly licensed to Steve Kruse, an individual who has been repeatedly cited for violating animal-welfare regulations. County records indicate Kruse still owns the business and the property.
On Nov. 18, the USDA’s notified Snakenberg her license was being suspended for 21 days. That action appears to be tied to a Nov. 5, 2026, visit to the property by USDA inspectors, although the federal agency has yet to publish its full inspection report on that visit.
During the suspension, the USDA says, Snakenberg is barred from buying, selling, transporting or exhibiting dogs or any other animals whose care is regulated by the Animal Welfare Act.
Federal records indicate that in February 2026, Snakenberg had a total of 435 dogs on the property, which would make the West Point kennel one of Iowa’s largest dog-breeding operations.
Among the allegations listed in the notice of suspension sent to Snakenberg:
Fraud: The USDA alleges Snakenberg “interfered with APHIS officials in the course of carrying out their duties by providing false statements and fraudulent records to APHIS officials.
No veterinarian: Snakenberg “failed to employ an attending veterinarian under formal arrangements” to care for animals at the kennel, the USDA says.
Veterinary care: Snakenberg failed to establish and maintain “a program of adequate veterinary care” that was approved by an attending veterinarian and used appropriate methods to prevent, diagnose, and treat disease and injuries, according to the USDA.
Exercise space: The USDA asserts that Snakenberg failed to develop and follow an appropriate, approved plan to provide dogs with an opportunity for exercise.
Vet visits: Snakenberg allegedly failed to have in place a veterinary care plan that regularly scheduled visits, at least once a year, by an attending veterinarian to ensure the  adequacy of all aspects of animal care on the premises.
Annual exams: The USDA alleges Snakenberg had no approved plan that provided for a complete, annual physical examination, from head to tail, of each dog by an attending veterinarian.
Vaccinations: Snakenberg had no approved veterinary care plan that provided for vaccinations against contagious or deadly diseases specific to dogs, such as rabies, parvovirus and distemper, the USDA alleges. In addition, the agency says Snakenberg had no approved plan that provided for the testing and treatment of parasites and other pests, such as fleas and heartworm.
Snakenberg and Kruse each tied to the kennel
In court filings, the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals has alleged that Kruse didn’t cease operations at the West Point facility with the loss of his USDA license in August 2025, but instead expanded what the ASPCA calls “illegal activities” intended to facilitate the sale of puppies and dogs.
According to the ASPCA, within days of Kruse’s license being canceled in August 2025, the USDA approved Snakenberg’s application for a license to do business at the same West Point address where Kruse had for years operated what was then called Stonehenge Kennels.
County real estate records show that in July of this year, Kruse transferred ownership of the West Point kennel to a newly formed limited liability corporation, Tipsy Tail. That company’s officers are not publicly disclosed, but its mailing address – which is where the property-tax bills for the West Point kennel are sent — is a $723,000 residence located 3.5 miles west of the kennel on the same road, Highway 16. That home was purchased by Kruse in March of this year, according to county records.
The ASPCA alleges in its lawsuit the transfer of the license into Snakenberg’s name is part of a puppy-laundering scheme designed to conceal Kruse’s ownership of the kennel. The organization claims the license transfer enables the West Point kennel to sell dogs to brokers and retailers in states that restrict the purchase of dogs acquired from licensees who are repeat violators of the Animal Welfare Act.
Federal records show that prior to the license transfer, Kruse had been cited for numerous animal-welfare violations, including throwing a bag of dead puppies at an inspector, but continued to operate under a USDA license.
The ASPCA’s lawsuit, which is aimed at the USDA and alleges a lack of enforcement by the agency, is still pending in federal court. The USDA has denied any wrongdoing.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Snakenberg or Kruse for comment.

title: Indiana risks missing out on millions in federal mental health funding as deadline nears
description: Indiana mental health providers are urging Gov. Mike Braun to expand a federally backed behavioral health program before a December deadline, warning that the state is already missing out on millions of dollars in funding that could improve access to care. The push comes more than three years after Indiana lawmakers committed $100 million to […]
text:
Republican state Sen. Michael Crider, of Greenfield, speaks at the Indiana Statehouse on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, about the need to expand Indiana's Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic program. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana mental health providers are urging Gov. Mike Braun to expand a federally backed behavioral health program before a December deadline, warning that the state is already missing out on millions of dollars in funding that could improve access to care.
The push comes more than three years after Indiana lawmakers committed $100 million to overhauling the state’s mental health care system and nearly two years after eight community mental health centers began participating in a federal Medicaid pilot program intended to improve access to mental health and addiction treatment.
Those eight centers cover 35 of Indiana’s 92 counties. Providers want to extend the program to the remaining 57.
Doing so could bring Indiana an estimated $55 million annually in additional federal Medicaid matching dollars, said Zoe Frantz, president and CEO of the Indiana Council of Community Mental Health Centers.
The state would still be responsible for a portion of the Medicaid costs, but the enhanced federal match reduces Indiana’s share. It’s unclear how much additional state funding, if any, would be needed to expand the program statewide.
“This is not about a provider getting rich,” Frantz said. “This is about a provider providing services to those who need it most.”



Quotation







This is not about a provider getting rich. This is about a provider providing services to those who need it most.


– Zoe Frantz, president and CEO of the Indiana Council of Community Mental Health Centers


But the state must submit paperwork to federal officials by Dec. 1 to move forward with a Jan. 1 expansion.
“Gov. Braun has led on this issue and supported the funding of the CCBHC program since taking office, committing over $115 million since 2025,” a spokesperson for the governor said in a statement to the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “The governor will evaluate this program in the context of all Medicaid-related spending with the Medicaid forecast in December.”
Indiana’s Family and Social Services Administration did not respond to the Capital Chronicle’s requests for comment.
Indiana’s 22 community mental health centers collectively serve 375,000 Hoosiers across all 92 counties, but only eight participate in the federal Medicaid pilot program, formally known as the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic (CCBHC) demonstration.
“From my perspective, it would just be a tragedy for us to not continue moving forward,” said Republican state Sen. Michael Crider, of Greenfield, who joined mental health care providers, local government officials and law enforcement representatives at the Indiana Statehouse on Tuesday. “We will not achieve what  the collective goal is any other way.”
Millions in federal funding at stake
Indiana lawmakers laid the groundwork for the state’s current behavioral health system in 2023 with the passage of Senate Enrolled Act 1, authored by Crider.
The legislation sought to establish a statewide system in which Hoosiers experiencing mental health emergencies have someone to call, someone to respond and somewhere to go for treatment. Those three components are the state’s 988 suicide and crisis hotline, mobile crisis response teams and crisis stabilization units.
Zoe Frantz, president and CEO of the Indiana Council of Community Mental Health Centers, urges state officials on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, to pursue additional federal funding for behavioral health services. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Lawmakers appropriated $50 million annually in the 2023 state budget to get the system off the ground. That fell short of the roughly $130 million in annual funding the Indiana Behavioral Health Commission had recommended to support a fully developed crisis response system.
Under the CCBHC model, participating clinics receive Medicaid reimbursements based on the anticipated cost of providing comprehensive care rather than relying solely on payments for individual services.
The pilot program provides Indiana with enhanced federal Medicaid matching funds and was intended to help the state expand the model statewide and establish a sustainable funding structure for behavioral health services.
Clinics must meet federal standards and provide a range of services, including mental health and substance use treatment, round-the-clock crisis response, care coordination and specialized services for veterans. They must also serve patients regardless of their ability to pay.
Frantz said the state is forgoing about $4 million in potential federal funding each month that the demonstration is not expanded statewide.
“The state is leaving federal match dollars for infrastructure, for workforce, for behavioral health needs — that’s an extensive amount to be able to use,” Frantz told reporters Tuesday.
Based on her conversations with state officials, Frantz said the administration’s top concern appears to be how Indiana would pay for those services once the demonstration ends in late 2028 and the enhanced federal match is no longer available.
She maintained, however, that providers have presented the state with options for sustaining the model beyond the demonstration period.
Crider said he had not spoken directly with Braun about the issue but has met with FSSA officials. The senator said he’s willing to consider modifications to the model to address any of administration’s financial concerns.
Story continues below.
Sen. Crider CCBHC LOS 10.26.26
 
“If you talk to the folks who are running the pilot sites, you’ll see that the the data is really positive,” Crider said, adding that he would also be open to an incremental expansion if state officials are unwilling to extend the program to all remaining counties at once.
“Can they go five more? Can they go 10 more?” Crider said. “I think that’s the discussion.”
In an Oct. 26 letter to Braun, Crider and 17 other senators from both sides of the aisle urged the administration to continue participating in the pilot program, allow additional providers to join as they meet state readiness requirements and establish a timeline for statewide coverage.
Lawmakers also asked the administration to outline how Indiana would sustain the Medicaid reimbursement model after the pilot program ends and fund crisis services in the meantime. They cautioned against delaying or replacing the model before the state can fully assess its costs and effectiveness.
“A custom approach should not replace the legislatively chosen pathway without clear evidence that it will preserve these standards, sustain the crisis continuum, and deliver equal or better access statewide,” the senators wrote.
Getting more Hoosiers into treatment
Frantz said the state’s investments in behavioral health infrastructure have dramatically shortened the time it takes for Hoosiers to get help.
“When I started five years ago, it was about six to eight months to get someone in, and now we’re getting people in same day,” she said.
“Game changer” bill aims to revolutionize mental health care system

Before the 2023 legislation took effect, mobile crisis teams were responding to emergencies in just 16 Indiana counties. By June 2024, that number had grown to 59 counties.
Between July 2025 and July 2026, Indiana recorded 14,676 mobile crisis dispatches and 23,781 visits to crisis stabilization units.
Crider and other legislators noted that community mental health centers and certified clinics operate nearly all of Indiana’s crisis stabilization capacity.
A May report from the National Council for Mental Wellbeing found that 12 Indiana providers operating under the CCBHC model collectively served more than 119,000 people — a 31% increase since adopting the model.
All 12 reported providing behavioral health services in schools, child care facilities or other settings that serve young people. All also reported partnerships with courts.
Nationally, the council estimated that certified clinics served 3.4 million people in 2025. Providers responding to its 2026 impact survey reported an average 42% increase in the number of patients served since becoming certified clinics.
Frantz said a statewide expansion is especially important in rural communities, where providers have historically struggled to recruit mental health professionals and patients can face long waits or have to travel substantial distances to get treatment.
Story continues below.
1784127743354
 
Local governments have made their own investments, too.
Hamilton County Commissioner Mark Heirbrandt pointed to the county’s partnership with community mental health provider Aspire Indiana Health to open the Rely Center in 2025.
He said his interest in improving local access to mental health treatment dates back to the 2018 shooting at Noblesville West Middle School. Hamilton County has since invested millions of dollars in behavioral health services.
“While there’s been a lot of good work that’s been done in our counties and also on the local level, we need the partnership with state government to make a greater impact on our local communities,” Heirbrandt said.
Easing burdens on Indiana’s jails and hospitals
Law enforcement officials have likewise backed a statewide expansion, arguing that better access to treatment outside of hospitals and jails could reduce the number of Hoosiers cycling through the criminal justice system.
Steve Luce, executive director of the Indiana Sheriffs’ Association and a former Knox County sheriff, said addressing mental illness and substance use disorders has been among the biggest challenges facing county sheriffs for years.
He said sheriffs want more resources to help people return to their families and become productive members of their communities after leaving jail.
“Law enforcement cannot solve the behavioral health crisis alone,” Luce said. “Certified community behavioral health clinics are proven they are essential allies in improving public safety and quality of life.”
Indiana is additionally grappling with the cost of providing psychiatric treatment to criminal defendants deemed incompetent to stand trial.
Competency restoration is intended to ensure defendants understand the criminal proceedings against them and can participate in their own defense. The state spends about $80 million annually on competency restoration, Crider said.
Indiana lawmakers, mental health care providers and local officials gather at the Indiana Statehouse on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, to call for the statewide expansion of a federally backed behavioral health program. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
The senator said problems can arise when defendants are sent to state psychiatric hospitals for treatment and then returned to local jails, where their mental health can deteriorate again before trial.
Community-based providers could help maintain continuity of care and, in some cases, provide restoration services closer to home.
“We want them taken care of. We want them to understand the ramifications of the criminal proceedings against them,” Crider said. “It’s an obligation the state has.”
Expansion of the certified clinic model was among the recommendations made following a summer study of the competency restoration issue through the state’s Justice Reinvestment Advisory Council.
Crider said the goal is also to get Hoosiers into treatment before their mental health deteriorates to the point that they require hospitalization or become involved in the criminal justice system.
The senator said he witnessed the issue firsthand while working in hospital security, where he regularly encountered families who sought emergency psychiatric care but left without an immediate option for follow-up treatment.
“What you often saw was, under the old model, somebody would leave the emergency room with nothing fixed,” Crider said. “They’ve got a card to go see a counselor in 30 or 60 days.”
Expanding the model, he said, could also help address gaps in care between urban and rural communities.
“We don’t want access to care by geography,” Crider said.
What comes next?
Frantz told reporters on Tuesday that providers are pushing for action this week — ahead of the Dec. 1 deadline — because of the Thanksgiving holiday.
Additional providers can join the pilot at subsequent quarterly intervals, but each delay would shorten the amount of time those clinics could participate and receive the enhanced federal match.
Frantz said providers would likely seek $30 million annually from state lawmakers during the 2027 budget-writing session if the administration does not proceed. That money would come without the enhanced federal match.

“That’s not to expand,” Frantz said. “That’s really just to sustain our crisis services.”
Crider indicated that he, too, would pursue legislative solutions if the administration does not move forward, although he said the state would be better positioned financially if it could take advantage of the available federal funding.
“I could come back as a legislator and ask for the the whole amount to be funded,” Crider said. “But it really doesn’t make sense to not get the federal match, right?”
Among those advocating Tuesday for the expansion was Donnisha Duncan, an Army veteran and peer recovery specialist who spoke about her own experience living with schizophrenia and helping others manage their mental health.
She emphasized that peer recovery specialists draw on their personal experiences with mental illness or substance use disorders to help others navigate treatment and recovery.
“Hoosiers want the care provided by CCBHCs. Hoosiers want to get and feel better. They want to fill a place in society and feel productive,” Duncan said. “We can’t leave work unfinished. We can’t leave clients without care or without hope.”
“On my journey to recovery, in years of being a peer support specialist, I have never seen anything remotely like CCBHC,” she continued. “We need its expansion, not its extinction.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: State of Iowa certifies 2026 election results, with no changes from unofficial results
description: Iowa State Board of Canvass certified election results Tuesday for Iowa’s Nov. 3, 2026 election, which saw a voter turnout of 62.35%.  Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate said there had been a “shift more and more” toward early voting, and this most recent election showed that more early voters are choosing to vote in […]
text:
Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate spoke with reporters in his office at the Iowa State Capitol Nov. 24, 2026, with other members of the Iowa State Board of Canvass joining virtually, to certify the results of the 2026 midterm election. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa State Board of Canvass certified election results Tuesday for Iowa’s Nov. 3, 2026 election, which saw a voter turnout of 62.35%. 
Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate said there had been a “shift more and more” toward early voting, and this most recent election showed that more early voters are choosing to vote in person at the auditor’s office or at satellite sites. Nearly 30% of all ballots were cast in person before Election Day, according to Pate. 
The board’s certification is the final step for the state in all races and issues on the ballot, aside from the governor and lieutenant governor race, which will be canvassed by the Legislature at the start of session. Certificates for federal positions, U.S. Senate or U.S. House of Representatives, will be sent to respective offices in Washington, D.C. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bailey Kelley, the state director of elections, said Tuesday there was one recount this election, in Pottawattamie County for an Iowa House race. The recount found no discrepancies, meaning Republican Rep. Brent Siegrist maintained his seat in the House. 
“Overall, there were no balancing discrepancies to report for the 2026 general election,” Kelley said. 
Winneshiek County had the highest voter turnout, according to Pate, with 70.34%.
Pate said overall, there were about 12% more ballots submitted in this election compared to the last midterm election in 2022. 

The Iowa State Board of Canvass includes: Pate, Gov. Kim Reynolds, Treasurer Roby Smith, Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig and Auditor Rob Sand. 

He attributed the high turnout to the competitive nature of the races on the ballot and the millions in advertising spent in Iowa for the election. According to reporting from the Des Moines Register, there was about $525 million spent on 2026 election ads in Iowa. Pate said “it was a pretty expensive election cycle, to put it candidly.” 
“When you have an open governor’s race and an open U.S. Senate race and several congressional races, the way they were situated, I think there’s something for everybody, and then on top of that, a constitutional amendment,” Pate said. “That should have been appealing enough to get a lot of people out to vote.” 
According to the Secretary of State, about 36% of all ballots cast were absentee ballots and of those, about 23% were sent via mail. 
“So satellite voting … was a bigger channel than the mail was,” Pate said. 
He said he believes part of this change has to do with voter concerns of whether or not the “mail moves fast enough.” 
Mail-in voting has also been targeted by the Trump administration, which sought to add regulations to the process.
Moving forward, Pate said there is always some “technical tweaking” to be done following an election, but he said “nothing major came out” of the election in terms of process. Pate said the state had about 10,000 poll workers. 
Pate said his office is still analyzing demographic data from the election and finalizing legislative priorities for the upcoming session, which begins in January.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: As Florida prepares for next execution, Uthmeier slams California for death sentence commutations
description: As the state of Florida prepares for its 40th execution in the past two years next week, Attorney General James Uthmeier is condemning California Gov. Gavin Newsom for his commutation of death sentences of all 548 inmates on that state’s death row. While California remains one of 27 states that still has the death penalty […]
text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom promotes his book during a Feb. 21, 2026, stop in Nashville at Oz Arts, a visual and performing arts facility. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)As the state of Florida prepares for its 40th execution in the past two years next week, Attorney General James Uthmeier is condemning California Gov. Gavin Newsom for his commutation of death sentences of all 548 inmates on that state’s death row.
While California remains one of 27 states that still has the death penalty on its books, the Golden State hasn’t executed anyone since 2006. And Newsom guaranteed that wouldn’t change when he issued a moratorium on the death penalty after he took office in 2019.
Since 2019, 14 states have held executions, according to the State Court Report. Of those, four — Florida, Alabama, Texas, and South Carolina — carried out 72% of them in 2025. Forty percent of those executed last year were in Florida, and the state’s 20 executions this year are more than all the other states combined, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
The state executed 70-year-old Thomas Mitchell Overton Thursday night.
The next inmate set to be executed by Florida is Ricardo Gonzalez, 56, convicted of the first-degree murder of a North Miami police officer in 1992. Gonzalez was one of five men who robbed the Kislack National Bank in North Miami. The officer was working an off-duty job at the bank and tried to stop the suspects before he was shot and killed.
A jury convicted Gonzalez in 1994 and, in the penalty phase, recommended death by a 7-5 vote. He appealed, and in 1997 the Florida Supreme Court affirmed his conviction but reversed his death sentence. During a second penalty phase in 1998, the jury recommended death by a vote of 8-4. The state Supreme Court affirmed that sentence in 2001. (Some of that information is provided from the Tracking Florida’s Death Penalty Substack page.)
Gonzalez’s attorneys have raised claims that his intellectual limitations and brain injuries as a youth raised questions about whether he can understand why the state intends to execute him. A state commission examined Gonzalez on Nov. 18 and reported to the governor that he has the mental capacity to understand the nature of the death penalty and the reasons it is being used against him.
“It seems like the state commission is very good at greenlighting these executions over and over and over again,” the Rev. Dr. Jeff Hood said Tuesday in a remote press conference. “We have seen people who have major intellectual issues who have not received proper engagement before, so it is no surprise that this execution has been greenlit by folks who so regularly greenlight other executions.”
In addition to Gonzalez, death row inmate Willie Crain is scheduled to be executed Dec. 10.
“These two executions are quite possibly the last two executions in Gov. Ron DeSantis’ treacherous tenure,” Hood said. “Forty executions in the last two years. It’s also unbelievable that this many people have been executed. It’s not just unbelievable with regards to Gov. DeSantis and his desire to make this happen; it’s also unbelievable as to what this has cost in terms of the lives of corrections officers. In terms of the loss to victims’ families. In terms of the lives of families of the condemned.”
Hood has served as spiritual adviser to 15 death row inmates around the country, including Reinaldo Dennes of Texas, put to death last week. His execution took more than an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the intravenous needles carrying the lethal injection drugs before they inserted them in Dennes’ left foot and on the left side of his neck, according to the Associated Press.
 State attorneys general
Uthmeier was one of 14 Republican attorneys general who signed a letter Monday to Gov. Newsom condemning his decision on Nov. 5 to commute the death sentences of his state’s death row inmates.
“These are not victims of a broken system,” the letter says of the convicted death row inmates. “They are murderers, each convicted by a jury beyond a reasonable doubt and sentenced to death only after a separate penalty trial. Among them are men who murdered children, police officers, and the innocent, some on several occasions. With one stroke of your pen, you overrode hundreds of juries, the courts that upheld their verdicts, and the families who were promised justice.”
President Trump also criticized Newsom Monday during a speech at U.S. Department of Justice headquarters in Washington, D.C.

title: Newborn vaccination rates for hepatitis B drop sharply
description: The percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccine has declined sharply in recent years, falling to 65.6% in June 2026 from 79.8% in 2022, according to a new study published today in the New England Journal of Medicine. The authors of the peer-reviewed study looked at health records from more than 1.3 million infants […]
text:
A worker applies an adhesive bandage to a child at a vaccination clinic in Minneapolis’ Corcoran Park in August 2023. A new study found the nationwide percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccination has declined sharply since 2023. (Photo courtesy of the City of Minneapolis)The percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccine has declined sharply in recent years, falling to 65.6% in June 2026 from 79.8% in 2022, according to a new study published today in the New England Journal of Medicine.
The authors of the peer-reviewed study looked at health records from more than 1.3 million infants and found that the percentage of babies receiving the hepatitis B vaccination within one day of birth began declining around 2023. The study also found that fewer mothers testing positive for hepatitis B got the vaccine for their babies, from around 98% of those infants in 2025 to around 94% in 2026. 
A panel of federal vaccine advisors, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, voted in December 2025 to end the longtime recommendation for infants to receive the hepatitis B vaccination at birth even if the mom tested negative. That decision is on hold pending legal challenges.
The study was based on data from Truveta, a health data and analytics company owned and governed by 30 health systems across the nation.
In explaining the December change, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said screening of pregnant women is highly reliable and can spot disease early. But Nina Masters, an author of the new study and a principal applied research scientist at Truveta specializing in infectious disease and maternal health, told Stateline that “not every mother is tested during pregnancy, and not every person who gets tested has a known status.”
“And screening is imperfect,” she said. “This birth dose has been a universal recommendation to be a safety net to catch those kids that might fall through the cracks, and what we’re seeing here is that that safety net is kind of falling apart.” 
Hepatitis B is a contagious liver infection that can cause symptoms of fatigue, loss of appetite and jaundice, and potentially lead to cancer. But it can be prevented through a vaccination. The virus can be passed down from an infected mother to a baby, so since 1991, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recommended that all newborns receive the hepatitis B vaccination within a day after birth to prevent early infections, especially when mothers test positive. 
A 2023 study by CDC researchers found that between 1990 and 2019, with the recommendation for newborn vaccination, there was a 99% decline in reported cases of acute hepatitis B among people younger than 19 years old. 
It’s official: Measles is endemic again in the US

But amid growing vaccination skepticism, the new study found that fewer babies are getting the shot. The shift began a few years before vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. became secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in February 2025. 
Researchers noted the decline in vaccination rates for hepatitis B comes as the federal government and many conservative states walk back vaccine mandates for children. Just this month, the United States lost its status as a country that had eliminated measles, as the transmission of measles has risen in the last year. Children are particularly susceptible to the disease. 
“When messaging gets confusing and there’s different recommendations coming from different medical bodies and different kinds of assessments of vaccine safety that are being publicized, I think it can become scary and hard to make the right choice,” Masters said. 
“And I think that’s what we’re seeing is just extreme confusion as a result of the level of misinformation and changing recommendations around pediatric vaccines.” 
Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org.

text:
Highmark Health Options Delaware has launched a pilot program to help family caregivers of eligible Medicaid members manage day-to-day care and find support in their communities.
The 18-month program gives caregivers of eligible members who use self-directed attendant care one-on-one guidance and help finding local services.
WILMINGTON, Del. — Highmark Health Options Delaware has launched a pilot program to help family caregivers of eligible Medicaid members manage day-to-day care and find support in their communities. Highmark is offering the program in partnership with Carallel.
Caregivers can speak one-on-one with an adviser about their family’s needs, get help finding and navigating local services and use online tools and educational materials. Carallel delivers the services through a team with backgrounds in nursing, social work and caregiver support. The team reaches out to eligible caregivers by phone and text, Highmark said.
The 18-month pilot began Oct. 5, and Highmark announced it Nov. 24 during National Family Caregivers Month. It is available to family caregivers of eligible Highmark Medicaid members who use self-directed attendant care, including members who receive it through long-term services and supports. That option gives members more control over who provides their care and how it is delivered, according to Highmark’s member handbook.
Jessica Sebastian, Highmark Health Options’ director of social determinants of health, said the program recognizes the physical, emotional and financial strain that can come with caring for a loved one.
A 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving estimated that 197,000 Delaware adults, or 24%, had cared for a family member or friend in the previous year. Nationally, nearly four in 10 family caregivers reported emotional stress, and 23% said caregiving made it difficult to take care of their own health.
Highmark is offering the pilot as an additional resource outside its covered plan benefits. The insurer said it will track how caregivers use the service and look for ways to improve it. Highmark plans to expand the initiative into Pennsylvania in 2027 and has identified Medicaid and Medicare populations for broader expansion.
To Go Box
Who — Family caregivers of eligible Highmark Health Options Delaware Medicaid members who use self-directed attendant care.
What — One-on-one coaching, online tools, educational materials and help finding local services.
When — The 18-month pilot began Oct. 5, 2026.
Where — Delaware. The program contacts eligible caregivers by phone and text.
Why — To help family caregivers manage day-to-day care and ease the strain of caregiving.
How to learn more — Ask the member’s Highmark case manager about the caregiver support pilot or call Highmark’s Delaware long-term services and supports line at 855-401-8251 (TTY 711).

name: Source New Mexico
title: Federal judge orders Kalshi to stop allowing sports gambling on some New Mexico tribal lands
description: A federal judge on Monday ruled in favor of three New Mexico pueblos and one tribe in their lawsuit alleging the online prediction market Kalshi is allowing sports gambling on their lands and therefore violating tribal sovereignty.
text:
U.S. District Court Judge Margaret Strickland on Nov. 23, 2026, ruled that online prediction market Kalshi must cease allowing sports betting within the boundaries of three pueblos and one tribe in New Mexico. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A federal judge on Monday ruled in favor of three New Mexico pueblos and one tribe in their lawsuit alleging the online prediction market Kalshi is allowing sports gambling on their lands and therefore violating tribal sovereignty. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
U.S. District Court Judge Margaret Strickland issued a 29-page ruling that orders Kalshi to prohibit users from accessing the platform within the boundaries of the Sandia, Isleta and Pojoaque pueblos or the Mescalero Apache reservation. Those are the four tribal plaintiffs that sued Kalshi in May. 
Their lawsuit alleged that the company was violating state gaming compacts and federal law by allowing users in New Mexico to place online wagers on the outcomes of sporting events. In New Mexico, sports gambling is allowed only at tribal casinos.
Kalshi’s lawyers have countered that the federal Commodities Exchange Act trumps the federal  Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, as well as state gaming compacts, and that regulating the platform is under the sole discretion of the Commodities Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that oversees prediction markets.
The company also argued that it is not subject to gaming compacts that it is not a party to, and that it can’t be held to tribal laws when its offices aren’t on New Mexico tribal land. 
However, Strickland’s ruling dispenses with the company’s arguments by citing recent rulings in other states and by determining that the Commodities Exchange Act is not intended to “preempt or displace all state gaming laws” nor “the ability of Tribes to enforce” their own compacts. 
She also wrote that she is “unpersuaded by Kalshi’s argument” that conducting its business over the internet with off-site servers insulates it from state gaming compacts or federal law. 
As part of the lawsuit, the plaintiffs instructed tribal employees to access Kalshi while on tribal lands and identify which sports wagers were available. One Mescalero gaming agent wrote in a court declaration that the “wagers or bets are materially the same as those offered” in the tribe’s Inn of the Mountain Gods or Casino Apache. 
Information technology specialists for the three Pueblo plaintiffs also reported approximately 30,000 visits to Kalshi’s website over a three-week period on their respective Wi-Fi networks, though they did not identify how many wagers users placed. 
Prediction market Kalshi registers as New Mexico lobbyist employer ahead of legislative session

Strickland’s ruling orders Kalshi within the next 14 days to establish a virtual “geofence” or otherwise find a way to block access to Kalshi sports betting on those tribal lands. The lawsuit notes that the app has similar geofences established in more than 50 other jurisdictions around the world. 
The judge’s ruling is a preliminary injunction issued while the lawsuit otherwise proceeds in federal court. 
A spokesperson for Kalshi declined to comment in an email to Source NM.. Leaders of the four tribal governments that sued the company did not immediately respond to Source NM’s requests for comment Tuesday.

On Monday, a federal district court judge approved a settlement for $950,000 for the family of 44-year-old Justin Grant, who was shot and killed on May 6, 2024, during a police stop near the West Virginia State Fair[...]
text:
(Getty Images)A settlement has been reached between the state of West Virginia and the estate of a man shot and killed by State Police in Greenbrier in 2024.
On Monday, a federal district court judge approved a settlement for $950,000 for the family of 44-year-old Justin Grant, who was shot and killed on May 6, 2024, during a police stop near the West Virginia State Fairgrounds.
Grant, according to a news release from the family’s attorneys, was walking to meet his girlfriend when stopped by a state trooper. At the time, he was carrying a garden tool, which attorneys say he never displayed in a threatening manner.
Grant was shot multiple times in the back, a news release states.
Barbara Burdette, Grant’s mother, is quoted in the news release as stating she hopes police will reform their practices moving forward.
“Justin has finally received a measure of the justice he deserves,” she said. “We are grateful for the efforts of the entire legal team in pursuing accountability on his behalf through the civil justice system. We hope this case leads to better law enforcement training and de-escalation practices so that no other family has to endure what ours has.”
Attorneys representing State Police did not return an email seeking comment.
The estate was represented by L. Danté diTrapano, Amanda J. Davis, and Charles
F. Bellomy of Calwell Luce diTrapano PLLC; W. Jesse Forbes, Jennifer N. Taylor, and Michael Heidenreich of Forbes Law Offices, PLLC; and Larry Forman of Forman & Associates in Louisville, Kentucky.

text:
Dear Reader,
Today, you have the chance to double your impact for Vermont. A group of three donors have generously pledged to match all donations to VTDigger’s Thanksgiving Drive. 
That means a special year-end gift today will go twice as far before 11:59 p.m. on November 26 — supporting local journalism and helping provide meals through the Vermont Foodbank.

2X your gift & send 10 meals

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: State launches new tourism office to boost outdoor recreation in Kentucky
description: Kentucky tourism officials are launching a new office to boost outdoor recreation as a part of the state’s multi-billion dollar tourism industry. The Office of Outdoor Recreation, created through an executive order by Gov. Andy Beshear, will work to “help expand outdoor opportunities” and bring more visitors to the state, according to a Tuesday afternoon […]
text:
Creation Falls is a favorite hiking destination for tourists in Wolfe County. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Jamie Lucke)Kentucky tourism officials are launching a new office to boost outdoor recreation as a part of the state’s multi-billion dollar tourism industry.
The Office of Outdoor Recreation, created through an executive order by Gov. Andy Beshear, will work to “help expand outdoor opportunities” and bring more visitors to the state, according to a Tuesday afternoon release. 
The new office will also administer the Kentucky Trail Town Program, a group of highlighted communities throughout the state with notable outdoor recreation opportunities, including hiking and biking.
“Our record-breaking $14.6 billion tourism industry is essential to our commonwealth’s success, and outdoor recreation is a major driver that this industry and our local communities depend on,” Beshear said in a provided statement. 
Beshear said the office would expand recreation opportunities across the state and “further support jobs, local businesses and communities across our commonwealth.”
Seth Wheat, who served as the director of interpretation and engagement for Kentucky State Parks, will be the new office’s executive director. The new office will also have a dedicated license plate that will be available for purchase online, according to the release.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota oil contamination poses challenges that could ‘cascade,’ regulators say
description: The discovery of contaminants in North Dakota crude oil being exported out of state has created a headache for the energy industry that could become a serious problem.  Two major oil export routes, the Dakota Access Pipeline and Enbridge’s pipeline to Minnesota, have begun requiring all crude oil deliveries be tested for organic chlorides before […]
text:
Justin Kringstad, director of the North Dakota Pipeline Authority, provides an update on oil and gas infrastructure on Dec. 19, 2025. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)The discovery of contaminants in North Dakota crude oil being exported out of state has created a headache for the energy industry that could become a serious problem. 
Two major oil export routes, the Dakota Access Pipeline and Enbridge’s pipeline to Minnesota, have begun requiring all crude oil deliveries be tested for organic chlorides before entering the system, North Dakota regulators said this week. The corrosive contaminant was first detected at Enbridge’s hub in Minnesota, according to media reports.
That has left at least Enbridge’s pipeline operating at a reduced capacity as oil companies rush to submit samples to overwhelmed commercial labs and find storage space to hold crude oil produced while they wait for results, according to state officials. 
Enbridge confirmed its pipeline system, which crosses North Dakota from the Bakken oil field to Minnesota, is experiencing delays due to the organic chloride contamination. 
“We expect delays to continue in the short term, until feeders deliver product clean of organic chlorides continuously,” the company said in a statement. “Enbridge is working with shippers to return service to normal operations as quickly as possible.”
A spokesperson for Dakota Access Pipeline developer Energy Transfer did not respond to a request for comment.
North Dakota Pipeline Authority Director Justin Kringstad said he estimates oil production in the state has decreased between 40,000 and 60,000 barrels per day as a result, a small slice of the state’s 1.1 million barrels of daily production. But that may only last for as long as companies have storage space for oil waiting to be tested.
“We’re probably getting to the point where tanks are full,” Kringstad said Monday during a meeting of the North Dakota Industrial Commission. “This could cascade quickly.”
He noted storage capacity varies by company, and predicting when space will run out is “totally speculative.”
The organic chloride contamination is not a public safety risk, Kringstad said. But it is corrosive, and can damage equipment such as pipelines and refineries. Two refineries have reportedly stopped accepting deliveries of North Dakota crude oil, though Kringstad said he has not independently verified those reports. 
Part of the problem is even a few gallons can be enough to contaminate tens of thousands of barrels of crude oil, Kringstad said. 
“It does not take much of this organic fluoride to contaminate large volumes,” Kringstad said.
Organic chloride does not naturally occur in the Bakken formation, which means it can only have been introduced by an external source. Nathan Anderson, director of the Department of Mineral Resources, said it could have been in chemicals used at a well site for tank cleaning or well servicing. 
But identifying the source of the contamination is easier said than done. 
“You’re looking for a needle in a haystack,” Anderson said. 
Kringstad said producers are being required to test their crude oil before major pipelines will accept it. But those tests have to be sent to commercial labs, such as those in Minot and Bismarck, which are experiencing a backlog. 
“Those testing facilities, I was told, are bringing in additional staff and resources to increase the speed of it,” Kringstad said.
He noted the issue has not affected the refinery in Mandan or other retail products sold in North Dakota. 
Anderson does not expect it to be a long-term issue. 
North Dakota’s state government is heavily reliant on the tax revenue generated by crude oil production.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.
