title: Gov. Kay Ivey appoints William Cole to Alabama Supreme Court
description: Gov. Kay Ivey on Tuesday appointed William Cole, a state Court of Criminal Appeals judge, to the Alabama Supreme Court. The appointment followed the U.S. Senate confirmation of Justice Greg Cook to be the U.S. District Court Judge for the Northern District of Alabama on Nov. 12. Cole was elected to the Alabama Court of […]
text:
Gov. Kay Ivey appointed William Cole to the Alabama Supreme Court on Nov. 24, 2026, following the confirmation of Justice Greg Cook to be the U.S. District Court Judge for the Northern District of Alabama. Cole's nomination is Ivey's sixth to the state's high court, a record among Alabama governors. (courtesy of Gov. Ivey's office)Gov. Kay Ivey on Tuesday appointed William Cole, a state Court of Criminal Appeals judge, to the Alabama Supreme Court.
The appointment followed the U.S. Senate confirmation of Justice Greg Cook to be the U.S. District Court Judge for the Northern District of Alabama on Nov. 12.
Cole was elected to the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals in 2019. In 2005, he was appointed circuit judge in Jefferson County by Gov. Bob Riley and was subsequently elected to two terms in the Criminal Division, according to a release from Ivey’s office. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Bill Cole is well known to the people of Alabama, and he brings decades of judicial experience to our state’s Supreme Court,” Ivey said in a statement on Tuesday. “Alabama is a state that ensures justice is served, and Bill’s vast experience with criminal cases, in particular, make him exceptionally qualified to serve the people of our state.”
Cole earned a law degree from The University of Alabama School of Law in 1992. Prior to his appointment to the Jefferson County Circuit Court, he had a private practice involving criminal, civil, domestic relations, family and probate law, according to the release. 
Cole said he is honored that Ivey is confident in his judgement through her appointment in a statement.
“After serving as a circuit court judge and as a judge on the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals for over 20 years, I am excited to accept this new responsibility,” Cole said. “Having been born and raised in Alabama and having developed a love for the law at an early age, I cannot think of any higher honor than being able to serve the people of the state of Alabama as a member (of) our Supreme Court.”
Cole’s appointment is Ivey’s sixth to the Supreme Court bench, a record among Alabama governors. The justices are elected, except in cases of a vacancy. All nine justices are Republicans. 
Ben Baxley tapped to Court of Criminal Appeals
Gov. Kay Ivey appointed Elmore County District Judge Ben Baxley to the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals to fill a vacancy left by an Alabama Supreme Court nomination on Nov. 24, 2026. (courtesy of Gov. Ivey’s office)
To fill Cole’s vacancy in the Court of Criminal Appeals, Ivey appointed Elmore County District Court Judge Ben Baxley.
“When I tapped Ben to the district court in Elmore County, he answered the call and has been very effective. I know he will continue serving our state well on the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals,” she said.
Ivey appointed Baxley to the district courtship in 2024. Another University of Alabama School of Law graduate, Baxley started his legal career in Tuscaloosa as Assistant District Attorney in 1990 where he handled drug prosecutions, according to the release. 
“Serving the people of Elmore County as a district court judge has been a privilege. That work has reinforced for me how much is at stake for the people who come before our courts and how important it is that every case receives careful and impartial consideration,” Baxley said.
Both appointments are effective immediately. Ivey will make another appointment to fill Baxley’s vacancy at a later date.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi opioid settlement council finalizes yearly recommendations as some raise concerns with new grading process
description: Members of the Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council listen and take notes at the group's meeting in Jackson, Miss. on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026.
text:
The Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council decided on roughly $39 million in its top 2026 funding recommendations Monday as its members raised new concerns about their adjusted roles in an altered application scoring process. 
After the council received 149 applications from 120 different organizations this fall, the Steadman Group, a Colorado-based behavioral health consulting firm, reviewed the proposals seeking some of Mississippi’s expected $431 million from companies that contributed to over 10,000 Mississippi overdose deaths. 
The Mississippi Attorney General’s office, which runs the council, sent committee members summaries of the firm’s grading on Nov. 17. Steadman provided members access to its notes for each application, which requested about $143 million in total, the next day.


At Monday’s meeting, the council accepted most of Steadman’s assessments but boosted up lower-scored state agency applications totaling about $14 million to the top-ranked tier, even as many council members said they didn’t know what issues the Colorado consulting firm had with the proposals. 
Jennifer Dick, a Mississippi Public Health Institute project specialist who’s been in addiction recovery for over a decade, said after the meeting that regardless of which groups are applying for funds, she wished the council better understood the initial grading rearranging the rankings.
“If we move everything on feelings, then why are we in this room doing this?” she asked.
The council’s grading process differed from the previous year, when small groups of council members were the first people to assess the applications. During that process, members raised concerns about how each group approached grading proposals, and how some on the council had opportunities to lobby for organizations they were affiliated with. 
Months later, the Mississippi Legislature changed state law to require the council to partner with an outside group like Steadman, in addition to strengthening council rules aimed at preventing potential conflicts of interests among committee members. 
Using the same scoring rubric as the council approved in 2025, Steadman highly recommended some applications from organizations that won Mississippi opioid settlement money last cycle. But the consulting firm also scored over two dozen applications from currently-funded groups in the bottom half of grades. 
Like it did last year, the full council had the power to adjust Steadman’s grades. But throughout the meeting, some council members expressed confusion and discomfort about how they should approach those decisions without having thoroughly reviewed the applications themselves. 
Many members said they hadn’t read all of the Steadman reviewers’ notes on the 149 applications in the five days since getting access to the files, and some expressed unease about tinkering with the consultant firm’s grades without that knowledge. 
Mississippi Department of Education Chief Operating Officer Kym Wiggins, right, listens to another council member at the Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council meeting in Jackson, Miss. on November 23, 2026 Credit: Allen Siegler / Mississippi Today
Kym Wiggins, chief operating officer of the Mississippi Department of Education, questioned Joseph Sclafani, Gov. Tate Reeves’ attorney, as he sought to raise three applications from the state’s Department of Mental Health — requesting about $5.4 million in total — to the council’s highest tier of recommendations.“Is it an issue with the quality of the proposals?” Wiggins asked. “Is it resulting in a low score, as compared to some of the private entities?” 
Sclafani said he couldn’t answer that question because he hadn’t looked as thoroughly at all the applications as he did last year. But he said he looked closely at the mental health department’s proposals, and he believed they should be funded. 
“I don’t think you’re going to find people who are more dedicated and committed to this mission than the employees of the Department of Mental Health,” he said.
Joseph Scalfani discusses agenda items during the Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council meeting at the Carroll Gartin Justice Building in Jackson, Tuesday, Dec. 2, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Sclafani made a similar motion for applications from the Mississippi Supreme Court, all related to drug intervention courts run by the state’s Administrative Office of Courts. Sclafani asked that four proposals — in total asking around $8.5 million and each receiving mediocre grades from Steadman — all be moved to the council’s highest recommendation level.
He said seeing the applications from an organization funded by the Legislature last year graded poorly didn’t sit well with him. Sen. Nicole Boyd, a Republican from Oxford and a council member, said she wanted to learn more about what Steadman graders saw in the drug court applications that concerned them.
“Maybe they didn’t hire a grant writer? Or did they consider there to be significant pieces missing in the application?” Boyd asked the council members. “We just need a little more feedback.”
Wiggins echoed Boyd’s concerns and said it might be perceived as arbitrary to move graded Department of Mental Health and court applications up in the rankings without knowing whether Steadman had identified major holes in the proposals. 
“It is not against these entities,” she told the council. “These entities are amazing entities. So, it is just me preserving the integrity of the process.” 
No graders from the Steadman Group attended the meeting, and the Attorney General’s office only read their application notes for one group they identified as a “submission irregularity.” Dr. JK Costello, Steadman’s behavioral health consulting director, said in an email after the meeting that the group scored proposals only on the application material a group submitted and graded based on the rubric the council approved. 
Deputy Attorney General Doug Miracle leads the Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council meeting in Jackson, Miss. on November 23, 2026. Credit: Allen Siegler / Mississippi Today
Wiggins asked council members if it would be possible to ask the Steadman Group questions about the applications before deciding what to do about the seven mental health department and supreme court applications. Mississippi Deputy Attorney General Doug Miracle, representing council chair and Republican Attorney General Lynn Fitch, said the group could make those final decisions at a tentatively scheduled Nov. 30 meeting. 
But the council members ultimately decided to cancel that meeting and finalize recommendations this week, and they voted to move all seven applications to the highest recommendation tier without asking Steadman those questions.
While discussing what to do with these grants, several council members with vested interests in the organizations applying for opioid settlement money followed the new conflict-of-interest procedures Miracle outlined at the beginning of the meeting. Members, such as committee co-vice chair and Department of Mental Health Executive Director Wendy Bailey, left the room when their applications came up, and they told Miracle they wouldn’t be voting on the proposals. 
Mississippi Supreme Court Justice Jenifer Branning, a member who joined the council in July, chose not to leave the room when the body discussed the drug intervention court applications. Instead, she told others on the council that funding the proposals would be “common sense.” 
“I, like many of you, have been boots on the ground for years and am comfortable with the work of these agencies,” she said to the other members.
After the meeting, Branning told Mississippi Today that unlike judges presiding over intervention courts, supreme court justices are not directly intertwined with the drug courts. Despite the applications being listed as Mississippi Supreme Court proposals, she said her body is funded through a different budget than those programs, and she did not have a conflict of interest. 
“We checked all that out to make sure,” she said. 
Jenifer Branning, a Mississippi Supreme Court Justice, speaks at a Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council meeting in Jackson, Miss. on Nov. 23, 2026. Credit: Allen Siegler / Mississippi Today
Michelle Williams, chief of staff for Attorney General Fitch’s office, said after the meeting that despite the application listing on the grading packet, the state’s administrative judicial office was the applicant rather than the Supreme Court itself. 
Beyond unease with changing individual application grades, some on the council worried about problems that could emerge in this new setup. James Moore, the Hattiesburg father of a child who died of an opioid overdose, told his peers that he worried the council’s reduced role in vetting applications could lead to the Legislature funding ineffective organizations. 
During last year’s cycle, after Moore said he found an organization applying for funds prohibited patients from using evidence-based opioid addiction medications, the council voted to require that all funded organizations must allow their participants to continue with their prescriptions. On Monday, he said the Steadman group told him it hadn’t inquired about applicants’ policies around medications.
“There may be some facilities that have slipped through the cracks that are not practicing the best science that is available for recovery treatment,” Moore told the other council members. 
Williams told Mississippi Today that while Steadman didn’t verify the medication policies of every organization, the group assessed whether an applicant used evidence-based practices. 
Now that the council has finalized its decisions, Williams said Fitch’s office will compile the recommendations and send them to the Legislature by Dec. 4.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bristol artist Gloria ‘Glo’ Sessions returns to her roots
description: The exhibition, at the Carousel Museum through Dec. 31, paints a portrait of an artist, mother and educator who was deeply curious.
text:
It’s the light, falling over the red and yellow brick of Bristol’s Main Street, that draws in the viewer.  Beneath a cluster of low-hanging gray clouds, three brick buildings line the road, quiet as cars trundle past. From a smear of blue sky above, mid-afternoon light spills down, making the brick glow. 
And yet, it’s too quiet here, in what’s supposed to be the beating heart of a Connecticut city. The hustle and bustle of a self-sustaining Main Street is conspicuously absent. 
Gloria “Glo” Sessions’s undated “What’s Left of Main Street” is one of hundreds of canvases, etchings, pen-and-ink drawings, and watercolor compositions that build “Glo Sessions Returns to Bristol,” an exhibition at the Carousel Museum running through Dec. 31 of this year. 
A retrospective of Sessions’s work that becomes a vibrant celebration of her life, the show paints a portrait of an artist, mother, educator and Bristol resident who was deeply curious about the world around her, and eager to document a city and its people over half a century of change. 
It marks Sessions’s fourth exhibition at the museum, where she was an active volunteer for years, and the second since her death in November 2011. 
“I think what’s most impressive about her work, that I also love the most, is that she really picked this [practice] up in her 30s,” said Jenny O’Connor, director of development at the museum. “I think because of that, her study of people is different. She appreciated the everyday moments, the mundane, and that is so beautiful.”
Siblings Ruth, left, and Don Sessions talk about on of their mother’s pieces as staff, volunteers and family members get the Glo Sessions Returns to Bristol exhibit ready at The Carousel Museum in Bristol on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
She motioned to a painting of Sessions’s youngest daughter, Molly, wearing a striped shirt and stretched out on a couch. “It’s not just people doing fantastic things. It’s just people. I find that timeless.” 
Sessions’s work, and the decades of life she spent in Bristol, are very much intertwined. Born and raised in Waltham, Mass. (her son, Don Sessions, said that her name came from the phrase “Gloria in Excelsis Deo,” which her father proclaimed after a long and complicated birth), Sessions’s early creativity led her to study visual art at Skidmore College, a path that brought her to New York City after graduation.
From the early to the mid 1940s, she worked for Macy’s New York offices, using her art background in the advertising department. Then she met Lt. James (Jim) Sessions, with whom she would have and raise five children across multiple cities, and ultimately make a home in Bristol. Within a year of marrying in 1945, they had moved across the country to California, and welcomed their first son, Paul. They were there for just roughly a year before James returned fully to civilian life.   
In the late 1940s, the growing Sessions family returned to James’s native Bristol so he could  take over the long-running family business J.H. Sessions & Son, where six generations of his family produced the small, indispensable parts for trunks and foot lockers from 1854 into the 1990s. Years later, she would document every detail of the building for an anniversary catalogue, from its timekeeping fixtures to the equipment that made its machinery run. 
Ruth Sessions sorts through her mothers prints as staff, volunteers and family members get the Glo Sessions Returns to Bristol exhibit ready at The Carousel Museum in Bristol on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
What no one expected, perhaps even Sessions herself, was the degree to which her work would become a record of a city in the midst of a transformation. In the mid 1960s, as urban renewal projects were gaining speed across the country, Bristol began a demolition of its Main Street district to make space for a shopping mall that — after several fits and starts — materialized in 1969, changed hands in 1973, and struggled under multiple owners for the next two decades.  
Sessions, who had come to love her adopted home, became — quite by accident — both an artist and an activist. By then, she had expanded her practice to the family’s J.H. Sessions building, where she had both a studio and taught classes to other local artists and art students. Her daughter Ruth, who by that time had followed in her mother’s footsteps at Skidmore and then studied ceramics at UConn, remembered how deeply her mother opposed the development, and mourned the city she loved as it changed before her eyes. 
“She was so angry and so involved with what happened to Main Street,” Ruth said, remembering multiple letters her mother wrote to a local newspaper, most likely the Bristol Press. “She would walk all over Bristol” and chronicle the city, creating a historical record in the process. In the 1980s, she did a number of paintings of the city’s Main Street for the Bristol Historical Society which still live in the organization’s collection. 
Staff, volunteers and family members sort through prints as they get the Glo Sessions Returns to Bristol exhibit ready at The Carousel Museum in Bristol on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Before that, she raised her children, and figured out how to make a way for her artistic practice. Even as Sessions became a mother five times over — after Paul came Don, then Tulis, Ruth, and Molly — “she found the time to draw,” Don remembered as he helped install the show with his sister Ruth and wife Roxanne last week. At first, the drawings came in fits and starts as she raised her children, the eldest of whom was in college while the youngest was in diapers. And then, when she was in her late 30s, Sessions started to hit her stride.
“She would just draw all the time,” said Ruth, remembering the excitement with which her mother reacted to the first magic markers, which became widely available in the 1960s. As she built her practice, Sessions kept a notebook of the artists who inspired her, from the French Impressionists to American neoclassicists like Maxfied Parrish and his contemporaries. “She was a consummate draftswoman.”
As Sessions found more time to dedicate to her practice, she became especially interested in picturing the world around her, especially the small, pedestrian details of life in a small Connecticut city. It was not uncommon, Don Sessions remembered, for his mother to scale Bristol’s South Mountain and paint the city from above, or to pull over on the side of a street to jot down a quick study, sometimes for a work that became a painting or, slightly later, an etching that she produced at home.  
Etching, which falls under the umbrella of intaglio printmaking, is a process in which an artist covers a metal plate in wax, creates a design with their etching implement (usually a needle), and then submerges the plate in acid, which eats away at the parts of metal that have been exposed. The artist then inks the plate, a process that must be done in precise and meticulous detail multiple times for a color print, aligns it with the paper or substrate on which they are printing, and passes it through the press. Everything is done in mirror image, so that an artist essentially has to be thinking in reverse when they create the design. 
Ruth Sessions points out a plate her mother used for prints as staff, volunteers and family members get the Glo Sessions Returns to Bristol exhibit ready at The Carousel Museum in Bristol on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Often, Sessions carried around a camera, and “would just take pictures of people” she found interesting, Don said. They came from all walks of life: waitresses, store attendants, staff and visitors at bed and breakfasts she stayed at on her travels, homeowners and the houses they lived in, her own children. Last Thursday, both Ruth and Don Sessions gravitated toward one such image, a quickly-dashed-off study that became a subject of her etching practice as it deepened. 
In the initial drawing, done in charcoal that has smudged with time, two women — or maybe it’s the same woman, pictured twice — stand back to back, their hair pulled up into messy chignons. One, on the right, leans over a pad of paper, scribbling something down quickly. Sessions, even in her haste, has captured fine details: the crinkle of her apron, a row of round buttons beneath it, the flyaway bangs that hang over her eyes. Beside her, a woman tilts her head just slightly to the right, hands clasped at her waist. 
Don said it came from her travels. His mother was just like that — she loved drawing people, and found them inherently interesting simply because they were there.    
By the time Sessions was in her 40s, she had drawers full of thousands of photographs, some of which she returned to over and over again. Around that same time, she took a class in printmaking at the Farmington Arts Center, “and she was bitten by the bug.” Ruth’s smile as she spoke suggested that the etching pun was fully intended. 
Within years, Sessions’ home studio space included a Charles Brand printing press, a massive piece of hardware on which she created both black-and-white and color etchings for the remaining decades of her life. One, of a hairdresser named Rose, channels the whimsy and quirk of artists like Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, with clementine-colored hair and a patterned, burnt orange background that seems to set the print ablaze. Another features a woman leaning back, her face rendered in blue and orange inks that highlight her tight crown of curls. 
Museum Manager Marita Damenia, left, and Volunteer Michael Brauer make sure pieces are level as staff, volunteers and family members get the Glo Sessions Returns to Bristol exhibit ready at The Carousel Museum in Bristol on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
As she installed the exhibition last Thursday, Museum Manager Marita Damenia said that she’s excited for attendees to experience not just the breadth of Sessions’ work, and the intimate journey that it takes through Bristol’s history, but the care that she poured into her artistic process.  
In the gallery that welcomes visitors to the show, for instance, several of Sessions’ old paintbrushes fill mugs that she molded herself. Nearby, there’s a poster showing the progression of a single oil painting, which Sessions photographed obsessively as she worked on it. 
“It’s very interesting!” Damenia said. “Definitely she has a very unique technique. My goal is to show people her technique, and to show her as a person.”

title: Democrats plan investigations of Trump. Here’s how his Justice Department is fighting back.
description: As the Trump administration prepares for Democrats to launch an onslaught of investigations in the next Congress, the U.S. Department of Justice is turning to a three-word phrase to preemptively fight back: “Legitimate legislative purpose.”The Justice Department has sent letters in recent days to leading Democratic lawmakers raising the possibility they’ll f[...]
text: As the Trump administration prepares for Democrats to launch an onslaught of investigations in the next Congress, the U.S. Department of Justice is turning to a three-word phrase to preemptively fight back: “Legitimate legislative purpose.”The Justice Department has sent letters in recent days to leading Democratic lawmakers raising the possibility they’ll face criminal prosecution for conducting aggressive oversight of President Donald Trump and his aides. Legal experts have widely dismissed the threats as empty because the U.S. Constitution affords lawmakers wide protections from prosecution for official actions taken in Congress.But the letters — and that short phrase within them — offer a blueprint for how the White House will try to undermine the investigations themselves, in addition to discrediting the investigators. Democrats will take control of Congress with majorities in both the House and Senate in early January.Line of attackThe Justice Department is signaling it will attack congressional subpoenas seeking documents and testimony from federal officials as driven by retribution and outside the bounds of traditional oversight. The government appears ready to argue such requests cross a line into illegality. The DOJ letters allege Democrats intend to violate federal laws that prohibit individuals acting in an official capacity from violating the constitutional rights of others. In this case, those supposedly having their rights violated would be Trump’s associates.“As you should know, whatever investigations you and your fellow Democrats have planned must have a legitimate legislative purpose,” U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz, the top Justice Department official in the Southern District of Texas, wrote on Nov. 19 to Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat.Reitz, a former Republican candidate for Texas attorney general, included similar language in letters to Rep. Robert Garcia and Sen. Adam Schiff of California, Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. All are Democrats likely to play prominent roles in investigating the Trump administration after the party takes control of Congress in January.Additionally, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, in a Nov. 9 letter to Garcia wrote that “abusive and capricious threats” were spreading among Democratic legislators. He warned that the Trump administration “will not be extorted” and expected lawmakers to investigate within settled constitutional limits.Rocky 2 years aheadThe defiant posture comes as Trump braces for a final two years in office marked by aggressive oversight from House and Senate committees, as Democrats probe alleged corruption and mismanagement. Many Democrats credit the blue tsunami that gave the party large majorities in both chambers to voters’ frustration with self-enrichment by Trump and other government officials.In addition to the Justice Department letters, Trump on Nov. 20 signed an executive order that requires federal contractors to notify the White House of any congressional requests for information. Contractors are also required to abide by any White House instructions to withhold communications that the Trump administration says are covered by executive privilege.Democrats are now on a collision course with the Trump administration that could end up in the courts.Raskin pressed forward with his oversight efforts in the wake of despite Reitz’s letters. The ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, Raskin sent letters on Nov. 20 to the DOJ, FBI, Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the U.S. Bureau of Prisons — demanding that they preserve all records, including Signal chats, which can be set to auto-delete.Slotkin responded to Reitz in a letter last week, calling congressional oversight an important constitutional responsibility. She called the DOJ official’s threats frivolous and a violation of his ethical duties as an attorney. The nonpartisan watchdog group Campaign for Accountability has filed a complaint against Reitz with the State Bar of Texas.“I’m not going to participate in some sham investigation,” Slotkin said in a video response to Reitz. “Every American has freedom of speech. In particular, senators have special privileges and special responsibilities given by the Constitution for oversight.”White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told States Newsroom that Trump is willing to work with anyone “to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans.” “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,” Bis said in a statement.The Justice Department didn’t respond to a request for comment.The U.S. Supreme Court has previously ruled Congress has broad power to investigate the federal government. Broad oversight authorityConstitutional law experts interviewed by States Newsroom said that while lawmakers don’t have unlimited investigative power, their oversight authority is sweeping, rooted in the need for lawmakers to have information before legislating.“Although they are not stated in the Constitution, there is a clear line of cases that say as long as investigations are related to possible legislation, then they can proceed,” said John Vile, a professor of political science at Middle Tennessee State University who has written books on constitutional law.In 1957, the Supreme Court found that the U.S. House Un-American Activities Committee had exceeded the bounds of congressional power after labor organizer John Watkins was prosecuted for refusing to answer lawmakers’ questions about whether certain individuals were members of the Communist Party. The court threw out Watkins’ conviction, finding his due process rights were violated.Retiz cites the case, known as Watkins vs. United States, in his letters to Democrats as he warns lawmakers that their planned investigations could be unlawful. In the court’s 6-1 decision, Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that investigations solely to punish or for the “personal aggrandizement” of the investigators weren’t permissible.Unmentioned by Reitz is that earlier in the same paragraph, Warren wrote that Congress’s power to investigate is “broad” and encompasses looking into both how current law is being applied and possible future law.“It includes surveys of defects in our social, economic or political system for the purpose of enabling the Congress to remedy them,” Warren wrote. “It comprehends probes into departments of the Federal Government to expose corruption, inefficiency or waste.”As recently as 2020, the Supreme Court reaffirmed the sweeping scope of Congress’ investigatory powers. In a 7-2 decision in a case called Trump vs. Mazars USA, the justices didn’t immediately allow a congressional subpoena for Trump’s personal financial records to proceed, but they repeated Watkins’ description of lawmakers’ sweeping oversight authority.“The congressional power to obtain information is ‘broad’ and ‘indispensable,’” Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in the majority opinion.The speech or debate clauseWhatever the courts may decide about future subpoenas, constitutional scholars in recent weeks have been virtually unanimous in arguing that the Constitution’s speech or debate clause will protect Democratic lawmakers from criminal cases for launching congressional investigations into the Trump administration. The clause says of lawmakers that “for any Speech or Debate in either House, they shall not be questioned in any other Place.” The provision has its roots in England, where members of Parliament used to fear prosecution for offending the crown.Its protections have been on display as recently as October, when federal agents searched the D.C. residence of Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Democrat. Recently unsealed court documents show a federal judge asked prosecutors for additional information on the “potential Speech or Debate Clause implications” of the search before signing off on a warrant.Steve Vladeck, a professor of federal courts at Georgetown University Law Center and a leading expert on the Supreme Court, wrote on Nov. 23 that an indictment alleging lawmakers had conspired to deprive individuals of their rights through a “weaponized” oversight process would mean proving the illegitimacy of the investigation’s subpoenas, hearings or committee votes.“Every one of those is a legislative act, for which the members’ motives are off the table,” Vladeck wrote in his newsletter, One First. “When the oversight itself is the alleged crime, the Speech or Debate Clause is arguably at its zenith.”Lawmakers also can’t be sued for their speech in Congress, a protection that they sometimes use to make remarks that might otherwise open them up to allegations of defamation. Last year, Rep. Nancy Mace, a South Carolina Republican, accused her ex-fiance and three other men of being sexual “predators” in an explosive speech on the House floor. A federal judge later dismissed a defamation lawsuit brought against Mace by one of the men.Illegal orders videoThe Trump administration has also so far failed in other efforts to target Democratic lawmakers over their communications.Just over a year ago, several lawmakers with military or national security backgrounds, including Slotkin, posted a video telling members of the military and intelligence community that they should refuse illegal orders. Trump called the video evidence of seditious behavior and as recently as this month asked whether the lawmakers would ever face prosecution.The Department of Defense attempted to demote one of the lawmakers, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired U.S. Navy captain. A federal judge has temporarily blocked the demotion, but the Trump administration has appealed the decision.But even without prosecutions, Molly Nixon, a senior fellow in executive power at the libertarian Cato Institute, said the White House can still work to slow down investigations. The letters and the recent executive order serve as “markers” that could deter cooperation with Congress, she indicated. Individuals pressed for information might weigh the pros and cons of quick and full compliance.“The fact that if I were a member of Congress I would not be particularly worried about a successful criminal prosecution doesn’t mean the administration doesn’t have a lot of tools at its disposal,” Nixon said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Murray calls for probe into sale of WA immigrant detention center
description: U.S. Sen. Patty Murray is pushing for an oversight investigation into the Trump administration’s purchase of a controversial immigrant detention center in Tacoma.  In a letter sent Tuesday morning, Murray requested the inspector general within the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to immediately investigate the $453 million sale of the Northwest ICE Proce[...]
text:
The Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, which is one of the largest immigrant detention facilities in the western U.S. (Grace Deng/Washington State Standard)U.S. Sen. Patty Murray is pushing for an oversight investigation into the Trump administration’s purchase of a controversial immigrant detention center in Tacoma. 
In a letter sent Tuesday morning, Murray requested the inspector general within the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to immediately investigate the $453 million sale of the Northwest ICE Processing Center.
Announced last week, the sale would transfer the Washington facility, with roughly 1,600 beds, from private ownership by the Florida-based GEO Group to the federal government. GEO, one of the nation’s top private prison operators, expects to net $340 million from the transaction after taxes, which will go toward stock buybacks. 
The most recent assessment of the detention center site set the property’s value at $72.6 million. Earlier this year, GEO valued the detention center at $67 million, according to The Intercept.
“The Office of Inspector General must investigate this egregious waste of taxpayer dollars, which serves to enrich a private detention contractor to maintain unsafe conditions in immigration detention,” Murray wrote in her letter to Inspector General Joseph Cuffari.
Murray, a Democrat who is poised to become chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, wants Cuffari to determine how GEO and the Department of Homeland Security landed at the hefty price.
“This waste and abuse of taxpayer dollars to pursue President Trump and Stephen Miller’s cruel and extreme immigration agenda deserves immediate attention before the sale is finalized,” Murray wrote, referring to the president’s new chief of staff and the architect of his immigration agenda.
Federal ownership could allow the Tacoma facility, which for years has faced numerous allegations of mistreatment and human rights violations, to evade oversight under a state law seeking to inspect the detention center. The state and GEO Group have been in court for years as the company has batted down the state’s attempts to investigate thousands of complaints.
The legal question has been whether the state can regulate a federal contractor, but if the feds own the facility, constitutional doctrine could bar state officials from inspecting under the 2023 law. 
The Trump administration has been rumored to be looking at buying detention facilities across the country to evade oversight. Last month, GEO sold its 1,940-bed facility in Adelanto, California, to the Department of Homeland Security for $950 million. 
Meanwhile, a number of Trump administration officials have worked or consulted for the company.
GEO will continue to run the Tacoma facility under a recently signed, 10-year, $1.5-billion contract with the federal government, which houses immigrants detained under the president’s crackdown.
“In short, taxpayers are sending nearly $2 billion to GEO Group to execute President Trump’s cruel immigration agenda,” Murray wrote in her letter.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Company CEO George Zoley said in a statement last week that GEO looks forward to “continuing to provide high-quality secure support services at the Northwest ICE Processing Center.”
U.S. Reps. Pramila Jayapal and Emily Randall have vowed congressional committee inquiries into the sale when Democrats retake Congress in January. 
“We are going to continue to fight to do oversight, and next year in 2027, when Robert Garcia is the chair of the Oversight Committee, you better believe that we will be calling in witnesses to testify about how this deal happened, who got rich, and what the cost is for actual human beings who are being warehoused in this facility,” said Randall, a member of the committee.
Jayapal, meanwhile, is slated to become chair of the House Subcommittee on Immigration, Integrity, Security, and Enforcement.
A Homeland Security spokesperson said last week that the agency “purchased the Northwest ICE Processing Center on November 18 to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations.”
The “big, beautiful bill” that congressional Republicans passed in summer 2025 featured tens of billions of dollars to increase the number of immigrant detention beds by tens of thousands. But a U.S. Government Accountability Office report this fall found Immigration and Customs Enforcement has “wasted funds on unsuccessful detention initiatives and lacks important information about the long-term affordability of its investments.”
A follow-up last week from the accountability agency found ICE “has neither determined the scope and costs to purchase more facilities nor updated its spending plan to reflect its current efforts.”
“ICE also hasn’t assessed the cost effectiveness of these investments,” the report reads. 
In the report, ICE officials “noted that while they do not expect the effort to result in cost savings, it will help ICE fulfill its mission in locations where state governments may resist expanded detention efforts.”
Another private prison giant, CoreCivic, offered a detention center to the state of Minnesota for $75 million, only for ICE to buy it this year for $495 million. Democrats in the U.S. Senate are investigating the purchase.
GEO said last week that the company is in active negotiations that could result in the sale of three more of its facilities by the end of the year.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: ICE detainees held in solitary confinement, strip-searched at Anchorage jail, Alaska lawmakers hear
description: Some people arrested and detained for civil immigration warrants in Alaska have been placed in extended solitary confinement, subjected to strip searches after visits with attorneys and denied regular access to phone calls, showers, recreational time and medical care while held in the state-run Anchorage Correctional Complex, Alaska lawmakers heard on Friday[...]
text:
Rep. Chuck Kopp, R-Anchorage, and Rep. Andrew Gray, D-Anchorage, listen to testimony at a Nov. 20, 2026, hearing in Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Some people arrested and detained for civil immigration warrants in Alaska have been placed in extended solitary confinement, subjected to strip searches after visits with attorneys and denied regular access to phone calls, showers, recreational time and medical care while held in the state-run Anchorage Correctional Complex, Alaska lawmakers heard on Friday.
The House Judiciary Committee held an investigatory hearing on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in Alaska and conditions of confinement for people held in state prisons. ICE detainees are held in state custody while awaiting civil immigration proceedings or before being transferred to federal detention facilities in the Lower 48. 
It was the third such hearing on state detention policies under the Alaska Department of Corrections since the start of the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda in 2025. The committee held a similar hearing following the transfer of 41 men in ICE custody to Alaska which raised similar concerns of punitive conditions of detention, violations of due process and criminal confinement.  
Rep. Andrew Gray, D-Anchorage, chair of the Judiciary Committee, criticized the department for its treatment of ICE detainees. People arrested by ICE are under administrative custody, and not charged or convicted of any criminal offense, Gray noted.
“Lockdowns, strip searches, missing medications, lawyers who cannot access their clients — those are the same things documented at our June 2025 hearing, where we were assured that DOC would do better,” he said. “Seventeen months later, it appears that little has changed.”
No DOC officials were present at the hearing. Officials with DOC declined to participate, but would answer written questions from the committee, Gray said.     

The entrance of the Anchorage Correctional Complex is seen on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Officials with DOC did not respond to a list of questions Monday on the department’s policies for placing ICE detainees in solitary confinement, subjecting them to strip searches and allowing access to regular phone calls, visits, showers and recreational time. Officials did not respond to questions about lawmaker concerns that DOC has violated federal standards of confinement. 
Gray said Alaska and the Legislature need to do more to strengthen oversight and protections for ICE detainees in state custody. He said they should review cooperative agreements between DOC and the federal government, and potentially ban ICE arrests in state courthouses, schools and other public facilities. 
Alaska has seen a surge in the number of people arrested and detained by ICE with the Trump administration’s nationwide immigration crackdown, rising from 13 people in 2024 during the Biden administration to 99 people in 2025, according to DOC data compiled by the ACLU of Alaska. That is a 662% increase.
This year, from January through Oct. 19, DOC has detained 130 people. The majority of people have been detained at the Anchorage Correctional Center. DOC has an agreement with ICE to hold federal detainees at a cost of $243.24 per person per day.
One of the people detained this year was Latyr Barreto, who shared his experience being incarcerated at ACC with the committee.  
He told lawmakers he came to Alaska in 2020 after marrying a U.S. citizen, and has worked as a certified nursing assistant, including in home care and hospice, in Anchorage and the Matanuska-Susitna Valley for the last six years. 
Barreto was arrested by ICE for a civil violation, not criminal charges, he said. He was jailed at ACC for the first 11 days with two other ICE detainees in a cell with only two beds, where he slept on the floor. They experienced frequent lockdowns, which prohibited calls with his attorney, showers and leaving the cell. One day after he complained, he was transferred to solitary confinement.
He remained there for the next four months, while fighting his case.
“I spent 117 days in solitary confinement. I was alone in my cell approximately 23 hours a day. I was allowed one hour of recreation and would shower every other day. This was my daily routine for nearly four months,” he said. “The restrictions affected my ability to maintain relationships, communicate with people outside, access legal resources and participate in ordinary daily activities.”
He could make calls through a phone that was passed through the food slot in his cell, which was physically difficult, he said. Calls and visiting hours were restricted to certain times.
After in-person visits with his attorney, he was routinely strip searched in a public area.  
“A dozen times, every one of those strip searches took place in a room where a camera was pointed directly at me. Staff also left the door open. People walking through the area, including detainees, being escorted and other staff members could see me naked, male or female. I repeatedly asked staff to provide privacy,” he said. “My requests were never honored.”
He urged lawmakers to examine DOC standards of detention, use of solitary confinement and policies for detainees to access basic services, including communication with their attorneys — “because the next person who finds themselves in that situation might not have the opportunity to tell the story. I do,” he said.
Anchorage Republican Rep. Mia Costello thanked Larreto for his testimony and said it was “disturbing.”
“Your testimony today is meaningful and will most likely result in changes from this committee or future legislatures,” she said. “I appreciate your courage and coming forward and speaking with us in person.” 
Costello lost her re-election bid earlier this month to Democrat Denny Wells. 
Another unidentified 55-year-old ICE detainee submitted an affidavit to the committee with a similar experience of being held in solitary confinement, routinely strip searched and denied access to services including medical care, which resulted in physical and mental health effects. 
“Being treated like a criminal is dehumanizing and demoralizing,” they wrote. 
Kristine Quint, an immigration attorney with Cascadia Cross Border Law Group who is representing Barreto, told lawmakers she was shocked to learn her clients were strip searched after seeing her. “I find that absolutely abhorrent,” she said. 
“I’ve since learned that it’s standard procedure at the ACC for criminal inmates as well,” she said. “Every time there’s a contact visit with an attorney, everybody is strip searched, and it is just so normal that nobody really comments on it anymore.”
“But I do believe it is avoidable, especially when meeting with an attorney to review necessary legal documents,” she added. She said she and Barreto did not get an answer from ACC officials on why he was kept in solitary confinement for so long.     

Attorney Nicolas Olano tesitfies at a Nov. 20 hearing in Anchorage of the House Judiciary Committee. The hearing was about the impacts on Alaska of federal immigration enforcement policies. Rep. Genevieve Mina, D-Anchorage, was participating online and is seen on the screen in the background. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

Nicolas Olano, another immigration attorney with the Nations Law Group, told lawmakers strip searches are not standard practice for detainees meeting with their attorneys in other federal immigration facilities.
According to ICE’s policy for standards in non-dedicated facilities, detainees should be searched “in the least intrusive manner as appropriate.” “Absent reasonable suspicion that a detainee is concealing contraband, detainees shall not be strip searched,” it says. 
Anchorage Democrat Genevieve Mina asked why ICE detainees in administrative custody for immigration issues appear not to have the same access to basic amenities as prisoners in the general population, and whether Alaska could be held liable for violating state and federal standards. 
“My thinking just revolves around this same conversation that we had last summer,” she said. “That No. 1 — the conditions that people have been experiencing are unconstitutional and unjust. But number two, we have a contract with the federal government, and what liability do we risk as a state, knowing that people are still under terrible conditions over a year later? And I want to make sure that we are going to change and we have good state safeguards.”
Challenges to communication between immigration attorneys and clients
Quint testified that it’s difficult for those arrested by ICE in Alaska to contact and hire an immigration attorney, and in turn, it’s logistically difficult for attorneys to reach clients in DOC custody due to constraints to visitation and phone hours. ICE detainees can be transferred quickly out of state with no notice, she said.
“So if I schedule an appointment today to see somebody tomorrow, it’s possible they will be gone, and I won’t actually get in to see them. That’s obviously a huge concern,” she said.
Quint said there’s no public record of how many people have been arrested by ICE in Alaska and not held in DOC custody, but transferred immediately out of state. “I do believe that the number of arrests that are occurring here are probably much higher than we are aware,” she said. 
A spokesperson for ICE responded to a request for information about the number of people arrested by ICE in Alaska with a link to a White House dashboard that reports 107 people were arrested in Anchorage from Jan. 2025 to May 2026. 
Quint recounted several stories she had heard about from colleagues doing immigration work in Alaska. 
“An Indigenous man from Mexico was detained here this summer. He has a wife and child here in Alaska. He was swiftly deported to Mexico and disappeared, and is now presumed dead,” she said.
Quint and other immigration attorneys told the committee that they are filing more habeas corpus petitions to challenge ICE detentions. Additionally, they said a change in August in the immigration court process prohibiting attorneys from representing clients virtually over WebEx video streams is barring Alaska-based attorneys from representing clients detained in Tacoma, Washington. That is the location of the nearest ICE detention facility. 
Olano said generally Alaska attorneys now have to turn down clients detained in the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, due to prohibitive costs to fly there to represent them in person. 
“It’s extremely unfair in the sense that these people chose their attorney here, they chose him because it was somebody that can contact their family, get the documents needed — work with Kotzebue, work with Juneau, work at a local level to get them out,” he said. “And now they cannot have that.”
Fear of ICE has reverberating effects
Laura Nations, an immigration attorney with the Nations Law Group, said Alaska families are living in fear of ICE, and the effects are reverberating through communities, schools and places of employment, as well as the criminal justice system.     

Attorney Laura Nations testifies at a Nov. 20 hearing in Anchorage of the House Judiciary Committee. The hearing was about the impacts on Alaska of federal immigration enforcement policies. Rep. Genevieve Mina, D-Anchorage, who participated online, is seen on the screen in the background. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

She said that means they aren’t reporting crimes because they are fearful of ICE involvement if they contact the police.
“I have done a lot of work, particularly in the labor trafficking space over the years, and I have seen since January of 2025 a real breakdown in the ability to seek justice for people who have been the victims of crimes,” she said. “And also just the extreme fear that folks in our community and across our state are experiencing that is causing them not to make reports.”
Nations emphasized its a public safety issue for all Alaskans when perpetrators are not held accountable. “When people are not being held accountable for criminal behavior, they continue to do that, and that causes harm beyond just the immediate impact,” she said. “It also makes all of us and everyone in our state less safe.”
People are particularly fearful of traveling and risking arrest at airports, she said, as the U.S. Transportation Security Administration coordinates with ICE and can flag people who have immigration warrants or deportation orders. 
“That curtails both obviously personal travel, but also business,” she said. “And those are costs that we are all bearing in various ways because all of those things end up having a ripple effect.”
While the state does not have jurisdiction over federal immigration enforcement, Nations urged lawmakers to take action where the state has authority, including reviewing state cooperative agreements with ICE and ensuring protections of due process rights. 
“None of this is inevitable, and we don’t have to bear some of these costs,” she said.
Lawmakers pledge to take legislative action, increase oversight
Members of the House Judiciary Committee from across the political spectrum called the testimony “shocking” and “disturbing” and said legislative action was needed.
Gray, chair of the committee, closed the hearing by outlined some of the policy areas the Legislature could take up beginning in January.     

Rep. Andrew Gray, D-Anchorage, asks a question at a Nov. 20, 2026, hearing in Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

“We need independent routine oversight of conditions for everyone held in state custody,” he said. “Second, we need minimum protections written into statute for civil civil immigration detainees, protecting them from things like unnecessary strip searches.”
Gray said the state should prohibit taking custody of ICE detainees from other states, as DOC officials agreed to do in June 2025. He said Alaska also should follow other states in banning ICE arrests at courthouses, schools and other public facilities. 
Additionally, DOC has a Warrant Service Officer Program agreement with ICE, signed in 2020, to deputize correctional officers to serve immigration warrants on people in state custody, prior to their release on state charges. The ACLU of Alaska estimates 31%, or 40 of 130 people have been detained under the agreement since January 2025.  
Gray said legislators should review those agreements, “and decide whether or not we should continue any of them.” 
In an interview Monday, Gray said there should be accountability for what ICE detainees have endured in Alaska, and he’s hopeful for new leadership under the Kreiss-Tomkins administration. 
“My hope for the hearing this close to a new administration coming in, is that whoever comes in knows that this happened, and makes sure that nothing like this ever happens again,” he said. “Look at what has been happening — this is not who we are. We are not going to allow this to happen. We are not going to do this to people.”

name: California
title: What the blue wave means for California’s economy
description: The Trump administration put its thumb on the scale to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia and the stock market rejoiced. We’ll see how that plays out. Today we’re looking into what the Dems’ big victory means for the Golden State economy. Gov. Gavin Newsom gave an exit interview to the Sacramento Press Club, and […]
text:
Matt Licklider, owner of LIOCO Wines, talks with guests at the winery’s tasting room in Healdsburg on Nov. 21, 2026. Photo by Chad Surmick for CalMatters




The Trump administration put its thumb on the scale to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia and the stock market rejoiced. We’ll see how that plays out. Today we’re looking into what the Dems’ big victory means for the Golden State economy.
Gov. Gavin Newsom gave an exit interview to the Sacramento Press Club, and it sounded to our reporters like a warmup to 2028.
If you’re in CalPERS, you don’t want to miss our story about new rules that could shape who can work while taking home a pension.
Voters elected Democratic candidates in a historic blue wave in part because of their pledges to lower the cost of living and act as a check to President Donald Trump’s policies, including economic ones, that have been responsible for rising costs. 
But how would California’s economy be affected by more Democrats in office?
CalMatters’ Levi Sumagaysay explores this question through key sectors of the state’s economy, including agriculture and artificial intelligence. 
California’s agriculture has taken a beating during Trump’s second term. Inflation, driven by tariffs and the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, caused the price of nearly everything to rise, including transportation and supplies. The U.S.-Canada trade war, triggered by Trump’s tariffs, led the state’s vegetable and melon exports to Canada to drop by about 27% in 2025 from the previous year, or from $1.14 billion to $837 million.
Winemakers have also lost overseas business, and Matt Licklider, the owner of LIOCO Wines in Healdsburg, is worried about the long-term effects on global trade. 

Licklider: “The American brand was so damaged by tariffs and the toxic politics of the day. We have done almost no export business since Trump took office (the second time).”

Trump put his foot on the gas to help investors in another California industry: Technology. A Democratic Congress could mean much more scrutiny for Silicon Valley, which stirred mixed reactions from Wall Street. 
Though the reinstatement of Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang caused the stock market to jump on Monday, the market dipped before that amid concern that Democrats would rein in AI and data centers.
Read more.
In other economic news: California had a banger month of employment gains, adding 47,000 jobs in October. The Employment Development Department reported the state added 148,700 jobs in 2026, which it said accounted for 17.3% of the nation’s job growth.



CalMatters Ideas Festival: 2027 Ideas Festival will expand to Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Francisco. One full day of candid conversations in each, with the leaders, innovators and changemakers shaping California’s future. Learn more.

Other Stories You Should Know


CA sues to protect kids in mixed-status families


A “for rent” sign outside an apartment building in Fresno on Feb. 22, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters




California is suing the Trump administration over new rules barring households with mixed immigration status from receiving federal housing assistance, writes CalMatters’ Ben Christopher.
More than 7,000 households in California could be affected by the rule change. Immigrants who are in the country illegally can’t receive federal housing subsidies, but the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development is required by Congress to provide assistance in proportion to the share of members who have legal status. 
Starting Dec. 14, however, federal aid would end for these households, including housing vouchers or the ability to live in public housing. 
California — as well as other local governments including Los Angeles, San Diego and San Francisco in a separate lawsuit — is suing to stop the rule from taking effect, arguing that the Trump administration is overstepping its authority by overriding a congressional statute.
Read more.



New CalPERS rules for working retirees


The CalPERS regional offices in Sacramento on March 15, 2022. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




The California Public Employees’ Retirement System voted last week to advance new rules related to members who want to work part-time after retirement without losing their pension, writes CalMatters’ Adam Ashton.
For government employees, unclear and complex CalPERS rules can make post-retirement work especially fraught: Last year, the city of Sacramento laid off dozens of reserve police officers after a CalPERS employer audit. There have also been instances of CalPERS demanding government workers to repay hundreds of thousands of dollars in pension income because they allegedly violated California retirement law.
To clear things up, CalPERS is trying to make new rules about who can work while receiving a pension and for how long. One set of rules lays out a clear timeline for how long a government agency can hire what CalPERS calls a retired annuitant, meaning someone who works while receiving a pension. Previously, retired part-timers could work for a “limited duration,” but that duration was never clearly defined.
CalPERS’ rules are not yet final and will be subject to a public comment period.
Read more.



And lastly: Does Newsom have any regrets?


Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks during a press conference at the Bay Area Discovery Museum in Sausalito on Sept. 10, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




Gavin Newsom is winding down his time as California governor and preparing to run for president in 2028. He defended his record — and the headline-grabbing promises he made as governor — at the Sacramento Press Club on Monday. Read more from CalMatters’ Maya C. Miller.

name: California
title: What the blue wave means for California’s economy
description: The Trump administration put its thumb on the scale to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia and the stock market rejoiced. We’ll see how that plays out. Today we’re looking into what the Dems’ big victory means for the Golden State economy. Gov. Gavin Newsom gave an exit interview to the Sacramento Press Club, and […]
text:
Matt Licklider, owner of LIOCO Wines, talks with guests at the winery’s tasting room in Healdsburg on Nov. 21, 2026. Photo by Chad Surmick for CalMatters




The Trump administration put its thumb on the scale to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia and the stock market rejoiced. We’ll see how that plays out. Today we’re looking into what the Dems’ big victory means for the Golden State economy.
Gov. Gavin Newsom gave an exit interview to the Sacramento Press Club, and it sounded to our reporters like a warmup to 2028.
If you’re in CalPERS, you don’t want to miss our story about new rules that could shape who can work while taking home a pension.
Voters elected Democratic candidates in a historic blue wave in part because of their pledges to lower the cost of living and act as a check to President Donald Trump’s policies, including economic ones, that have been responsible for rising costs. 
But how would California’s economy be affected by more Democrats in office?
CalMatters’ Levi Sumagaysay explores this question through key sectors of the state’s economy, including agriculture and artificial intelligence. 
California’s agriculture has taken a beating during Trump’s second term. Inflation, driven by tariffs and the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, caused the price of nearly everything to rise, including transportation and supplies. The U.S.-Canada trade war, triggered by Trump’s tariffs, led the state’s vegetable and melon exports to Canada to drop by about 27% in 2025 from the previous year, or from $1.14 billion to $837 million.
Winemakers have also lost overseas business, and Matt Licklider, the owner of LIOCO Wines in Healdsburg, is worried about the long-term effects on global trade. 

Licklider: “The American brand was so damaged by tariffs and the toxic politics of the day. We have done almost no export business since Trump took office (the second time).”

Trump put his foot on the gas to help investors in another California industry: Technology. A Democratic Congress could mean much more scrutiny for Silicon Valley, which stirred mixed reactions from Wall Street. 
Though the reinstatement of Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang caused the stock market to jump on Monday, the market dipped before that amid concern that Democrats would rein in AI and data centers.
Read more.
In other economic news: California had a banger month of employment gains, adding 47,000 jobs in October. The Employment Development Department reported the state added 148,700 jobs in 2026, which it said accounted for 17.3% of the nation’s job growth.



CalMatters Ideas Festival: 2027 Ideas Festival will expand to Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Francisco. One full day of candid conversations in each, with the leaders, innovators and changemakers shaping California’s future. Learn more.

Other Stories You Should Know


CA sues to protect kids in mixed-status families


A “for rent” sign outside an apartment building in Fresno on Feb. 22, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters




California is suing the Trump administration over new rules barring households with mixed immigration status from receiving federal housing assistance, writes CalMatters’ Ben Christopher.
More than 7,000 households in California could be affected by the rule change. Immigrants who are in the country illegally can’t receive federal housing subsidies, but the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development is required by Congress to provide assistance in proportion to the share of members who have legal status. 
Starting Dec. 14, however, federal aid would end for these households, including housing vouchers or the ability to live in public housing. 
California — as well as other local governments including Los Angeles, San Diego and San Francisco in a separate lawsuit — is suing to stop the rule from taking effect, arguing that the Trump administration is overstepping its authority by overriding a congressional statute.
Read more.



New CalPERS rules for working retirees


The CalPERS regional offices in Sacramento on March 15, 2022. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




The California Public Employees’ Retirement System voted last week to advance new rules related to members who want to work part-time after retirement without losing their pension, writes CalMatters’ Adam Ashton.
For government employees, unclear and complex CalPERS rules can make post-retirement work especially fraught: Last year, the city of Sacramento laid off dozens of reserve police officers after a CalPERS employer audit. There have also been instances of CalPERS demanding government workers to repay hundreds of thousands of dollars in pension income because they allegedly violated California retirement law.
To clear things up, CalPERS is trying to make new rules about who can work while receiving a pension and for how long. One set of rules lays out a clear timeline for how long a government agency can hire what CalPERS calls a retired annuitant, meaning someone who works while receiving a pension. Previously, retired part-timers could work for a “limited duration,” but that duration was never clearly defined.
CalPERS’ rules are not yet final and will be subject to a public comment period.
Read more.



And lastly: Does Newsom have any regrets?


Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks during a press conference at the Bay Area Discovery Museum in Sausalito on Sept. 10, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




Gavin Newsom is winding down his time as California governor and preparing to run for president in 2028. He defended his record — and the headline-grabbing promises he made as governor — at the Sacramento Press Club on Monday. Read more from CalMatters’ Maya C. Miller.






California Voices
America’s two largest cities will be led by Indian Americans, but rather than fitting in a model minority mold, they both rose to prominence by taking on the establishment, writes Sara Sadhwani, an associate professor of politics at Pomona College.
