name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: After another tough year for loons, one lake exemplifies their struggle
description: It was another difficult summer for New Hampshire’s loons. After some improvement last summer, this year the loons that nest, fish and make their voices heard on the state’s lakes saw a dip in their parenting success. Fewer than half of mated loons successfully raised a chick through the summer, with a final tally of […]
text:
A lone loon dives for fish in Great Bay Estuary, near Durham, on Aug. 10. Common loons are state-listed as "threatened" in New Hampshire by the state Fish and Game Department and protected by the New Hampshire Endangered Species Conservation Act. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)It was another difficult summer for New Hampshire’s loons.
After some improvement last summer, this year the loons that nest, fish and make their voices heard on the state’s lakes saw a dip in their parenting success. Fewer than half of mated loons successfully raised a chick through the summer, with a final tally of 0.43 surviving chicks per breeding pair, according to the Moultonborough-based Loon Preservation Committee.
That’s below the level of 0.48 needed for the loons to sustain a stable adult population, according to Tiffany Grade, Squam Lake biologist with the committee.
“It’s really disturbing,” she said. “… The loons are continuing to struggle.”
As biologists digest the season’s data, they are also absorbing the findings of a report from Grade and other Loon Preservation Committee biologists on the broad prevalence of dangerous pollution in loon eggs, published in a peer-reviewed journal this year. The report showed the near-ubiquitous presence of contaminants in egg samples from across the state. In particular, eggs from Squam Lake, a focus of the study, showed high levels of certain contaminants as well as thin, relatively weak shells and smaller overall size, raising a red flag for biologists.
The findings highlight what the species is up against, and why humans should pay attention, said Grade and Micah Miller, director of the loon and Arctic programs and co-director for the Center for Ecotoxicology at the Biodiversity Research Institute in Maine, who was not involved in the study.
“Across the board, we know that the environmental and human health risks of having contaminants in the environment, that alone is enough reason to try to reduce exposure,” Miller said. 
A challenging coexistence
Of the various threats loons must contend with in New Hampshire’s waters, most are human-caused. 
The birds’ need for clean, clear lakes and plentiful freshwater fish bring them to the same lakes that attract throngs of human visitors every summer.
Those visitors include the anglers and boaters who love New Hampshire’s lakes but who can also present unique hazards to loons. Ingestion of lead fishing tackle remains the “most immediate” threat to loon populations, according to Grade. And disturbance — whether from wakes washing over a nesting site, humans approaching too closely and spooking would-be parents, or deadly boat-loon collisions — is another problem.
In fact, considering last year’s relatively successful loon season, the cold, rainy start to summer may have been a beneficial factor, Grade said: Unfavorable weather could have reduced boat traffic on New Hampshire lakes during the most crucial window of early-season nest building.
But rain isn’t always helpful to loons. Particularly strong storms, like those increasing in severity with climate change, can harm their nests, too. And climate change has also contributed to the increasing incidence of certain illnesses, like avian malaria. 
There is also the matter of chemical pollution.
The Loon Preservation Committee has been privately funding the testing of loon eggs from different water bodies around New Hampshire, after high PCB levels were detected at Squam Lake. (Courtesy of the Loon Preservation Committee)
The Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry study, authored by Grade and fellow Loon Preservation Committee coauthors R. Wesley Flynn and Harry Vogel, assessed a range of major contaminants that affect loons and their habitats, from industrial chemicals to pesticides, PFAS, and metals like aluminum, lead and mercury. 
These pollutants are persistent in nature, said Miller, who was not involved in the study. Many remain in an ecosystem for years after they are released, making them a continual threat to wildlife. As top-of-the-food-chain predators, loons get a magnified dose.
For the study, over a period of nearly 30 years, the Loon Preservation Committee collected eggs that they determined were not going to hatch from 28 lakes across New Hampshire. They then tested 92 eggs for contaminants and measured their overall volume, as well as the thickness of their shells.
The results reveal the widespread presence of organic and metal pollutants in the loon eggs. While the Loon Preservation Committee has previously raised the alarm over these contaminants during the course of the study, the paper’s publication was the first peer-reviewed research to confirm the presence of PFAS “forever chemicals” and flame retardant chemicals known as BDE in common loon eggs, according to the committee.
In many cases, the chemicals were observed at levels that alarmed the biologists because of their documented ability to cause negative effects in other species. Even in the group of eggs that biologists believe most closely resembles the “baseline” egg for New Hampshire loons, about half contained a higher level of contaminants than that known to cause negative effects in other birds, Grade said. 
Other groups surpassed those levels. One of particular concern was the cluster of eggs from central New Hampshire’s Squam Lake, located just northwest of Lake Winnipesaukee.
Squam Lake as a mirror
In some ways, that wasn’t surprising, the researchers said. In fact, Grade said, concern over the loons in Squam Lake was what initially touched off the analysis that ultimately led to this paper. In the winter of 2004-2005, the population of loons on Squam Lake shrank to about half of what it had been the year before. For years after, loon pairs on Squam struggled to reproduce, Grade said. 
The Loon Preservation Committee initiated intensive monitoring and management of the Squam loons at that point, in an effort to help them thrive, Grade said. But despite their work, the loons on Squam have continued to struggle to some degree in the years since. Within the last eight years, the average success rate on Squam Lake has been 0.3 surviving chicks per mating pair, according to Loon Preservation Committee data. 
There are many reasons for this, Grade said. The July report shed light on one in particular: The eggs on Squam Lake were disproportionately affected by certain contaminants, including PCBs, PFAS, and the pesticide DDT.
High exposure levels also appear correlated to weaker eggshells and smaller egg volumes, Grade said. While eggs from other lakes across the state were typical on average, the eggs from Squam were both smaller and thinner-shelled than expected.
This has implications for the health of loons overall, as the quality of an egg is generally indicative of the health of a mother bird, Miller said. 
“If she has a high contaminant load that’s interfering with her ability to lay down nutrients into that developing egg at the right time, you’re going to get, you know, some sort of malformations and so forth,” he said. 
With clear indication that contaminants are widespread in New Hampshire’s loons, the study is a first step toward assessing what is happening to the birds as a result, Grade said. 
While Squam Lake is a “more extreme” example, concerning levels of contamination were found in eggs from all over the state, Grade said. 
“What we saw in this paper is the widespread nature of this contamination in loon eggs across the state,” she said.
Other water bodies were also singled out in the report for the high PFAS content in eggs from their shores, including Canobie Lake, Lake Winnipesaukee and Arlington Mill Reservoir. The report noted the relative proximity of Canobie Lake and the Arlington Mill Reservoir to the former Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics factory.
“The exposure patterns are vastly different depending on where you are looking and what the source might be,” Miller said. 
The study is limited to some degree by the fact that the eggs collected for analysis were, by study design, all eggs that had failed to hatch. 
While some eggs were prevented from hatching due to external factors, like human disruption, others may have stopped developing due to internal factors. Some of the contaminant levels observed in the study exceeded those known to cause embryo mortality in other bird species, according to the report. The result? The samples may be biased somewhat toward higher contaminant levels, since heavily contaminated eggs are more likely to be collected for research, Grade and Miller said. 
(Both said, however, that this way of conducting egg studies is much preferred by biologists, especially when a bird species is imperiled, as loons are. Grade said she believed the bias in the results was insubstantial.)
Also by virtue, in part, of the difficulty of collection, the egg samples were limited in number, with some geographic gaps in data, Miller noted. But he added that the study was a valuable and unique example of long-term monitoring effort. 
Loons as a mirror
Fortunately for loons, despite the headwinds they face, the species seems to be increasing — albeit slowly — in prevalence in northern New England, Miller said. But their continued improvement is not a given, and the presence of high contaminant levels in their eggs is still concerning, for loons and other wildlife, he said. 
Just as eggs can signal the health of parent birds, loons themselves can be a window into the wellbeing of an ecosystem as a whole, Grade said. The contamination of loon eggs has concerning implications for them and for New Hampshire’s waterways, she said. 
Grade called for more widespread testing, for the sake of both environmental and human health. Already, testing connected to the project has resulted in a fish consumption advisory for Squam Lake related to elevated PCB content. 
Grade added that action to reduce chemical emissions was crucial to prevent the plight of the loons on Squam Lake from becoming more widespread. 
“Squam is really kind of holding up a mirror to the rest of the state, and as far as we know, the loon population,” she said. “And in some ways, it may be almost an early warning signal, you know, to what could happen. But we’re working very hard to try to make sure it doesn’t happen throughout the rest of New Hampshire.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Democrats demand answers from Oz after delay in $50B rural health awards
authors: Sarah Jane Tribble / KFF Health News
description: Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans. Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services […]
text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, speaks at the Health Connect South conference in Atlanta on Sept. 17, 2025. (Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder)Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans.
Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz late Thursday. The letter pointed to what it called “an alarming lack of public transparency” and said the fund “lacks sufficient guardrails to protect rural hospitals at greatest risk of closure.”
Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski said her state “got no explanation from CMS as to why” it got $3 million less in its second-year Rural Health Transformation Program allocation. It was a roughly 1.5% reduction from its $193.4 million first-year award. State leaders have not received information about an appeals process, she said.
Any delay in knowing how much they received and any reduction in their base funding is significant, Budzinski said, because states need to plan for an “acute impact” from the loss of other federal funding.
In the first year, states competed for their initial share of the $50 billion, which is handed out at $10 billion a year for five years. They won awards ranging from $147 million to $281 million. Most of the lawmakers who signed the letter were from states that lost funding this year. Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama, which got $4.1 million less, along with Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado, which saw a nearly $3 million drop, also spearheaded the letter along with Budzinski.

One concern, Budzinski said, is “making sure that the money isn’t going to consultants, that it’s actually getting to the rural providers that it is supposed to be getting to.” The lawmakers asked Oz for a response to detailed questions by Nov. 25. They also requested a briefing about the delays to the funding announcement, which was first reported by KFF Health News, and the impact on states.
The second-year awards were due to be announced by Oct. 31, but an Oct. 30 letter from CMS stated officials “discovered an additional administrative process requirement.” Instead, second-year funding was announced Nov. 9.
Those kinds of delays prevent state officials from being able to “fully prepare for what’s to come,” Budzinski said.
CMS oversees the fund and its newly formed Office of Rural Health Transformation. Agency officials did not respond to questions for this article before the given deadline.
Republicans passed the Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to offset other ramifications of President Donald Trump’s signature budget law, including an estimated $137 billion in Medicaid spending cuts for rural America over 10 years.
That rural money is “retail therapy for Congress,” said Cara James, president and chief executive of Grantmakers in Health, while speaking at a Milken Institute event this month.
Because the same tax law cut Medicaid spending, which rural hospitals and people disproportionately use, as well as supplemental food assistance and other government grants, the short-term money would not “help sustain people” in rural America, James said.
Then, she posed a persistent fear about the fund: “If it’s even getting to the communities.”
Five rural hospitals have closed or been converted into lower-level facilities since the rural fund was created, including one in Michigan that shuttered beds and switched to providing only emergency services to survive, according to a list curated by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research at the University of North Carolina.
The letter stated lawmakers’ concerns that too much of the rural fund “could flow to large consulting and technology firms rather than supporting providers and communities on the ground.”
After the law passed last year, state leaders had just over seven weeks to write applications as they competed for the first-year funds. All 50 states won funding with allocations determined by a federal scoring process. Each year, officials are to revisit the funding allotments.
Most states saw their funding change by less than 2%. North Dakota and Iowa won the largest gains; New Jersey, Florida, and Vermont saw the biggest reductions.
Although federal officials have created state data maps, released a slew of press announcements, and led sessions on the complicated scoring of state applications, it’s not enough, said Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association.
The association, which represents hospitals and community clinics nationwide, sent its own letter to federal officials Nov. 9. Morgan said that the way states win money needs “to be articulated in a way that success can be replicated by all states going forward.”
Morgan said his association’s analysis found that state leaders are sending the federal money to local hospitals and clinics because communities and individuals are “relying on rural hospitals to be there to deliver care.” But it’s unclear, he said, how much of the overall rural fund local hospitals are actually receiving versus how much is benefiting other entities, such as consultants.
In their letter, Budzinski and the other Democrats asked if CMS would establish a searchable database that tracks spending. They also asked for an explanation of how federal officials will evaluate state performance and allocate awards.
It was just the latest congressional letter to federal health officials on this issue.
In August 2025, a month after the law passed, Democrats sent a letter about the program’s rollout to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. And last November, Budzinski reached out to Oz on behalf of Illinois. Bennet, along with Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and others, signed a letter in June asking that the funds be targeted to rescue rural hospitals and clinics.
“We haven’t gotten full responses to any of these inquiries,” said Budzinski, who will become chair of the House’s largest Democratic caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: Rolling the dice on prediction markets: North Carolina’s warning for Indiana
description: Are prediction markets financial forecasting tools, or simply gambling by another name? For Indiana lawmakers, the answer carries significant consequences. As prediction markets expand into sports wagering, they threaten to undermine the gaming laws, consumer protections, and regulatory framework established by the Indiana General Assembly. Indiana need only[...]
text:
Will Indiana lawmakers regulate prediction markets that allow trading on sports, politics and more? It's a key question for the 2027 General Assembly. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Are prediction markets financial forecasting tools, or simply gambling by another name?
For Indiana lawmakers, the answer carries significant consequences. As prediction markets expand into sports wagering, they threaten to undermine the gaming laws, consumer protections, and regulatory framework established by the Indiana General Assembly.
Indiana need only look to North Carolina to understand why this issue deserves attention.
Earlier this year, North Carolina lawmakers handed prediction markets a regulatory free pass. Through legislation signed into law by Gov. Josh Stein in July, the state expressly recognized federally regulated prediction markets as lawful without requiring state gaming licenses or compliance with the regulatory framework governing traditional sportsbooks.
The legislation imposed a modest 6% tax on prediction markets’ net trading fee revenue. Meanwhile, North Carolina increased the tax on licensed sportsbooks from 18% to 23% of gross wagering revenue.
Although the taxes apply to different revenue bases, the disparity is striking. North Carolina welcomed a new class of sports wagering competitors under a separate, less restrictive regulatory structure while increasing the burden on sportsbooks already operating under state law.
Rather than protecting its existing gaming framework, North Carolina created an alternative pathway for gambling-like products to reach consumers.
Indiana should pay attention, because much is at stake when it comes to protecting vulnerable residents.
Consider the most glaring inconsistency: age restrictions.
Election betting is booming as the midterms near. Do states have the power to curb it?

Indiana law requires individuals to be at least 21 years old to legally place a sports wager. Licensed sportsbooks must verify customers’ ages and comply with requirements enforced by the Indiana Gaming Commission.
Prediction market platforms such as Kalshi allow individuals as young as 18 to participate, including in sports-related contracts. That means an 18-, 19-, or 20-year-old Hoosier who cannot legally wager on a Colts game through an Indiana-licensed sportsbook can purchase a contract predicting the outcome of that same game through a prediction market.
The consumer risks money on the same sporting event, hoping for the same financial return. The only meaningful difference is what the company calls the transaction. In 2025 alone, individuals under the age of 21 exploited this loophole to wager an estimated $3.9 billion on sports and parlay-type “contracts,” as Kalshi calls them, on that platform.
The problem extends beyond age restrictions.
Indiana’s licensed sportsbooks operate under a regulatory system requiring state licensure, gaming taxes, responsible gaming safeguards, and ongoing oversight.
Prediction market operators, meanwhile, contend their products are federally regulated financial contracts under the jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, rather than state-regulated gambling.
Under that interpretation, companies offer sports-related contracts to Indiana residents without obtaining Indiana sports wagering licenses or complying with the same requirements imposed on licensed operators.
Even more concerning, established sports betting companies are entering the prediction market business themselves, creating the possibility of offering substantially similar products through two entirely different regulatory systems.
Why should one company follow Indiana’s gaming laws while another offers essentially the same product without doing so?
Indiana lawmakers have repeatedly considered, but declined to authorize, internet casino gaming, commonly known as iGaming. Whether one supports or opposes iGaming, that decision belongs to Indiana’s elected lawmakers.
But if companies can use federal commodities regulation to offer products functioning like sports wagers outside Indiana’s gaming laws, what prevents that same approach from eventually extending to casino-style gambling products?
Don’t just take our word for it. BetMGM CEO Adam Greenblatt recently warned that if prediction markets survive, “it’s a matter of time before casino-like products emerge in some other form.” In other words, the prospect of prediction markets becoming a backdoor to iGaming isn’t merely hypothetical — it’s a concern being actively raised by the gaming industry itself.
Prediction markets are not currently equivalent to full-scale online casinos. Nevertheless, their expansion raises the possibility of opening a back door to iGaming, allowing gambling-like products to enter Indiana without legislative authorization or the safeguards that would ordinarily accompany it.
That should concern anyone who believes Indiana, not private companies operating under a disputed interpretation of federal law, should determine the future of gambling within its borders.
The legal questions surrounding prediction markets remain unresolved. Courts are weighing competing claims of federal commodities regulators and state gaming authorities.
But Indiana lawmakers need not ignore the practical consequences while those disputes unfold.
North Carolina’s decision to grant prediction markets favorable treatment demonstrates the risks of creating exceptions to established gaming frameworks. Indiana has an opportunity to examine those consequences before following a similar path.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Some CT parents say kids don’t belong in self-contained special ed classrooms
description: Two New Haven families say their kids were placed in special education classrooms without proper evaluation and received inadequate services.
text:
American special education, by law, is supposed to strive for inclusion — providing students with as much time with their nondisabled peers as possible, even if it takes extra support. 
The reality for some children doesn’t measure up.
In New Haven, two families are speaking out after they say their children were pushed into restrictive special education classrooms without proper evaluation, where they received woefully inadequate services.
Both families have children with autism. The parents said New Haven didn’t conduct key assessments before placing their children in self-contained classrooms, and they said the experiences made the children’s behaviors worse at home. According to one parent, her child’s classroom was lacking a certified special education teacher for part of the year.
Attorneys with the Center for Children’s Advocacy who represent the parents said these experiences are not uncommon in New Haven and elsewhere in the state. They described understaffed systems that don’t take basic steps to assess children’s needs and struggle to meet their legal obligations under federal special education law. 
Under these circumstances, the attorneys said, some kids are pushed into restrictive classrooms where they end up learning very little.
CCA attorney Sarah Mervine likened it to a daycare. 
“I’m gonna take all these kids, smush them together, so three [paraeducators] can deal with 10 people, instead of saying, ‘Wait a minute, where is the best way I could integrate these children?’” she said.
Her colleague Kathryn Meyer called it “a failure to invest in inclusion.”
State lawmakers are expected to take up the issue in earnest during next year’s legislative session, which starts in January. And New Haven Mayor Justin Elicker has been an outspoken critic of Connecticut’s school funding system, which has increasingly left cities like his on the hook for ballooning education costs; special education is one of the main pressure points.
Connecticut also has an acute shortage of special education professionals, making it almost impossible for schools to hire the staff they need — especially if they don’t have the money to offer competitive salaries. New Haven, which lacks taxable property wealth relative to the size and needs of its student body, is a case in point.
New Haven Public Schools could not comment directly on any individual cases because of student confidentiality rules. The executive director of student services, Typhanie Jackson, provided The Connecticut Mirror with a written statement.
“We understand and respect that some parents will feel frustrated as we work to provide appropriate support to students who may have complex learning needs,” Jackson said. “Our goal will always be to provide the right support for each child as an individual.”
She added, “The challenges facing school districts in providing special education services are well known. We are working with our legislators in the hope that they may be able to help us augment state funding for public education, and particularly special education, this year.”
But parents say they can’t just wait for the state or the district to catch up. They worry about their kids falling behind and failing to learn essential skills they’ll need as they age out of the school system. Special education is where they build those skills, and its shortcomings have far-reaching implications.

Jay Vazquez, 6, center, plays cars with his mother Ziomary Vazquez and sister Nellianys Ruiz, 11, at their home in New Haven on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Pushed toward self-contained classrooms
Ziomary Vazquez didn’t know at first that her son Jaysiel had been moved to a self-contained classroom.
Jaysiel has autism and sometimes struggles with his behavior. He can speak, but it can be hard to understand him — though when he’s talking about, say, the BMW M4, “He’ll tell you the whole entire specs of the car, just like that, without hesitation,” Vazquez said.
In the 2023-24 school year, Jaysiel attended two different part-time preschool programs: one at LULAC Head Start and one at the Reginald Mayo Early Learning Center, which is run by New Haven Public Schools. At LULAC, he was in the same space as all the other kids, and Vazquez said he was doing well there. But the situation was different at Reginald Mayo.
One day, Vazquez arrived to pick Jaysiel up from school and found him in a classroom with just one other student. A staff member told Vazquez her son was in a self-contained classroom after throwing a tantrum.
Because of that, Vazquez said, Reginald Mayo had decided the general education classroom wasn’t a good fit for her son. None of that sat well with Vazquez. As far as she knew, Jaysiel had been doing well in a general education setting at LULAC. There, he was learning with other kids and could eat and use the bathroom on his own.
(The Connecticut Mirror emailed LULAC for comment and did not receive a response.)
At the end of the school year, Vazquez decided not to send Jaysiel back to Reginald Mayo. He still had another year of preschool, and he spent it exclusively at LULAC — where, she said, his behavior improved markedly. 
The following year, Jaysiel returned to New Haven Public Schools to start kindergarten at Hill Central Music Academy. For a few months, Vazquez said, everything was fine, but then she began receiving reports of problems, some highly distressing. In one case, Vazquez said, the school lost track of her son for two hours — eventually discovering him hiding in his locker.
It was becoming clear Jaysiel needed some kind of additional support. What exactly that looked like, however, became a source of tension between Vazquez and the school. The school argued Jaysiel couldn’t function in general education and needed to go back into a self-contained classroom. 
Vazquez maintained her son could stay in general education with a one-to-one paraeducator. 
In her corner was Jennifer Wheeler of the Center for Children’s Advocacy. Wheeler said she was convinced Jaysiel was suited for a general education classroom the first time she met him.
“[Vazquez] had given me a list of names, and he sat over my shoulder and he started reading them, including Everleigh, E-V-E-R-L-E-I-G-H,” Wheeler said. “OK, this is a kid who can read and function and learn really well.” He seemed to Wheeler like the perfect example of a kid who could thrive if he just had a dedicated paraeducator to help manage his behavior.
When a child exhibits problematic behavior, a school is supposed to conduct a functional behavior assessment, or FBA. It’s how everyone figures out what is causing those behaviors and how to address them. A one-to-one paraeducator, a self-contained classroom — those interventions stem in theory from the FBA.
But Jaysiel had never had an FBA.
In early March, Wheeler joined Vazquez and school officials at a Planning and Placement Team meeting about Jaysiel. Wheeler said when she asked about the FBA, there were “blank stares.”
Wheeler said the school agreed to provide a part-time, one-to-one paraeducator. Two weeks later, Jaysiel was still struggling, and a supervisor again recommended the self-contained classroom. 
“I said, ‘Well, let’s get the para full time before we make that decision,’” Wheeler recalled. To Wheeler’s surprise, the supervisor told her the paraeducator hadn’t even started yet.
The paraeducator started two days later, and Jaysiel’s behavior improved almost immediately, Wheeler said. “In April, when I checked in, I was told that ‘this is a kid who absolutely does not belong in a self-contained classroom,’” Wheeler said.
‘The failure to invest in inclusion’
CCA attorney Kathryn Meyer said her organization has deep concerns about how kids like Jaysiel are ending up in self-contained classrooms.
Per the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act — known as the IDEA — every student is entitled to a free appropriate public education in what is known as the least restrictive environment. That standard means kids should go into the most inclusive setting they can manage.
In other words, if children can learn in the same classroom as their neurotypical peers, that’s probably where they should be. If they need extra support — like a one-to-one paraeducator who works with them to manage disruptive behaviors — so be it.
For other kids, the least restrictive environment may look different. It may be a separate room where they go to build certain skills or learn concepts at a different pace. It may include time in a resource room where they can cool off if they’re having a bad day. Whatever it is, the IDEA mandates it should be as inclusive as the child can manage.
Over the past several years, Meyer said, she’s seen growing resistance from some schools toward investing in more inclusive services — especially hiring one-to-one paraeducators. She said some districts, New Haven included, have told her they just “don’t do” that anymore. 
“To say that we have a blanket policy is the opposite of making an individualized determination,” Meyer said.
It’s no secret schools are in a very difficult position when it comes to special education. Legally, they have to provide whatever is in a child’s Individualized Education Program, or IEP, no matter the cost. If they agree to a one-to-one paraeducator for a kid, they just have to find the money.
[RELATED: These Meriden moms want CT to do better on special education]
Except many districts can’t — at least, not easily. Years of rising costs have taken chunks out of strained school budgets. Those costs have increasingly fallen on individual towns because the state’s share of public education funding does not rise with inflation. For cities like New Haven, where property wealth doesn’t fill the gap, the end result is cuts and shortages throughout the district.
Justin Harmon, a spokesperson for New Haven Public Schools, said Meyer’s claim that New Haven doesn’t do one-to-one paras is untrue.
“There is no such policy. We use 1:1 paras when programmatically appropriate and in alignment with IDEA requirements,” Harmon wrote in an email.
Jackson, the special education director, said in her written statement that the district is working on increasing “the number and range of specialized programs for students with complex learning needs in order to successfully maintain more such students within our district community.”
And, she said, the district is “augmenting training opportunities for educators regarding best practices for co-teaching, with an eye to improving opportunities for special education students in the general education classroom.”

East Rock Community Magnet School in New Haven on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

‘They’ve ruined a lot of things’
CeeCee Crooks thought she knew who her son Carter’s special education teacher was. The woman worked in Carter’s self-contained classroom at East Rock Elementary in New Haven, and she had the air of someone in charge.
But while visiting the school one day, Crooks began to feel unsure.
“I’m like … ‘She’s the teacher, right?’ And they’re like, ‘No, no,’” Crooks recalled. “I’m like, ‘Who’s the teacher?’ And they kind of all muted.”
It turned out the classroom had no teacher. The woman Crooks had been watching was a paraeducator — support staff for a leader who didn’t exist. Confused, Crooks contacted CCA attorney Sarah Mervine.
“It’s like we put these kids in self-contained classrooms so we don’t see them,” Mervine said.
Crooks’ son Carter has autism and was identified as nonverbal. The self-contained classroom he attended was supposed to be a space to learn important academic and life skills in a manageable environment. In reality, Crooks said, “he wasn’t learning anything.”
“They had a big projector screen. They would watch Cocomelon and spin in their chairs and go to recess and go to gym and go to music. That was it,” she said.
The school finally hired a new special education teacher, but Crooks said Carter was still left to spin in a chair and stare at his phone for hours at a time. Carter has diabetes and the phone is there to monitor his blood sugar, but he’s not supposed to use it. His FBA — which, like Jaysiel’s, was delayed — found phone use to be a major trigger for his negative behaviors. 
Crooks said Carter’s behavior at home also changed for the worse. He started flipping furniture, which Crooks suspected he learned from a classmate. He also got “a little rough” with his siblings.
She said they were understanding. Her 3-year-old daughter would “rub his back and say, ‘It’s OK, Carter. We have to breathe. We have to calm down.’”
Mervine said what she and Crooks really wanted for Carter was to have a proper one-to-one paraeducator assigned to him. She couldn’t say whether Carter would have done well in a general education setting, but she expressed doubt that the school had properly assessed him in the first place.
“A lot of times they don’t even know what the child in front of them is capable of,” Mervine said.
Mervine said there was also a pervasive lack of documentation. In one instance, Mervine said, Carter’s blood sugar dropped to 40. He was with a paraeducator at the time, and the school nurse thought he had gone home; no one told her he was actually still in the building. There was no incident report.
Not knowing what was happening was a source of significant concern for Crooks. Part of the problem — well-known to parents of nonverbal children — was that Carter himself couldn’t tell her. It’s one reason some parents, Crooks included, believe self-contained classrooms should be equipped with cameras.
(A bill mandating such cameras cleared the Education Committee with unanimous support in the 2026 legislative session but died without a vote in the House. The Connecticut Education Association, one of the state’s two teachers unions, submitted testimony in opposition to the bill, raising concerns about student privacy and suggesting the perceived lack of trust might dissuade people from becoming special education teachers. CT Mirror reached out to New Haven’s teachers union for comment but did not receive a response.)
By June, Crooks was fed up.
“It’s been a nightmare. They’re a nightmare,” Crooks said. “They’ve ruined a lot of things and set my son back in so many ways.”
The problem of funding
There is growing interest among state leaders in reforming how Connecticut approaches special education.
In April, Gov. Ned Lamont convened a Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability to, as its website states, “deliver a top-to-bottom overhaul of how the state funds its public schools.” The commission has met regularly since June and will issue a final set of recommendations on Jan. 15.
One popular idea the commission has discussed is boosting the state’s main school funding mechanism, the Education Cost Sharing or ECS grant, and then tying it to inflation. That would alleviate a large and growing source of strain for towns, as health care, transportation and other costs have risen faster than state aid. More money could mean more staff and better training for schools.
In a similar vein, the commission has looked at expanding the SEED grant, a relatively new pot of money the state set aside in 2025 to begin paying for in-district special education programming. Previously, the state covered only the costliest out-of-district placements for children with the most severe needs. The grant was designed to provide around $180 million in funding, but the General Assembly ultimately allocated only $30 million.
But even a relatively modest ECS increase could amount to an additional $400 million in one year, and that’s before factoring in the $150 million or more for a fully funded SEED grant. Finding that money will be difficult, especially given Connecticut’s stringent budget caps. Some advocates have argued that legislators could raise the state’s income tax to foot the bill, but there, they would likely run into another roadblock: Lamont.
At a press conference the day after the election, Lamont told reporters he doesn’t want to raise the income tax unless “absolutely necessary.” Asked whether school funding qualified, he replied, “I don’t want more money for the status quo.” And he pointed out that Connecticut has already put millions more into school funding in the past few years — though that only brought ECS up to a funding level set in 2013.
There is another idea Lamont seems to prefer: bolstering regional services schools can access for, among other things, special education.
“Talk about regional back-office savings, there’s a place where the state can take a real lead,” Lamont said at the post-election press conference.
That might involve staffing up Connecticut’s Regional Educational Service Centers to provide special education services or training at scale, rather than making each town build its own programming from the ground up. The Blue Ribbon Commission is looking at that idea, too, and its members seem enthusiastic so far.
A more ambitious proposal around special education came from the Connecticut Citizens’ Assembly on Property Taxes in late October. The 98-member group of everyday citizens was convened in July to develop a comprehensive plan for local property tax relief. Among the solutions it put forward: shifting all special education costs fully onto the state. That would amount to $3.3 billion a year out of the state budget.
The question of design
Beyond the money, there’s a pedagogical question about what special education should look like in the first place — particularly whether the model of a self-contained classroom makes sense.
The CCA’s Kathryn Meyer isn’t sure.
“What we do not think is appropriate or lawful is for students with disabilities to be isolated from their peers. … That means it’s not any less restrictive than an outplacement would be,” Meyer explained.
Meyer said districts should instead work to create a “spectrum of services” for kids. 
Ideally, she said, schools would create a separate hub — a kind of “home base” — for kids with special needs. The home base would be in a neighborhood school and would include an environment appropriate for children’s needs, as well as related service providers from the community. The staff-to-student ratio would be kept as low as possible.
Crucially, Meyer said, the point is not to suppress behaviors but to develop skills. Kids should also have plenty of chances to spend time outside the hub with their general education peers. “I would say that’s the underlying principle to it all,” Meyer said.
Although every student’s needs and development will look different, Meyer said that over time, a program like this should enable a growing number of students to enter progressively less restrictive environments. That’s another general goal of special education, though critics say it is often unrealized.
Meyer acknowledged implementing this kind of system isn’t always easy. 
“In order to build these programs successfully, you need to have the expertise, and most school districts don’t have that expertise,” she said.
That brings up another challenge in special education: There just aren’t enough people in the workforce. 
As of Nov. 12, there were 330 unfilled special educator teacher positions and 1,264 unfilled special education paraeducator positions in Connecticut, according to the state’s education data portal EdSight. Those are roles districts are actively hiring for — not roles they’d create if their budgets were bigger.
The state is trying to close that gap. 
Earlier this year, the State Department of Education announced a new training program for aspiring paraeducators, with the aim of training 250 in the first year. The state also has scholarship programs for aspiring teachers and recently won a federal grant to expand its Teacher Registered Apprenticeship Program, which pays student teachers to work in the classroom. The program puts an emphasis on training new special education and early intervention teachers.

Jay Vazquez, 6, plays cars with family members at their home in New Haven on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

A new school year begins on better footing
Jaysiel transferred to Fair Haven this year, and so far, he seems to be doing much better — though Wheeler cautioned that kids often have a honeymoon period of a few months in a new setting. 
He still has a part-time one-to-one paraeducator in his IEP; had the district denied the transfer, Wheeler said, she would have kept pushing for a full-time paraeducator instead.
Vazquez said Jaysiel was doing well academically in his new school.
“He can read and write just fine,” she said. He reads age-appropriate books for a first grader and is particularly fond of those about cars and police. She added that he has one of the highest scores in his class.
As for Carter, the district agreed to send him to an outplacement after the delayed FBA found no lessons were taking place in the classroom, according to Mervine.
“We were ready to file due process to get it, but they gave it to us because they know they failed him,” said Mervine.
Over the summer, it also became clear that Carter could both read and speak, raising further questions about whether a self-contained classroom was really his “least restrictive” learning environment.
The outplacement, she said, gives Carter more freedom of movement than he had at his previous school. Kids can walk down the hall and go up the stairs on their own — further evidence, Mervine suggested, that the self-contained classroom model should be reimagined.
“Not every self-contained teacher is terrible. A lot of them are wonderful,” Mervine said. “But the system is not a good system. We could imagine a better system.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi’s outlier election laws face new scrutiny after tight U.S. Senate race
description: DeSoto County Election Commissioners Laura Edler and David Ross prepare to start counting affidavit ballots in the 2026 midterms at the commission's office in Hernando, Mississippi, on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026.
text:
Democrat Scott Colom’s upset victory in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race is drawing new scrutiny to the state’s unusual election laws, which make it harder for some voters to cast ballots.
Mississippi law can prevent voters from casting a normal ballot after election officials receive information suggesting they have moved, even if the information hasn’t been verified. That’s led to questions about whether Mississippi may be running afoul of federal election laws meant to prevent voter disenfranchisement.
“I suspect a court will decide this at some time, but on the face of it, it certainly feels like it is absolutely turning people into second-class voters,” said Ben Hovland, a former chairman of the U.S. Election Assistance Commission who was a Democratic member of the bipartisan federal agency from 2019 until earlier this year. 
The issues largely stem from Mississippi’s voter roll maintenance law, which is out of step with other states and appears to conflict with Justice Department guidance on how states should comply with federal election law.
Secretary of State Michael Watson speaks during the Mississippi Economic Council’s annual Hobnob at the Mississippi Coliseum in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 30, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
After the state Legislature changed the law in 2024 to give election officials broad authority to turn to any source to clean the voter roll as long as it was considered “reliable information,” Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson’s office authorized county election officials statewide to use unverified address data from the credit bureau Experian for voter roll maintenance last year.
His office announced the partnership with Experian would bring “a new level of reliable data” to maintaining the roll, though records show the office signed off on disclaimers that the company could not guarantee the “accuracy or reliability” of the information.
Also, 11 years earlier, Mississippi had sued Experian over “significant inaccuracies” in the company’s credit files. Experian denied Mississippi’s allegations and agreed, along with credit bureaus Equifax and TransUnion, in 2016 to pay the state a $7 million settlement.
Mississippi Today first reported in March 2026 that properly registered voters had discovered they were wrongly inactivated by errors in the data since the state began experimenting with Experian’s information in early 2024. After Mississippi’s close U.S. Senate race earlier this month, Watson responded to criticism by saying it was county election commissioners’ legal responsibility to vet the data.
Thomas Minor, photographed March 18, 2026, at his local polling place in Fulton, discovered during the March 10 primaries that his name was missing from the poll book. County election officials had mistakenly inactivated him after the secretary of state provided them with incorrect address information sourced from Experian’s data. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
“Their job is to make sure they verify the information,” Watson said on a talk radio show the week after Election Day. “And I’ve heard people say, ‘Well, you pass the buck.’ What I am doing is explaining how the law works. I cannot make an election commissioner do his or her job.”
But election experts and state lawmakers say Mississippi’s use of credit bureau data is just one part of the problem. 
Mississippi’s voter roll maintenance law imposes unusual hurdles
Under state law, Mississippi approaches voter roll maintenance differently from other states that have used Experian’s data to clean the rolls, including West Virginia, Maryland and Montana. There, election officials give voters a chance to confirm their addresses before moving them from active to inactive status, by mailing them a notice and waiting for a response. In West Virginia and Montana, for example, that waiting period is 30 days. 
That aligns more closely with guidance from the Justice Department, which states that election officials may mark voters inactive if they don’t respond to the notice by the voter registration deadline for the next election.
But under Mississippi law, there is no waiting period. Election commissioners must inactivate voters upon sending them a notice to confirm their address. By the time voters even get the notice, they’re already inactive.
A copy of a confirmation notice sent out by Washington County election officials asks inactive voters suspected to have moved to confirm their address. The notice is pictured in Greenville, Mississippi, on Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
This automatic process means election officials can inactivate voters based on address information that was never verified. 
“There’s zero discretion,” said Amir Badat, a Mississippi voting rights attorney with the advocacy group Fair Fight Action. “If you’re an election commissioner, and the secretary of state is telling you that we have this new, reliable data source to do list maintenance and specifically cites this part of the statute, you shall send a confirmation notice and shall make that person inactive.”
To make matters worse, voters may never even receive the notice. Watson said Wednesday in an interview with a Mississippi Public Broadcasting talk radio show that his office discovered some election officials may have violated state law by failing to mail notices.
“That’s a problem, so they need to do their jobs a little bit better,” Watson said. “I have no idea what they were thinking, number one, to say that.”
Mississippi Today also identified cases in which election officials mailed the notice to incorrect addresses pulled from Experian’s data. As a result, some properly registered voters were inactivated without ever realizing it, until they showed up to vote.
Affidavit ballot envelopes are pictured in Hernando on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
State law prohibits inactive voters from casting regular ballots, and their names are not listed in precinct pollbooks. Instead, they must cast an affidavit ballot, which must be signed by the voter and a poll worker and reviewed by election officials before it can be counted.
“That doesn’t even give a person a chance to be able to vote regularly because the confirmation card is missing,” said Democratic state Rep. Zakiya Summers of Jackson, a former Hinds County election commissioner.
Mississippi’s law is out of step with many other states. For example, in Texas, voters whose addresses have been called into question can verify their residence at the polls, and then can vote a regular ballot.
Watson’s spokesperson, Elizabeth Jonson, defended the state’s voter roll maintenance process, stressing that inactive voters are not immediately purged from registration lists.
“The voter is not removed from the voter roll book simply by being marked ‘inactive,’” Jonson wrote in an email. “The voter has two federal election cycles to cure this designation by voting via affidavit ballot to restore the ‘active’ status.”
A line snakes out of a polling place in DeSoto County to vote in the 2026 midterms on November 3, 2026. Credit: Courtesy of Deborah Williams
But voting rights advocates say Mississippi’s process creates additional barriers and makes it less certain that inactive voters’ ballots will count. Election commissioners say the rollout of Experian’s data led to a surge in the number of inactive voters before this month’s election, causing long voting lines, confusion at polling places and an uptick in affidavit ballots, which officials spent over a week verifying and counting after Election Day.
“Requiring affidavit ballots for inactive voters is bonkers,” said Quinn Raymond, the co-founder of VoteShield, a tool from the nonprofit Protect Democracy that monitors changes to voter registration records. 
Amid criticism over the Experian deal, Watson told Mississippi Public Broadcasting that his office has been taking steps to fill gaps in Mississippi’s voter roll maintenance process. He said the online database that election commissioners use to clean the voter roll will now give officials the option to send notices to the new address flagged for a voter who may have moved and to the address that the voter originally used when registering, to ensure the notice actually reaches the voter.
“They could’ve already done that,” Watson said. “There is no restriction on how many of those confirmation cards they send, but we’re going to put it at the touch of their finger to where they can actually do that now on a much easier basis.”
Watson said the change will make it easier for election officials to send multiple notices to a voter when they are unsure whether a flagged address is accurate. He said his office’s switch from Experian to a new commercial data broker, IDI, will also help because the new vendor gives a score conveying how likely it is that a flagged address is accurate.
Raymond said the issue is less about the credit bureau data and more about how Mississippi law directs election officials to clean the voter roll in a way that prevents voters from casting regular ballots, especially when the sources they rely on are unverified.
Outrage over Experian deal renews hopes to change law
As the 2024 law faces new scrutiny and potential legal challenges in the wake of the midterms, Democratic state lawmakers from the legislative Black caucus are looking to bring Mississippi’s voter roll maintenance process in line with the rest of the nation.
Their goal is to work with voting rights advocates, attorneys and Republican legislators to amend the law, known as House Bill 1310, in the next legislative session. They say they hope to prevent the same issues from arising when voters turn out to the polls during Mississippi’s state elections next November, when the Legislature and top state offices will be on the ballot — including Watson’s bid for lieutenant governor.
“Mississippi voters should not have a system where you have to use an affidavit ballot for things that are out of your control,” said Ari Savitzky, a senior staff attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union’s Voting Rights Project. “The Mississippi Legislature is going to be back in session in January, and I hope they take a long, hard look at this and say, ‘We can do better than this.’”
Rep. Zakiya Summers, D-Jackson, center, and other members of the Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus speak at a press conference at the state Capitol on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, calling for an investigation into Secretary of State Michael Watson’s deployment of Experian data to local officials to make changes to voter rolls. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Summers said when the Legislature returns, the “first thing” on her priority list is overhauling the law, which opened the door for Watson’s partnership with Experian. 
“Voter roll maintenance should not be utilized to punish voters,” Summers said. “We’ve got to make sure we are protecting them, versus weeding people out.”
Before the Legislature passed HB 1310, Mississippi had for years solely relied on government data, such as U.S. Postal Service address data and death information from the Social Security Administration, to clean the roll of voters who may have moved or died.
But a little-debated clause within the new law broadly allowed election officials to use “reliable information” indicating that a voter had moved from their registered residence as grounds to mark them inactive. 
The bill did not specify any standards that the information had to meet to be considered reliable, but the examples it provided were all government sources. The bill made no mention of credit bureau data.
Rep. Cheikh Taylor, chair of the Mississippi Democratic Party, gives remarks on Gov. Reeves’ cancellation of the special session and ongoing Republican redistricting efforts during a press conference at the Mississippi Democratic Party headquarters in Jackson, Tuesday, May 19, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Rep. Cheikh Taylor of Starkville, the chair of the state Democratic Party, said he plans to introduce a bill that gives voters an opportunity to confirm their addresses before they’re inactivated.
Because Republicans have had supermajorities in the House and Senate for over a decade, GOP support would be essential to passing any reforms. In the past, Democratic lawmakers’ efforts to loosen Mississippi’s unusually strict voting laws — including proposals to allow no-excuse early voting and no-excuse absentee voting — have stalled year after year.
But as state lawmakers from Watson’s Republican Party also criticize his deployment of Experian’s data in the wake of the midterms, the Black caucus is hopeful it can build the bipartisan backing needed to change the law.
“My message is very simple to you: We can disagree politically, but we should never disagree about making sure that every eligible Mississippian has a fair opportunity to cast his or her vote,” Democratic Rep. Timaka James-Jones of Belzoni, who represents the southern Delta, said at a Thursday news conference at the Capitol. “When a voter encounters a problem at the polls, our responsibility is not to create another barrier.”
Mississippi’s inactive voter restrictions build on legacy of discrimination at the polls
Mississippi has a historical reputation, stretching back to the Jim Crow era, for creating discriminatory hurdles for voters. Voting rights advocates say the state’s history of erecting barriers to voting for Black residents casts a long shadow over the current debate surrounding the Experian deal.
“Mississippi has such a fraught history of voting,” said Deborah Williams, chair of the DeSoto County Democratic Party. “It was so long when voting was just the right of white voters. And then when you wanted to vote, you had to pay a poll tax and bring all kinds of documentation.”
U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Decades later, Mississippi still ranked last in the nation in a 2024 academic study measuring the time and effort required to vote in each state.
Watson has defended HB 1310 and stated that it has helped improve “election integrity.” 
In response to concerns that Experian’s data fueled an uptick in affidavit ballots during the midterms, Watson wrote in a statement last week that the 21,484 affidavit ballots cast this month was about the same as the 21,321 cast in 2024. 
“The process worked exactly as it has in prior elections, and the volume reflects a normal, high-engagement election, not a breakdown in the system,” he wrote.
However, according to data from the University of Florida, Mississippi’s voter turnout in the 2026 election was significantly lower than in 2024, meaning that those 21,000 ballots represented a higher share of the total this year. 
In reality, the portion of voters who had to cast affidavit ballots increased from about 1.7% in 2024 to 2.2% in 2026.
Three-quarters of the affidavit ballots this year were accepted after being checked, according to Watson. 
Voters fill out their ballots at the G. Chastaine Flynt Memorial Library in Flowood during the midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
In the wake of criticism over the increase, Watson has pointed to Mississippi’s high election integrity rankings. The conservative Heritage Foundation ranks Mississippi as tied for 14th place with Kentucky for “election integrity,” which considers factors, such as voter ID laws and the accuracy of voter lists, that Watson has described as priorities for his office.
“Maintaining accurate voter lists ensures the integrity of our elections and prevents voter fraud,” Watson wrote in a recent assessment of the November election.
But before the midterms, records obtained by Mississippi Today show a coalition of civil and voting rights groups warned him that “a list-maintenance program built on that data raises serious concerns” that it is out of step with federal requirements prohibiting discrimination in voter roll maintenance.
The groups also said state law allows voters to be inactivated “based only on ‘reliable information’” and said the Experian data didn’t meet the standard.
A 2025 study by the Election Assistance Commission of Mississippi and other jurisdictions’ use of Experian’s information to clean their voter rolls found ZIP codes with high numbers of rental housing and certain groups of voters — including Black, Native American, and young and elderly voters — correlated with more new addresses in the credit bureau data. 
This has heightened advocates’ concerns that minority and low-income voters were disproportionately affected by Mississippi’s use of Experian’s data.
Harya Tarekegn, director of advocacy and policy for the Mississippi Center for Justice, speaks during a voting rights rally at the Capitol in Jackson on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“Black Mississippians won the right to vote at enormous cost,” the groups, including the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, ACLU of Mississippi and Southern Poverty Law Center, wrote to Watson. “They should not have to win it again at the polling place because a credit bureau guessed wrong about where they live.” 
Savitzky, who was arguing a redistricting case in Mississippi last week, said the ACLU is considering whether to challenge the state law that allows election officials to mark voters inactive, preventing them from casting a regular ballot. 
Recently, Mississippi has seen among the fewest voting rights lawsuits in the nation. Mississippi ranked 42nd out of 50 states in election-related lawsuits from 2018 through 2024, according to the State Democracy Research Initiative, a nonprofit research program at the University of Wisconsin Law School. That even takes into account a high-profile challenge to the state’s mail-ballot receipt deadline that went to the U.S. Supreme Court this year.
Advocates and state lawmakers say the errors tied to the Experian deal broke voters’ trust in Mississippi’s commitment to protecting the right to vote. Rebuilding that trust, they say, will take changes.
“There’s an ugly history here with regard to voting,” Williams said. “Don’t mind me if I don’t trust your motives now.” 
Votebeat editorial director Jessica Huseman contributed reporting. 
Madeline Nguyen is an investigative reporting fellow at Mississippi Today and is based in Jackson. Contact Madeline at mnguyen@mississippitoday.org.
Dion Nissenbaum is a senior national reporter for Votebeat and is based in Houston. Contact Dion at dnissenbaum@votebeat.org.
