name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Close Osborn and invest in the way home
description: Closing Osborn is about the health and safety of staff and incarcerated individuals alike, and right now we are failing both.
text:
I spend a lot of time with the families this issue touches. In my district, I hear from mothers, wives, and children who have a loved one inside a Connecticut prison, and I hear from the correction officers and staff who walk those same tiers every shift. 
They are all my constituents, and they are all telling me versions of the same story. The conditions inside our oldest facilities are wearing people down, body and spirit, and everybody inside the walls knows it.

Christopher Rosario

Dallas Bailey’s story, reported this week by the Connecticut Mirror, is what that looks like up close. About a year into his time at Osborn Correctional Institution in Somers, Bailey reported significant gastrointestinal bleeding. A physician recommended a colonoscopy or an at home test, and it still took another ten months, and a trip to the emergency room, before he received the testing he needed. 
Doctors eventually diagnosed an H. pylori infection, the kind that can spread through contaminated food and water, and Bailey believes he contracted it from Osborn’s drinking water. Plaintiffs’ lawyers made claims about that same water in a 2016 class action over conditions at the prison that the state settled in 2024. A decade later, we are reading the same story with a different man’s name on it.  
When the same failures keep surfacing at the same facility, we are no longer talking about isolated mistakes. We are talking about a building that Connecticut has been patching for years while the men incarcerated there, and the staff who work there, pay the price with their health. Correction officers breathe the same air and work in the same deteriorating conditions. Closing Osborn is about the health and safety of staff and incarcerated individuals alike, and right now we are failing both.
Here is where our values have to mean something. We say Connecticut believes in dignity, in second chances, in treating people like people. If we believe in Connecticut values, that applies to all of us, including the men and women who are on their way back into society. Nearly everyone inside Osborn today will come home to a Connecticut neighborhood. The only real choice is whether they come home healthy and ready, with a fair shot at rebuilding a life, or come home sick, bitter, and set up to fail. 
A state that means what it says about redemption does not warehouse people in a facility that makes them ill and then act surprised at the outcome.
Connecticut’s prison population has fallen dramatically from its peak, and we have closed facilities before when the numbers and the conditions called for it. We also have to be honest about what happened last time. We had the opportunity to take the savings from that closure and build something lasting with them, and instead we folded the money into the base of the budget, where it quietly disappeared into everything and nothing. 
The men and women coming home saw none of it. We cannot make that mistake twice. Every dollar saved at Osborn should be dedicated, on purpose and in the open, to reentry programs that actually work, the kind that meet a person at the gate with identification, housing, treatment, and a real path to a job. That is not soft. That is how you lower recidivism, how you keep neighborhoods safe, and how you honor the belief that people coming home deserve the chance to become who they are trying to be.
We can keep paying to warehouse people in a facility that makes them sick. Or we can close Osborn, protect everyone inside it, and invest in the work of return. Connecticut values point one way. It is time we followed them.
 Christopher Rosario represents Bridgeport’s 128th District in the Connecticut House of Representatives, where he serves as Deputy Speaker Pro Tempore.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: It’s time for CT to lead again on climate, justice, and public health
description: Gov. Lamont has a chance to build a legacy as a climate and environmental champion. Here are three priorities that should be at the forefront of his agenda.
text:
As Gov. Ned Lamont begins his new term and lawmakers prepare for the 2027 legislative session, Connecticut has a real opportunity. Families are struggling with some of the highest energy costs in the nation, the state is falling behind on its own climate and environmental justice commitments, and too many communities still breathe dirty air and live with toxic hazards.
These problems are connected, and so are the solutions: policies that protect our environment also make life more affordable, improve public health, and build a stronger future for Connecticut families. Governor Lamont has a chance to tackle these challenges together and build a legacy as a climate and environmental champion. Here are three priorities that should be at the forefront of his agenda.
Get our climate and clean energy strategy back on track 
Connecticut has a history of climate leadership. We were among the first states to write binding emissions limits into law, were a founding member of the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, and are home to the nation’s first green bank. 
But in recent years, our follow-through hasn’t matched our ambition. The Department of Energy and Environmental Protection reports that we are not on track to meet our statutory climate requirements. The state’s Comprehensive Energy Strategy is eight years old and four years overdue. (DEEP is working to update it now.) Lawmakers cut our 2030 renewable energy requirement from 40% to 29%, scaled back clean transportation commitments, and repeatedly diverted energy efficiency funds to balance the budget.
Meanwhile, Connecticut families and businesses are struggling with some of the highest electricity prices in the country, driven largely by our reliance on natural gas and utility infrastructure spending. 
The affordability crisis and the climate crisis are related problems and share the same solutions. The cheapest energy is the energy we don’t use, so the state should fully fund efficiency and weatherization, and help families, especially renters and lower-income households, upgrade to efficient heat pumps. We should build as much solar and storage as can be responsibly sited, starting with rooftops, parking lots, and brownfields, and work with our neighbors to revive offshore wind. 
We should stop expanding a gas system that customers will be paying off for decades. And we should reward utilities for performance, not for costly capital projects.
Realize our commitment to environmental justice
Connecticut enacted its first environmental justice law in 2008. In 2023, Governor Lamont signed a law allowing DEEP to consider the cumulative pollution a community already bears when deciding whether to permit a new polluting facility. 
Three years later, those protections still aren’t in effect, because the regulations to implement them haven’t been finalized. Until they are, neighborhoods located near highways, power plants, and waste facilities have no assurance that the next project will be judged against the pollution burdens they live with every day.
The administration should finalize strong cumulative impact rules without further delay and give residents a real voice before decisions are made, not after. Justice also means making sure the clean energy transition reaches the people who need it most. And it means reliable, affordable, and cleaner bus and rail service for residents who depend on it. Your Zip code shouldn’t determine the quality of the air you breathe, the size of your energy bill, or whether you share in the benefits of a cleaner economy.
Protect our families from toxic chemicals and pollution
Connecticut has also led on toxics. We’ve banned PFAS “forever chemicals” in firefighting foam and food packaging and will phase them out of many consumer products by 2028. We’ve strengthened protections for children from lead poisoning and restricted harmful pesticides like chlorpyrifos and neonicotinoids.
Now the state must deliver. That means implementing these laws on schedule, without carve-outs or delays, and speeding up lead pipe replacement and cleanup of lead hazards in older homes. And with the federal Environmental Protection Agency rolling back chemical safety protections, states must take the lead in safeguarding their residents from toxic chemicals. 
Connecticut should require manufacturers to prove their chemicals are safe and regulate chemicals by class, so companies can’t dodge the rules with slightly altered substitutes.
We also face a waste crisis. Since the state’s largest trash incinerator closed in 2022, Connecticut has shipped roughly 40% of its trash to out-of-state landfills, driving up disposal costs for municipalities and residents. The answer isn’t more burning or dumping in already overburdened communities. It’s reducing waste, expanding recycling and composting, and making producers responsible for their packaging.
A legacy within reach
With Washington actively sabotaging climate and environmental protection efforts, the states must lead, and Connecticut has led before. Governor Lamont can be remembered as the governor who let the state’s commitments slip, locked families into another generation of volatile fossil fuel costs, and left the same neighborhoods to carry the same burdens. Or he can be remembered as the governor who delivered: who lowered energy bills by building a clean energy economy, made sure every community shared in the benefits, and left Connecticut’s air, water, and neighborhoods healthier than he found them. 
The tools are in his hands. Connecticut is ready to lead again.
James Flynn is Conservation Law Foundation‘s Vice President for Connecticut

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Gov. Lamont must help ICE-impacted families
description: I join with others in calling on the governor to create a $10 million fund for legal defense and family stability for families impacted by ICE abductions.
text:
“When a foreigner resides among you in your land, do not mistreat them. The foreigner residing among you must be treated as your native-born.” Leviticus 19:33–34

My faith teaches me to put love at the center, and as a person who strives toward moral character, I am called to welcome the stranger. I believe this is a community commitment we should live out together in Connecticut. 

The Rev. Sierra-Marie Gerfao

Gov. Ned Lamont has the power to act right now. Connecticut established a $500 million federal cuts response fund, of which about $250 million remains unused, and the governor has expansive discretion in how to use it. I join with others in calling on the governor to create a $10 million fund for legal defense and family stability for families impacted by ICE abductions.
Though I live in New Haven, I work as Director of Family Ministries at the Unitarian Universalist Congregation in Danbury, CT, and a couple years ago, I joined Danbury Unites for Immigrants. When a family reaches out for support after a loved one is taken by ICE, I work with volunteers to get them the support they need, whether that is financial assistance and items like groceries and diapers, emotional support, or connecting with legal services.
What residents of Connecticut need to know is that ICE removing individuals from our towns doesn’t make our communities safer, strengthen our communities, nor enhance the economy (economic research indicates that heavy immigration enforcement harms the economy, making conditions worse for all of us).
In my work with families who have been impacted by ICE, on a daily basis I see negative ripple effects that extend far beyond the individual taken, to parents, children, siblings, cousins, friends, employers, schools and peers, faith communities, and more. One of our volunteers described the heartbreaking scene she encountered visiting the family of a young man detained by ICE, only to find the young man’s little brother selling his toys in a tag sale to help the family.
One way we can lessen these negative impacts is to ensure that family members have a way to keep food on their tables after an income-earner has been taken, that families don’t have to choose between paying rent or paying for an attorney, and teenagers don’t have to become breadwinners for their families.
I am grateful that my congregation has been able to house the fund that, through individual donations, supports the families that Danbury Unites for Immigrants serves, but the level of need is far greater than philanthropy alone can address. 
This is a case in which the state is fully justified in stepping in. A Legal Defense and Family Stability Fund would help ensure that people fighting detention and deportation can access legal representation and that their families can get immediate financial assistance for basic needs. The governor says he is in support of keeping immigrant neighbors safe. He built a re-election campaign with promises like that. Now it is time for him to act.
The Rev. Sierra-Marie Gerfao lives in New Haven.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Auditor announces $443K in restitution for Montanans since July
description: State Auditor James Brown announced Monday his office helped secure more than $443,000 in restitution for victims of securities fraud in Montana since July. The money is for victims to financially recover when getting full restitution from fraudsters is not possible, the agency said in a news release. It said the auditor and Montana Legislature […]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.State Auditor James Brown announced Monday his office helped secure more than $443,000 in restitution for victims of securities fraud in Montana since July.
The money is for victims to financially recover when getting full restitution from fraudsters is not possible, the agency said in a news release.
It said the auditor and Montana Legislature created the fund in 2011, called the Lynne Egan Memorial Securities Restitution Assistance Fund.
Brown will ask the 2027 Montana Legislature to renew it so it doesn’t expire in June 2027. The news release said renewal is a legislative priority for Brown.
The funds come from voluntary contributions, legal settlements with the agency, and a portion of fees paid by companies offering securities in Montana, the news release said. No general fund dollars are used, according to the Auditor’s Office.
Brown said the fund is a critical tool that helps victims of fraud recover from “life-changing losses” and get back on their feet.
“Oftentimes, the restitution only covers a fraction of the total loss, but it can mean all the difference to victims of fraud,” Brown said in a statement.
An agency committee reviews applications for restitution on a quarterly basis, and Brown approves them for payment, the news release said.
It said the fund has provided $569,000 in restitution so far in 2026, including $443,000 the last three months.
Ethan Holmes, spokesperson for the Auditor’s Office, said the figures have been the following in recent fiscal years:

$341,000 in 2022,
$11,700 in 2023,
$125,000 in 2024, and
$0 in 2025.

Holmes said the office received just one referral in 2025, but it was not for a case their office handled. Generally, he said, payments are escalating.
“We’re just seeing, in general, bigger fraud losses,” Holmes said.
He said the increase also may be due in part to an increased threshold for payments to vulnerable people.
The news release said victims of securities fraud who have had their cases prosecuted or handled by the Auditor’s Office may receive up to $25,000 or 25% of their losses, whichever is less.
However, victims considered a “vulnerable person” under Montana law, which includes people older than 60, can receive as much as $50,000 or 50% of their losses.
Additional information is available at csimt.gov/restitution-assistance-fund.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Gov.-elect Kreiss-Tomkins announces attorney general pick
description: Alaska Gov.-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has named Jim Torgerson, a longtime Anchorage-based trial and appellate lawyer to be the state’s next attorney general, according to an announcement on Monday. Torgerson will step into the role in early 2027, the announcement said, and his appointment is subject to a confirmation vote by the Alaska State Legislature [...]
text:
Jim Torgerson has been selected as the next attorney general by Gov.-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins. (Photo courtesy of Stoel Rives LLP)Alaska Gov.-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has named Jim Torgerson, a longtime Anchorage-based trial and appellate lawyer to be the state’s next attorney general, according to an announcement on Monday.
Torgerson will step into the role in early 2027, the announcement said, and his appointment is subject to a confirmation vote by the Alaska State Legislature in the spring. 
Kreiss-Tomkins will announce an acting attorney general to serve in the interim, according to the announcement. 
As attorney general and Alaska’s chief legal officer, Torgerson will lead the Alaska Department of Law and serve as advisor and legal counsel to the governor, state agencies and the Legislature. 
“Jim understands Alaska, the importance of public service, and the responsibility that comes with serving as our state’s chief legal officer,” Kreiss-Tomkins said in a statement with the announcement. “The Department of Law has a vital role to play in ensuring state government works effectively, fairly, and in the best interest of Alaskans. I’m thrilled Jim has agreed to take on this role, and I’m grateful to have him as part of our team.”
Torgerson is a longtime litigator, with more than four decades of trial experience and 25 years of legal management experience, the announcement said. 
Torgerson is registered as a nonpartisan voter. 
“I’m honored by the opportunity to serve Alaska in this capacity,” Torgerson said in a statement. “I look forward to working with the dedicated professionals at the Department of Law and carrying out the responsibilities of this office with integrity, fairness, and a commitment to the people of Alaska.”
Torgerson is a partner at the national law firm Stoel Rives LLP, where he’s worked since 2008. The firm is recognized for legal work in the energy and natural resources industries, according to its website. He has represented Alaska Native corporations, energy and natural resource companies and individual Alaskans from across the state, the announcement said. 
Melissa Jones, the firmwide managing partner at Stoel Rives LLP, praised the selection in a statement Monday.
“Those of us who worked alongside Jim saw firsthand how hard he worked to bring people with different views together,” she said. “Time and again, he listened carefully, got to the heart of the issue and helped us make difficult decisions with sound judgment. The people of Alaska will be well-served by Jim.”
Torgerson previously worked as a federal prosecutor, heading the civil division and the criminal division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Alaska, where he worked from 1991 to 1998, according to his LinkedIn profile. He holds a law degree from the University of Washington and a bachelor’s degree from Bethel College in Minnesota.
Torgerson will replace Acting Attorney General Cori Mills, who was appointed in May after Stephen Cox, the former acting attorney general appointed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy, was rejected by the Legislature in a confirmation vote, amid concerns he pursued political and ideological policies over Alaskans interests. Cox was tapped to replace the former attorney general Treg Taylor, who served from 2021 to 2025. He stepped down to run as a Republican candidate for governor this year.  
Kreiss-Tomkins is expected to announce more leadership and cabinet picks in the coming weeks, and is scheduled to be sworn in on Dec. 7.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Court lifts administrative stay on Army’s lead-explosives detonation permit
description: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit on Monday evening lifted its administrative stay on a permit pertaining to the U.S. Army’s plan to intentionally detonate approximately 9,700 pounds of lead azide in southeast Iowa. The Army had previously decided it would act regardless of the court’s stay, based on an emergency exclusion, […]
text:
U.S. 8th Circuit Court of Appeals at the Thomas F. Eagleton Courthouse in St. Louis. (Photo via Google Earth)The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit on Monday evening lifted its administrative stay on a permit pertaining to the U.S. Army’s plan to intentionally detonate approximately 9,700 pounds of lead azide in southeast Iowa.
The Army had previously decided it would act regardless of the court’s stay, based on an emergency exclusion, but President Donald Trump on Monday advised the Army to postpone the detonation – most recently scheduled for Nov. 25 – until the federal court ruled. 
Trump also conditioned the decision on Gov.-elect Rob Sand, who said in a statement later in the day that “everyday Iowans” should have access to the information he received about the situation from the federal government. Sand did not say if he supported the intentional detonation in the statement on X.
“The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks,” Sand wrote.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Monday developments are the latest in an on-again, off-again situation around the planned detonation of the lead-containing explosive at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. 
The detonation was initially scheduled for Nov. 20, then delayed shortly after environmental groups filed a lawsuit, for which the court later granted an administrative stay, meaning the Army was unable to detonate until the court ruled on the permit. But the government responded in the lawsuit, saying the Army intended to detonate the lead azide, regardless of the court stay, to avoid the potential of an unplanned detonation from the unstable barrels of explosives.
On Sunday, the Army said it planned to detonate Nov. 25 — the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. As of Monday evening, the Army had not shared new information.
Judges say environmental groups were unlikely to win the suit
The environmental groups sued the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over its permit to the Army for the intentional detonation, arguing EPA did not fully consider alternative containment methods for the lead azide, nor the human health and environmental impacts of the intentional detonation, which has the potential to release lead particles into the environment. 
The opinion from a group of appeals court judges lifted the administrative stay on the permit, saying the environmental groups were not likely to win in their petition to review the permit.
The U.S. Department of Justice opposed the environmental groups, on behalf of the EPA, and submitted declarations from an Army explosives expert and the EPA region 7 administrator, who held that the crystallization in the lead azide drums presented an “immediate threat” of an uncontrolled explosion. 
The government response to the lawsuit said actions such as removing the lids, disturbing the area with heavy machinery and temperature fluctuations could cause an unintentional detonation, which it argued would be more damaging to surrounding communities and environment than an intentional detonation with safety precautions in place. 
The court opinion, which was attributed to Judges Justin Smith, L. Steven Grasz and Bobby Shepherd, held that EPA “adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead dust into the environment and mitigate the risks associated with potential exposure” in issuing the permit. 
Smith and Grasz were appointed by Trump, while Shepherd was appointed by President George W. Bush.
The judges also wrote that the Army evaluated a “full range” of alternative containment methods, but concluded in-place intentional detonation was the “best course of action.”
“While Petitioners disagree with that determination, the record does not provide a sufficient basis to conclude that the EPA failed to meaningfully consider safer alternatives or that its reliance on the Army’s technical assessment was unreasonable,” the judges wrote. 
Throughout the case filings, all parties have agreed that the detonation, controlled or not, has a risk of environmental and public health harms through the release of lead, which is toxic.
“However, that alone does not entitle petitioners to a stay,” the judges wrote. “… Here we are faced with a situation in which the risk is between a controlled detonation and an unplanned explosion, not between the risk of a controlled detonation and no explosion at all.”
The opinion noted that because the case pertains to the EPA permit, the court cannot and does not opine on the government’s filing that the Army intends to detonate without the permit if the stay remained.
“We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army’s planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide,” the opinion said. “However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place.” 
Who has the final say?
Trump’s Monday post on Truth Social said he had “ordered” the Army not to move forward until the court agreed they could do so. But he also said he was “making this decision fully subject” to Sand “agreeing to the operation.” 
The court lifted the stay, but Sand’s statement did not reveal if he supported the detonation. A subsequent request for comment about the court’s decision Monday night was not returned by Sand’s team. 
U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley criticized the politicization of the issue and said decision makers should “keep their eye on what’s most important—the health and safety of Iowans” in what he called a “life-or-death situation.” 
“Iowans expect government to be transparent and trustworthy,” Grassley said in a statement Monday. “Unfortunately, the situation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant has turned into political finger pointing from all sides.” 
The Iowa Republican said his office has been in contact with the Army about the situation since March when the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant closed for a period of time to conduct a safety review and remove lead azide, according to reporting at the time. In the statement, Grassley also noted that while the Army held an open house in Middletown in October about the planned detonation, “it’s clear it wasn’t enough” in terms of communication and transparency.
“My position remains clear—a controlled, safe removal of the lead azide far outweighs a spontaneous catastrophe,” Grassley said. “Final plans should be clearly and expeditiously communicated to the public and all government partners so Iowans can plan accordingly. I will continue to share resources as they are available for Iowans.”
Iowa U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek said on social media Monday night that Iowans need more information.  “Yes. Iowans deserve to know how we got here, why the Trump administration believes this is the best path forward, what is being done to keep Iowans safe, and how we can prevent such a communication failure from ever happening again,” said Turek, a Democrat.
“The safety of Iowans is my foremost concern and Iowans deserve transparency and to know that every possible safety protocol is being implemented to mitigate health risks,” he wrote.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Some FBI Files In Bribery Cases May Have To Be Released, Court Says
description: Civil Beat has been seeking the federal investigative records since 2023. Judges say the public has a right to know more about them.
text:
A federal appeals court has sided with Civil Beat in our legal fight to obtain the government’s investigative files on two of Hawaiʻi’s state lawmakers who were convicted of bribery in 2022.
The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday agreed that the FBI and U.S. Attorney’s Office can’t withhold records in a case of such high public interest just by saying, sorry, there’s an ongoing investigation so everything has to remain secret until we say it’s over.
Instead, the appeals court said — just as the Public First Law Center had argued on our behalf — the government has to prove that release of a document would jeopardize its case. A blanket refusal isn’t good enough.
“We conclude that the FBI has not met its burden to justify the challenged withholding,” the court ruled in a 2-1 decision. “The FBI has not provided a detailed and specific explanation of how the release of any documents or types of documents from the closed files would interfere with its ongoing investigation.”
In this case, the investigative files include more than 38,000 pages pertaining to former state Rep. Ty Cullen and former state Sen. J. Kalani English as well as about 30 minutes of video and tape recordings.
“Perhaps some of the records would disclose such information, but would every one of the more than 38,000 pages of responsive records that the agency identified?” the court’s majority asked in its ruling. “The FBI has not carried its burden of showing that they would.”
English and Cullen were arrested in 2021 after a yearslong FBI investigation into bribery that continues to ripple through Hawaiʻi today. The recent state charges against five people —former Lt. Gov. Sylvia Luke, former state Rep. Ryan Yamane, former Department of Transportation airports administrator Ford Fuchigami, former Public Utilities Commission chair Leo Asuncion Jr. and businessman Tobi Solidum — flow from the Cullen-English case.



A Special Commentary Project
Civil Beat is focusing on transparency, accountability and ethics in government and other institutions. Help us by sending ideas and anecdotes to sunshine@civilbeat.org.





Read More

The arrests of English and Cullen weren’t made public until 2022. Both men soon pleaded guilty to bribery-related charges and were sentenced to prison time. Milton Choy, the businessman who paid them tens of thousands of dollars to sway legislation, also was convicted and sentenced to prison, where he later died.
Once the cases were closed, Civil Beat asked for the FBI’s files but was turned down. In 2023, we filed a federal Freedom of Information Act lawsuit. Because none of the defendants went to trial, very little is actually known about what Cullen and English did or how the federal government went about making its case. And, as the 9th Circuit judges point out in Monday’s ruling, the public has a legitimate interest in knowing how the FBI is handling investigations in general.
In 2025, Hawaiʻi U.S. District Court Judge Shanlyn Park ruled in favor of the FBI that the files should remain off limits. And Civil Beat appealed to the 9th Circuit, which heard arguments in June.

Former lawmakers J. Kalani English, left, and Ty Cullen were convicted and served time in prison for accepting large sums of money to influence legislation. (Civil Beat/2022)

For years, the FBI has continued to insist there is still an ongoing investigation related to the English and Cullen cases and that the release of any more information could tip off suspects and jeopardize further prosecutions.
But the government only has five years under the statute of limitations to charge a crime. That means time is running out for crimes that might have occurred while Cullen, in particular, was cooperating with the FBI and was in a position to surreptitiously make a recording or provide information. Legal experts have pegged the end of that timeframe unofficially as February 2027, five years after Cullen’s role became publicly known and the FBI no longer needed him to cooperate with them.
The case has taken many twists, including when the U.S. attorney filed a memo explaining why officials thought Cullen deserved a lighter sentence for his assistance, which had redactions for information they believed should remain private. Unfortunately for the government, the U.S. Attorney’s Office screwed up when redacting key parts of the document and Civil Beat was able to see through the blacked-out sections. 
That allowed us to inform the public that the feds were also looking into another “influential state legislator” who appeared to have accepted $35,000 from someone they were also investigating. That money was apparently meant to be used in the lawmaker’s political campaign.
That part of the investigation was, as we all know by now, handed over to the stateAG’s office and led to the indictments of Luke, Yamane and the others. The identity of that influential lawmaker remains unknown to the public to this day.
Defendants in the state’s bribery case, which spun off the FBI investigation, appeared in court in July with their attorneys after they were initially charged.  (Jamm Aquino/Star Advertiser pool photo/2026)
That’s why it’s more important than ever that the public be allowed to see the original cases against Cullen and English, track the investigation carried out by the FBI and see for ourselves how it was handled and, frankly, whether there even has been an ongoing federal investigation all this time.
The judges wrote in their ruling that the public has a substantial interest in how an agency like the FBI carries out its duties, including how it approaches public-corruption investigations. The court also noted that Choy first bribed Cullen and English to support a bill funding research on cesspools, septic systems and sewers and then bribed them to kill the legislation.
“It may seem odd that someone would pay legislators both to advance and to defeat the same piece of legislation,” the judges said, “but Choy did not pay the bribes with his own money. Choy was cooperating with the FBI: When he bribed English and Cullen to support or oppose the cesspools bill, he was acting at the direction of the FBI. And it was the FBI that gave him the money to pay the bribes.”
Still, as Public First Law Center Executive Director Brian Black points out, it will be months if not longer before we can hope to see any more information about these cases coming from the federal government.
First, the government has 45 days to decide whether it will ask for a re-hearing in the 9th Circuit. And if there’s no re-hearing the case still goes back to Park in the Hawaiʻi District Court where she will preside over further review of thousands of pages of documents using the guidelines set out by the 9th Circuit to decide what is public and what is not.
So we’re not quite there yet. But, as Black, who argued the case before the 9th Circuit judges, says, this was an important victory for the public and its ability to hold a powerful government agency accountable.
“If the 9th Circuit had accepted the FBI position it would have eviscerated FOIA whenever a case involved an FBI investigation,” he says. “The court reaffirmed the importance of an agency publicly justifying denial of access and the District Court’s robust role to independently confirm that justification.”
​​

name: Nevada Current
title: Democrats plan 12 debates for 2028 presidential primary
description: Democrats plan to hold a dozen debates for candidates seeking the party’s 2028 presidential nomination — and will include a new set of conditions for participants — the Democratic National Committee announced Monday. The first primary debate will take place in June 2027, roughly seven months ahead the nation’s first primary. South Carolina, the first […]
text:
Democrats on the debate stage in Las Vegas Feb. 19, 2020. (Photo courtesy NBC News)Democrats plan to hold a dozen debates for candidates seeking the party’s 2028 presidential nomination — and will include a new set of conditions for participants — the Democratic National Committee announced Monday.
The first primary debate will take place in June 2027, roughly seven months ahead the nation’s first primary. South Carolina, the first in the nomination calendar, will have its primary on Jan. 22, 2028.  Nevada will host the second primary, on Feb. 1, 2028.
Under the DNC framework, there will be five debates in 2027 and seven in 2028, with the final debate taking place ahead of Super Tuesday in March 2028. The DNC said all early-state debates will be held in 2028.
“Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” said DNC Chair Ken Martin in a statement. 
No candidates have officially announced their 2028 presidential bid, however, the Democratic field is expected to be crowded following a commanding midterm performance that helped Democrats flip both the House and Senate.
Several names have been floated as potential candidates, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris, Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez of New York. Several possible contenders, including U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna of California, have held events in Nevada this year.
Candidates will be required to follow a new set of conditions to participate in the debates, including signing a pledge agreeing to denounce any spending from super PACs or political nonprofits that support their campaigns or oppose their rivals.
The “Fair Campaign Practices Pledge” is meant to limit the influence of dark money and outside spending in the Democratic presidential primary, said the DNC. 
The DNC said it would announce more details for the 2028 presidential primary debates, including dates, locations and media partners, in January.
Candidates will also need to meet certain polling and fundraising thresholds to be eligible to participate in debates, which the DNC said it would announce in January. 
In the event of a crowded field, the DNC said early debates could be spread out over two nights with the number of participants capped at 20 across the two nights. The DNC did the same thing with the first two debates in 2020.
That year, Las Vegas hosted the the ninth debate of the cycle, in February.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah’s 2026 election results are certified, solidifying Democrats’ gains in the Legislature
description: It’s official. Utah’s 2026 general election results were certified by the state Board of Canvassers — solidifying a blue wave election that doubled the Utah House’s Democratic caucus and shattered that chamber’s Republican supermajority for the first time in more than three decades.
text:
Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson speaks to reporters after the State Board of Canvassers certified the state's 2026 general election results at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Nov. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)It’s official. Utah’s 2026 general election results were certified by the state Board of Canvassers on Monday — solidifying a blue wave election that doubled the Utah House’s Democratic caucus and shattered that chamber’s Republican supermajority for the first time in more than three decades. 
The board — made up of Utah’s top election official, Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, Attorney General Derek Brown, Auditor Tina Cannon and Treasurer Marlo Oaks — voted unanimously to certify the results. 
On election night, there were no surprises from Utah’s congressional races. Democrat Ben McAdams won the newly-drawn 1st Congressional District. Republican Reps. Celeste Maloy, Mike Kennedy and Blake Moore will return to Congress representing the state’s other three congressional districts. 
‘Blue tsunami’ hits Utah: House Republicans on pace to lose 17 seats, breaking supermajority

But the blue tsunami that swept the nation also washed over typically ruby red Utah in an unexpected way: 14 Democrats and two unaffiliated candidates flipped a total of 16 Republican seats in the Utah House. 
That doubled the House Democratic caucus from 14 legislators to 28, knocking the House GOP’s two-thirds control down to a simple majority and therefore breaking Republicans’ veto-proof supermajority control over the Legislature. 
In the Senate, Republicans took back one seat from the Forward Party’s only currently elected legislator in the country, Sen. Emily Buss, who narrowly lost to Republican Brooks Benson. 
However, Senate Republicans also lost two seats to Democrats. That included one held by the Senate’s No. 2 highest ranking Republican, Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore, who lost to Democrat Shana Anderson. And they also lost an open seat previously held by retiring Sen. Ann Millner, flipped by Democrat “CJ” Christina Hernandez.
Senate Republicans will maintain two-thirds supermajority control in that chamber, but Senate Democrats gained two seats, bringing their members from six to eight, while Republicans’ ranks dipped from 22 to 21. 
From left, Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, Attorney General Derek Brown and Treasurer Marlo Oaks vote as the State Board of Canvassers to certify the state’s 2026 general election results at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Nov. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
‘Not a normal election’
Monday’s certification capped off an unusually exciting election year that had stunning election night results — far from the norm in Republican-controlled Utah, where usually the real contest happens in the June primaries. 
It was also a highly contentious cycle for election officials, including Henderson, a Republican who has made national headlines for calling out President Donald Trump and his administration’s “gamesmanship” with voting rights. 
Utah’s top election chief says Trump admin’s ‘gamesmanship’ with voting keeps her up at night

Henderson has refused to release private voter data despite threats of criminal prosecution by the U.S. Department of Justice. And earlier this fall, she learned the DOJ was investigating her as a result of her refusal. 
But while the months leading up to Election Day were stressful for election officials, Henderson told reporters Monday that the election itself went smoothly. 
“It was not a normal election on my end. It did not feel normal for me in the months and weeks and days leading up to the election,” Henderson said. “But Election Day itself, it was very smooth considering all of that.”
This year’s election turnout landed at 59.3%, or just over 1 million votes cast out of Utah’s nearly 1.8 million active registered voters — typical for a general election with no presidential or gubernatorial ticket. 
The dynamics that propelled Democrats’ blue wave included many loyal MAGA or Trump Republicans who didn’t vote, while middle-ground voters like independents or moderate Republicans opted to vote for Democrats instead, according to recent research conducted for Brigham Young University’s Center for the Study of Elections and Democracy. 
Analyzing Utah’s blue wave: Many Republicans didn’t turn out; others crossed over to vote blue

Even after individual counties had already canvassed their results in the weeks since the Nov. 3 election, Henderson in a social media post over the weekend said she received a “whopper” of a letter from what she called the “‘enthusiast’ wing of the Republican Party demanding we not certify election results” due to unverified concerns of election security. 
Henderson told reporters after the statewide certification on Monday that other Republican secretaries of state have received similar pushback — and that the concerns listed in the letter had no merit. 
“We worked really, really hard throughout every single step of the process to make sure things are done well, they’re done securely, they’re done in the open,” she said. “And if there are any concerns at any step along the way, we’d like to know about them. (But) right before we canvass the statewide results is not the time to bring up these issues.” 
She noted that the State Board of Canvassers has one duty under the law: compute and determine the final vote tallies for ballot initiatives and statewide and multi-county races. 
“That’s it,” she said. 
In a time of distrust, how do we know Utah’s elections are secure? Clerks show us

Canvass documents — including individual county reporters — are available to view and download on the state’s election results website. 
Final results on close races
While the leading candidates in several state legislative races flipped several times since election night due to narrow margins, Monday’s certification finalized the following results for those tight contests. 
None of these margins are narrow enough to qualify any of the races for a recount under Utah law.
Senate District 11: Republican Brooks Benson beat Forward Party incumbent Sen. Emily Buss with 50.19% (16,358 votes) to Buss’ 49.81% (16,236). 
House District 4: Democrat Zane Woolstenhulme won with 51.76% (10,006 votes) to Republican Rep. Tiara Auxier’s 48.24% (9,326). 
House District 8: Democrat Kim James beat Republican Rep. Jason Kyle with 49.88% (7,430 votes) to Kyle’s 45.9% (6,837 votes). Forward Party candidate Libby Shelton had 4.22% (628 votes). 
House District 11: Republican Rep. Katy Hall won a challenge from Democrat Dave Calder. Hall got 51.84% (5,970 votes) to Calder’s 48.16% (5,546 votes).
House District 16: Republican Bob Stevenson won against Democrat Abigail Treasure with 51.48% (6,673 votes) to Treasure’s 48.52% (6,290 votes). 
House District 20: Democrat Phil Graves beat Republican incumbent Rep. Melissa Ballard. Graves had 51.31% (6,713 votes) to Ballard’s 48.69% (6,369).
House District 45: Republican incumbent Rep. Tracy Miller won against Democrat Rod Moser with 53.96% (8,333 votes) to 46.04% (7,110 votes).
House District 48: Republican incumbent Rep. Jake Hunsaker narrowly beat Democrat Benyde Walker with 50.65% (7,492 votes) to Walker’s 49.35% (7,301 votes).
House District 59: Democrat Celeste Johnson won with 51.35% (9,799 votes) to Republican Luke Searle’s 48.65% (9,282 votes). 
House District 61: Republican incumbent Rep. Lisa Shepherd won against Democrat Alan Jimenez with 48.81% (4,878 votes) to Jimenez’s 47.21% (4,718 votes). Constitution candidate Jennifer Doud got 3.97% (397 votes).

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota landowners push back on wetland easement rules
description: JAMESTOWN, N.D. — Ryan Pederson called signing a conservation agreement with the federal government the “greatest single mistake” that ancestors of North Dakota landowners ever made.  Pederson, who farms in Rolette County, told Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, a former governor of North Dakota, “it is your mistake to have to deal with.” The Interior Departmen[...]
text:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, left, speaks with Rolette County farmer Ryan Pederson after meeting about wetland rules in Jamestown, North Dakota, on Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)JAMESTOWN, N.D. — Ryan Pederson called signing a conservation agreement with the federal government the “greatest single mistake” that ancestors of North Dakota landowners ever made. 
Pederson, who farms in Rolette County, told Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, a former governor of North Dakota, “it is your mistake to have to deal with.” The Interior Department oversees the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which holds the conservation agreements. 
About 200 people filled a room at the North Dakota Farmers Union headquarters in Jamestown on Monday, discussing how to correct a history of poorly documented conservation agreements with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and how to best ensure that ducks and other wildlife can thrive on North Dakota wetlands. The agreements provided the landowners with a payment in return for agreeing not to disturb the wetland. 
Outraged over ‘illegal’ wetlands rule, Sen. Cramer blocks dozens of Trump nominees

Burgum called it a national issue but with a disproportionate share of the problem falling on North Dakota, which has prime habitat for breeding ducks. Many in the room were descendants of landowners who signed conservation agreements in the 1960s. 
More than 50% of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service easements are in North Dakota, said U.S. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., who organized the meeting. Cramer said there are more than 16,000 such agreements in the state. Another 30% are in South Dakota. 
Cramer said the problem of poorly mapped easements has been exacerbated by a setback rule enacted by the Biden administration. The rule expands the area around wetlands where farmers are not allowed to install drain tile, or plastic tubing buried in the ground that drains excess moisture. 
Violating the rules can result in criminal charges.
Sen. Kevin Cramer, left, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum discuss wetland easement rules at a meeting Nov. 23, 2026, in Jamestown, North Dakota. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Landowners showed maps with wetlands as small as less than 1 acre — sometimes less than one-tenth of 1 acre. 
With the setback, Burgum said the areas taken out of agriculture production are sometimes more than five times the size of the original easement. 
Cramer said the small wetlands often no longer hold water and instead have become heavy with salt deposits, making the area poor for wildlife and farming. 
“There are no ducks on saline divots,” Cramer said. 
The Fish and Wildlife Service has started a pilot program to try to address the issue. 
The agency has met with 18 landowners — 17 in North Dakota and one in South Dakota –  to try to agree on  new maps that protect a similar number of acres to the original agreement, though the areas protected may shift to create larger protection areas. 
Most of the people who spoke at the meeting identified themselves as landowners dealing with restrictions on drain tile and vague records of what was agreed to in the 1960s. 
Drew Courtney farms in Dickey County near the South Dakota state line. He said most farmers agree on being good stewards of the land. 
“We love our land, we love wildlife habitat, and we love hunting, too,” said Courtney, who showed a map of small wetlands in a farm field and how the setback rules limit his ability to use drain tile. 
Jill Shaffer, a retired ecologist, speaks in favor of preserving small wetlands at a meeting Nov. 23, 2026, in Jamestown, North Dakota. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Others spoke in favor of preserving small wetlands. 
Jill Shaffer is a retired ecologist from the Northern Prairie Wildlife Research Center who lives south of Jamestown. She said habitat areas of less than 1 acre and seasonal wetlands are important to ducks and other wildlife species. 
“They are your everything,” she said. 
While the Fish and Wildlife Service pilot program addresses updating maps, changing the Biden-era setback rule is a different challenge. 
The agency in August announced in August it would pause a change on the rule as it reviewed more than 200,000 comments. 
Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., thanked Cramer for leading the North Dakota effort to get the rule changed, but said it may have to go beyond administrative rule changes and include action by Congress or a legal challenge. 
Cramer called the rule “theft of property” and a breach of the contract signed by landowners who have lost trust in the federal government. 
“We’re here to rebuild that trust,” he said. 
Cramer had put a hold on Trump administration confirmations in the Senate while advocating for the Trump administration to change the wetlands rule. He said he has been releasing those as there have been more conversations about the rule change, including visits to North Dakota by Fish and Wildlife officials. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Outcry over intended Medicaid cuts grabs lawmakers’ attention
description: LINCOLN — Uproar over changes coming to a broad spectrum of Nebraska Medicaid services swept through healthcare and low-income advocate circles Monday. The concern followed announcements late Friday afternoon by Gov. Jim Pillen’s administration. The Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services notified health care providers of a variety of changes and Me[...]
text:
A stir is created by the latest Medicaid-related changes announced by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services. (Courtesy of  IronHeart/Getty Images)LINCOLN — Uproar over changes coming to a broad spectrum of Nebraska Medicaid services swept through healthcare and low-income advocate circles Monday.
The concern followed announcements late Friday afternoon by Gov. Jim Pillen’s administration. The Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services notified health care providers of a variety of changes and Medicaid reimbursement rate cuts in programs ranging from dental to at-home personal care to hospital operations.
Tony Green, director of the disability and aging services for Nebraska at a news conference in 2023. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Those who received emails expressed outrage and disappointment. By Monday, groups and individuals had contacted state lawmakers and efforts were underway to try to stop changes that DHHS officials say are necessary to sustain the Medicaid insurance programs in light of escalating healthcare costs.
“These changes represent difficult, but responsible decisions intended to preserve access to essential services over the long term, not simply to obtain short term savings or abandon the individuals who depend on Medicaid,” said a letter from Jeremy Brunssen, interim director of Medicaid and long-term care for DHHS.
Center of controversy 
At the center of the shifts, said a press release from the Nebraska Hospitals Association, is a proposed 3% reimbursement rate cut in 2027 to physicians, dentists and other providers who accept Medicaid. Another 3% cut is to follow the next fiscal year.
“These state cuts, combined with Medicaid cuts enacted by the federal government, will be a devastating blow to our already fragile rural healthcare infrastructure,” said Jeremy Nordquist, the association’s president and CEO. “Nebraska patients and Nebraska communities will feel the pain.”
Nebraska’s projected budget deficit set at $1.1 billion heading into 2027 legislative session

Kris Perkins is the co-owner of A Place At Home, a private agency that provides non-medical home care to hundreds of elderly and disabled Nebraskans, a portion of whom are Medicaid recipients. 
She said she opened an email sent to her at 4:12 p.m. Friday from Tony Green, director of DHHS’ Division of Disability and Aging, announcing what she called significant reductions in reimbursement rates effective Jan. 1.
“That gives agencies just 41 days to prepare for a decision that could fundamentally change the availability of home care services throughout Nebraska,” Perkins said.
She, Nordquist and others believe that public health aid for low-income and vulnerable populations is the brunt of the state’s financial woes. 
Said Perkins: “You can’t balance the budget on the backs of your most needy populations.”
State Sen. Victor Rountree of Bellevue said he and other lawmakers have been flooded with concerns from people including those representing Nebraskans with disabilities — ”many feeling they’re numbers on a spreadsheet.”
The state faces a newly revised projected shortfall of about $175 million for the current budget period ending June 30, 2027, and about $1.124 billion for the 2028-29 biennium that starts in July. Pillen has said the financial predicament means the state will need to find trims and make “tough decisions” over the next three years.
State tried to ‘minimize’ impact
A state DHHS spokesman said the agency researched rates in the region to come up with adjustments that would minimize the impact on both providers and beneficiaries while keeping Nebraska in line with neighboring states. 
Over the years, said Jeff Powell, the spokesman, Nebraska’s Medicaid costs have increased significantly and the state had to respond. He said that nationally, Medicaid expenses have risen more than 40% since 2020.
DHHS ‘error’ in case of Nebraskan with disabilities hits home with state lawmaker

“DHHS will still need to request approximately $500 million in additional funding from the Legislature during the upcoming session to address rising Medicaid and waiver costs,” Powell said. “Without these adjustments, the additional funding request could exceed $1 billion.”
Rountree, who found out about the additional cuts Friday night, said it was unfortunate especially as the holiday season approached. He said he had a busy weekend and Monday fielding concerns and lawmakers are deliberating next steps.
The Nebraska hospital association is among groups calling for the Legislature to curb the “devastating cuts.” The association said that in addition to the 3% cut in provider reimbursement rates, concerns include:

New copay requirements for people receiving certain Medicaid services
Cuts to mental health and substance use treatment reimbursement, and changes to certain behavioral health services 
Changes to inpatient and outpatient hospital reimbursement 
Changes to specialty drug reimbursement
New limits on adult dental coverage, capping Medicaid benefits at $2,000 annually
A 4% cut in in provider rates in 2027 and again in 2028 for those who receive services through the Developmental Disabilities Waiver

Nordquist said Nebraska has already seen some rural clinics close, and “underpaying providers” drives up financial pressures elsewhere.



Quotation







When a rural hospital closes its dialysis or labor and delivery unit or shuts down entirely, every resident in that community loses access to care, whether they are on Medicaid, Medicare or private insurance.


– Jeremy Nordquist, head of the Nebraska Hospital Association



“When a rural hospital closes its dialysis or labor and delivery unit or shuts down entirely, every resident in that community loses access to care, whether they are on Medicaid, Medicare or private insurance,” he said.
Powell, in response, said Nebraska hospitals and healthcare providers are important parts of a healthcare system the Pillen administration values. He cited the governor’s signing of the Hospital Quality Assurance and Access Assessment Act in 2024 that “generates nearly $1 billion annually in additional funding for hospitals statewide.”
A grandma and a business owner 
From Perkins’ vantage point, elderly and disabled Nebraskans are in jeopardy of losing access to essential care, as agencies like hers may not be able to employ caregivers. 
According to intended changes, Perkins said, Medicaid reimbursement to agencies such as hers that deliver personal care will be reduced to a flat rate of $26.32 per hour, down from her current rate of $31.69. She said reimbursement rates currently vary according to the provider.
Independent providers are to receive $17 an hour.
Sarah Maresh, director of health care access for Nebraska Appleseed. (Courtesy of Nebraska Appleseed)
Perkins recalled a study the state conducted five years ago, which identified about $43 as the hourly rate necessary to operate a home care agency while accounting for caregiver wages, payroll taxes, workers’ compensation, insurance, administrative costs and more.
“This isn’t just about business,” she said. Perkins said she wants to employ caregivers at a rate that lets them pay bills. She also is the grandmother of a profoundly autistic, nonverbal 7-year-old whose speech therapy, she said, is in jeopardy.
Green, in his email to A Place At Home, said the state recognizes the impact on providers, families and others. 
“Our responsibility is not only to maintain services today but also to ensure Nebraska can continue providing meaningful, quality services well into the future,” wrote Green, who recently announced his February retirement from DHHS, the state’s largest agency.



Quotation







Our responsibility is not only to maintain services today but also to ensure Nebraska can continue providing meaningful, quality services well into the future.


– Tony Green, Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services


Sarah Maresh of Nebraska Appleseed called Friday’s Medicaid-related announcements “mind-boggling and sweeping.” 
She pointed out as “extremely harmful” Nebraska’s accelerated implementation of copays for certain Medicaid services and recipients. Maresh said Nebraska is calling for the new copays 21 months earlier than what is required under the Big Beautiful Bill.  
According to a state notice, copays are between $4 and $35 for services ranging from vision-related treatments to inpatient hospital stays. Certain populations are exempt, including pregnant women and people in nursing homes or other medical institutions.
Anticipated savings to the state from the copays, Maresh said, is roughly $6,000, which she describes as more “punitive” to poor people than a monetary boost to the state.
Angie Lauritsen, director of Nebraska For Us, noted that Nebraska for two months has not released new data related to the impact of previously implemented  changes related to work requirements for certain recipients of Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 
At last report, about 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied or lost Medicaid coverage since Nebraska launched the requirements in May — eight months ahead of the federal deadline.
“Now Nebraska wants to fast-track implementation of even more cuts,” Lauritsen said. “For a program based on financial need to force patients to come up with additional funds they do not have, this move makes it clear that the ‘Republican Tax Law’ hurts people in need to fund tax cuts for the wealthy.”
She noted a sign of how well the rollout is going: “The Trump administration is now giving the rest of the country an additional six months to execute changes that are well underway here. Nebraska has no plans to slow down.”
Not a ‘race worth winning’
State Sen. John Fredrickson of Lincoln, who is vice chair of the Legislature’s DHHS Committee, took to social media to challenge the state’s latest moves.
State Sen. John Fredrickson of Omaha. Dec. 6, 2023. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“Being first to make it harder to see a doctor isn’t a race worth winning,” he wrote. 
He said his priority bill last session would have let Medicaid cover copays. “It passed 31-18 with support from both sides of the aisle. The Governor vetoed it. … Nebraska can do better.”
Maresh said advocacy agencies “won’t stop”; they plan to participate in public comment periods and hearings, and will urge action by state policymakers and lawmakers.
 “I’m guessing there is going to be a busy legislative session coming up to protect healthcare access for all Nebraskans,” she said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Scholarship program would tackle rural primary care doctor shortage
description: The program would target medical students who commit to practicing primary care in “shortage areas,” such as rural corners of the state.
text:
Physicians, lawmakers and university leaders gathered at the Connecticut state Capitol complex Thursday to call on the state to address a shortage of primary care doctors in certain geographic areas.
“Connecticut has a primary care shortage,” said Quinnipiac University President Marie Hardin. “It’s felt perhaps most acutely in our rural areas. The consequences are real, and they impact the healthspan and the lifespan of our residents.”
Hardin and others called for a scholarship program that would target medical students who commit to practicing primary care in “shortage areas,” such as the rural northeast and northwest corners of the state.
“Connecticut is in the bottom 10 states in the nation at retaining our [medical] residents,” said Dr. Lisa Coplit, dean of Quinnipiac’s Frank H. Netter MD School of Medicine.
“Why don’t they stay here?” Coplit said. “The average Netter graduate leaves medical school with about $250,000 in debt… [and] primary care pays about 28% less than other specialties, so you put those together, and the math is really pushing our graduates towards higher-paying specialties or out of the state where cost of living is lower.”
“Who loses the most? It is our most underserved communities,” Coplit said.
“Our primary care workforce covers only 45 to 48 percent of our state’s need, and nowhere is that clearer than in rural Connecticut,” Coplit said. “In Fairfield County, there are 97 primary care physicians for every 100,000 residents. In Litchfield County, there are 56, and in Windham County, there are 45.”
State Senator. Saud Anwar speaks with medical professionals and Quinnipiac University President Marie Hardin during the National Rural Health Day event at the Legislative Office Building in Hartford, Connecticut November 19, 2026.  Credit: Francesca Fontanez / Connecticut Public
Dr. Saud Anwar, a South Windsor Democratic state senator and co-chair of the General Assembly’s Public Health Committee, said addressing the rural primary care physician shortage would be a priority in the upcoming legislative session.
“Our ZIP codes should not determine our outcomes,” Anwar said. “If you look at the data, it’s embarrassing, because the lifespan can be 17 to 20 years different from one part of the ZIP code to another part of the state.”
“This is a policy failure,” he said.
This story was first published Nov. 19, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming AG asks high court to rebuff ruling on 3 abortion laws
description:
Appeal asserts judge applied incorrect legal standard when striking down mandatory ultrasounds and other restrictions.  
The post Wyoming AG asks high court to rebuff ruling on 3 abortion laws appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A Wyoming district judge erred when he struck down an ultrasound requirement and two other anti-abortion laws in June, lawyers for the state argue in a recently filed appeal.
Judge Thomas T.C. Campbell incorrectly applied a more strenuous legal standard to decide the constitutionality of two laws passed by legislators in 2025, state lawyers argue in their appeal to the Wyoming Supreme Court. One of those laws enacted a mandatory ultrasound requirement and 48-hour waiting period for patients seeking abortions. The second required abortion clinics in Wyoming to operate under a more stringent set of regulations — rules that reproductive rights advocates maintain are really intended to make running such a facility unfeasible.

Keith Kautz, photographed here toward the end of his tenure as a Wyoming Supreme Court justice, now serves as the state’s attorney general. (Ana Castro for WyoFile)

The appeal from Wyoming Attorney General Keith Kautz and two other lawyers in his office further asserts Campbell erred when he blocked a 2025 law governing the prescription of off-label medications, which critics say would indirectly ban common abortion medications. The state’s lawyers maintain the law does not “impose any restrictions at all” on abortion providers.
The appeal is the latest in a series of legal battles over abortion in Wyoming that began when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, finding the U.S. Constitution did not protect the right to an abortion. 
In the years since, the Wyoming Legislature has repeatedly passed new restrictions on abortions, including attempts to ban the practice in most circumstances. The Wyoming courts, including the state’s high court, have repeatedly batted down those laws, concluding they violated a 2012 amendment to the state constitution that protects a competent adult’s “right to make his or her own health care decisions.” At the same time, it allows the Wyoming Legislature to set “reasonable and necessary restrictions” on that right in order to protect health and general welfare.
The amendment was enacted amid conservative backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare.
In striking down the three abortion-related laws passed in 2025, Campbell used a legal standard called strict scrutiny, typically the most strenuous standard of review that courts employ when they weigh whether a law is constitutional. (A 2025 U.S. Supreme Court decision noted it was “the most demanding test known to constitutional law.”) The standard requires the government to clear a challenging hurdle: showing restrictions are “necessary to achieve a compelling state interest” and that less restrictive alternatives weren’t an option. 
In January, a divided Wyoming Supreme Court used the same strict scrutiny standard in State v. Johnson, when it struck down Wyoming’s two previously passed abortion bans as unconstitutional. “The majority determined the State did not present enough evidence to show the restrictions (and exceptions) on performing abortions and the ban on medications (and exceptions) are no more restrictive than necessary to serve the State’s interest in protecting prenatal life. Therefore, the majority held that those laws are unconstitutional,” the court explained in a summary released along with its decision.
Anti-abortion billboards can be seen along some Wyoming highways.  (Tennessee Watson/WyoFile)
Campbell’s ruling “illustrates the incongruity” of the Johnson case, Kautz and his attorneys wrote. The Johnson decision recognized that the same constitutional amendment that protected Wyomingites’ right to make their own healthcare decisions also provides the Legislature with the authority to restrict those rights in some circumstances.
However, “it effectively negated that authority by holding such laws are subject to strict scrutiny review,” the appeal states. “As a result, even modest regulations like those in the laws here cannot pass constitutional muster.”
Kautz, a former Wyoming Supreme Court Justice, asked the high court to require Campbell to reevaluate the ultrasound and surgical center laws based on the rational basis test, a lower hurdle for the government to overcome. As for the off-label medication law, Kautz argued it was constitutional regardless of what legal standard it was assessed under.
Abortion remains legal in Wyoming as this latest case winds through the system. The state is home to only one clinic that provides procedural abortions: Wellspring Health Access in Casper.
A University of Wyoming survey released last month found the state’s residents broadly divided on abortion access. About 36% of Wyomingites believe abortion should always be available as a matter of personal choice. The same percentage supported restricting abortion except for cases involving rape, incest or when a woman’s life is in danger. About 15% said it should be permitted for other reasons, but only after the need had been clearly established. Roughly 14% backed a total ban.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commission rejects allegation that eavesdropping on closed meeting violated open-meetings law
description: PIERRE — The South Dakota Open Meetings Commission found no violation of law occurred when a person allegedly eavesdropped on the non-public portion of a city council meeting, but the commission decided to reprimand another city council for failing to adequately disclose its reasons for closed-door sessions. The Open Meetings Commission considered those and [...]
text:
Members of the South Dakota Open Meetings Commission, from left, Katelynn Hoffman, Michael Smith, Lance Russell and Austin Hoffman, listen to testimony from Stephanie Budihas during a meeting in Pierre, South Dakota, on Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/112326-Open-Meeting-Commission-web.mp3
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
PIERRE — The South Dakota Open Meetings Commission found no violation of law occurred when a person allegedly eavesdropped on the non-public portion of a city council meeting, but the commission decided to reprimand another city council for failing to adequately disclose its reasons for closed-door sessions.
The Open Meetings Commission considered those and other cases Monday. The commission’s five members are county prosecutors, known as state’s attorneys, and are appointed to the commission by the state attorney general.
Eavesdropping not a violation
State law requires public bodies to conduct most of their business in public, but with a majority vote of their members, they can enter a non-public executive session to discuss legal matters, the performance of a public employee and a limited list of other topics.
A resident of Gary, a small town in northeastern South Dakota, accused the city council of a violation for not preventing the city finance officer from sitting close enough to the door of a closed-door meeting to overhear what was discussed.


For broadcasters

Produced 1 minute, 13 second audio story with host intro script



According to Rachel Hinsvark’s complaint, the finance officer “positioned herself directly outside the executive session room, in the hallway between the library and city office — close enough to hear the ongoing discussion.” Hinsvark also alleged city council members included city employees in executive session without voting to approve their presence in the meeting.
Hinsvark told commissioners “there must be procedures in place that do not rely solely on trust” for meeting attendees to vacate an executive session, and that the city council “has a responsibility to safeguard executive sessions.”
“This is not simply about an employee sitting at the door,” Hinsvark told commissioners. “It’s about public trust, accountability and ensuring the rules governing public bodies mean something.”
Commission members voted unanimously to dismiss the complaint after finding nothing in the state’s open-meetings laws addressing eavesdropping on a closed meeting.
“What statute would’ve she specifically violated?” Austin Hoffman, a commission member, said of the finance officer. “I’m not certain there’s anything directly pertaining to that situation.”
Commission members also found nothing in state law requiring a vote about who’s allowed to attend an executive session.
Tripp City Council violations
State law says a motion to enter executive session must state the specific law containing a justifiable reason for the executive session.
According to a complaint from resident Stephanie Budihas, Tripp City Council members went behind closed doors in July without stating a purpose.
Commission Chair Michael Smith said that was clearly improper.
“I don’t think there’s any way to defend the violation,” Smith said.
The commission voted unanimously to reprimand the city council for that.
During another meeting in August, Budihas said, council members entered an executive session while citing “general descriptions ‘personnel & legal,’” and minutes published afterward did not cite specific sections of state law used to justify the executive session.
The commission voted 4-1 to reprimand the city council for that instance.
Smith cast the sole no vote.
“I felt like it was improper, and I still do, that we’re asking laypeople to cite the statute,” Smith said. “I mean, while we as legal counsel need to ensure that what they’re going into executive session for is defensible legally, I don’t expect a farmer or a retired individual to have that state law recitable.”
Hoffman agreed with that sentiment but still voted for the reprimand based on what’s in the existing state law.
“I’m not saying I think it’s right. I think there needs to be broader language there,” Hoffman said. “But I think that’s what meets that statute.”



Other cases
In other cases Monday, the commission:

Voted to reprimand the city of Egan Board of Trustees for failing to provide notice of a public meeting.
Voted to reprimand New Effington’s Board of Trustees for conducting an executive session without adequately explaining the reason.
Voted to reprimand the Town of Hermosa Board of Trustees for gathering at a campaign meeting for a board member with a majority of members present, and with the possibility of discussing public policy, but without notifying the public.
Approved written reprimands arising from two hearings in April, including violations by the city of Gary for disallowing public participation in a public meeting and the Hermosa Town Board of Trustees for discussing city business an hour before the official start of meetings.
