title: Certified election results affirm record turnout, expanded Democratic majorities in Legislature
description: Mainers turned out to vote in record numbers in November to expand Democratic control of the Legislature and decide other local and federal races, according to the official election results certified by the Secretary of State on Monday. “More voters turned out for this midterm election than any other midterm in the state’s history,” Secretary […]
text:
Maine Senate President Mattie Daughtry speaks to Democratic Party supporters at a post-election watch party in Portland on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger / Maine Morning Star).Mainers turned out to vote in record numbers in November to expand Democratic control of the Legislature and decide other local and federal races, according to the official election results certified by the Secretary of State on Monday.
“More voters turned out for this midterm election than any other midterm in the state’s history,” Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said in a statement. 
With 731,486 total ballots cast, comprising just more than 63% of Maine’s estimated citizen voting age population, Bellows expects that total to put Maine among states with the highest midterm turnout. 
That turnout led to Democrats getting a 13-seat majority in the Maine Senate and a 26-seat majority in the Maine House of Representatives in the upcoming Legislature. 
In the Nov. 3 election, in which every legislative seat was on the ballot, Democrats grew their majorities in both chambers, and gained a supermajority in the Senate; whereas the GOP now has historically small numbers in both. 
In the Senate, there are now 24 Democrats and 11 Republicans, compared to last session with 20 Democrats, 14 Republicans and one Republican turned independent. In the House, there are now 87 Democrats, 61 Republicans and three independents, while last session Democrats only had a narrow 74-73 majority, with three independents and one vacancy. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Democratic supermajority in the upper chamber gives their caucus the power to pass emergency legislation and override vetoes without GOP support, as those measures require a two-thirds vote. Though Republican support will still be needed for two-thirds of support in the lower chamber. 
The races for two of the seats Democrats flipped in the Senate, previously held by GOP incumbents Scott Cyrway from Benton and Bruce Bickford from Auburn, had some of the highest outside spending. Outgoing Sen. Rick Bennett, a former Republican who ran for governor as an independent, will be replaced by Democrat Elizabeth Bosworth, a win confirmed by a hand-recount completed last week.
Two other recounts last week also affirmed the margins in the House. Democrat Bradley Youngs defeated incumbent Republican Barbara Bagshaw. On the other hand, Republican Kerryl Lee Clement defeated Democrat Luke Jensen for a seat covering Lewiston. Some of the other seats Democrats flipped in the lower chamber included those covering Sanford, Windham and Auburn. 
Legislative leadership this upcoming session will be made up of some new and some returning faces. 
Senate Democrats stuck with the same leadership team: President Mattie Daughtry of Brunswick, Majority Leader Teresa Pierce of Falmouth and Assistant Majority Leader Jill Duson of Portland, who became the first all-female leadership team in the upper chamber when they initially assumed those roles in 2024.
House Democrats kept Ryan Fecteau of Biddeford as speaker and Matt Moonen of Portland as majority leader, while selecting Rep. Ambureen Rana of Bangor as the new assistant majority leader. 
Senate Republicans kept their same minority leader, Trey Stewart of Aroostook, while choosing Sen. David Haggan of Hampden as assistant minority leader. In the House, Rep. Ken Fredette will lead the GOP, after previously serving in the role from 2014 to 2018. Rep. Alicia Collins of Sidney was chosen to serve as assistant minority leader.
Election night results are based on unofficial returns, so the certified results also provide clarity on the exact vote totals for races. 
Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree received 391,364 votes, while Republican Bobby Charles received 272,710 and independent Rick Bennett received 58,241. 
Democratic U.S. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson received 379,629 votes, while outgoing Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Susan Collins received 338,596 votes.
Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree received 252,194 votes, while her Republican challenger Ron Russell received 130,155.
Maine’s 2nd Congressional District outcome was decided by ranked-choice tabulations. Republican U.S. Rep.-elect Paul LePage received 170,890 in the final round of tabulations, while Democrat Matt Dunlap received 165,432.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. party chairs reflect on Election Day and what comes next
description: State party chairs Eugene DePasquale, with the Democrats, and Sen. Greg Rothman, with the Republicans, previewed their parties' respective futures.
text:
The state Capitol building in Harrisburg. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Following a decisive midterm election that gave state Democrats their first governing trifecta in decades, leaders for the Pennsylvania Democratic and Republican parties made a joint appearance to preview what comes next for the commonwealth. 
Democratic Party Chairman Eugene DePasquale, said there were a few factors that boosted his party’s success: a popular governor running for reelection, good voter turnout and independents voting blue. 
“We had a popular governor who had an agenda that most Democrats agree with, which I think helped us attract state legislative and state Senate candidates, even in districts that were tough for us to win because they wanted to push that agenda,” said DePasquale. 
Eugene DePasquale, the chair of the Pennsylvania Democratic Party, talks to reporters on Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Sen. Greg Rothman (R-Cumberland), who serves as the state Republican Party chair, agreed that independents sided with Democrats, but noted that Gov. Josh Shapiro’s enormous cash advantage hardly won him any new voters when compared to 2022 numbers. Between the two election cycles, both won with over 3 million votes, Shapiro gained an additional 8,600 votes.
“If every person who had voted for Donald Trump in ‘24 in Pennsylvania had voted for Stacey Garrity, she would have won by a half million votes. That’s significant,” said Rothman. Trump received 3.5 million votes in 2024. “So why did they stay home two years later?”
Such questions will prompt some self-reflection, he added, saying donors opted not to support Republican Stacey Garrity’s gubernatorial campaign.
“She couldn’t get money early because everyone said she wasn’t going to win, and it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy,” Rothman said. 
Shapiro, who outraised Garrity 10-1, had enough cash that he could support candidates lower on the ballot.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“But, clearly, where he spent the money made a difference in those (Pa.) Senate seats,” he said, noting narrow victory margins in a handful of seats that tipped the scales. With those wins in hand, Democrats will control the upper chamber for the first time since the early 1990s.
Taking the chamber was “sort of our moonshot,” said DePasquale. For Republicans, keeping the Senate was the main objective, “but we failed miserably,” added Rothman. 
“Obviously, the challenge for us moving forward … It’s now time to govern politically,” DePasquale said.
 Legislative priorities

Democrats have named several priorities going into the next state legislative session: codifying abortion rights, addressing transit funding and tackling high prices for energy, housing and childcare. 
But the one expected to hit Shapiro’s desk first is an increase to the state’s minimum wage, which currently sits at $7.25/hour. House Democrats have repeatedly advanced proposals increasing the rate to $15, but Republican senators opted not to advance them.
Rothman signalled an openness to discussing a hike, but said it would increase prices — a claim that supporters refute.
Sen. Greg Rothman (R-Cumberland), the chair of the Pennsylvania Republican Party, talks to reporters on Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“That is not going to make things more affordable if you get more money … That’s not how it works. You have to have more supply, and if we don’t increase supply and we just give people more money, it actually has the opposite effect,” said Rothman. “Prices are going to continue to go up.”
“I don’t know how you create more affordability without creating more productivity and more things.”
He said he supported exemptions for small businesses, teenage employees, amusement parks and nonprofits. There was a risk that some people would lose their jobs, especially low-level positions that could be automated, he continued.
“There should be discussion about the best way to implement this, but we ran on raising minimum wage and that’s what we’re going to do,” said DePaqaule. “But it also is not the only thing we ran on.”
Data centers also played an outsized role, and have faced bipartisan pushback as proposals move forward around the state. 
“I think things will calm down a little bit, and people will say, ‘Wait a minute, we need the data,’” said Rothman, who has reportedly personally profited from a data center development in Cumberland County. 
Some projects generated massive protests, while others have moved forward with smaller fanfare, he noted.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“You’re using data, and if you’re using the computer and the data, we need data centers. If we’re going to have data centers, they need to be in the United States, not in China,” he continued. “And if they’re going to be in the United States, why not have them in Pennsylvania?”
“Local communities clearly want safeguards on these,” DePasquale added. “I think there was a lot of frustration if some of the bigger entities were able to — for lack of a better phrase — bulldoze their way into getting a permit. I think that’s what people want protection from.”
 A call for civility

DePasquale declined to weigh in on whether U.S. Sen. John Fetterman would win a Democratic primary if he chose to run for re-election. The first-term lawmaker has taken unpopular positions and openly criticized his party, fomenting rumors that he could try to switch to the Republican Party. 
“John Fetterman is a Democrat. And he has said publicly and to me privately, he doesn’t plan to switch,” DePasquale said.
“There are some issues that John Fetterman and the Republican party agree on — the border, the support for Israel — but I think that probably still 90% of the issues that are important to Republicans … he’s going to say no,” Rothman said. “I can’t imagine he wins a Democratic primary, but I don’t know if he wins a Republican primary either.”

DePasquale also demurred when asked whether Shapiro should run for president in 2028, saying the party would be focused on 2027 judicial retention races. 
When asked about turning down the political temperature, Rothman said people were “cynical about politics because of the way we treat each other,” adding that “we have to do more of ourselves showing that we can work together.”
Rhetoric accusing rival parties of being fascists or communists are “not helpful,” he continued, pointing to ever-escalating attacks on politicians, including arson at the governor’s residence last year. 
“We can set an example. I think that’s what we have to do. I would say that to every elected official,” Rothman said. 
“There is zero place for any political violence. Period. Full stop. End of story,” DePasquale added. “There is a difference between us having a vigorous debate about a policy initiative … (and) when you call someone a bad human being.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Lawsuits pile up over HUD mixed-status rule as AGs sue to block crackdown on immigrant tenants
description: Both suits argue that the “arbitrary and capricious” rule change exceeded the agency’s authority and violated federal law, including the Administrative Procedure Act.
text:
THE US DEPARTMENT of Housing and Urban Development is facing yet another legal challenge to a rule that would require households receiving federal housing assistance to prove that every member has citizenship or eligible immigration status. 
Days after a coalition of public tenant advocates and residents filed a federal class-action lawsuit on behalf of mixed-status families whose housing is endangered by the new rule, a coalition of 22 state attorneys general dropped their own suit Monday arguing that the change illegally reverses nearly 30 years of federal policy. 
The rule “leaves families no real choice because they must either break apart, forcing ineligible members out of the home so that the rest of the family can keep its HUD assistance, or be driven out of assisted housing altogether, at grave risk of homelessness,” wrote the tenant and public housing group in its complaint. “Families forced out of assisted housing will be thrown into a housing market that is already desperately short of affordable units.” 
Both suits argue that the “arbitrary and capricious” rule change exceeded the agency’s authority and violated federal law, including the Administrative Procedure Act. 
The tenants also claim that the rule and requirement that residents produce substantial documentation violate the equal protection and due process guarantees of the Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution. 
Since 1996, Congress has allowed families whose members have different legal immigration statuses to live in federally funded housing so long as the assistance was pro-rated so that only eligible household members received support. 
HUD did not immediately respond to a request for comment on either lawsuit. 
But HUD Secretary Scott Turner said earlier this month that the rule change reflects that “the federal government is not good at providing housing,” and long-term subsidies are “not the way that it’s intended to be. 
The attorneys general argue what HUD wants is irrelevant. 
“Federal financial assistance is not a slush fund that executive agencies can redirect at will to the groups they favor,” they assert in the complaint. “HUD is charged with administering a statutory scheme in furtherance of Congress’s goals, which are clear: Congress seeks to ensure a decent home and suitable living environment for all American families, and Congress’s definition includes mixed- status families.”  
Tenants and the attorneys general are asking a Massachusetts federal judge to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it against the states, their local governments, and their public housing authorities.   
Around 20,000 mixed-status families, totaling 78,100 people, could lose their housing assistance under the new rule. The state prosecutors note that this estimate includes 55,000 people who are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, many of whom are children and seniors. In Massachusetts, about 910 households would likely be impacted.  
One of the class-action plaintiffs is a Massachusetts mother of four. She has lived in the country for 15 years and is currently authorized to live and work in Massachusetts, but her immigration status is not among those deemed eligible. She lives in a Section 8 subsidized apartment with her four children, all of them 12 or younger and three of them US citizens. 
“Under the mixed-status rule challenged in this case, the family would lose their housing subsidy entirely,” the suit asserts. Because her “citizen children cannot live independently from her, the family would face eviction and homelessness.” 
The City of Boston announced on Monday that the city and the Boston Housing Authority would join the tenant and public housing organization suit. More than 500 Boston families could have federal housing assistance stripped away, according to city officials. 
“Almost every family we house at the Boston Housing Authority has previously suffered through a period of homelessness,” said Kenzie Bok, administrator of the Boston Housing Authority. “These are Boston kids, they are eligible for federal housing in their own right, and they deserve to stay safely in their homes.” 
Lawyers and advocates cautioned that although the new rule is set to take effect on December 14, that does not mean immediate withdrawal of benefits. Housing authorities would have about a month to begin sending out notifications to impacted families. Those families would then have until March 14 to verify the eligibility of every family member.  
Zafiro Patiño, director of organizing for the Massachusetts Union of Public Housing Tenants, one of the groups in the class- action suit, urged families to be prepared but patient.  
“We are basically saying to people, ‘Do not sign anything yet.’ The law still is the same, so do not panic,” she said. The group has already heard that some housing authorities are already sending out notices, which Patiño expects will spook many households. 
The class-action group emphasized that a severe regulatory burden will land on tenants and housing authorities if the rule takes effect. “We expect that the housing authorities already are feeling terrorized with this because they have a lot of work,” said Patiño, “and now it’s going to be even more.” 
HUD’s impact review estimates that sheltering people displaced by the rule could cost state and local governments between $20,000 and $50,000 per person each year. 
About 8.8 million tenants across the country will be impacted, because all tenants would have to verify their status, said Annette Duke, a senior housing attorney at the Mass Law Reform Institute. 
That burden, she noted, will fall disproportionately on people of color, women, children, and people with disabilities.  
“The rule really seeks to divide the communities,” she said, “and what’s great is this lawsuit shows that people are standing together to fight this.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado sues Trump administration over housing assistance rule that excludes immigrant families
description: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser joined a lawsuit challenging a federal rule that would exclude an entire household from receiving housing assistance if it contains at least one ineligible immigrant member.  The lawsuit, filed by 23 states in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts, seeks to invalidate a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development[...]
text:
Gov.-elect Phil Weiser spoke to reporters at a press conference on Nov. 4. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser joined a lawsuit challenging a federal rule that would exclude an entire household from receiving housing assistance if it contains at least one ineligible immigrant member. 
The lawsuit, filed by 23 states in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts, seeks to invalidate a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule that would withhold benefits from any household that includes someone who is not a U.S. citizen or eligible immigrant. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Weiser, a Democrat whom voters this month elected to be Colorado’s next governor, said the rule will require families who live with a relative not eligible for benefits to “choose between keeping their housing or keeping their family together.” 
“Those most affected by this cruel policy are seniors and children,” Weiser said in a statement. “Once again, the federal government overreached and came up with an illegal rule, and we’re suing to stop it and protect housing for families.”
The federal housing assistance program already reduces the subsidies for “mixed status” families so that only eligible household members receive benefits. Congress in 1997 implemented this protection to ensure low-income families who live with ineligible members can still receive financial support.
U.S. citizens will also need to verify their citizenship when applying for federal housing assistance under the newly approved rule, which is set to take effect in mid-December.
The Department of Housing and Urban Development estimated that 20,000 mixed-status families will lose housing assistance under the new rule, including 55,000 people who are fully eligible for federal housing assistance.
The lawsuit says the rule exceeds the agency’s authority and violates federal law that allows for prorated assistance for immigrant families. It says the department also violated the Administrative Procedures Act. The lawsuit asks the court to block the federal government from enforcing the rule in plaintiff states and declare it unlawful.
A group of attorneys general, including Weiser, in April wrote comments in opposition to the rule. They argue it will result in increased homelessness as families who become ineligible for benefits lose access to housing. 
Weiser has filed nearly 90 lawsuits against the federal government since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025. He has been successful in more than 50 of them so far, with many still pending.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. health officials report 9th measles-related death in Centre County
description:
The most recent death occurred in Centre County, the state Department of Health announced, noting 49 new measles cases since Nov. 18 that brought the total for 2026 to 1,638.

From @peterhall
text:
Vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy in Mill Valley, California, in a 2015 file photo. (Photo illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)A ninth person has died after testing positive for measles, Pennsylvania health officials said Monday, as the highly contagious virus continues to spread mainly among unvaccinated people.
The most recent death occurred in Centre County, the state Department of Health announced, noting 49 new measles cases since Nov. 18 that brought the total for 2026 to 1,638.
The department did not provide identifying details of the victim, which are protected under state law. The Centre County Coroner’s Office, which may release more information, did not respond to a message Monday. 
Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak started in April and reached a peak in early September, when 143 cases were reported between Sept. 7 and 14, according to the Health Department’s measles dashboard. 
As Pennsylvania’s measles-associated death toll rises, the CDC’s count lags. Why?

Measles is a respiratory virus that can cause short- and long-term health problems including pneumonia and brain swelling. Nearly 20% of cases reported to the Health Department have involved hospitalizations.
The virus spreads when a person who is infected breathes, coughs or sneezes and it remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours. Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose and red watery eyes followed by a rash on the head that spreads down the body.
The death reported Monday is the first in Centre County. The other deaths were reported in Clinton, Jefferson, Lancaster, Mifflin and Montour counties. Fewer than 1% of the infections have been in people who received the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
Around 300 Health Department staff are working with community organizations and health care providers to fight the outbreak by providing fact-based information and access to the MMR vaccine. 
Staff at state health centers have administered more than 7,400 vaccinations are pop-up clinics in the affected communities. The department recommends children older than 12 months who have not received two doses of the MMR vaccine should receive one immediately and a second dose at least 28 days later.
Adults who have received only one dose or who do not have their vaccination records should contact their health care provider or pharmacist about getting vaccinated.
People who believe they were exposed to measles and have symptoms should contact a health care provider or call the Health Department at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258).

In a 59-page ruling, U.S. District Court Judge Mary S. McElroy found HUD an[...]
text:
The exterior of U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island at 1 Exchange Terrace, Providence. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)A federal judge in Rhode Island struck down the Trump administration’s plan to set aside $1.3 billion in homelessness funding for new transitional housing and supportive-services projects, ruling Friday that the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development exceeded its authority.
In a 59-page ruling, U.S. District Court Judge Mary S. McElroy found HUD and its cabinet-level secretary sidestepped congressional requirements by steering funding away from existing programs and permanent housing through its Continuum of Care grant program toward shorter-term solutions.
“Although Congress delegated to the secretary the power to create additional criteria for awarding funds, this residual clause cannot be read as allowing HUD to nullify the other congressionally established mandatory factors,” McElroy wrote. 
McElroy was appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term.
A coalition of states and another group of cities and nonprofit organizations took HUD to court in July, arguing its new funding rules would upend the federal government’s longstanding emphasis on moving people into permanent housing.
Lead plaintiffs in the latter case include the National Alliance to End Homelessness and the National Low Income Housing Coalition, along with Providence-based nonprofits Crossroads Rhode Island and Youth Pride Inc. Several cities and counties across the country also joined the suit.
The coalition of plaintiffs welcomed the ruling, saying in a joint statement they would protect communities’ ability to compete for federal homelessness funding without facing penalties for their housing policies or service approaches.
“At a time when so many people are struggling to find and maintain stable housing, these resources are too important to be tied to arbitrary and unlawful restrictions,” they said.
Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha, whose office joined the multistate lawsuit, also welcomed the ruling, saying the administration’s proposed funding changes could have put thousands of Americans at risk of losing their homes.
“While the Trump administration remains committed to making life harder for our most vulnerable Americans, our coalition remains committed to holding this administration accountable,” he said in a statement to Rhode Island Current.
At issue was a June 1 funding notice for HUD’s roughly $4 billion Continuum of Care program, which sought to redirect funding toward new projects, favor transitional housing and supportive services, and impose new conditions on organizations seeking federal grants.
The July lawsuits followed a similar fight over HUD’s 2025 funding competition. McElroy ruled in June that the department’s November and December 2025 funding notices were unlawful, setting them aside. In August, she ruled that HUD had again violated federal law by trying to divert $4 billion in homelessness grants away from permanent housing programs, blocking the June 1 directive from taking effect. She declined to issue a permanent injunction barring the department from making similar changes in the future.
HUD threatened penalties for programs that use harm-reduction strategies and added requirements tied to local law enforcement’s efforts to clear encampments, diversity, equity and inclusion policies, and immigration-related restrictions.
Plaintiff groups argued the changes would undermine existing homelessness programs, discourage approaches that help people secure housing without preconditions and put federal funding at risk for organizations whose practices or policies ran afoul of the new criteria.
McElroy agreed that HUD’s $1.3 billion set-aside for new projects would sideline existing programs and prevent communities from weighing their track records and local priorities in deciding how to spend federal homelessness funding.
“Defendants offer no evidence contradicting Plaintiffs’ showing that the Set-Aside distorted the application process,” she wrote.
McElroy ordered HUD to allow applicants to amend and resubmit grant applications by Dec. 1. She pushed back the funding award deadline from Dec. 1 to Dec. 31.
HUD Secretary Scott Turner, in a statement to Rhode Island Current, called the ruling disruptive to the agency’s efforts to distribute $4 billion in homelessness funding.
“The plaintiffs’ ideological agenda threatens to cause gaps in funding,” he said. “HUD reserves the right to appeal. Our ‘Treatment First’ mission will not be deterred.”
In addition to Crossroads Rhode Island and Youth Pride, the coalition of providers and local governments includes Santa Clara County, California, and King County, Washington, and the cities of San Francisco; Boston and Cambridge, Massachusetts; Nashville; and Tucson, Arizona. 
The states’ lawsuit includes attorneys general from Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia. The governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania also filed on behalf of their states.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Makana Eyre: New Owners Add To The Mystery Of Historic Kona Hotel
description: Since I read about the sale of the Manago Hotel to an anonymous buyer last month, I haven’t been able to shake these two questions. Who is the new owner? What is in store for this cherished historic hotel perched high above Kealakekua Bay on the Kona coast? Opened in 1917 by Kinzo and Osame […]
text:
Since I read about the sale of the Manago Hotel to an anonymous buyer last month, I haven’t been able to shake these two questions.
Who is the new owner? What is in store for this cherished historic hotel perched high above Kealakekua Bay on the Kona coast?
Opened in 1917 by Kinzo and Osame Manago, the Manago has long felt like a relic of an increasingly bygone era in Hawaiʻi, like finding a weathered glass fishing float on the beach.
Family-run until its sale, it seemed to resist the increasingly standard — and blandly corporate – uniformity of hotels, restaurants and stores across America.
Sure, it could be a little rough around the edges. But it felt real, personal, atmospheric. And those views of the south Kona Coast. It’s hard to beat pūpū and a cold beer watching the vog-reddened sun dip beneath the horizon from a Manago balcony.
Kealakekua Bay glistens in the morning light. The Manago Hotel sits on the bluffs above with stunning views of the bay. (Nnachappa64/Wikimedia Commons)
After news of the sale broke, I spent a few weeks trying to get those questions out of my head. But my curiosity got the better of me and I decided to nose around in the public record. Here’s what I found.
It Leads Back To The Ninth Island
According to property deeds filed with the Hawaiʻi Bureau of Conveyances, the Manago Hotel was purchased by MTZ LLC, a Hawai‘i-registered company formed a month before the sale. Mortgage filings list a Las Vegas address for the company. 
The two people behind MTZ are Joseph and Brenda Tuttle. In sworn disclosures submitted to the Hawaiʻi County Department of Liquor Control, each identified themselves as owning half of the company.
So, who are the Tuttles? I phoned Joseph Tuttle to find out. The ensuing conversation left me a little perplexed – and with more questions than answers.
The first thing I asked was whether he and Brenda were indeed the new owners. To my surprise, he repeatedly avoided telling me.
Is he the hotel’s manager? He said no. What is his role then? He refused to say.
While he wouldn’t divulge his function or stake in the Manago, when I asked him why he’d acquired it, he said, “It’s a cool hotel. Who wouldn’t want it?” When I pressed for more information, he shifted the conversation, insisting that MTZ is the owner and the purchase was “a strategic business investment.”
Are he and Brenda from Hawaiʻi? Are they based in Hawaiʻi? Once again, he declined to say.

Read More

He did share some information about his plans for the hotel – which, again, he says, he doesn’t own or manage.
The rooms already, or soon will, have new pillows, mini fridges and lamps. In the longer term, he added, the hotel would get new furniture and fixtures alongside expanded restaurant hours. He didn’t plan to make any major changes.
“The heart and soul of the hotel stays the same,” he told me.
The more questions I asked, however, the more evasive Tuttle became. At a certain point, all he’d say was either “I don’t disclose personal information” or superlative-laced boilerplate on how the hotel is constantly sold out, doing great business, and that everyone is happy.
Over the course of our conversation, those assurances kept coming:
“Our customers absolutely love it. They love the positive changes we’re making.”
“The staff loves it. The staff is completely happy.”
“There are 30-year employees who’ve been there and they’re all staying on.”
“We have people returning from 40 years ago and they absolutely love the new ownership and all the employees love it.”
“The hotel is running sold out most nights. People coming in don’t have any problems. They absolutely love it.”
“The local community has supported and endorsed the new ownership” 
“It’s beautiful that MTZ LLC is continuing the Manago tradition.”
Somewhat Sober Dining, Pricey Financing
The hyperbole made it feel like I was talking to Donald Trump, if he’d been transformed into a local hotel owner in a rural corner of Hawaiʻi island. 
Since Tuttle was taciturn, what else could the public record tell me?
On Oct. 1, he appeared at a preliminary hearing in front of the Liquor Commission to petition it to allow him to take over the Manago’s liquor license.
In paperwork accompanying the liquor license petition, he and Brenda Tuttle describe themselves as real estate investors based out of Las Vegas.
The Tuttles have already made one previously unreported change – one that could be major or minor, depending on whom you ask.
During the hearing, Joseph Tuttle revealed that he and his wife have introduced a two-drink limit for any patron. The rule wouldn’t be posted, he explained, just something that waitstaff would know. He might, however, allow staff to serve a third drink, “if someone wasn’t intoxicated, and it wasn’t going to cause a problem.”
“We really don’t want to serve alcohol,” he explained, adding that he and his wife don’t drink. He made the two-drink concession, he said, because he was told that the local community would be very upset if he stopped serving alcohol altogether. 
Was financing from mainland investors also involved? According to filings submitted to the Hawaii Bureau of Conveyances, MTZ took out a $2.5 million loan on the Manago Hotel property.
The loan was arranged by Capella Mortgage Corp., a Nevada-based hard money lender. It is held by six lenders, including Capella and several private investors.
A hard money loan is typically short-term with a higher interest rate. Loans of this sort are often used in real estate as bridge financing or to buy or flip commercial properties. According to the filings, the loan comes due in August of 2028, unless repaid sooner or renegotiated.
This matters because the interest payments on a loan this size could be substantial. While the rate in this case was not disclosed, experts say it’s common for hard money lenders to charge between 9 and 14%. Capella currently advertises rates of “9% to 14%, with most loans priced 12% to 14%.”
Can the Manago, a relatively small historic hotel, shoulder such a debt burden? We’ll have to wait and see.
Still, there are some reasons to be optimistic. The restaurant, known for its pork chops, will be open longer hours and more days than before. The Tuttles appear to be making some improvements to the property.
It’s also true that for several years prior to the MTZ purchase, there were signs that the Manago was in distress. In 2024, a deal to convert it into affordable housing collapsed. It stopped renting rooms the same year and then went on the market for $7.5 million. In 2025, the family dropped the sales price to $5.75 million.
According to the County of Hawai‘i Real Property Tax Office, MTZ bought the hotel and adjacent lot for a combined $3.7 million.
Why All The Secrecy?
Kailua landing on the Kona Coast, 1900-1920. (Courtesy: Hawaiʻi State Archives)
There’s nothing inherently wrong about people from the continent owning treasured local businesses. In fact, there’s an argument to be made that the Tuttles deserve some credit for assuming what is surely a monumental undertaking – and keeping the doors open. After all, the Manago family themselves nearly sold the property knowing full well that it would be closed as a hotel.
Yet there’s something off-putting about the secrecy of it all. Why attempt to be anonymous? Why buy the hotel? What is the plan to honor its legacy? The Tuttles might very well have good answers. It’s a pity they refuse to share much of anything with the community.
In mid-October, the Manago family listed a curious Craigslist ad. “MANAGO HOTEL SALE! FURNITURE, ANTIQUES AND MORE,” its headline read. The listing included pictures of some of the items for sale: several lucky cats, traditional Japanese dolls, a wooden usu and kine (for making mochi), a Hawaiian stone adze, old dressers, glass fishing floats, vintage aluminum cookware, and much more. The proceeds, the listing noted, would be donated to the community. 
A lot of it looked like the sort of thing you’d clean out of a deceased elderly relative’s home. Nothing was essential to the hotel. But up for sale were the little things that make a place feel individual, that add character. I wonder what of the original decor is still intact.
Among Joseph Tuttle’s many grand pronouncements to me was this: 
“It’s one of the coolest experiences you’ll ever have, staying at the Manago, and eating those famous pork chops.”
Despite the oversell, Tuttle does get that right. The Manago is special. Its restaurant is a part of local heritage – though I’ve always preferred the miso butterfish to the pork chops. This is why people care so much. This is why I’m writing a column about it.
Despite my reservations as to how they’ve handled the sale, I hope – sincerely, unironically – that Joseph and Brenda succeed. A piece of Hawai‘i is now in their hands. May they rise to the challenge.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Recount set in northeast Alabama Senate district
description: A recount is scheduled for Wednesday in a tight state Senate race in northeast Alabama. State officials on Monday certified the Nov. 3 general election and started the process for an automatic recount in Senate District 10, which includes Cherokee, DeKalb and Etowah counties.  Independent candidate Jesse Battles had 72 votes over incumbent Sen. Andrew […]
text:
Secretary of State Wes Allen (right) certifying the 2026 general election on Nov. 23, 2026, in the Old House Chambers in the Alabama State Capitol in Montgomery, Alabama. The certification of the general election triggered the automatic recount in a tight race in Senate District 10. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)A recount is scheduled for Wednesday in a tight state Senate race in northeast Alabama.
State officials on Monday certified the Nov. 3 general election and started the process for an automatic recount in Senate District 10, which includes Cherokee, DeKalb and Etowah counties. 
Independent candidate Jesse Battles had 72 votes over incumbent Sen. Andrew Jones, R-Centre as of Nov. 10. Battles claimed victory and was sworn in on Nov. 10. Jones did not concede, saying he would wait for the recount. 
The margin of votes between Battles and Jones was less than 0.5%, which triggered the automatic recount. 
“When we certify today, the official winner of District 10 will not be included in what we submit to the Secretary of State,” said Alabama Director of Elections Jeff Elrod.
Jesse Battles is running as an independent candidate in Senate District 10. (Via jessebattles.com)
The automatic recount process is initiated by the certification of the general election, Secretary of State Wes Allen said on Monday. The recount will be conducted on Wednesday by the district’s probate judges in Etowah, Cherokee and DeKalb counties.
“It just takes coordination. It’ll go fine. I trust these guys that are in these three counties. They’ll do a fabulous job, just like they did on November 3,” said Allen, a former probate judge.
A message seeking comment from Battles was left Monday afternoon. Jones declined to comment on Monday afternoon, but said he would issue a statement following the recount.
Sen. Andrew Jones, R-Centre, looks up to the gallery in the Alabama Senate on March 10, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
Battles originally sought to challenge Jones in the Republican primary for the district, but was removed from the ballot by the Alabama Republican Party in February. According to The Anniston Star, Battles faced allegations that he had done work for former Alabama House Minority Leader Craig Ford, D-Gadsden, who ran against Jones as an independent candidate in 2018.
Battles accused the “Montgomery establishment” of removing him from the primary, and gathered enough signatures to win ballot access as an independent.
Jones, who started the campaign with about $432,000, reported raising $1 million and spending $1.2 million on the race, according to campaign finance reports. Battles raised $142,000 and spent about $135,000.
Should the general election results hold, there will be 24 Republicans, 10 Democrats and one independent in the upper chamber. 
The Legislature will convene for the 2027 Regular Session on Feb. 2.

name: Maryland Matters
title: All Maryland Matters readers are winners — or at least 3 of our election contestants are
description: The results of our election contest are in, and we have not one, but three winners, all tied with 14 correct answers to 20 questions, and no correct tiebreakers. Not only was it our first multiple-winner contest, we had our first woman winner and our first repeat winner.
text:
Two Question 3 campaign signs - one for and one against - in Calvert County on the last day of early voting this fall. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)It’s been like watching the odometer as it nears 100,000 miles. Or the calendar when you’re a kid waiting for Christmas. But after weeks of hitting the refresh button on the Maryland Board of Elections site, the number of ballots remaining to be counted all rolled to zero Saturday night.
That’s good enough for us to declare the election over, even though it will be another week before the returns are officially certified. More importantly, that’s good enough for us to tally up the results and declare a winner to our regular election contest.
And we came up with not one, but three winners for this election, the results of which were apparently just as hard to predict for the contestants as they were for everybody else: The winners each got just 14 of 20 possible answers. And they all went zero for four in the tiebreakers, though they came close. (Note to self: Easier tiebreakers next time around.)
Since this is not the Hunger Games, we’re good with three winners: Anne Zmuda, the vice president of government relations at the Maryland Food Bank. Henry Snurr, the deputy caucus director for the House Democratic Caucus; and Del. Vaughn Stewart (D-Montgomery).
This was a contest of firsts: Besides our first multiple winners, Zmuda is the first woman to win the contest and Stewart is the first repeat winner, after winning way back in 2018.
Former Montgomery County Del. Kirill Reznik and Anne Arundel County Councilmember-elect Spencer Jones, who won our primary election contest, both came close with 13 correct answers each in this latest contest.
The results, for those keeping score at home:
1) Ballot Question 3, the redistricting amendment, is seen as a way to enable Democrats in the legislature to redraw the state’s congressional boundaries before the next U.S. Census. Will the proposed constitutional amendment pass? Yes, it will pass. And what percentage of the vote will “yes” and “no” garner? 62.06% yes, 37.94% no. You’ll get one point for correctly picking the result, and another point if you’re within 2 points of predicting the “yes” vote.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
2) Who will have the biggest margin of victory over their Republican challengers: Gov. Wes Moore (D), State Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D), or Attorney General Anthony Brown (D)? Attorney General Anthony Brown, with a margin of +39.59 percentage points (edging the comptroller by 0.21 percentage points and the governor by 4.65 percentage points).
3) Which of those three statewide incumbents will have the biggest raw vote? Attorney General Anthony Brown, with 1,560.746 votes to Comptroller Brooke Lierman’s 1,547,104 and Gov. Wes Moore’s 1,470,907.
4) Who will win the 1st District race for the U.S. House, incumbent Republican Rep. Andy Harris or Dan Schwartz, the Democratic challenger? Andy Harris. What will the victor’s percentage of the vote be? 52.12%. You’ll get one point for correctly picking the result, and another point if you’re within 2 points of predicting the winner’s percentage of the vote.
5) Which of Maryland’s other seven members of Congress will have the biggest margin of victory? Rep Glenn Ivey (D-4th), with a margin of +83.29 percentage points over perennial candidate George McDermott.
6) Which of the other seven members of Congress will have the smallest margin of victory? Rep. Andy Harris with a squeaker, for him, of 4.41 points over Dan Schwartz.
7) Who will win the election for Frederick County executive – Democratic Jessica Fitzwater, the incumbent, or Jeff Holtzinger, the Republican challenger? Jessica Fitzwater. Predict the margin of victory +18.94 percentage points. You’ll get one point for correctly picking the result, and another point if you’re within 2 points of predicting the winner’s percentage of the vote.
8) In the 2022 election for Harford County executive, Republican Bob Cassilly took 64.1% of the vote compared to 35.64% for Democrat Blaine Miller. Will Cassilly, who is seeking reelection, surpass that percentage of the vote in his race against Democrat Barbara Kreamer? No, Cassilly beat Kreamer by 9.94 percentage points.
9) How many seats will Republicans win on the five-member Talbot County Council? Three of five.
10) How many seats will Republicans win on the seven-member Anne Arundel County Council? One of seven.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
11) Who will have a bigger percentage of the vote, Julian Jones, the Democratic nominee for Baltimore County executive, or Allison Pickard, the Democratic nominee for Anne Arundel County executive? Jones got 64.99% of the vote in his race while Pickard won 60.98%.
12) Who will win the District 30 state Senate race between incumbent Democratic Sen. Shaneka Henson and Republican challenger Jessica Haire? Shaneka Henson, by a convincing 59% to 41%.
13) Apart from the District 30 Senate race, will any Senate incumbents lose their reelection bids? Yes. If so, who will lose? Republican Sen. Bill Folden was unseated in Frederick County’s 4th District by Democrat Lara Westdorp.
14) Who will win the District 38B House of Delegates race in Wicomico County, between Del. Barry Beauchamp (R) and Wicomico County Councilmember Josh Hastings (D)?Josh Hastings, by a 61% to 39% margin.
15) Who will win the District 30B House of Delegates race in Anne Arundel County, between Del. Seth Howard (R) and Democrat Matt Johnston? Seth Howard, 51.72% to 48.22%.
16) Who will win the District 29B House of Delegates open seat race in St. Mary’s County, between Democrat Adrianne Mathis and Republican BJ Hall? Adrianne Mathis, 59.65% to 40.24%.
TIE-BREAKERS

How many seats will Democrats hold in the House of Delegates? 106.
How many seats will Democrats hold in the state Senate? 35.
How many seats will Democrats hold in the U.S. Senate? 56.
What percentage of the vote will Robin Ficker get in the 6th congressional district race? 37.63%.

description: WisconsinEye announced Monday that Jon Henkes, the president of the organization who helped found it and recently led it through financial troubles, is retiring at the end of 2026. The organization started as an independent nonprofit in 2007 and provides livestream coverage and archives of government meetings and legislative sessions. The announcement stated[...]
text:
WisconsinEye President Jon Henkes, who helped cofound the organization that livestreams and archives Wisconsin state government proceedings, will retire at the end of 2026. WisconsinEye was among reporters who covered Gov. Tony Evers signing the 2025-27 state budget in July. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)WisconsinEye announced Monday that Jon Henkes, the president of the organization who helped found it and recently led it through financial troubles, is retiring at the end of 2026.
The organization started as an independent nonprofit in 2007 and provides livestream coverage and archives of government meetings and legislative sessions. The announcement stated that under Henkes’ leadership, WisconsinEye was able to make state government more visible and accessible. 
Henkes said in a statement that he was proud of the work he and his team had done to make state government proceedings available to Wisconsinites. 
“WisconsinEye exists to serve the public – not a party, an interest group or a point of view,” Henkes said.
Henkes’ final year at the nonprofit was marked by a battle to raise funds from donors and the state Legislature to continue its operations. For most of its history, WisconsinEye has relied on donations and is run independently from the state Legislature, but Henkes told the Examiner last year that since the pandemic, the organization had struggled with raising funds. 
WisconsinEye briefly shuttered coverage and pulled its archives down last year. But it was able to come back  online due to a short-term cash infusion from lawmakers. The organization then expanded its fundraising efforts over the last year and engaged in a lobbying effort to secure state funding to help support its work.
In July, Wisconsin lawmakers on the Joint Committee on Legislative Organization approved a $250,000 infusion of funds to be paid out to WisconsinEye in $50,000 increments each month. The money will take the organization through the end of December. 
In his farewell, Henkes thanked elected officials past and present for helping allow WisconsinEye to “operate independent of state control, as a model for the nation.” He also thanked Diane Hendricks, the Beloit billionaire businesswoman and philanthropist, for providing financial support from the start and Margaret Farrow, who has served as board chairperson. “Both gave generously and continually, never once exerting pressure or influence on programming or coverage decisions.” 
New Democratic majorities in the Legislature will take over in January 2027 and WisconsinEye could again turn to lawmakers to seek future funding for the service.
WisconsinEye said that Henkes will remain in his role through December 31, and it will share information about leadership transition plans at a later date.

name: VTDigger
title: Historic bridge month shines light on landmarks
description:
From Tunbridge’s covered bridges to Royalton’s steel trusses, Vermont’s historic crossings tell stories of ingenuity, preservation and change.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Historic bridge month shines light on landmarks.
text:
One of dozens of bridges built as replacements after the great 1927 flood, the green steel-truss bridge, like the Foxstand Bridge in Royalton, became a signature design for generations. Photo by Rose Curtis/Herald

This story by Rose Curtis was first published in the White River Valley Herald on Nov. 12, 2026.
November is Historic Bridge Awareness Month, an opportunity to appreciate the bridges that have connected Vermont communities for generations and to consider what it will take to preserve them for the future.
The observance was established unofficially in 2006 by HistoricBridges.org to encourage public awareness of historic bridges and the importance of preserving them. November was chosen partly to commemorate a bridge lost to demolition and to reflect on historic structures lost during the preceding construction season.
In the White River Valley, residents don’t have to travel far to find examples of this engineering heritage. Tunbridge alone has five historic covered bridges: the Howe, Cilley, Mill, Flint and Larkin bridges. Nearby Chelsea has the Moxley Covered Bridge, while the Randolph area has three more: the Kingsbury, Gifford and Johnson bridges, the last also known as the Braley Bridge.

The Kingsbury covered bridge in South Randolph was featured in Alfred Hitchcock’s 1955 film “The Trouble With Harry.” Photo by Rose Curtis/Herald

Phill Gatenby, a member of the Vermont Covered Bridge Society, has visited and documented all 100 of Vermont’s covered bridges for his YouTube series, Vermont’s 100 Covered Bridges.
“There used to be 600 covered bridges at any one point in Vermont. Today we have 100,” Gatenby said.
Originally from Manchester, England, Gatenby developed his fascination with covered bridges after moving to Vermont and discovering structures unlike anything he had previously encountered.
His curiosity grew into an ambitious project to research and film the state’s covered bridges, documenting their histories, construction and surroundings. He began filming in September 2024 and completed the filming in June of this year. The episodes are being released weekly on YouTube.
“I’ve finished. I did them all. I’ve done all 100,” he said.
Gatenby’s work recently earned him the Vermont Covered Bridge Society’s Member of the Year award, presented at the organization’s fall meeting in Tunbridge.
The society was founded in 2001 following efforts to save the Cambridge covered bridge in Cambridge Junction. Its mission grew from that preservation effort into a broader commitment to protecting Vermont’s remaining covered bridges.

Spanning the White River, South Royalton’s present steel-and-granite bridge was built in 2002 at a crossing with more than 150 years of history. Earlier structures at this location included a wooden toll bridge constructed in 1848 and a Parker through truss bridge built in 1935. The crossing is recognized as a contributing feature of the South Royalton Historic District. Photo by Rose Curtis/Herald

But preserving these landmarks is not always straightforward.
JB McCarthy, a project manager in the Vermont Agency of Transportation’s structures section who chairs the agency’s covered bridge committee, said covered bridges occupy a special place in Vermont’s transportation history.
McCarthy said Vermont places a high priority on preserving its historic covered bridges, generally favoring rehabilitation over replacement while maintaining their original appearance and character.
Unlike modern bridges, many historic covered bridges were constructed for horse-drawn vehicles and much lighter traffic. Today’s heavier trucks, changing transportation needs and decades of exposure to the elements present significant challenges.
John Dumville, of South Royalton, Vermont’s retired historic-site operations chief and state historian, said a bridge’s historical importance goes beyond its age. Unusual designs, distinctive engineering and rare construction methods can make a bridge historically significant.

Just out of sight from Route 110, the Flint Bridge in Tunbridge sports a view to the First Branch below. Photo by Rose Curtis/Herald

He pointed to the importance of routine maintenance, including cleaning debris from bridge pockets each spring. Road salt, corrosion and deferred maintenance can gradually undermine historic structures, while increasing traffic and heavier vehicles add to the strain.
Gatenby identified another major danger. “It’s the weather, storms.”
He cited Vermont’s devastating 1927 flood and Tropical Storm Irene as examples of the destruction that severe weather can inflict on historic covered bridges.
Preservation sometimes requires compromises. Gatenby explained that steel I-beams have been installed beneath some wooden covered bridges to support their weight and prolong their useful lives.

Tunbridge’s historic Mill Bridge was rebuilt in the 1990s. Photo by Rose Curtis/Herald

McCarthy said the state generally prefers repairs using traditional materials and construction methods because steel supports can alter a bridge’s historic structural character. Such reinforcement may help save a bridge, but preservation specialists generally consider it a less desirable alternative to maintaining the original timber structure.
The choices become especially difficult when a historic bridge can no longer accommodate the needs of its community.
Preservation and practicality
In Stockbridge, the Gaysville steel truss bridge, constructed in 1929 after the 1927 flood, has been the subject of years of discussion involving the town, the Transportation Agency and historic preservation officials.
McCarthy said the bridge’s narrow, single-lane design and weight restrictions have made it unsuitable for some emergency vehicles, town maintenance equipment and logging operations. Although preservation officials sought to retain the structure, the town favored replacement.

The Gifford Bridge in East Randolph reflects in the Second Branch. Photo by Rose Curtis/Herald

After approximately five years of project development and discussions, the Transportation Agency moved forward with plans for a new bridge.
Other White River Valley communities face similar decisions, with different outcomes.
Dumville said the Foxstand Bridge is slated for replacement, while the Royalton village steel truss bridge has been rehabilitated. According to Transportation Agency project information, the Royalton bridge was built in 1928, has a 165-foot span and was previously rehabilitated in 2007.
Brookfield’s Floating Bridge offers another example of how a historic structure can survive through changes to its original components. Its pontoons have been replaced multiple times (most recently in 2015, when it was completely rebuilt), but Dumville said the bridge retains its historical identity through the preservation of its distinctive design concept.
Funding also plays an important role in determining which bridges survive.
McCarthy said the state has been working to direct preservation resources toward historic bridges before deterioration becomes too extensive.
McCarthy emphasized the importance of addressing deterioration early, explaining that once a historic bridge deteriorates beyond a certain point, rehabilitation may no longer be feasible, leaving replacement as the only practical option.
For communities, the cost of maintenance and rehabilitation must be weighed against the expense of replacement, as well as public safety and the demands of modern transportation.
Historic Bridge Awareness Month offers an opportunity to consider those choices before another construction season begins.
For residents of the White River Valley, the region’s covered bridges, steel trusses and unusual floating bridge are more than ways to cross rivers and streams. They are reminders of earlier generations’ engineering skills, the changing needs of Vermont communities and the ongoing work required to keep historic landmarks standing.

description: About 7,000 California families stand to lose subsidized housing under a Trump administration policy denying HUD assistance to households with mixed immigration status.
text:
In summary
About 7,000 California families stand to lose subsidized housing under a Trump administration policy denying HUD assistance to households with mixed immigration status.


California, along with 21 other states and Washington D.C., filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging a Trump administration rule that would bar tens of thousands of low-income households from receiving federal housing assistance, including more than 7,000 in California. 
Earlier this month the Trump administration finalized a rule to bar all households with “mixed” immigration status — meaning, those with some members who are citizens or legal residents and others who live in the country illegally — from receiving housing vouchers or living in public housing. 
The new rule would terminate aid for all of these households on Dec.14. The states’ lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts argues that the Trump administration overstepped its authority in overriding a congressional statute and asked the federal court to freeze the new rule from going into effect. 
Undocumented immigrants have been banned from receiving federal housing subsidies for decades. But starting during the Clinton administration, Congress has required the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to provide assistance in proportion to the share of members who have legal status. A family with two undocumented parents and two citizen children, for example, would receive half the eligible aid. 
“California won’t stand idly by while the Trump administration forces families to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta in a press conference announcing the suit.
In a written response, the HUD press office said the rule “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”
“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing,” the statement, attributed to Secretary Scott Turner, continued. “This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”
Since the Trump administration published the final version of the rule earlier this month, local public housing agencies have been racing to figure out how to comply while minimizing the eviction of residents and financial collateral damage for the agencies themselves. Some warn that many U.S. citizens and legal residents may struggle and ultimately fail to comply with the more stringent requirements to prove eligibility. They also warn that housing agencies will be squeezed financially as they evict lower-cost mixed status households and replace them with households entitled to full benefits.
Housing agencies and local governments across the country, including in Los Angeles, San Diego, San Francisco, Fresno, Santa Barbara and Santa Clara County, filed their own suit on Monday.

name: California
title: Miles de familias californianas con estatus migratorio mixto perderán sus viviendas bajo nueva norma del gobierno de Trump
description: Una nueva norma que prohíbe a las familias con estatus migratorio mixto acceder a viviendas financiadas con fondos federales afectará a California más que a ningún otro estado.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Las autoridades de vivienda de todo el estado están haciendo todo lo posible para evitar que sus clientes se queden sin hogar, mientras se preparan para una nueva norma de la administración Trump que podría retirar los subsidios federales a 7,000 hogares de California.
A partir del próximo mes, el Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano de Estados Unidos (HUD, por sus siglas en inglés) planea prohibir el acceso a viviendas financiadas con fondos federales a todas las familias con estatus migratorio mixto. Se prevé que esta medida afecte a California, con su numerosa población inmigrante, más que a ningún otro estado.
 “Esto es algo muy importante”, dijo Sanford Riggs, director de operaciones de la Autoridad de Vivienda del Condado de Santa Bárbara. “Es un cambio enorme”.
 Las agencias que administran los subsidios de vivienda están intentando elaborar planes de emergencia para las familias con estatus migratorio mixto, procurando transferirlas de programas financiados por el gobierno federal a programas financiados con fondos municipales, del condado, estatales o de donaciones filantrópicas. Sin embargo, el éxito de este esfuerzo variará considerablemente de un condado a otro, dependiendo de los recursos disponibles en cada uno.
 La administración Trump ha presentado esto como una forma de retirar los subsidios a los inmigrantes indocumentados y dárselos a veteranos sin hogar y ciudadanos discapacitados o ancianos. “El presidente Trump advirtió que se acabarían los días en que los inmigrantes ilegales y los no ciudadanos que no cumplían los requisitos se aprovechaban de los programas de asistencia social financiados por el gobierno”, dijo el secretario de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano, Scott Turner, en un comunicado.
 Pero este cambio podría perjudicar incluso a los ciudadanos estadounidenses que no viven en hogares con estatus migratorio mixto. Esto se debe a que, en algunos condados, por un tecnicismo, los vales que quedan libres cuando las familias con estatus migratorio mixto se marchan por cualquier motivo desaparecen por completo en lugar de reasignarse a otros solicitantes.
 Otros condados afirman que podrán atender a menos personas en general porque las familias con estatus migratorio mixto pagan más alquiler y reciben un subsidio menor que los ciudadanos estadounidenses. Si el Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano (HUD) las obliga a marcharse y las reemplaza con familias ciudadanas, habrá menos fondos disponibles y menos familias podrán acceder a una vivienda. 
 ¿Cómo cambia las cosas la nueva normativa del HUD?
 Los fondos federales para vivienda siempre se han reservado únicamente para ciudadanos estadounidenses o personas con un estatus migratorio que cumpla con los requisitos, como la residencia permanente (tarjeta verde). Sin embargo, históricamente, las familias con estatus mixto podían recibir ayuda proporcional; es decir, una familia de cuatro personas con dos ciudadanos que cumplen con los requisitos y dos inmigrantes indocumentados recibía la misma ayuda que una familia de dos.
 Según la nueva normativa, que entrará en vigor el 14 de diciembre, esas familias no recibirían nada. Los ciudadanos estadounidenses que vivan con familiares indocumentados tendrían que separarse de ellos o perder también su vivienda.
Un análisis de datos de 2024 realizado por el Centro de Prioridades Presupuestarias y Políticas reveló que 7,190 hogares con estatus migratorio mixto recibían ayuda federal para la vivienda en California. El único otro estado que se acerca a esta cifra es Texas, con 4,500.
 El Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano (HUD) propuso este cambio normativo una vez más durante el primer mandato del presidente Donald Trump en 2019, pero lo revocó tras la indignación pública. En esta ocasión, ya se han presentado demandas para impedir que la norma entre en vigor, incluida una interpuesta por un grupo de familias y defensores de los derechos de los inquilinos con sede en Los Ángeles.
 La Autoridad de Vivienda del Condado de Santa Clara cuenta con 157 hogares con estatus migratorio mixto en su programa, incluyendo 290 niños, quienes se verán afectados por la nueva normativa. En muchos casos, los niños son los únicos miembros de la familia que cumplen los requisitos para recibir ayuda federal, por lo que no existe la opción de que la familia se separe para que los miembros elegibles puedan conservar su vivienda, explicó Angie Garcia-Nguyen, subdirectora ejecutiva de la autoridad de vivienda del condado.
 El condado previó este cambio y se preparó para el recorte de fondos. La comunidad cuenta con un plan de contingencia para ayudar a las familias en riesgo de desplazamiento, explicó García-Nguyen. No quiso revelar la cantidad de dinero recaudado ni su procedencia para evitar generar sospechas. Sin embargo, señaló que cualquier ayuda no federal que puedan brindar es solo temporal, lo que significa que esas familias aún necesitan un plan a largo plazo.
 “Creo que las familias van a tener que tomar decisiones muy difíciles”, dijo García-Nguyen. “El condado de Santa Clara no es el lugar más asequible para vivir sin un subsidio. Algunos hogares tendrán que decidir si se quedan o no”.
 Una vez que la norma entre en vigor, podrían pasar más de un año antes de que se produzcan los desalojos. Las autoridades de vivienda tienen la opción de conceder prórrogas de hasta 18 meses. 
Se solicita a las personas mayores que verifiquen su estatus migratorio
 En el condado de Santa Clara, el efecto dominó de la nueva norma podría extenderse incluso más allá de las 157 familias con estatus migratorio mixto.
El Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano (HUD) también exigirá a algunas personas que antes estaban exentas que presenten documentación que acredite su ciudadanía o estatus migratorio. La autoridad de vivienda está ayudando a 12,000 adultos mayores y casi 9,000 niños que no han verificado su estatus migratorio. Ahora, estas personas deberán hacerlo o perderán sus subsidios de vivienda. No está claro cuántos de ellos podrán hacerlo, dijo García-Nguyen.
 En el condado de Santa Bárbara, Riggs dijo que no tiene conocimiento de ningún fondo municipal, del condado o estatal que pueda ayudar a las 131 familias con estatus migratorio mixto que reciben subsidios federales a través de su agencia.
 “Es muy posible que algunos acaben sin hogar ”, dijo. “No cabe duda”.
 Según Riggs, muchos de los vales que quedan libres cuando las familias con estatus migratorio mixto se mudan no se volverán a emitir a ciudadanos estadounidenses, ni a nadie más. El costo de la vivienda en el condado de Santa Bárbara, por ejemplo, es tan elevado que el Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano (HUD) proporciona fondos adicionales, además de los vales de vivienda habituales, para cubrir el alquiler. Pero hay una condición. A cambio, una vez que alguien renuncia a un vale (ya sea por fallecimiento, desalojo u otro motivo), el HUD no permite que la autoridad de vivienda lo vuelva a emitir a otra persona.
 La Autoridad de Vivienda de la Ciudad de Los Ángeles presta servicios a 1709 familias con estatus migratorio mixto que se verían afectadas por la nueva normativa. Estas familias pagan más de su propio bolsillo y reciben subsidios menores que los hogares donde todos sus miembros tienen un estatus migratorio que les permite acceder a ayudas.
 La autoridad de vivienda afirmó que eliminar a todas las familias con estatus migratorio mixto del programa la obligaría a recortar al menos 800 vales de vivienda de la Sección 8 para cubrir el aumento de los costos, lo que significa que 800 familias menos se beneficiarían.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont students give thanks—and give back
description:
Five Vermont students are thankful for the teachers who believed in them and the communities that cheered them on. This Thanksgiving, Sam, Nettie, Soren, Mya, and Parker share their gratitude and their goals, from classrooms to forests, and from the open road to the sky above.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont students give thanks—and give back.
text:
This Thanksgiving, we give thanks to the students who share their stories—and their journeys—with us. Thanks to the support of their families, employers, and college and career mentors, they are on their way to giving back in a big way. The experiences of Sam, Nettie, Soren, Mya, and Parker remind us how powerful encouragement from teachers, families, and communities can be.
Sam Lucci of Fair Haven was able to go back to college thanks to Freedom & Unity 
Sam Lucci has known for the last ten years that he wanted to finish his education but felt like he couldn’t commit until he made a plan to pay for it. In the meantime, he held off and entered the workforce. When he learned about Freedom & Unity from Martha McCaughin, an outreach counselor with VSAC’s Educational Opportunity Center, Sam was excited. “It was as easy to get Freedom & Unity as I was promised,” he said.
Freedom & Unity is funded by the Vermont Legislature and administered by VSAC, in partnership with Vermont State. Open to new or returning students of any age who do not already have a bachelor’s degree, Freedom & Unity is an opportunity for Vermont students with a family income of $85,000 or less to attend Vermont State tuition free.
In addition to taking classes full-time, Sam is on the Fair Haven selectboard. He says that serving and engaging on a local level really appeals to him, combining his interests in local government, civic engagement, and political science.
“There might be a point where I have to weigh the cost of college against everything else,” Sam said. “But as long as there is Freedom & Unity, I can plan my life and my next semester and a path to my degree.”
A senior at Oxbow High School, Nettie Morse is applying to college to be able to give back as an OT  
Aneta “Nettie” Morse is a senior at Oxbow High School in Bradford. She’s a three-season athlete and one of the founding members of VSAC GEAR UP Leads, the first-ever student-led leadership club in VSAC’s GEAR UP, a federally funded program that helps students access college and careers after high school.
Nettie herself has benefited from VSAC’s GEAR UP program. She’s working with her VSAC GEAR UP outreach counselor, Kassidy Moore, on her college applications and financial aid paperwork.
Nettie is grateful for Kassidy’s help. “Kassidy just knows everything,” Nettie laughed. “When I first started working with her, I was really not sure where I wanted to go. I knew I wanted to do pediatric occupational therapy (OT), but I didn’t have a sense of where I wanted to go to school. At that point, all I knew was that I needed financial aid to get there.”
She added, “I saw a collage of photos of someone playing with kids on mats, blocks, swings, and what the OT was doing with the kids working on sensory and motion and skills. I kept going, diving deeper and looking more and it was just so cool to me.” Nettie shared that she would be “honored and really excited and grateful to have that opportunity and to play that role in someone’s life.”
Soren Stelma-Leonard of Westfield is thankful for being able to go to school while staying connected to the outdoors 
Soren Stelma-Leonard aspires to a career as a game warden. For him, it’s about spending as much time as possible outside in the woods, an experience he’s always found peaceful and grounding.
To meet the requirements of the game warden job, Soren will need, at a minimum, an associate degree in environmental studies, or a bachelor’s degree in a related field. He started working with his VSAC GEAR UP counselor, Amanda Frattaroli, in his junior year at Craftsbury Academy. Soren applied to a few colleges in Vermont and in neighboring states and ultimately landed on the University of Vermont (UVM). 
“Financial aid was a huge factor in my decision,” he noted. Soren was especially excited to learn about the UVM Promise, which covers in-state tuition after scholarships and grants for income-eligible students. A VSAC GEAR UP scholarship is helping as well.
Soren is confident that he’s made a solid choice. He’s finishing his first semester at college now and is excited for the opportunity to stay connected to so many of his passions: spending time in the woods, hunting, sugaring, and his home community.
Mya Adams of Hardwick is grateful for mentors who sparked her desire to be a professional pilot
A chance conversation between her mom and a coworker led Mya Adams to Habitat for Aviation. It’s a Vermont nonprofit, founded and directed by Beth White, that provides people with the opportunity to fix, build, and fly planes. Mya felt at home there from her very first day. It’s been three years since she started, and Habitat—and airplanes—take up almost every moment of her life.
Mya’s VSAC counselor, Michelle Legere, also helped. Michelle is an outreach counselor in VSAC’s Talent Search, a program that helps students explore career and postsecondary education options and enroll in education programs after high school. Michelle helped Mya keep on top of the many deadlines for financial aid. “She was so available and responsive,” Mya added. “I’m really grateful for that.”
Mya is so passionate that she applied to exactly one school when it came time for her to go to college: Vermont State University. Vermont State has a professional pilot program, and Mya knew she wanted to go. “Having a college that offers that program this close to home is a dream,” she shared. “Why wouldn’t I go?!” 
Parker Hoblin of Colchester earned his Commercial Driver’s License, enabling him to open opportunities and change careers
A few years ago, Parker Hoblin saw a chance to open up a new career path by getting his Commercial Driver’s License (CDL) at Stafford Technical Center in West Rutland.
Working with VSAC outreach counselor Martha McCaughin of VSAC’s Educational Opportunity Center, Parker was ultimately awarded money to cover tuition at Stafford through VSAC’s Vermont Trades Tuition Benefit Program. “The financial aid from VSAC was what made it so I could take the class and get my Class A CDL,” he said.
It was a tough few months. The class started in the dead of winter on Saturdays, and required Parker to leave home before sunrise and return after sunset. “I’d be there all day on Saturday, leaving at 5 AM to drive the two hours to Rutland, where I’d be in class until 4:30 PM, and then would need to drive the two hours home,” he said. Luckily, it was only four months, and he had his Class A CDL by April. 
Parker now works as a driver for Lamell Lumber and welcomed a son with his wife, Claire, earlier this year. When he reflects on his career trajectory, he expresses gratitude for the opportunities he’s had that led him to where he is today. And he’s grateful for Martha. “Bless her, what a wonderful person,” he said. 
Each of these students is an inspiration. If you or someone you know is interested in pursuing a career, changing careers, or sharpening their job skills, reach out to VSAC at vsac.org/contact. From all of us at VSAC, Happy Thanksgiving!

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. Our grant, scholarship, and workforce development programs create opportunity, help students re-skill or learn new skills, and grow the economy. VSAC’s loan, loan refinance, and loan forgiveness programs provide competitive education financing to students and families. Find us at www.vsac.org or visit Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn.
