name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Union Pacific says a merger would make shipping cheaper. Farmers, labor and shippers are skeptical.
description: More consolidation could be coming to the railroad industry as federal regulators enter the latest phase of reviewing a merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern.  If approved, Union Pacific would become the largest railroad in the country, and the first railroad to serve both coasts. The nation’s rail network is divided between the east […]
text:
Nate Lee, a rail worker with BNSF and the local chairman for the Brotherhood of Maintenance Way Employees, stands near the West Haymarket Pedestrian Bridge in Lincoln, Nebraska, on Nov. 7. His union and company are opposed to the merger. (Daniel Wheaton/ The Midwest Newsroom)More consolidation could be coming to the railroad industry as federal regulators enter the latest phase of reviewing a merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern. 
If approved, Union Pacific would become the largest railroad in the country, and the first railroad to serve both coasts. The nation’s rail network is divided between the east and west, with the Mississippi River as a rough border. Many Midwestern cities, including Chicago, Kansas City and St. Louis, serve as interchange points where goods move from one rail line to another. Despite promises from Union Pacific, workers fear job losses across the Midwest, where the two railroads meet. 
“If this goes through, they will be a mega-railroad,” said Clark Ballew, the communications director for the Brotherhood of Maintenance Way Employees. “Quite literally. Obviously the biggest and largest railroad that’s ever existed in the United States. Unforeseen to this point.” 
The merger is being reviewed by the federal Surface Transportation Board, which uses existing precedent on rail mergers to make its decisions. 
Public comments on the merger were due to the board on Nov. 18. 
Rows of freight cars fill a rail yard on Saturday, July 18, 2026, in North Platte, Nebraska. The city’s railroad roots date to 1866, when its first Union Pacific train arrived. (Brian Munoz/St. Louis Public Radio)
Opponents to the merger rebut Union Pacific’s claims that the merger will cut shipping costs, and have formed a unified front: The Stop The Rail Merger Coalition. The coalition includes labor unions, shippers, farmers and transportation groups. 
They worry that further consolidation, from six major railroads to five, could force the remaining railroads to seek mergers as well.
Skepticism over the merger’s approval increased this fall, after a video circulated of Union Pacific CEO Jim Vena threatening to raise rates for businesses that didn’t support the merger. 
“I’ll probably increase everybody’s rates that said they didn’t want a seamless railroad by 3 or 4% just to teach you a lesson,” Vena said during a March meeting of the Southwest Association of Rail Shippers. 
Union Pacific sought to keep the video private, but a federal judge ordered it released to the public in late October. The company released the video and provided additional context. 
“Let us be clear: Union Pacific does not retaliate against customers,” the post with the video states. “A customer’s position on the merger will not determine its rates or how we deliver service. Customers should participate freely and candidly in the Surface Transportation Board’s (STB) review. We also welcome direct dialogue with our customers. Their perspectives matter to us.” 
Regardless of what the board rules, this merger has the potential to cause inflation, opponents say, just after voters provided a national rebuke to the Trump administration’s economic policies. 
A Union Pacific branded engine travels the rails in an undated archive photo from Nebraska Public Media’s “Great Plains Rail Tales” show. (Tom Jurgens/Provided)
Railroaders worry about safety 
On a Saturday afternoon in November, dozens of train cars passed underneath the West Haymarket Pedestrian Bridge in Lincoln. Empty freight cars snaked west, likely headed toward Wyoming for a new load of coal, and a row of tanker cars rumbled east — possibly containing ethanol refined from Great Plains corn. 
Those tanker cars are a reminder of what the worst scenario is for a railroader: a train derailment. 
In 2023, a Norfolk Southern train carrying hazardous materials derailed near the town of East Palestine, Ohio. The cargo caught fire and sent a toxic cloud over the town, leading to evacuations. A lawsuit alleged the toxic fumes contributed to multiple deaths. That case has yet to be adjudicated. 
“Across the country, you have the potential for an East Palestine-type incident pretty much every single day,” said Nate Lee, a rail worker with BNSF and the local chairman for the Brotherhood of Maintenance Way Employees. “It’s up to us folks maintaining the railroads to make sure that that doesn’t happen. And unfortunately, we have our jobs cut out for us nowadays.” 
Lee, the BNSF rail worker, said he’s worried that a merger would reduce the total number of workers repairing rail lines, and investor pressure might mean job cuts to improve the bottom line.
“You can only run a person ragged for so long before it starts to wear on you,” Lee said. “And unfortunately, what happens when people get tired? People get worn out. Things that shouldn’t be missed may get missed.” 
A freight train travels through Lincoln, Nebraska, on Nov. 7. BNSF operates the majority of track near the city. (Daniel Wheaton/The Midwest Newsroom)
Union Pacific announced a “Jobs For Life” promise for union workers on both sides of the merger this spring. The International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers Union, which supports the merger, negotiated with the company on the agreement. Members of the Brotherhood of Maintenance Way Employees do not trust the agreement and cite the promise as a reason why they are opposed. 
Concerns about the relocation of managerial Union Pacific workers to Atlanta arose in the Nebraska Legislature last session, when a bill was passed, aimed at keeping high-paying jobs in the state through tax credits to large employers. 
If a merger goes through, Norfolk Southern employees would have to adapt to the safety standards of Union Pacific. While both railroads are required to follow standards from the Federal Railroad Administration, new safety operations generate an awkward period of adapting that might increase risk, Lee and several other BMWE union members said. 
Several rail tracks bisect Lincoln, Nebraska, on Nov. 7. Most trains carry coal from Wyoming or ethanol out of state. (Daniel Wheaton / Midwest Newsroom)
Lee said the work of maintaining the rails is unpredictable. October storms dropped nearly 8 inches of rain across southeast Nebraska, resulting in washouts in track in the region where Lee works. During those periods, Lee and his crew worked overtime to prevent derailments. 
Even in normal conditions, Lee’s team needs to weld rail lines back into place and level out ballast, the small rocks that support rail lines, to ensure the trains won’t overturn. 
Rail companies have been using longer trains in recent years, as a way to reduce labor costs and move more goods faster. These “super trains” put more stress on the rail infrastructure, and also can cut off road access when a stopped train closes a crossing. 
“So when you had a train that was half a mile long, and now you have trains that are a mile and a half, two miles long,” Lee said. “It takes a long time for that train to stop.” 
Local governments won’t have much say if rail causes more traffic problems across the country. Existing legal precedent says that only the federal government can regulate railroads, putting local leaders in a bind. 
“You’ll have a bunch of people at your meetings, and they will be angry and upset, and they will have valid reasons to be,” said Ballew of the BMWE. “And if you’re a politician, there isn’t much you can do to help.” 
Does consolidation mean inflation?
Union Pacific argues that the merger would allow for more cost-effective freight service by eliminating the transfers that occur when a load of freight moves from one service area to another. 
“The creation of America’s first single-service transcontinental railroad will eliminate time consuming rail interchanges that will improve service for shippers, reduce costs for consumers and strengthen the nation’s supply chain,” Union Pacific spokesperson Robynn Tysver said in an email. “A shift from road to rail will ease congestion, reduce taxpayer-funded road maintenance, cut emissions and deliver cargo faster and more reliably.” 
Union Pacific declined requests to make a spokesperson available, instead sharing the statement above and providing additional information on their site. A spokesperson deferred to Norfolk Southern to speak for the merging partners. 
A freight train travels through Lincoln, Nebraska, on Nov. 7. BNSF operates the majority of track near the city. (Daniel Wheaton/The Midwest Newsroom)
As an industry, railroads are sometimes considered natural monopolies because the cost of creating a rail network far exceeds the cost of adding a train. Natural monopolies come with a higher level of governmental regulation that monitors the company while still ensuring it’s profitable. 
“The typical things that happen as monopoly power rises in a market are increases in price or reductions in service or product quality,” Elena Prager, an assistant professor of economics at the Simon Business School at the University of Rochester, said. “In general, you’re looking at higher prices, lower quantities and worse quality.” 
Transportation consultant Bob Granatelli, who has been in the transportation business since the 1970s, said that businesses with few options, known as captive shippers, are the most at-risk of having to pay higher costs. 
“This is frightening for a captive shipper,” Granatelli said. “It will make captivity even stronger.” 
The American Chemistry Council joined the coalition against the merger because many of its members are captive to one rail shipper — especially in the petrochemical industry along the Gulf Coast. 
“That exposes them to higher rates, less responsive customer service,” Jeff Sloan, the senior director of regulatory affairs for the American Chemistry Council, said. “Essentially, if you’re not afraid of losing your customer, you treat your customer differently.” 
Chemical manufacturers and the businesses they serve are at a disadvantage because their commodities are often not shipped in intermodal shipping containers — the large, standardized steel or aluminum boxes commonly seen on the tracks. Instead, they require tanks or hopper cars. Those commodities can’t easily go from rail to road. 
It’s a similar problem for farmers.
“If a grain elevator can only ship on one railroad now, and they set the pricing, that’s going to affect all of the farmers that get grain to that elevator, and so now those farmers may have to eat more costs,” Ash Anderson, education director for BMWE, said. 
Union Pacific locomotives line the tracks on Saturday, July 18, 2026, in North Platte, Nebraska. The railroad began mainline operations through the city in 1867, following the arrival of its first train the year before. (Brian Munoz/St. Louis Public Radio)
It also could mean that different loads get prioritized by a new, larger railroad, and smaller rail lines may shut down or be absorbed by the dominant company. Union members said they fear this merger might be the first domino that ends in a consolidated market. 
“The trickle-down effect is very evident in this merger because we’re talking about a transcontinental merger and basically a duopoly,” Paul Bellows, the vice chairman of the Unified System Division at BMWE, said. “Every citizen in the United States is going to be affected, and possibly even, you know, people in Canada and Mexico.” 
Mike McClellan, the senior vice president and chief strategy officer of Norfolk Southern, downplayed the inflationary concerns, because the combined railroad would compete better with trucking. In their merger application, the rail companies argue their improved service will result in a decline of some 2.1 million truckloads on the road annually. 
“People use railroads because we’re cheap, right?” McClellan said. “Trucks will always present essentially the ceiling on what we can do with pricing.” 
The two companies are planning for a future where there are more autonomous trucks on the road, so they hope to keep rail viable for that future. 
In general, rail is a better proposition for longer haul trips, or with materials that are too large or too dangerous to be on the nation’s highways. McClellan said rail struggles compared to trucking in the area about 250 miles east and west of the Mississippi River. This is because a nearby transfer point means two trips: one short haul to the transfer point, and a theoretical longer haul to the destination. By removing a transfer from one railroad to another, he said, shippers might consider rail over trucks when shipping across the greater Midwest. 
“I will say that we are doing this to grow rail business, not to shrink it,” McClellan said. “You’re going to do it by improving your service and improving the competitiveness of rail.” 
A ruling to come 
The Surface Transportation Board will continue to hear comments from other federal agencies on the merger throughout the winter, with more hearings planned for the spring. 
While the board is independent and its members sworn in by the Senate, politics has played a role in this transaction. Three of the five-member board are Republicans and were sworn in by President Donald Trump; a fourth seat is held by a Democrat, and there is one vacancy created by the firing of Robert Primus. He was the only member to vote against the 2023 merger of Canadian Pacific and Kansas City Southern.
William C. Vantuono, editor-in-chief of Railway Age, said this merger attempt is motivated by investors who saw an opportunity following the reelection of Trump. 
“I think the investment community, [the] Wall Street community, got excited because: Oh, you know maybe there’s going to be some regulations scuttled,’” Vantuono said. “And this big transcontinental merger was announced last year.” 
In October 2025, just months after the announcement of the merger in July, Union Pacific donated $2.5 million for the construction of the White House ballroom. Vena, the CEO, publicly denied that the gift was meant to persuade Trump to back the merger. Still, Vena’s messaging has also garnered bipartisan attention from Congress, with Sens. Tammy Baldwin and Roger Marshall asking the board to scrutinize the plan. 
Vantuono is confident the Surface Transportation Board will follow existing precedent and won’t bend to political pressure. Both Vantuono and Granatelli said that the ruling will likely be decided on the extent a merger would affect competition in the market. 
“I know most of the Surface Transportation Board members personally,” Vantuono said. “They are the most ethical people you’d ever come across.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Federal investigators to probe plane crash that killed two healthcare workers
description: Dr. Derek Culnan, 48, died Saturday, November 21, 2026 along with Zachary Myrick (not pictured), 40, co-owner of Buckner Prosthetics and Orthotics following a plane crash in Jackson. In 2023, he was seen here offering remarks about the Mississippi Baptist Medical Center being designated as a Level III trauma and primary pediatric center and a Mississippi bur[...]
text:
The cause remains unknown of a plane crash that killed two healthcare workers in Jackson on Saturday.
Dr. Derek Culnan, 48, the medical director of the Mississippi Burn, Hand and Reconstruction Center in Jackson, and Madison-based Zachary Myrick, 40, co-owner of Buckner Prosthetics and Orthotics, died in the crash. The aircraft was a Cirrus SR22 and the incident took place at Hawkins Field Airport at 12:16 p.m. that day, according to the National Transportation Safety Board. 
An NTSB investigator is traveling to the accident site, agency spokesperson Peter Knudson told Mississippi Today Monday. Knudson said he expects a preliminary report to be made within 30 days of the accident, but the probable cause of the crash will likely be detailed in the final report, which he said he expects in 12-24 months.  
On Sunday, the Mississippi Burn, Hand & Reconstruction Center, a partnership of Baptist Medical Center, released a statement from Culnan’s wife. Genevieve Culnan testified to her husband’s legacy as a partner, father and surgeon who she says helped thousands of patients in Mississippi live better lives. 
“He showed up every day and gave his all to every case, every situation, every person,” she said. “Not enough can be said about how much this one man did to support our team, our patients, our community and our state. But not enough will ever be said about the love, patience and compassion he showed his family. He was an amazing father and husband.”
In 2023, Culnan led efforts to open Baptist Medical Center’s burn center. He worked to open the new facility following the 2022 closure of the state’s only burn center at Merit Health Central in Jackson.
Buckner Prosthetics and Orthotics also released a statement Sunday announcing the loss of Myrick, co-owner of the organization, on social media. 
“There are simply no words to express the devastation we feel,” the statement said. “Zach devoted himself to Buckner Prosthetics bringing passion and enthusiasm to everything he did. His impact on our profession, his patients and our team will never be forgotten. His legacy will live on in the many lives and communities he touched.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: US measles outbreak prompts bipartisan call for more wastewater testing
description: A bipartisan group of lawmakers in Congress are lining up behind legislation to strengthen wastewater disease monitoring in the United States. Their proposal comes days after the U.S lost its measles elimination status and amid growing criticism for the Trump administration’s public health policy decisions.
text:
Wastewater effluent in Hammond, Louisiana. Legislators from Louisiana and a cohort of other states are sponsoring legislation to support continued public health monitoring of wastewater to track diseases like COVID-19, flu and measles. (Photo by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)A bipartisan group of lawmakers in Congress are lining up behind legislation to strengthen wastewater disease monitoring in the United States. Their proposal comes days after the U.S lost its measles elimination status and amid growing criticism for the Trump administration’s public health policy decisions.
U.S. Reps. Troy Carter, D-New Orleans, Russely Fry, R-South Carolina, and Chrissy Houlahan, D-Pennsylvania, have collaborated to author the PREDICT Act. It calls for the federal government to continue and expand funding for wastewater testing to track the spread of measles and other diseases. A similar measure has emerged in the U.S. Senate with Democratic, Republican and independent co-authors. 
“With the expansion of this cost-effective technology, Congress and CDC can protect Americans’ health and stop the spread of deadly diseases like COVID-19, measles and more,” Carter said in a news release Friday.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention coordinates the National Wastewater Surveillance System to monitor measles and other highly contagious viral diseases such as avian influenza and monkeypox. Relying on state data, it also keeps tabs on common respiratory illnesses such as the seasonal flu, COVID-19 and RSV. The system provides a snapshot to health officials of how concentrated a disease is amongst a population without the need to navigate the logistics of human testing.
The CDC’s data comes from roughly 140 million citizens, representing less than half of the U.S. population.
“It can be a harbinger, or like a forewarning, of an outbreak,” said David Hamer, professor of global health at Boston University’s Center on Emerging Infectious Diseases. 
“It was during the COVID pandemic that we showed how useful it could be,” he added. 
Money from the American Rescue Plan Emergency Fund, related to tracking and managing COVID-19 in 2020, began CDC’s monitoring program, which then proved to be useful for other diseases. 
“Basically, the money is running out,” Hamer said. “We need long term funding to keep this going.”
The proposed PREDICT Act would direct the CDC to increase its monitoring programs and lab testing capabilities, and it seeks the creation of a central database of disease monitoring records for public health officials. It also would require the CDC to generate a national plan outlining how it will strengthen wastewater monitoring nationwide and maintain an early warning system capable of detecting emerging health threats.
The legislation was introduced just after news broke that the U.S. lost its status of effectively eliminating measles in the country. 
The Pan American Health Organization, which rescinded the United States’ measles eradication status last week, reports 58,213 confirmed cases globally and 82 deaths so far in 2026. As of Nov. 18, the CDC had logged 5,838 U.S. measles cases this year. 
The current epicenter for the U.S. measles outbreak is Pennsylvania, where public health officials have reported nearly 1,600 cases and eight deaths this year, more than any other state. Pennsylvania officials have clashed with the CDC, which has attributed only six deaths nationwide directly to the measles. Another Kennedy policy change ended the CDC’s longstanding practice of relying on state data to track the impact of measles spread.    
Hamer said wastewater monitoring is central to helping predict areas that a measles outbreak could arise, given widespread vaccine skepticism. 
“Measles is a disease you really need to maintain, like, 93 to 95% coverage (in a population), ideally with two doses, and we’ve just fallen well below that in many places,” he said. “Wastewater has become a really good tool for tracking, early identification of outbreaks and then tracking the progress of outbreaks.”
Before the measles vaccine was created in 1963, major epidemics occurred about every two to three years and caused an estimated 2.6 million deaths each year, according to the World Health Organization. The number was 95,000 in 2024, mostly among unvaccinated or under-vaccinated children younger than 5.
Increased calls for expanded public health measures are primed to take center stage once the next Congress, with its new Democratic majority in both chambers, convenes Jan. 3. 
Democratic lawmakers are expected to increase scrutiny of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and its secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Vaccine hesitancy, health misinformation and an overhaul of the CDC and much of the federal public health apparatus have marked his tenure. 
Though Kennedy has said he recommends the measles vaccine, a CDC advisory panel he handpicked has repeatedly gone against widely accepted medical practices and the science that supports them. Its proposed changes, which are being challenged in federal court, include ending the hepatitis B vaccine for newborns and removing the mercury-based preservative thimerasol from flu vaccines, despite widely debunked claims of it being harmful.
Last week, CDC scientists independently published a public health alert that said at least 112 pregnant women and 13 newborns in the U.S. have been diagnosed with the measles. The complications reported included maternal pneumonia, preterm delivery and neonatal complications. Their research found that 98% of the pregnant women with measles had not received the MMR vaccine or did not know their vaccine status.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Gould retiring from New Hampshire Supreme Court
description: Associate Justice Bryan Gould is retiring from the New Hampshire Supreme Court before the end of the year, the judicial branch announced Monday. A statement from the judicial branch said Gould is stepping down to deal with a family medical emergency and a medical condition of his own. Gould’s wife suffered a life-threatening aortic dissection […]
text:
New Hampshire Supreme Court Justice Bryan Gould listens to oral arguments between the state and attorneys for victims of the YDC abuse scandal on Oct. 14, 2026, in the Frank Roe Kenison Supreme Court Building in Concord. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Associate Justice Bryan Gould is retiring from the New Hampshire Supreme Court before the end of the year, the judicial branch announced Monday.
A statement from the judicial branch said Gould is stepping down to deal with a family medical emergency and a medical condition of his own. Gould’s wife suffered a life-threatening aortic dissection and rupture in May, it said. Gould himself has “a neurocardiogenic condition that is aggravated by stress.” He’s previously managed the condition with medication, but the stress of her hospitalizations, rehabilitation and care needs have exacerbated his own symptoms, the branch said.
Gould is the second state Supreme Court justice this year to step down. In September, Chief Justice Gordon MacDonald resigned amid an investigation by the judicial conduct committee and reporting from New Hampshire Public Radio, which revealed an unusual personnel move he orchestrated to allow an ally to collect nearly $50,000.
Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican, has not nominated anyone to replace MacDonald. All judicial nominees must be vetted and confirmed by the Executive Council before they can sit on the high court, per the state constitution. After November’s elections, which brought massive gains for Democrats, the Executive Council will move from a 4-1 Republican majority to a 5-0 Democratic council.
Several councilors-elect have said in interviews with the Bulletin that their first priority will be greater scrutiny of Ayotte’s judicial nominees. Democrat Karen Liot Hill, the only incumbent councilor returning next year, said on election night earlier this month that “there’s going to be an appetite for true accountability on the Supreme Court.” Luz Bay, a Democratic state representative just elected to the council, said the “baseline” for Supreme Court appointments will be that they have bench experience. Before being appointed last year, Gould was a lawyer with deep GOP ties but no judicial experience.
There are two remaining Executive Council meetings, on Dec. 2 and Dec. 16, before the new Democrats are sworn in. State law requires the council to give the public a seven-day notice before it conducts a hearing on judicial nominees. That means Ayotte could appoint new justices before the Democratic council takes power but the timeline would be tight. She would also need to get the current council, which despite being controlled by her own party has still clashed with her at times, on board. 
Gov. Kelly Ayotte speaks with reporters in her office Nov. 11, 2026. The Republican governor said she didn’t “have any set time frame” for nominating a new state Supreme Court justice. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Asked about MacDonald’s replacement earlier this month, Ayotte told reporters, “I don’t have any set time frame” for a nomination. She said her “standard is the same” despite the incoming Democratic council and that she’ll appoint someone when she finds a quality candidate with her judicial selection committee.
Ayotte released a statement Monday afternoon: “I want to thank Justice Gould for his service to our state. I wish him and his family the best and a speedy recovery.”
Gould will have served on the court less than two years before his retirement next month. Ayotte nominated him in August 2025 and the Executive Council confirmed him the next month. Gould turns 70, the mandatory retirement age, on Dec. 2, 2028.
The Frank Roe Kenison Supreme Court Building in Concord is shown here on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: AG Campbell sues feds over ICE courthouse arrests
description: “These aggressive actions in Massachusetts state courthouses are no accident,” Campbell's office wrote in its complaint. Federal agents “are intentionally disregarding state law and the sovereign interests of Massachusetts in regulating what happens inside its courthouses.”
text:
IT’S BEEN LESS than a month since a ban on warrantless civil arrests at Massachusetts courthouses took effect, and federal immigration agents have already detained 38 people on courthouse grounds. 
Amid public complaints that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement was blatantly violating the state’s courthouse arrest law, Attorney General Andrea Campbell sued Monday to protect what she says is the state’s constitutional right to limit immigration actions on its property. 
Arguing that an ICE directive to ignore state bans on courthouse arrests violates federal law and the Constitution, she wants a Boston federal judge to block the directive and declare that civil immigration arrests at state courts are prohibited unless state law permits them. 
“These aggressive actions in Massachusetts state courthouses are no accident,” her office wrote in its complaint. Federal agents “are intentionally disregarding state law and the sovereign interests of Massachusetts in regulating what happens inside its courthouses.” 
The PROTECT Act, signed into law on August 5, laid out an array of new rules for federal immigration agents. It immediately prohibited most civil arrests, including immigration arrests, without a judicial warrant or court order in “sensitive locations” including public K-12 schools, licensed child care centers, health care facilities, and state property.  
A provision restricting courthouse arrests took effect on November 3. 
Last year, immigration agents arrested 614 people on Massachusetts courthouse grounds, according to the Trial Court. 
But just hours after the new court restrictions kicked in early this month, agents detained a man in a Chelsea courthouse. Four other people were also arrested that day, according to the Trial Court, and dozens more were detained over the next two weeks in courthouses in Chelsea, Framingham, Marlborough, Peabody, and Medford. 
Courthouse arrests “damage our entire justice system by chilling access to courts,” wrote Lawyers for Civil Rights in a letter last week calling for action from Campbell’s office. “Faced with the risk of arrest and deportation, victims hesitate to report crimes, witnesses decline to testify, and families miss legal proceedings that decide their futures.” 
ICE officials did not immediately respond to request for comment, but have previously said that detaining people at courthouses is a “common-sense” move, because people there are already correctly identified and screened for weapons.  
In an October press release touting the arrest of a Dominican man, ICE lambasted the PROTECT Act. 
“Time and time again, sanctuary politicians in Massachusetts have made the dumbfounding choice to prioritize dangerous criminal illegal aliens rather than their law-abiding American citizens,” said acting ICE Boston Field Office Director Joseph Sher.  
The PROTECT Act created a right for people to sue ICE agents in state court alleging violations of their rights under the US Constitution. It also allowed the attorney general to sue if federal agents interfere with voting or arrest anyone in protected locations without a judicial warrant.    
Campbell argues the Bay State arrests violate Massachusetts’s sovereign authority. She filed her lawsuit under the Administrative Procedures Act and is also arguing a violation of the 10th Amendment.   
Immigration officers are making their arrests under a directive issued in May 2025 that said courthouse arrests “are often required when jurisdictions refuse to cooperate with ICE, including when such jurisdictions refuse to honor immigration detainers.” 
The directive was vacated by a California federal judge in June, in a decision the administration has appealed. 
The courthouse arrest suit drops Massachusetts into an ongoing legal quagmire about state and federal supremacy. 
Federal courts in Connecticut, California, New York, and Pennsylvania have blocked state laws that required ICE agents to identify themselves and barred them from wearing masks while making arrests. The Connecticut law also allowed the state to investigate and prosecute federal immigration actions it believes involve excessive force. 
The Supremacy Clause of the US Constitution prohibits states from “interfering with or controlling the operations of the Federal Government,” wrote US District Judge Vernon Oliver in his ruling on the Connecticut case, “and federal officers are immune from state prosecution when acting within the scope of their federal authority.” 
Before Donald Trump’s first presidency, for years federal immigration agencies had restricted immigration activities around sensitive locations like schools, courts, and places of worship. After the Trump administration rolled back that guidance last year, Massachusetts lawmakers moved to enshrine those restrictions in state law. 
Sen. Cindy Friedman, a Democrat who was one of the lead negotiators of the PROTECT Act, said Monday that lawmakers are confident they are “on really solid constitutional grounds” after deploying “an enormous amount of energy, resources and research” to craft it. 
“Everything that we put in the PROTECT Act, we felt like we were walking right up to the constitutional line of what we were well within our rights as a state to do,” added Rep. Andy Vargas, another member of the bill-negotiating team and chair of the Legislature’s Black and Latino Legislative Caucus. 
He contrasted the Massachusetts law with measures in other states that aimed to place new restrictions on how ICE agents do their jobs, including bans on wearing masks. 
Asked if he had expected ICE to ignore the law, Vargas replied, “No, by no means.”  
While the state is generally barred from interfering with immigration enforcement, a task reserved for the federal government, Campbell’s office said immigration agents are not acting within a purely federal capacity. 
Rather, the office wrote, ICE is “commandeering state personnel and resources by using the infrastructure of state government to enforce federal immigration law. Specifically, they are relying on state-generated information, state infrastructure, state law enforcement, and state security systems to identify, locate, disarm, and contain federal targets.” 
The relationship between ICE, courthouses, and law enforcement is already under active consideration at the state’s highest court. 
Supreme Judicial Court justices are considering a bundle of cases revolving around the power of state courts to demand the return of criminal defendants who are whisked away by immigration enforcement during the trial.  
Campbell referenced such disruptions on Monday. 
“That individual could spend months in ICE custody, only to be released if ICE cannot establish a legal basis for deportation,” she said. “Meanwhile, the criminal charges remain unresolved. The defendant has not been held accountable to our justice system, or provided an opportunity to mount the defense, and the victim has been denied the opportunity for justice. How does that make anyone safer?” 
Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan — who back in 2019, along with then-Suffolk District Attorney Rachael Rollins, unsuccessfully challenged ICE’s patrolling of courthouses for immigrants to detain — said this state suit was on much firmer footing. 
While that suit aimed to protect the courts’ ability to create and enforce their own policies around how to handle immigration arrests at their courthouses, she said, this complaint is defending state law on state infrastructure. 
In an interview, Ryan described ICE arrests during prosecutions as deeply disruptive. Not only does the state’s plan to prosecute get interrupted, she said, but defendants disappearing and sometimes reentering the country without notice makes it difficult for victims to make safety plans. 
Under President Trump, Ryan said, “the communication has been nonexistent. I’ve been a prosecutor for a long time. We’ve always dealt with ICE. They’ve always brought people back and forth. We were able to figure that out. Now we just have no idea.” 
The SJC heard arguments on three ICE cases in early October and is now weighing whether state courts are empowered to order defendants be returned to Massachusetts, whether they must try to secure their return, and whether prosecutors should have to inform the court if they are aware ICE may be eyeing a defendant for removal. It’s expected to rule early next year. 
Campbell’s courthouse arrest suit introduces another legal dispute over state versus federal supremacy. 
“This is really a new area of the law, because we haven’t faced a federal administration that’s tried to step into the states and take away their authority before,” said Carol Rose, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union of Massachusetts. “So all of this is cutting-edge law.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC food pantries see a surge in demand as inflation, federal cuts hit household budgets
description: As Thanksgiving preparations get underway, more people are turning to food pantries to help meet daily needs, not just to provide the basics for holiday meals.  The more than 700 food pantries, meal delivery programs and other food distribution sites supplied by the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina have seen numbers of […]
text:
Volunteers at the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina sort food ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday on Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)As Thanksgiving preparations get underway, more people are turning to food pantries to help meet daily needs, not just to provide the basics for holiday meals. 
The more than 700 food pantries, meal delivery programs and other food distribution sites supplied by the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina have seen numbers of people seeking food assistance jump anywhere from 20% to 60% in the last year, said Jason Kanawati Stephany, vice president for communications and public policy at the Food Bank. 
“We haven’t seen numbers like this since at least the Great Recession,” he said. “There are more people facing food insecurity today than at the peak of the pandemic.”
Inflation is a factor in the increased demand, he said. Even people working more than one job have trouble affording enough food after they pay their rent, buy gasoline and purchase other necessities. 
People are working,” he said. “It’s just the math that doesn’t work anymore.”
Jason Kanawati Stephany of the Central and Eastern North Carolina Food Bank and U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross, D-Wake County, talk about the increased demand for food assistance at a Nov. 23, 2026 news conference. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)
Cuts to SNAP, the federal food assistance program are also a factor.
Last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act expanded work requirements for SNAP recipients and made some non-citizens ineligible. For example, people admitted to the United States for humanitarian reasons and victims of trafficking are no longer eligible for SNAP.
The law also requires North Carolina counties to pay for a bigger share of administrative costs. And starting next October, states will shoulder part of the cost of SNAP benefits, based on their error rates.
The number of North Carolina households enrolled in SNAP declined 7.7% between August 2025 and August 2026, according to the latest information from the  U.S. Department of Agriculture.
“Children, seniors, our veterans – they are all going without,”  U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross, D-Wake County, said at a news conference at the food bank in Raleigh. 
“‘These cuts can be reversed by Congress,” she said. “That is the important thing to know.”
Reversing the SNAP cuts is “absolutely on the agenda,” with Democrats controlling Congress starting next year, Ross said during a brief interview. “Speaker-to-be (Hakeem) Jeffries has already said that’s a priority.”
In addition to the SNAP cuts that hit households, food banks have also had to adjust to federal funding cuts. 
In early 2025, the USDA eliminated a program that reimbursed organizations for buying food from local farmers. 
As federal support has ebbed, demand has increased, Kanawati Stephany said.
NC counties now paying more to help feed hungry people

“It has been by the grace of our community and the generosity of the community that we’ve been able to fill that void, but that is not sustainable.”
However, charitable organizations cannot fill the federal government’s role in addressing food insecurity, he said. 
Every donation to the food bank through the end of this year will be matched, so every dollar donated will equal six meals, Kanawati Stephany said. People who need food can search for a food pantry at foodbankcenc.org.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: ​Complaint over AI-generated Colorado political video dismissed
description: A hearing officer in the Colorado secretary of state’s office last week dismissed a complaint over a video that state Sen. Cathy Kipp alleged violated the state’s law against unlabeled “deepfake” political content. Hearing officer Macon Cowles determined that the video is parody and satire, and therefore not covered by a 2024 law that requires […]
text:
Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Fort Collins Democrat, speaks on the Colorado Senate floor in April. (Screenshot from Colorado Channel YouTube)A hearing officer in the Colorado secretary of state’s office last week dismissed a complaint over a video that state Sen. Cathy Kipp alleged violated the state’s law against unlabeled “deepfake” political content.
Hearing officer Macon Cowles determined that the video is parody and satire, and therefore not covered by a 2024 law that requires a disclosure when a video uses generative artificial intelligence to depict a political candidate close to an election.
“No reasonable viewer would suppose that the sponsor of Proposition NN agreed to play a cashier who keeps a customer’s money in an advertisement urging a vote against the measure,” Cowles wrote in the Nov. 19 decision.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The video in question is from the right-leaning Independence Institute and criticized Proposition NN ahead of the Nov. 3 election. The proposition was a measure referred to the ballot by the Legislature and sponsored by Kipp. It passed with over 57% of the vote. It allows the state to retain more taxpayer revenue for public education. The video is AI-generated and shows Kipp as a grocery store cashier refusing to give a customer their change, a situation analogous to what the Independence Institute thought Proposition NN would do. The video has a closing line saying it was AI-generated, but it is not the text required by the state law.
Cowles wrote that the law applies to content that “falsely appears to be authentic and truthful.” But satire and parody falls outside of that, he wrote, because reasonable viewers wouldn’t believe it actually happened. Satire and parody are protected by the First Amendment.
The Independence Institute “concedes that what is portrayed in the video is not true: Sen. Kipp does not work in a grocery store and did not steal a customer’s grocery change in order to give it to children for their education,” Cowles wrote. “But it asserts that no one seeing the video would reasonably consider these things to be true.”
As a public figure, Kipp’s exposure to criticism such as the video, even though it is AI, is akin to a political cartoon in a newspaper, Cowles wrote.
“We’re grateful the hearing officer saw what every voter who watched it saw: a joke with a point,” Independence Institute CEO Jon Caldara said in a statement. “Nobody believed Sen. Kipp moonlights at a checkout counter. The point was that Prop NN keeps money that belongs to taxpayers, and voters deserved to hear that argument in a way that would actually stick.”
Kipp did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Cowles’ decision is subject to review by the deputy secretary of state before it becomes final.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: A mayor, a 19-year-old and a ‘Bachelorette’ alum: Beacon Hill’s incoming class
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: When the House and Senate gavel into the first sessions of the 195th General Court on Jan. 6, there will be at least 21 lawmakers new to their chambers, about a tenth of the 200-person legislative roster.
text:
MEET THE INCOMING CLASS of 2027.
When the House and Senate gavel into the first sessions of the 195th General Court on January 6, there will be at least 21 lawmakers new to their chambers, about a tenth of the 200-person legislative roster. 
Every freshman but one is a Democrat. While a handful cruised through the general election without challenge, at least four flipped seats in some tight races on November 3 by ousting Republican incumbents and turning the seats of two longtime, outgoing Republicans blue – including the House minority leader’s seat, which has been red for three decades. A South Coast seat held by a Democrat flipped red, in what was the MassGOP’s lone pickup.
New faces trudging up the hill come January include the Legislature’s new youngest member – a 19-year-old from Billerica – two 23-year-olds, a “Bachelorette” contestant and HGTV host, two Somerville city councilors, and the sitting mayor of Gardner. The classmates’ priorities mirrored each other in many ways, regardless of where they hail from. Addressing affordability, increasing government transparency, bringing in local aid, and easing the housing crisis were among their most promoted campaign issues. 
The 2nd Plymouth House race remains uncalled between Republican Rep. John Gaskey and Democratic challenger Sarah Hewins. Recounts were scheduled for Wareham on Friday, November 20, and in Carver on Monday, November 23. If Hewins, who was ahead of Gaskey by a small margin based on preliminary counts, beats Gaskey, she will be the 22nd newcomer in January and shrink the House’s minority caucus by another member.
Take a look at the three new senators-elect and 18 confirmed representatives-elect:
SENATE
Kate Lipper-Garabedian (D), Melrose
A former public school teacher, judicial clerk, legal counsel for the state’s education secretariat, and at-large Melrose city councilor, Lipper-Garabedian is one of two representatives moving down the hall. She has been in the House since winning a 2020 special election and will now fill outgoing Sen. Jason Lewis’s Fifth Middlesex seat in the Senate after cruising to election without challenge.
Erika Uyterhoeven (D), Somerville 
In a hard-fought primary against a fellow Somerville state rep, Uyterhoeven’s progressive agenda won over voters in retiring Sen. Pat Jehlen’s Second Middlesex District. A three-term lawmaker and self-described “antitrust economist,” she’ll be moving down the hall with a perspective that was not always highlighted in the House – Uyterhoeven has taken votes against House leadership and ran a campaign that included addressing issues with Beacon Hill’s transparency.
Persis Yu (D), Hyde Park 
The Hyde Park social worker and attorney beat Sen. Mike Rush in the Democratic primary in September for his Norfolk and Suffolk seat, and faced no challenger in the general election with a campaign based on a Massachusetts “where families – not corporations or billionaires – come first.” Yu, the daughter of an immigrant who fled fascism, went to college in Washington state, spent a decade at the National Consumer Law Center, and has worked five years at a nonprofit that aims to protect people from predatory lenders.
HOUSE
Lorena Betts (D), Chelmsford 
Betts says “Beacon Hill is broken” and “disconnected from the real struggles families face every day” and told voters she’s not a career politician. An interpreter, civic educator, and community organizer, she will take over former Rep. Rodney Elliott’s 16th Middlesex seat, returning to the State House where she used to work as a legislative aide and where she now plans to promote affordable housing, accessible care, and clean energy.
Daniel Darris-O’Connor (D), Billerica
The 19-year-old Billerica Select Board member defeated 16-year incumbent Republican Rep. Marc Lombardo for his 22nd Middlesex House seat with a campaign focused on his town government record and on the fact that “Billerica deserves a rep who shows up and gets things done.” Now a college student at the University of Massachusetts Lowell, Darris-O’Connor was also a student representative to the Billerica School Committee while in high school. He’ll be the youngest lawmaker on Beacon Hill in January, and one of the youngest in the state’s history.
John Drinkwater (D), Lowell
The former Lowell city councilor has lived his entire life in Tewksbury and Lowell and spent almost 17 years working at the Massachusetts AFL-CIO, five of them as the federation’s legislative director. Drinkwater has since worked as director of governmental affairs for the Union of Painters & Allied Trades District Council 35 and will assume the 17th Middlesex seat that now-Sen. Vanna Howard left vacant. He campaigned on helping working families and on his background as the son of a public school teacher and a pipefitter. Drinkwater first ran for state office in 2018, when he finished second in the primary for the First Middlesex Senate District to the late Sen. Ed Kennedy.
Ben Ewen-Campen (D), Somerville
The Harvard Medical School biologist whose research has taken him from studying birds in Alaska to beetles in Montana has spent almost nine years as Somerville Ward 3 city councilor. Ewen-Campen told 27th Middlesex voters – whose current representative, Uyterhoeven, is heading to the Senate – that he’ll fight on Beacon Hill to stabilize rents, for workers’ rights and green jobs, and against invasive surveillance technologies, pointing to his work on the city council passing progressive policies. 
Krista Ferrante (D), Princeton
Ferrante beat out her Republican opponent to flip the First Worcester District seat that’s been held by outgoing Republican Rep. Kim Ferguson of Holden for 16 years. A corporate archivist who has been working in tech as a records manager and data governance lead for over 12 years, she campaigned on regulating AI and protecting data privacy, supporting local agriculture, and improving government transparency. 
Chris Lambton (D), Dennis
The “Bachelorette” contestant, HGTV home and landscaping show personality, and former New York City public high school teacher and coach will assume outgoing Rep. Chris Flanagan’s First Barnstable seat. The longtime Dennis resident ran a campaign with priorities like affordable housing, the blue economy, and mental health awareness and assistance. He has also been chair of the Dennis Select Board and operated his family’s landscaping business and an oyster farm.
Lisa Lopez (D), Canton
Lopez told voters that she is “Retired. Ready. All in.” The Canton Select Board member has retired from her work at a medical device company. In the years since President Donald Trump’s first election, she has worked as a pro bono immigration attorney. She has sat on the town’s community preservation committee and is Canton Housing Authority chair. Housing, health care, and education are among her priorities alongside climate and clean energy, which she’ll push in outgoing Rep. William Galvin’s Sixth Norfolk seat.
Joe Markey (D), Lynnfield
Markey is a civil service commissioner, workers’ compensation attorney, former chair of the Lynnfield Housing Authority and six-term Lynnfield town moderator. He flipped outgoing House Minority Leader Brad Jones’s 20th Middlesex seat, beating out his Republican opponent in a district that has been red for three decades. Markey’s campaign focused on affordability, housing, local aid, and government transparency. 
Will Mbah (D), Somerville
The Cameroon native who studied in Sweden and then received a visa to work in the US is moving from his four terms on the Somerville City Council to outgoing Rep. Christine Barber’s 34th Middlesex seat. After working in city government for so long, he told voters that he “has seen just how many progressive policies require state-level approval to implement at the local level.” His campaign issues included immigrant rights, equitable public safety, and worker protections. 
Leila Migliorelli (D), Melrose
Migliorelli was a Melrose city councilor for six years and has spent two decades working in donor relations at Tufts University. She also created the Melrose Housing Trust and focused her campaign on affordability, expanding health care access and strengthening public schools in the 32nd Middlesex District, which Lipper-Garabedian vacated for her successful Senate bid.
Connor Murray (D), Andover 
The 23-year-old has advocated to reduce gun violence, lobbied for climate issues, and worked as an intern for now-Sen. Vanna Howard and as a field director for Rep. Tara Hong’s successful 2024 campaign. Murray will fill the open 18th Essex seat left by outgoing Rep. Tram Nguyen. He spent time at a DC think tank, graduated from college in New York in 2025, worked as a freelance actor and political consultant, and wants to “make sure that people who grow up here can afford to stay, build their lives, and succeed in the communities they love.”
Mike Nicholson (D), Gardner 
In his second term as mayor of Gardner, the city’s first Hispanic/Latin American elected official is heading to Beacon Hill – but not for the first time. Earlier in his career, Nicholson was a legislative intern for then-Sen. Jennifer Flanagan and outgoing Rep. Jonathan Zlotnik (whose Second Worcester seat he’s filling). Nicholson’s list of local government roles ranges from Rutland town administrator to mayoral aide, and the former UMass Minuteman Marching Band trumpet player and drum major’s priorities include economic development, housing, and education.
Ed Pacheco (D), Dartmouth 
Pacheco says he’s heading to Beacon Hill “to be a moderate, balanced voice who puts results over rhetoric,” and to focus on issues surrounding Dartmouth’s wastewater system, educator retention and recruiting, and “rising pressure” of 40B affordable housing developments. Pacheco has lived in Dartmouth for over two decades and will assume outgoing Rep. Chris Markey’s Ninth Bristol seat. The former night security officer at Dartmouth High School and nonprofit worker also opposes the development of large-scale data centers in the district.
Celina Reyes (D), Lawrence
Reyes is a Lawrence city councilor who was also the first president of SEIU 509’s Family Child Care Chapter, after she started her own family-run child care business. Her major campaign issues included housing and seniors, education and good government, and public health and safety. She cruised to election in the general after ousting Rep. Francisco Paulino in the September 1 primary for his 16th Essex seat following his indictment for alleged fraud. Paulino has pleaded not guilty.
Jack Richardson (D), Falmouth 
The 23-year-old, third-generation Falmouth resident ousted Republican Rep. David Vieira for the Third Barnstable House seat, campaigning on reducing housing and energy costs, cleaning Cape waters, and protecting people from federal immigration enforcement while not taking corporate PAC money. The former district director for Sen. Dylan Fernandes was also campaign manager for now-Rep. Thomas Moakley’s 2024 campaign and worked on former Sen. Susan Moran’s campaign. He went to American University, sat on the Falmouth Select Board, Housing Authority and town meeting, and is a longtime soccer referee. 
Ravi Simon (D), Sudbury
Outgoing Rep. Carmine Gentile’s sole staffer of almost five years will become his successor in the 13th Middlesex District with a priority list that includes quality education, climate action, and standing up for “Massachusetts values.” Simon’s resume features three years on the Lincoln-Sudbury School Committee, working as a speech and debate coach at Amherst College, and being a field organizer in 2018 for the committee to elect former Boston City Councilor Josh Zakim as secretary of state.
Jesse St. Gelais (R), Acushnet 
The GOP’s only flip came in the Eighth Bristol House District, where St. Gelais ousted Democratic Rep. Steven Ouellette with campaign priorities that included demanding the audit, supporting local aid and stopping “the climate agenda.” He has spent more than two decades in the insurance business, is a lifelong South Coast resident and ran on “common sense solutions” for the district.
Lora Wondolowski (D), Greenfield 
The founding executive director of the Massachusetts League of Environmental Voters campaigned on rural school funding, available and affordable housing, and farms and climate to win former Rep. Natalie Blais’s open First Franklin seat. After a close Democratic primary, Wondolowski beat an unenrolled candidate to secure the seat. A single parent, Wondolowski has raised money for progressive grassroots organizations at the Peace Development Fund in Amherst for more than four years.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV allocates more than $3M in Rural Health funds to biotech laboratory, Boone County hospital
description: The state of West Virginia will give $3.4 million of its federal Rural Health Transformation Program funds to Telostrand Laboratory to expand access to diagnostic testing, and to five initiatives at Boone Memorial Hospital, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Monday.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announces that the state will give $3.4 million of its federal Rural Health Transformation Program funds to Telostrand Laboratory and Boone Memorial Hospital in Madison, West Virginia on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)The state of West Virginia will give $3.4 million of its federal Rural Health Transformation Program funds to Telostrand Laboratory to expand access to diagnostic testing, and to five initiatives at Boone Memorial Hospital, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Monday.
“West Virginians deserve access to quality healthcare regardless of where they live,” Morrisey said in a news release. “These investments will help doctors catch health problems earlier, give patients better access to specialists, and make it easier for families to get the care they need closer to home. It’s about improving healthcare outcomes, keeping people healthy, and helping more West Virginians remain in or return to the workforce.”
According to the news release, the awards include: 

     $1,686,716 to Telostrand Laboratory to expand access to non-invasive diagnostic testing and shared laboratory services for rural healthcare providers. 
     $338,705 to Boone Memorial Hospital to expand inpatient remote patient monitoring across inpatient and observation beds, helping providers identify signs of deterioration sooner and reduce avoidable transfers and readmissions.
     $597,184 to Boone Memorial Hospital to expand at-home remote patient monitoring for high-risk patients managing diabetes, hypertension or complex needs following a hospital or emergency department discharge.
     $420,200 to Boone Memorial Hospital for artificial intelligence-enabled documentation and revenue cycle tools, helping reduce administrative burden and give healthcare professionals more time to focus on patients.
     $219,184 to Boone Memorial Hospital to improve Type 2 diabetes outcomes through nurse-led care coordination, nutrition and diabetes education, and glucose monitoring. Boone Memorial is adding its own funds for weekly food boxes and fitness classes for participants.
     $190,571 to Boone Memorial Hospital to expand specialty care in Boone County through two telehealth pods at the Comfort and Nellis clinics. The project will expand access to services including behavioral health, cardiology, podiatry, and pulmonary care.

The five-year federal Rural Health Transformation aims to “empower states to transform the existing rural healthcare infrastructure and build sustainable healthcare systems that expand access, enhance quality of care and improve outcomes for patients,” according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
West Virginia received $199 million in federal dollars from the program for 2026 and $202 million for 2027. The program was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made historic cuts to healthcare and food assistance spending.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ‘Dummymander’ helps propel Rep.-elect Smith to Congress in NC-03 victory
description: Four years ago, Smith lost his N.C. House seat to redistricting. This year, a new round of redistricting sent him to Congress.
text:
Raymond Smith seated at the far end of the table on the left, poses for a picture with the newest members of North Carolina's Congressional delegation. Democrats flipped seven U.S. House seats in North Carolina in the 2026 midterms. (Photo: Raymond Smith on X) GOLDSBORO, N.C. — Democrat Raymond Smith had a nine-hour heads up that he needed to get to Washington. He had become the representative-elect for North Carolina’s 3rd Congressional District. 
Smith trailed Republican U.S. House Rep. Greg Murphy by a slim lead of 233 votes at the end of Election Day. A week later on Nov. 10, provisional and absentee ballots were tabulated. They put Smith ahead by 293 votes, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. 
The following morning, Murphy conceded. 
Smith received a call around 9 p.m. on Nov. 11 saying he needed to be in Washington first thing in the morning. Orientation for newly-elected members of Congress had begun at the start of the week, but Smith said he wasn’t invited until his race was called. 
Virginia Foxx concedes long-held seat in NC’s closely watched 5th Congressional District

“I caught the first flight out of Raleigh, which was 6 a.m. I threw some stuff in a bag and got to Washington,” Smith said. “I lived that life while I was in the military, so I’m used to moving fast and packing quickly and packing light.”
Smith met the other new members of North Carolina’s congressional delegation at the U.S. Capitol, sharing a photo on social media. Each of the seven were Democrats who flipped seats in the Tar Heel State. 
Last year, North Carolina Republican state lawmakers tried to unseat Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Davis in the 1st Congressional District by making the district more Republican-leaning. They did so by moving some Democratic voters out of Davis’ 1st District and into Murphy’s 3rd District.
“Republicans were trying to grab one more seat, and in doing so, you have to do one of two things,” said Adam Newmark, a political science professor at Appalachian State University. “You either pack more Democrats into those three or four districts that you’ve crafted out as Democratic districts, or you have to shave off in some Republican districts from the sizable Republican advantage to try to create another district that’s for Republicans.”
U.S. Rep.-elect Raymond Smith (Photo: Campaign website)
The move made Murphy, who has held office since 2019, vulnerable to the blue wave. Some are calling the mid-decade gerrymander a “dummymander”: Davis won reelection, and Smith unseated Murphy.
Smith, who spent the week after the election raising funds for a potential recount, said it took a few days in Washington for his new reality to sink in.
“I started looking at the Capitol. I started looking at the Library of Congress. I started looking around at all of this history, and then it hit me,” Smith said. “I said, ‘Whoa, wait a minute. You’re a congressman now,’ and it became pretty emotional at that point.” 
Smith, 65, is an Army veteran who was born and raised in Goldsboro. He’s a former educator who served on the Wayne County school board before becoming a state legislator. 
In Raleigh, Smith represented Wayne and Sampson counties in the North Carolina House for two terms. North Carolina Sen. Gale Adcock, a Democrat from Wake County, was his mentor. 
“I just found him to be a delightful person,” Adcock said. “He’s very easy to talk to. He’s very approachable, very knowledgeable, well-spoken, friendly, willing to ask tough questions.”
NC Republicans eye 2028 comeback as two US House races move to recount

During his time at the legislature, Smith advocated for more funding for public schools, educators, and North Carolina’s HBCUs. He lost his seat in the 2022 election after a round of redistricting. 
Smith said education is one of his top priorities for Washington, but he also wants a voice in decisions related to transportation, agriculture, appropriations, healthcare, and the military.
His district contains the nation’s largest pork producer in Duplin County, as well as Eastern North Carolina’s only Level I trauma center in Greenville. There’s also Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune and Seymour Johnson Air Force Base. 
“I always tell people that the 3rd is the most eclectic district in the entire state of North Carolina,” Smith said. “As I look around the various committees and things of that nature, I’m struck by the need for more attention to armed services.”
If appointed to the U.S. House Committee on Armed Services, Smith would join Davis and Republican U.S. Rep. Pat Harrigan from North Carolina’s 10th Congressional District.

title: Candidate declines to seek recount in Fargo legislative district
description: North Dakota legislative elections are officially final after a third-place finisher in a Fargo district declined to demand a recount by Saturday’s deadline. Democrats Chris Tiongson and Stacy Heidenreich were the top two vote-getters in District 41 House, ahead of Republicans Jennifer Benson and Rich Slagle.  Benson trailed Heidenreich by 36 votes, which fe[...]
text:
Rep.-elect Stacy Heidenreich, left, and Rep.-elect Chris Tiongson, both Democrats from Fargo, smile for a photo at KFGO studios during the 2026 campaign. (Photo courtesy of Stacy Heidenreich)North Dakota legislative elections are officially final after a third-place finisher in a Fargo district declined to demand a recount by Saturday’s deadline.
Democrats Chris Tiongson and Stacy Heidenreich were the top two vote-getters in District 41 House, ahead of Republicans Jennifer Benson and Rich Slagle. 
Benson trailed Heidenreich by 36 votes, which fell within the margin for a demand recount. If requested, Benson’s campaign would have been required to fund a demand recount.
The secretary of state did not receive a request for a demand recount, Deputy Secretary of State Sandy McMerty said in an email Monday. That means the election results certified by the State Canvassing Board last week will stand, she said.
“I’ve been kind of waiting on pins and needles this whole week,” Rep.-elect Heidenreich said in an interview Monday. “I can just breathe a sigh of relief that it’s official.”
Benson did not return calls seeking comment.
North Dakota certifies 2026 election with 1 possible recount, court challenge looming

Heidenreich said District 41 is “very purple” after Republican Sen. Kyle Davison won reelection to the Senate in the same district that will send two freshmen Democrats to the state House. District 41 Republican Reps. Karen Grindberg and Jorin Johnson did not seek reelection.
The two Democrats have already visited with Davison about working together, Heidenreich said.
“Even though we are from different parties, we all have the same thing in mind,” she said.
Heidenreich is a 30-year veteran of the banking industry and an assistant vice president at Gate City Bank. 
Orientation for new state lawmakers and the organizational session are next week.
“I’m just really excited to get to Bismarck and work on the priorities that I heard from the community while I was doorknocking, which is daycare costs, general affordability, and protecting teachers and public education,” Heidenreich said. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: VTDigger
title: The best intentions often do more harm than good
description:
Truckloads of unrequested clothing and goods can bury relief workers after a disaster. This holiday season, the most useful gift is cash.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The best intentions often do more harm than good.
text:
This commentary is by Tessa Simson, an honors student at the University of Rhode Island majoring in political science.
Vermonters take pride in helping their neighbors. Whether it’s responding to floods that devastated our own community in 2023 and 2024 or donating to relief efforts across the world, we believe in helping others. But what if our values, expressed through well-intentioned donations, end up doing more harm than good? 
Take Hurricane Mitch, for example. In 1998, Hondurans were hit by a disastrous hurricane, which left millions homeless and claimed thousands of lives. For months following this tragedy, the affected community members were desperate for relief and the necessities that could save lives. However, when a plane full of necessary aid attempted to land on a runway in Honduras, the air crew found donated clothes — items that were neither requested by Hondurans nor needed at the time — blocking the runway, meaning the plane full of crucial aid was unable to land.
This situation is not unique to Hurricane Mitch. Disaster strikes, people and places are in shambles, often with no way to recover independently. Then the second disaster strikes. Unsolicited material donations arrive in large quantities, overwhelming storage units and airplane cargo capacity. Volunteers and relief workers have to deal with the donations instead of prioritizing essential aid distribution, and communities are left with huge amounts of unwanted items.

READ MORE

Vermont has a strong culture of giving and community service and is famous for its “neighbors helping neighbors” mindset, with a long-standing tradition of volunteerism and civic involvement. Its response is to donate to countries and people in need, which feeds directly into the second disaster.
When I was a student at Camels Hump Middle School, our art class was given blank shoes and asked to decorate them however we wanted. We were told they would be donated to communities affected by Hurricane Sandy, the 2012 storm that devastated the coasts of New Jersey and New York. As I painted the shoes, I imagined the people who might receive them, hoping that they would appreciate the thoughtful designs and bright colors I had used. Looking back, however, it’s clear we were focusing on how good it felt to give rather than thinking critically about making a noticeable impact in a devastated community. 
So what should we do instead? In scenarios like these, where communities did not request material donations, cash donations are the best option. They help communities and humanitarian organizations center their spending on the community’s actual needs. Relief organizations can purchase specific aid items and allocate cash to specific local businesses. This also reduces waste, since cash will not be discarded the way a material donation often is. 
Vermonters’ generosity and urge to help their own communities and others are beautiful traits of our small state. But we have to be mindful with our actions. With the holidays around the corner, I encourage all Vermonters to reflect on the unintended harm a physical donation may cause to a community or country that did not ask for it. Instead, take time to research the location and community you would like to help, and send money through a trusted source. As the saying goes, cash is king.

Lynn BreckenridgeFebruary 6, 1941 – November 15, 2026Rock Springs, WyomingShared by: Vase Funeral Home
Lynn Breckenridge, a beloved resident of Rock Springs, Wyoming, passed away peacefully on Sunday, November 15th, 2026, at the age of 85. He was listening to his favorite songs and surrounded by his loving family. Born on Thursday, February 6th, 1941, in Loveland, Colorado, Lynn was the cherished son of Elmer Breckenridge and Beulah Helen Cogdell and was lovingly raised by his grandparents, Arthur and Emma Breckenridge.
Lynn spent his early years in Colorado, attending local schools and graduating from Cache La Poudre in 1960. Following graduation, he married the love of his life, Jo, the mother of his four daughters. Although they later divorced, they remained lifelong friends. They moved to California where he had an adventurous job cleaning pools in Beverly Hills and met multiple famous people. He then went on to a rewarding career as a truck driver, traveling far and wide across the United States for various companies.
In addition to his professional pursuits, Lynn held a wide range of interests that brought joy and enrichment to his life. He had a deep passion for music, playing guitar at an early age, yodeling, attending concerts, Honky Tonkin’ and most of all singing and DJing karaoke. He was known for his storytelling, sense of humor, smoking a pipe with sweet cherry tobacco, and driving his ’56 Chevy Belair. He was a big reader and history buff. He also loved nature and animals, reveling in the beauty of the great outdoors which included finding hot springs, places to fish, and mountainous areas where he could view wildlife. His adventurous spirit took him on many memorable journeys, most notably Alaska and Costa Rica. Above all, he cherished spending time with his family.
Lynn’s kind and generous heart extended beyond his immediate circle. He was compassionate and loved helping animals and those in need. As a lasting tribute, his family requests donations in his memory be made to local animal shelters or homeless shelters, continuing his legacy of generosity.
Lynn completed his memoirs three weeks before he passed, which is now available on Amazon, titled “Happy Trails and Tears: Sentimental Memories” authored by Lynn Breckenridge.
Lynn is survived by his four devoted daughters: Tamela Lynn Moreno and her husband Rodolfo “Rudy” of Rock Springs, WY; Teresa “Roxan” Powell and her husband Frank of Erda, UT; Heidi Darlene Pamplin and her husband Shaun of Whitewright, TX; and Heather Jolyn Breckenridge and her spouse Teri Girtsman of Gaithersburg, MD. His enduring legacy lives on through his 13 grandchildren: Amador “Bubba” Moreno, Q’ra Reece, Na’keya Reece, Jazmine Suttles, Rusty Jones, Heather Jones, Josie Jones, Granger Powell, Trista Powell, Brady Hamilton, Haley Bunnell, Lane Pamplin, and Taylor Pamplin; 19 great-grandchildren: Dominic, Jade, Serenity, Jocelyn, Sydney, Alivia, Tyson, Lias, A.J., Laila, Olivia, Wylie, Theo, Ellie, Rustilynn, Zeriaa, Chelsey, Bree, Aurora; and two great-great-grandchildren: Macy and Zion. Lynn is also survived by five nephews: John Breckenridge, Brett Breckenridge, Tom Breckenridge, Hoby Breckenridge, and Dale Breckenridge; and one niece, Brenda Maile.
Preceding Lynn in death were his paternal grandparents, Arthur Breckenridge and Emma Harlow; maternal grandparents, David Cogdell and Nellie Turknett; parents Elmer Breckenridge and Beulah Helen Cogdell and her husband Harold “Pappy” Hedke; two brothers, John Breckenridge and David Breckenridge; a sister, Helen Florence Breckenridge; and a grandson, Riley Bunnell.
Cremation has taken place and a Celebration of Life in Northern Colorado will take place next summer. Details will be posted on Facebook.
Friends and family are welcome to express condolences and share memories at Vase Funeral Homes.
Lynn Breckenridge will be profoundly missed, but his spirit and kindness will continue to resonate through the many lives he touched.









Kenneth Edwin ChristoffersenJuly 25, 1941 – November 17, 2026Rock Springs, WyomingShared by: Vase Funeral Home
Kenneth “Hoss” Christoffersen, a beloved husband, father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and cherished friend, passed away peacefully on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at his home in Rock Springs, Wyoming.
He was born July 25, 1941, in Denver, Colorado; Ken’s journey was marked by a deep love for his family, an exemplary career, and tireless community service.
Ken graduated from Aurora High School in 1959. He often fondly recalled his schooling in Laramie, particularly his experiences at Nellie Iles, which he credited with providing him a strong foundation in life. An esteemed member of the United States Navy, Ken served his country with honor before returning home to work for OCI as a surface mechanic. His dedicated service spanned 36 years until his retirement on June 1, 2004.
He married the love of his life Doris Olga Stewart June 27, 1964 in Rock Springs, Wyoming.
Residing in Rock Springs, Ken was an integral part of the community. He was a valued member of the American Legion Archie Hay Post #24 and actively participated in the Memoirs Writing Club. Ken’s heart was made even warmer each Christmas season, as he volunteered as Santa Claus for over 50 years for various organizations. His commitment to serving others was also evident through his efforts at the Young at Heart Senior Center.
Ken savored the great outdoors, whether it was hunting, fishing, camping, or rock hunting. He took great joy in exploring the scenic landscapes of Wyoming, gardening, and delving into history, but his greatest joy came from time spent with his family.
Survivors include his wife Doris Christoffersen of Rock Springs, Wyoming; one son, Eric Christoffersen of Rock Springs, Wyoming; two daughters, Yvonne Peterson and husband Doug of Cheyenne, Wyoming; Becky Middendorf and husband Virgil of Billings, Montana; nine grandchildren, KJ Christoffersen and wife Meghan; Jacob Christoffersen and wife Wendy; Trey Christoffersen and wife Brooklyn; Gretchen Middendorf; Aaron Peterson; Sawyer Middendorf; River Christoffersen and companion Kallie; Kason Christoffersen; Ryan Peterson and companion Cynthia; ten great-grandchildren, Makenna Christoffersen; Cooper Christoffersen; Bailey Christoffersen; Cody Christoffersen; Cora Christoffersen; Waylon Sage; Sawyer Sage; Ava Peterson; Mila Peterson; Tobias Peterson; several cousins, nieces and nephews including Debbie Petrie Bullock; Josslynn Thomas; Jenille Thomas.
He is preceded in death by his parents, Edwin and Gladys Christoffersen; father and mother-in-law, John and Elaine Stewart, three brothers, Don Christoffersen and wife Laurie; Bob Christoffersen; Tom Christoffersen; two brothers-in-law, Doug Stewart; Ralph Stewart; two sisters-in-law, Carolyn Petrie and husband David; Judy Gray; one niece, Susan Christoffersen; one nephew, Mark Christoffersen.
The family respectfully requests donations be made in Ken’s memory to Young at Heart Senior Center, 2400 Reagan Avenue, Rock Springs, Wyoming or Rocky Mountain Home Health Care and Hospice, 175 Riverview Drive, Suite A, Green River, Wyoming 82935.
Cremation will take place; a Celebration of Life will be conducted at 10:00 am Friday, December 4, 2026 at Abundant Grace Ministries, 1515 Edgar Street, Rock Springs, Wyoming 82901. Military Grave Side Services and Inurnment will be in the Rock Springs Municipal Cemetery.
Condolences may be left at www.vasefuneralhomes.com
Ken’s legacy of commitment, kindness, and community service will forever remain in the hearts of those who knew and loved him.
