title: Democrats demand answers from Oz after delay in $50B rural health awards
authors: Sarah Jane Tribble | KFF Health News
description: Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans. Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services […]
text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz is administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. In this photo, Oz speaks at a March 15, 2022 press conference in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Pennsylvania Capital-Star).Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans.
Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz late Thursday. The letter pointed to what it called “an alarming lack of public transparency” and said the fund “lacks sufficient guardrails to protect rural hospitals at greatest risk of closure.”
Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski said her state “got no explanation from CMS as to why” it got $3 million less in its second-year Rural Health Transformation Program allocation. It was a roughly 1.5% reduction from its $193.4 million first-year award. State leaders have not received information about an appeals process, she said.
Any delay in knowing how much they received and any reduction in their base funding is significant, Budzinski said, because states need to plan for an “acute impact” from the loss of other federal funding.
In the first year, states competed for their initial share of the $50 billion, which is handed out at $10 billion a year for five years. They won awards ranging from $147 million to $281 million. Most of the lawmakers who signed the letter were from states that lost funding this year. Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama, which got $4.1 million less, along with Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado, which saw a nearly $3 million drop, also spearheaded the letter along with Budzinski.

One concern, Budzinski said, is “making sure that the money isn’t going to consultants, that it’s actually getting to the rural providers that it is supposed to be getting to.” The lawmakers asked Oz for a response to detailed questions by Nov. 25. They also requested a briefing about the delays to the funding announcement, which was first reported by KFF Health News, and the impact on states.
The second-year awards were due to be announced by Oct. 31, but an Oct. 30 letter from CMS stated officials “discovered an additional administrative process requirement.” Instead, second-year funding was announced Nov. 9.
“Those kind of delays prevent a state to fully prepare for what’s to come,” Budzinski said.
CMS oversees the fund and its newly formed Office of Rural Health Transformation. Agency officials did not respond to questions for this article before the given deadline.
Republicans passed the Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to offset other ramifications of President Donald Trump’s signature budget law, including an estimated $137 billion in Medicaid spending cuts for rural America over 10 years.
That rural money is “retail therapy for Congress,” said Cara James, president and chief executive of Grantmakers in Health, while speaking at a Milken Institute event this month.
Because the same tax law cut Medicaid spending, which rural hospitals and people disproportionately use, as well as supplemental food assistance and other government grants, the short-term money would not “help sustain people” in rural America, James said.
Then, she posed a persistent fear about the fund: “If it’s even getting to the communities.”
Five rural hospitals have closed or been converted into lower-level facilities since the rural fund was created, including one in Michigan that shuttered beds and switched to providing only emergency services to survive, according to a list curated by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research at the University of North Carolina.
The letter stated lawmakers’ concerns that too much of the rural fund “could flow to large consulting and technology firms rather than supporting providers and communities on the ground.”
After the law passed last year, state leaders had just over seven weeks to write applications as they competed for the first-year funds. All 50 states won funding with allocations determined by a federal scoring process. Each year, officials are to revisit the funding allotments.
Most states saw their funding change by less than 2%. North Dakota and Iowa won the largest gains; New Jersey, Florida, and Vermont saw the biggest reductions.
Although federal officials have created state data maps, released a slew of press announcements, and led sessions on the complicated scoring of state applications, it’s not enough, said Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association.
The association, which represents hospitals and community clinics nationwide, sent its own letter to federal officials Nov. 9. Morgan said that the way states win money needs “to be articulated in a way that success can be replicated by all states going forward.”
Morgan said his association’s analysis found that state leaders are sending the federal money to local hospitals and clinics because communities and individuals are “relying on rural hospitals to be there to deliver care.” But it’s unclear, he said, how much of the overall rural fund local hospitals are actually receiving versus how much is benefiting other entities, such as consultants.
In their letter, Budzinski and the other Democrats asked if CMS would establish a searchable database that tracks spending. They also asked for an explanation of how federal officials will evaluate state performance and allocate awards.
It was just the latest congressional letter to federal health officials on this issue.
In August 2025, a month after the law passed, Democrats sent a letter about the program’s rollout to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. And last November, Budzinski reached out to Oz on behalf of Illinois. Bennet, along with Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and others, signed a letter in June asking that the funds be targeted to rescue rural hospitals and clinics.
“We haven’t gotten full responses to any of these inquiries,” said Budzinski, who will become chair of the House’s largest Democratic caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia Democrats intend to look for ‘pathway’ to target state’s six-week abortion ban
description: It was the biggest applause line of the biggest event in Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms’ campaign, a rally featuring former President Barack Obama less than a week ahead of the Nov. 3 election. “I believe in a woman’s right to make decisions –” Bottoms said, then paused for more than 20 seconds of cheers and […]
text:
Protesters on both sides of the abortion issue clash outside the Georgia Capitol in 2022. A newly elected Democratic majority in the Georgia House could mean changes to the state's six-week abortion ban, but that wouldn't be easy.  Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderIt was the biggest applause line of the biggest event in Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms’ campaign, a rally featuring former President Barack Obama less than a week ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at the state Capitol about her transition into office on Nov. 6, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“I believe in a woman’s right to make decisions –” Bottoms said, then paused for more than 20 seconds of cheers and chants of “Keisha, Keisha.”
“ — a woman’s right to make decisions about her own body and her future,” she continued. “And as governor, I will fight to restore that right.”
Georgia has banned most abortions since a 2022 U.S. Supreme Court decision overturned the federal right to an abortion and left the issue to the states. With some exceptions, Georgia bans abortions once embryonic cardiac activity is detectable, typically around the sixth week of pregnancy. The ban remains in place while a challenge against it moves through court. Before Roe v. Wade was overturned, Georgia allowed abortions up to about 20 weeks of pregnancy.
Bottoms’ health platform included repealing that law and returning to “the Roe-era standard.”
Speaking to reporters at the Capitol the Friday after Election Day, Bottoms appeared to acknowledge obstacles to making that happen.
“If we see a pathway to do something about it this session, then we’re going to take that opportunity,” she said, referring to the annual lawmaking session set to begin in January. “And it may not be this session. If it’s not this session, then we’re going to take it at the first opportunity that we have.”
All pathways run through the Senate
Senate Majority Leader Jason Anavitarte speaks to members of the press. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Georgia Democrats outperformed expectations in this year’s midterm election, sweeping all statewide offices on the ballot and narrowly gaining control of the state House. But any pathway for Bottoms to change the abortion law, known as the LIFE Act, would need to run through the state Senate, which is set to remain under slim Republican control.
Republicans will have a two-seat majority in the chamber, which means GOP leadership will likely have final say over which bills are assigned to committee, a required first step toward becoming law.
And once a bill makes it to the full Senate, Democrats will need the support of at least two Senate Republicans to move legislation through the chamber.
Speaking on a recent episode of the Atlanta Journal-Constitution’s “Politically Georgia” podcast, Senate Majority Leader Jason Anavitarte indicated that the Senate’s Republican majority would not have much appetite to shift its priorities on issues like abortion.
State Sen. Josh McLaurin, who is set to become the next lieutenant governor. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
“Georgia elected a majority state Senate of Republicans,” the Dallas Republican said. “I mean, those are the electoral results, whether it was 29 or 31 or 32, they elected 29. So we’re going to stand by what we believe is the right thing to do, whether it’s on abortion or gun rights or the economy or taxes or whatever. We’re gonna have a deliberative conversation, and then we’ll make decisions.”
While the Senate will be under a Republican majority, a Democrat is set to preside over it. Sandy Springs Democratic state Sen. Josh McLaurin is set to become the state’s next lieutenant governor in January after winning the majority of votes in the midterm.
McLaurin said a majority is not the same thing as a mandate.
“Those 29 seats are gerrymandered,” he said. “If we had fair maps, Democrats would already have a majority. It’s a testament to the size of voters’ mandate this year that we flipped four Senate seats that were previously considered unwinnable because of gerrymandering. The majority leader should keep that in mind as he performs his moral calculus.”
Room for compromise?
Sen. Sally Harrell. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Some Democrats hope a full repeal is possible but believe a compromise is more likely.
“The compromise is going to have to happen in the Senate because that’s where you still have a narrow margin of Republicans,” said state Sen. Sally Harrell, an Atlanta Democrat who previously sought to overturn the abortion ban. “That’s where they have the majority, but there’s so much public support for being able to access abortions and support of reproductive freedom that you might find some Republicans who feel that pressure and who might be willing to enter into a dialogue about making some changes around the edges.”
Harrell said those changes might include reexamining the legal ramifications of fetal personhood, the idea that a fetus ought to be treated as a distinct legal person, or protecting doctors’ right to perform procedures on pregnant women that may harm the fetus.
Georgia’s abortion law seeks to provide these protections, including specifying that doctors are clear to act in cases of “medical emergency,” defined as “a condition in which an abortion is necessary in order to prevent the death of the pregnant woman or the substantial and irreversible physical impairment of a major bodily function of the pregnant woman.”
Some doctors and medical organizations say the language of the law isn’t compatible with the actual practice of medicine.
Rep. Michelle Au. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
State Rep. Michelle Au, a Johns Creek Democrat and a physician, said a prime example is the case of Amber Thurman, a 28-year-old medical assistant who died in 2022.
Thurman experienced a rare complication after undergoing a medication abortion. She went to the hospital with a severe infection, but doctors delayed treatment for 20 hours, and by then it was too late to save her life. Georgia’s maternal mortality review committee deemed her death preventable and found the delay largely responsible, ProPublica reported.
Au said all kinds of healthcare providers are regularly tasked with caring for pregnant women, not just obstetricians, and there are no bright lines establishing when a medical emergency exists. She said the law makes treating pregnant women more difficult, even when the consequences are not fatal.
“The law, which is not a clinical mechanism, it’s not a clinical recommendation, interjects itself in a way that does not harmonize with the way medicine is practiced, and it interferes with the way that medicine is practiced,” she said. “And that’s what we’re seeing, not just in these cases with catastrophic outcomes, but across the spectrum. Anytime that you are tasked with taking the best care of a patient the way you were trained to do and you hesitate because you’re like, ‘I’m not sure if I can do this now because of this legal regime,’ that impedes patient care.
Democrats and abortion rights advocates held a press conference in 2023 to unveil a proposal to repeal Georgia’s six-week abortion ban and protect access to the procedure. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
“That makes patient care worse,” she added. “It creates worse outcomes, even if the patient doesn’t ultimately end up dying.”
Au said lawmakers will be hearing from doctors and medical organizations about what changes they would like to see.
“The most important thing moving forward is we cannot have a law, we cannot have it written into statute that healthcare providers are criminalized for providing what we have been taught to be the best standard of care for certain clinical situations,” she said.
Elizabeth Edmonds, executive director of the Georgia Life Alliance, a nonprofit that advocates against abortion, said she thinks the law protects doctors as-is, but legislation to spell that out more clearly could be more palatable for conservative senators than an outright repeal.
“I don’t think it’s out of the question to maybe put together a piece of legislation that just spells that out but doesn’t touch any of the restrictions or other things established in the LIFE Act,” she said.
Other states have passed similar legislation. In Texas, it was called the “Life of the Mother Act.”
“They called it a ‘cleanup bill,’ even though it wasn’t really cleaning anything up, it was really more of a public education thing, letting people know doctors are allowed to provide these services and treatments, that a woman doesn’t have to be on the doorstep of death to receive life-saving care and things like that,” Edmonds said. “So I don’t think that that would be out of the question, and we would certainly work with anybody on either side if it helps to clear up that public confusion.”
Pressure from both sides
Cole Muzio stumps for Georgia religious liberty at the state Capitol in 2025. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
If Georgia’s new Democratic leadership decides that kind of compromise will be a goal for next year’s session, they can expect resistance.
Cole Muzio is founder and president of Frontline Policy Action, an influential rightwing evangelical lobbying group that has successfully pushed for culturally conservative legislation, including Georgia’s abortion law.
Muzio said the current law provides protections for doctors and he would resist changes to it.
“I don’t see a problem with the language of the law,” he said. “I think we’ve just got political narratives that have been pushed, and it would take a lot of convincing for me to see anything beyond the politics aiming to increase abortion.”
Muzio said he is hopeful Democrats will not exceed what he views as a narrow mandate from voters and that his organization is ready to work with them on legislation focused on bipartisan issues like boosting support for special education and children in foster care.
But he said Frontline is ready to defend outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp’s legacy, including the abortion ban.
“Our voters will not look kindly on any senator that participates actively in undoing what the governor achieved,” Muzio said. “I don’t believe or expect that will happen, but the unity of the caucus and a unified front behind caucus leadership will serve these individual members well as they go back to their districts.”
But legislators are likely to receive pushback not only from the anti-abortion side.
Kwajelyn Jackson, executive director of the Feminist Center for Reproductive Liberation, a health clinic in Atlanta providing abortions within the current law, said reproductive rights advocates will be lobbying for change as well.
“We will ensure that, whether or not there is waffling or hesitation, that it is made clear to everyone who is holding public office that we are demanding real change and that we are not willing to wait and see, that we actually want to see action being taken as quickly and as definitively as possible,” she said.

title: Ohio had more than 130 intimate partner-related fatalities in one-year span, according to new report
description: If you are experiencing relationship abuse, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-SAFE (7233) or text START to 88788.  Ohio had the second-highest number of intimate partner-related fatalities, according to a new report.  There were 134 intimate partner relationship fatalities in 101 cases from July 1, 2025 to June 30, according to a new […]
text:
A domestic violence awareness ribbon. (Stock photo from Getty Images.)If you are experiencing relationship abuse, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-SAFE (7233) or text START to 88788. 
Ohio had the second-highest number of intimate partner-related fatalities, according to a new report. 
There were 134 intimate partner relationship fatalities in 101 cases from July 1, 2025 to June 30, according to a new report from the Ohio Domestic Violence Network. There were 157 fatalities in last year’s report. 
“Domestic violence is very prevalent in Ohio and ultimately very deadly,” said Maria York, Ohio Domestic Violence Network’s director of policy and communications. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“There’s people behind the numbers, and so we always want to make sure that we remember that there’s people with lives and futures behind the data.”
This is the eleventh year of the report, which the Ohio Domestic Violence Network compiles using statistics from media reports of intimate partner relationship fatalities. 
Of this year’s fatalities, 89 were victims and 45 were perpetrators. There were 73 female fatalities and 61 male fatalities. 
The youngest person who died was seven months old and the oldest person was 88 years old, according to the report. 
There were 20 murder/suicides and four multiple murder/suicides. 
In nearly half of all the cases, the relationship was ending or had recently ended. 
More than 19,000 survivors reached out for emergency shelter last year, but not all can be taken in, York said. 
“Over half of the survivors who reached out for shelter were turned away just because we don’t have the capacity or the resources,” she said. 
“It’s probably very safe to say that there are survivors who are seeking help and are not getting served just because we can’t begin to meet the need.”
Ohio has 76 domestic violence programs. 
“There’s not a shelter in every county or a program in every county,” York said. 
“A lot of the neighboring counties are doing outreach to counties that don’t have a program. But southeast Ohio, like Gallia County, that area is pretty sparse.”
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine’s recently announced new initiatives designed to help domestic violence survivors including an additional $1 million will be directed toward the state’s domestic violence shelters recognized by the Office of Criminal Justice Services, among others. 
“Ohio must continue to be innovative in its work to protect both domestic violence survivors and the law enforcement officers who respond to calls for help,” DeWine said in a statement.
Three-fourths of domestic violence deaths were a result of gun violence, according to the Ohio Domestic Violence Network report. 108 people were shot in these cases, and only seven people survived. 
Nearly all of the other deaths were strangulations, traumatic brain injury, or stabbing, according to the report. One woman was beaten to death with a handmade wooden club while she was sleeping, according to the report. 
Five children were murdered, either by a parent or a stepparent. 
“These are children who are murdered by a parent, specifically in an effort to get back at the other parents about power and control,” York said. 
“So they’re using their kids as a message to say, ‘This is against you’ is why they’re killing the kids.”
More than 50 children witnessed their parent’s murder and three teenagers were murdered by someone they were dating. 
Most of the murders (87%) happened in a home. 
Ohio fatalities in the last 11 years: 

134 in 2026
157 in 2025 
114 in 2024 
112 in 2023 
112 in 2022 
131 in 2021
109 in 2020 
91 in 2019 
115 in 2018 
101 in 2017 
81 in 2016

title: Wisconsin DOA projects $4 billion budget surplus and $2 billion rainy day fund
description: The Wisconsin Department of Administration is projecting the state will end the 2026-27 fiscal year with $4.18 billion — over $1.8 billion higher than previously estimated — marking the sixth year of a state budget surplus.  The agency’s report released Friday stated that fiscally Wisconsin is “well-positioned for the future,” as Democrats prepare to write [[...]
text:
Wisconsin State Capitol (Baylor Spears | Wisconsin Examiner)The Wisconsin Department of Administration is projecting the state will end the 2026-27 fiscal year with $4.18 billion — over $1.8 billion higher than previously estimated — marking the sixth year of a state budget surplus. 
The agency’s report released Friday stated that fiscally Wisconsin is “well-positioned for the future,” as Democrats prepare to write the next state budget, but also said there are some factors that could change the projection. 
The state’s stabilization fund — also known as the rainy day fund — is nearly $2.1 billion, the largest in state history and over six times the balance at the end of fiscal year 2017-18. 
Gov. Tony Evers said in a statement that the report is proof of his administration’s work to “be good stewards of Wisconsinites’ tax dollars while still making smart, strategic investments in needs that were long neglected before I took office.” 
“We have one of the largest budget surpluses in state history, the highest ‘rainy day’ fund balance in state history, and some of the best, record-breaking years Wisconsin has ever seen for tourism, apprenticeship, unemployment, and much more,” Evers said. “Wisconsin’s in darn good shape, and it’s in large part due to the hard work of so many across our administration these last eight years.”
The report is the last before Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley and state lawmakers take office in January. Democrats will lead the state budget process for the first time since 2009. During the session that produced the 2009-2011 budget, Gov. Jim Doyle and lawmakers were dealing with the Great Recession and a $6 billion budget deficit. Under the resulting budget, most state programs had cuts of at least 1%, but many had cuts of 5% or more.
The DOA report projected the state’s finances in the future considering agencies’ requests for the next state budget. If all were approved, the state would have a $435.7 million surplus at the end of 2027-28 fiscal year and a $4 billion budget deficit at the end of the 2028-29 fiscal year. 
Most agencies were directed by Evers not to increase state spending, but exceptions were made in a few areas including K-12 schools aid, the University of Wisconsin system and Medical Assistance. 
Of all the agencies, the Department of Public Instruction is requesting the largest investment from the state, putting in a request totaling an additional $2.75 billion. State Superintendent Jill Underly is calling for the overhaul of the funding formula and investments to stop public schools’ reliance on local property tax increases to keep up with costs.
The University of Wisconsin system is seeking an additional $730 million from the state over the two-year period. The Department of Health Services is requesting an additional $1.8 billion in state funds in the 2027-29 budget to continue Medicaid services. 
“It is not uncommon for agency requests to exceed available projected revenues,” the report stated. “Again, this imbalance assumes that all state agency requests are approved, which is quite unlikely.”
Democratic lawmakers have said they will address high costs including for education, healthcare and local government. They’ll consider agency requests as well as input from across the state and from the incoming governor as they write the budget. 
The incoming chairs of the Joint Finance Committee Rep. Tip McGuire (D-Kenosha) and Sen. LaTonya Johnson (D-Milwaukee) said in a statement about the report that Wisconsinites “spoke loud and clear in November.”
“We are looking forward to crafting a budget that prioritizes working families and puts affordability first,” the lawmakers said. 
The report also identifies factors that could change the projections in the future including the war in Iran and artificial intelligence. It states that the conflict in Iran “poses a significant risk” to the economic forecast as there are higher energy prices, weakening consumer demand and the potential for higher inflation. 
Investments in AI, meanwhile, could go one of two ways. 
“Given the proportion of current economic growth and stability tied to investment in AI, an AI bust would heighten the risk of a recession or at least a sharp slowdown in growth,” the report states. “However, if AI investment proves to be substantially more additive than projected to productivity gains, growth could accelerate from its current trajectory.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio AG joins 42 others in fighting federal sports-betting maneuver
description: Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson and a bipartisan group of 43 state attorneys general are fighting an attempt by federal regulators to “expand federal control over sports betting and undermine states’ authority to protect consumers,” according to a statement from Wilson’s office. The Commodities Futures Trading Commission is proposing to define sports betti[...]
text:
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, left, has chosen Public Safety Director Andy Wilson, at podium, as interim Ohio Attorney General. (Photo by Morgan Trau, WEWS.)Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson and a bipartisan group of 43 state attorneys general are fighting an attempt by federal regulators to “expand federal control over sports betting and undermine states’ authority to protect consumers,” according to a statement from Wilson’s office.
The Commodities Futures Trading Commission is proposing to define sports betting in prediction markets as “swaps” and take control of regulating them from the states.
Sports betting has exploded in Ohio since it became legal at the start of 2023. With $10.3 billion wagered in 2025, it now has the fourth-largest market in the United States.
Being able to gamble so conveniently has come with serious social problems.   
The UCLA Anderson School of Management in 2025 reported that entire states’ average credit scores took a hit when sports betting was legalized in them. That’s not just the average credit scores of gamblers, but of everybody in the state. 
A separate study linked legalized gambling to increased crime — including violent crime.
Amid accusations that big-time athletes are rigging at least parts of games, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine a year ago told the Associated Press that he regrets signing Ohio’s sports betting law.
And those are problems associated with state-regulated and taxed sports-betting companies such as DraftKings. Wilson and his counterparts worry that the federal move will allow prediction markets such as Kalshi to offer sports betting without giving states much of a say.
A letter from the attorneys general to the Commodities Futures Trading Commission “warns that the proposal could encourage traditional sportsbooks to reorganize as prediction markets, effectively sidestepping state gambling laws and leaving consumers without established safeguards,” a written statement from the Ohio Attorney General’s office says.
It added, “Prediction markets allow users to wager on sporting events much like traditional sportsbooks, but without the same state oversight. The proposed rule could further open the door for these platforms to bypass licensing requirements, age restrictions and protections against problem gambling.”
In the statement, Wilson accused the commission of trying to override Congress and the courts.
“A sports bet isn’t a derivative just because the CFTC says so,” he said. “The agency doesn’t get to invent powers that Congress never gave it, ignore federal court decisions and bulldoze state consumer protections. If Congress wanted the commission running sports gambling, it would have said so — and headquartered it in Las Vegas.”
Wilson joined attorneys general from Kentucky, Maryland, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Tennessee and Utah in leading the coalition.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Commentary: Rural education matters: Save Mansfield University
description: The Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education (PASSHE) Chancellor Christopher Fiorentino announced the winding down of operations at the Mansfield campus of Commonwealth University.
text:
Students walk near Mansfield University's North Hall. (Photo courtesy of Mansfield University)In August 2024, flooding in the aftermath of Tropical Storm Debby destroyed homes in Westfield, a small town located in Tioga County. Gov. Josh Shapiro reacted swiftly using his authority to declare a state emergency. He was also instrumental in coordinating federal emergency relief to these affected areas.
In the aftermath of the crisis, Shapiro stood shoulder to shoulder with the Tioga County Commissioners and state Rep. Clint Owlett as he visited the affected areas. He showed up for people in a county where only 27% voted for him in the 2022 gubernatorial race.
In a 2026 book tour interview for his memoir, “Where We Keep the Light,” he said, “My natural inclination is to solve problems.”  It’s a leadership approach that he proudly promotes and has wide appeal. His getting stuff done (GSD) mantra has become a central component of his political ascendency. Early speculation gives him rather good odds to be a presidential candidate in 2028.
However, his leadership is being tested now.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Pennsylvanians in the northern tier were recently confronted with another crisis without warning.
In a press release, the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education (PASSHE) Chancellor Christopher Fiorentino announced the winding down of operations at the Mansfield campus of Commonwealth University to take effect by June 30, 2028.
The Commonwealth University President Jeff Osgood is directed to provide a plan for closure by December 8, followed by a vote of the PASSHE Board of Governors likely scheduled for mid-December.
Mansfield University integrated with Lock Haven University and Bloomsburg University in 2022 to form Commonwealth University.
Putting aside an unreasonable timeline and the questionable legal authority of the chancellor to order Mansfield’s closure, the people of Tioga County – home of the Mansfield campus – are faced with an existential crisis.
The following facts are not disputed: enrollment has declined significantly; campus space is not efficiently utilized; its energy costs are high; it has significant infrastructure needs; and prospects to increase enrollment from the top three counties it draws from are not optimistic in the university’s current form.
A recent sustainability report of the three CU campuses ordered by the chancellor neatly spells out all that is wrong with Mansfield, but it does not fully acknowledge all the ongoing work that is being done on the Mansfield campus to address the challenges it confronts.
The report was the pretense for the sudden closure directive, but sadly, it does not fully encapsulate the immeasurable value of the Mansfield campus, which was on display last Wednesday evening when over 1,000 students, staff, faculty, and community members turned up for a rally in an overcrowded auditorium to Save Mansfield.
Governor Josh Shapiro understands that spreadsheets and budget lines do not always tell the full story, which is why he makes a point of traveling the state that he leads. He has met the people of Tioga County, toured the Grand Canyon of Pennsylvania, and visited small businesses.
He knows what closing the Mansfield campus will do to the local economy as well as denying access for educational opportunities for underserved rural communities.
Regional public universities have served as anchors in communities across the state. Mansfield traces its roots back to 1857 when it first opened as a seminary school. When the state system was created in 1983, its mission included “to contribute to the economic, social, and cultural development of Pennsylvania’s communities, the commonwealth, and the nation.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While the chancellor makes a compelling argument, he clearly did not put in place a process for the problem to be resolved in some other way short of closure. He ordered this closure even after President Osgood had issued 108 retrenchment letters to address personnel costs.
The chancellor visited the Mansfield campus once and is betting that most of the state will ignore Mansfield’s closure given its rural location and low-population density.
The Mansfield campus, including its students and surrounding communities, deserve better. Governor Shapiro should delay a vote of the Board of Governors to close Mansfield.
Mansfield needs time to come up with a plan that includes emphasizing our role as an access university to underserved students, highlighting associate degree pathways to support local workforce needs, and adjusting our physical footprint to address inefficiencies.
Governor Shapiro should work with local stakeholders to keep this campus open. As he is fond of saying, “It’s time to get sh** done!”
 

Jonathan C. Rothermel is a political science professor at Commonwealth University-Mansfield. His work appears frequently on the Capital-Star’s Commentary Page.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Commentary: This is what we’re thankful for?
description: You live in Florida, you lucky, lucky dog. You know it’s paradise: the sand, the sea, the sun, the easy tanning, the undereducating, the overdeveloping. Florida is a beacon of red hope at the bottom of America, welcoming refugee despots, white nationalists, book-banners, and billionaires. You have boocoo reasons to be thankful for the Sunshine […]
text:
The Florida Capitol as of March 2024. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)You live in Florida, you lucky, lucky dog.
You know it’s paradise: the sand, the sea, the sun, the easy tanning, the undereducating, the overdeveloping.
Florida is a beacon of red hope at the bottom of America, welcoming refugee despots, white nationalists, book-banners, and billionaires.
You have boocoo reasons to be thankful for the Sunshine State this Thanksgiving, and you’d better be, damn it.
If you aren’t, we’ll track you down and deport you to Georgia.
So let us count the ways:

You don’t have measles!

Yet.
But that Morbillivirus hominis is one determined pathogen.
As of Nov. 7, Florida has reported 163 cases this year, the 11th highest number in the country.
It could be worse: Pennsylvania has racked up 1,500.

Your Florida Legislature is going to address this Amendment 3 thing.

Soon.
Pinky swear.
Gov. Ron DeSantis wants them to descend on Tallahassee for a special session before the end of the year. He says we need a “Taxpayer Bill of Rights.”
Legislators are not keen. I mean, Hannukah kicks off on Dec. 4, then there’s Christmas and New Year’s, then recovering from all that sugar consumption.
What’s the problem? As you recall, 62% of us poor, starving Floridians voted to lower our property taxes.
Otherwise, we wouldn’t be able to afford the basic necessities of life, including (but not limited to) DraftKings, DoorDash, Starbucks, ball caps, green fees, gas for the Ram 1500 TRX, Sam’s Club excursions, 25 different streaming services, and pool maintenance.
Why do local governments get all that taxpayer money, anyway?
How expensive can it be to fix potholes, pay firefighters, run health clinics, and maintain parks?
OK, the rural counties won’t have two pennies to rub together, but does Mayo really need a public library?
Your Florida Legislature will figure it out.
Eventually.

Speaking of Ron DeSantis, we must be thankful for his sake, whose gubernatorial term ends on Jan. 5, 2027.

He needs time to gear up for his 2028 presidential run, work on that smile, perfect those impressive people skills.

Manatees, those lovably, lumpy Naugahyde-sofa mammals are not yet extinct!

Endangered, but aren’t we all, one way or another?
It’s true, a lot of them keep dying for various reasons, but we must not overreact and over-regulate.
Check the Constitution: Floridians have a God-given right to jump on jet skis and drive speedboats at high speeds.
If a few manatee ribs get broken, so be it. Those sea cows must learn to get out of the way.

Great news for St. Petersburg’s beloved, indeed, iconic, 4th St. N. Chick-Fil-A.

The home of the fried nuggets and all-day chicken and waffles has long needed more space. Such is the importance of the Poultry Palace, the city has approved re-zoning enabling it to expand the parking lot and enlarge the drive-through.
Yes, some small businesses will have to close, and the income-challenged people living in the affordable housing complex next to the Poultry Palace will be put out on the street.
It’s capitalism. It’s the American Way.
As our president said, the income-challenged should have bought stock.

Whip out that Winchester, y’all, and celebrate. The bear hunt is ON!

Florida bears are out of control, digging into your trash can, hanging out in your back yard, crashing your barbecue.
Just because we’re building subdivisions in the wild places that used to belong to the bears (after we clear-cut them, of course) is no excuse for the bears to demand food.
Pesky environmental activists engaging in so-called “lawful protest” are on notice: If you oppose the bear hunt, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission can get your personal information from the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles — your address, your medical records, your Social Security number and license plate — and secretly track your movements.
The enviros claim this violates the Driver Privacy Protection Act, which is supposed to stop the government spying on motorists, but what do they know?
Socialists.

Aren’t you grateful the socialists didn’t win Florida?

The rest of the country is Going to Hell with radicals in charge of Congress, promising to fight racism, make healthcare affordable, raise the minimum wage, end the Iran war, investigate corruption, and impose higher taxes on the rich.
They even want to rein in our friends at ICE.
But our state rejected such commie notions and refused to elect Democrats, even though the vote was uncomfortably close.

Hooray! Florida will finally have not just a charter school advocate but a charter school entrepreneur in the Governor’s Mansion.

Not that Byron Donalds wants to live in the Governor’s Mansion. It’s in Tallahassee (ick) where there are too many Democrats and not enough beach.
Not that that Byron Donalds is the charter school entrepreneur, either. That would be his missus.
Erika Donalds’ companies make tens of millions of dollars from charter schools funded by the taxpayer.
And why not? (See capitalism above.)
Florida’s First Lady-elect earns that cash in the name of Jesus. She’s said education should be faith-driven and based on Christian principles.
Also, profitable.
As First Lady, she’s made it clear she’ll keep trying to shape Florida education policy and carry on running her businesses, as well.
Conflict of interest? Only fans of Government Schools (which some call Public Education), institutions designed to indoctrinate Our Youth into Wokery, could possibly object.

Our president has said, “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backward and poor.”

Well, there’s nothing backward and poor about us!
Except sometimes.
Our new gov was understandably cagey during the campaign. He was for data centers and against data centers, then back again.
That’s politics. You have to say stuff to get elected.
But now he’s been elected and the coast is clear, Florida’s going all-in on Big Data!
Those greenhouse gases belching into the air? That funny tasting water? That loud hum you hear in your back yard?
It’s progress. Get over it.

Poor Texas. The turkeys are sad, the cranberry sauce gone moldy.

No happy Thanksgiving in the land of the Longhorn: Texas screwed up big time in the midterms.
Sad.
But Florida will pick up the mantle!
We will carry on the noble fight against unwashed aliens, boys taking over girls’ volleyball teams, lefty professors, climate-change freaks, rainbow crosswalk-painters, foreign language speakers, drag queens, and uppity science nerds.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier stands ready to continue the righteous work of former Texas AG Ken Paxton and the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, scourge of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the FDA, the SEC (the money one, not the football one) and the EPA.
Ladies, keep those knees together and abortionists, beware: Uthmeier’s following Texas’ lead.
He promises to “take the enemy down” and outlaw all abortions.
Your body, his choice.
Uthmeier’s also suing to restrict access to mifepristone and advocating for fetal personhood.
God assures him that clump of cells clinging to the side of the uterus has as many rights as the uterus owner. Maybe more.
The uterus owner is, after all, only a woman.
And where do Florida women belong? In the kitchen mashing potatoes, making gravy, and tending to that turkey.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT must now confront the costs of past PURA decisions
description: Deferring maintenance or replacement does not stop pipes from aging or equipment from requiring attention.
text:
The men and women I represent at United Steelworkers Local 12000 work every day on Southern Connecticut Gas’s natural gas system, maintaining pipes, responding when problems arise and performing the work necessary to keep energy flowing safely and reliably to Connecticut homes and businesses.
That gives our members a practical perspective on energy regulation. Decisions made in hearing rooms and regulatory proceedings can seem far removed from the field, but over time they shape the work our crews can plan, the infrastructure they maintain and the ability of the system to serve customers and communities.
Under the previous leadership of PURA, one approach to limiting pressure on customer bills was to restrict or defer costs, including investments in the system. While that may have provided some near-term relief, it could not defer the physical needs of the system itself. Infrastructure continued to age, maintenance and replacement work remained necessary, and employees still had to keep the system operating safely and reliably. Deferring that work did not eliminate the need; it allowed projects to accumulate, making future planning more difficult and increasing the risk that routine infrastructure needs become larger, more complex challenges over time.
The new leadership at PURA inherited many of the challenges created by that approach. The current commissioners did not make those decisions, and they should not be asked to defend them. But they now have an opportunity to learn from that experience and establish a more predictable approach to the investments required to maintain the system over the long term.
Our members understand why that matters. Maintaining a gas system safely requires more than responding to the needs we can see today. Utilities and their workers need to look ahead, identify infrastructure that will need attention, anticipate where additional capacity may be required and build the skilled workforce necessary to perform that work.
When there is not a predictable approach to forward capital investment, that planning becomes much harder. Projects can be delayed or reprioritized, workforce needs become more difficult to anticipate, and decisions about hiring, training and developing the next generation of skilled workers become more uncertain. This is specialized work, and an experienced workforce cannot be created overnight. Maintaining those skills requires a steady and responsible pipeline of work.
The consequences also reach the infrastructure itself. Deferring maintenance or replacement does not stop pipes from aging or equipment from requiring attention. Instead, work that can be planned and performed methodically today can become more difficult to manage later. Our members would rather address infrastructure needs at a steady, responsible pace than continually push work forward until the need becomes more urgent.
That same need to plan ahead applies to the communities we serve. Across Connecticut, communities are looking to add housing, support local businesses and attract new employers and skilled workers. Reliable energy infrastructure is one part of the foundation needed to support that growth.
When parts of the gas system become constrained, the implications can extend beyond the utility. Limited capacity can make it more difficult to connect new customers, accommodate business expansion or support development in communities that are trying to grow. Planning ahead can help address emerging constraints before infrastructure becomes an obstacle to those opportunities.
That is why the distinction between the previous PURA and the PURA Connecticut has today matters so much. The lesson from the past is not that regulators should approve every investment a utility proposes. Regulators should scrutinize spending, demand accountability and make sure customers receive value for what they pay. But scrutiny and predictability can coexist.
A strong regulatory system can protect customers while providing enough visibility for utilities to plan necessary work, for employees to develop and maintain specialized skills, and for communities to know that infrastructure will be capable of supporting their future needs.
Connecticut cannot undo the regulatory decisions that brought us here, and the current commissioners should not be blamed for circumstances they inherited. What the new PURA can do is take a different approach going forward, one that recognizes that delaying investment does not delay the needs of the system.
For our members, that is ultimately what this debate is about. A more predictable approach to forward investment allows necessary work to proceed at a responsible pace, supports the skilled workforce needed to perform it and helps prevent infrastructure constraints from becoming larger challenges for customers and communities.
The new PURA inherited a difficult situation. It also inherited an opportunity to build something better: a regulatory approach that protects affordability while providing the consistency needed to maintain a safe, reliable system and support Connecticut communities for years to come.
Marcelo Assis is President of the United Steelworkers Local 12000 & 12000-1.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT families deserve to see every home for sale
description: We're in a housing crisis, and CT doesn't have enough homes for the people who want to live here. Private listings make that problem worse.
text:
The families I meet across Connecticut aren’t asking for much. Among other things, they all want a fair shot at buying a home, not a bidding war over a home they never knew they lost, or missing out on a house that sold before it ever hit the market.
As of October 1, Connecticut law now says they deserve better than that.

State Sen. Jorge Cabrera

As chair of the Senate’s Insurance and Real Estate Committee, I helped write and steer through the legislature Senate Bill 340, which Gov. Ned Lamont signed into law earlier this year. Now, real estate listings in Connecticut default to what’s called public marketing: a home is shown to the broadest possible pool of buyers, unless the seller signs a specific form acknowledging what they’re giving up by keeping it private.
I spent more than two decades as a union organizer before I came to the legislature, fighting for workers who too often got the short end of a deal that they didn’t fully understand. This new law follows that same principle: people deserve to know what they’re agreeing to before they sign away something valuable — in this case, transparency, the very thing that determines whether a family gets a fair shot at a home and whether a seller gets a fair price for it.
Here’s the problem that S.B. 340 solves. In recent years, more agents and brokerages have quietly marketed homes only within their own networks — sometimes called “private listings” or “pocket listings” by the industry — rather than putting them on the open market where everyone can see them. The financial incentive is obvious: when a brokerage controls both sides of the transaction, it collects the full commission. For the brokerage, that’s a win. For a family who never knew the house even existed, it’s something else entirely.
We’re in the middle of a housing supply crisis, and Connecticut simply doesn’t have enough homes for the people who want to live here. Private listings make that problem worse. When a home is marketed only inside a brokerage’s private network, it’s invisible to most buyers, and an invisible home might as well not exist. It is, in effect, a manufactured scarcity on top of real housing scarcity, and it distorts the very market mechanism that we’re all counting on to help solve the affordability crisis. More supply only helps if buyers can actually see what’s for sale.
S.B. 340 isn’t a ban on private sales. If a homeowner genuinely wants to keep a sale quiet, either for privacy, for a family transfer, or for any reason, they still can. What the new law requires is that they be told, clearly and in writing, what that choice will cost them. That’s the same basic consumer protection we already expect in almost every other major purchase we make.
Connecticut’s version of this law is among the strongest in the country. It closes a loophole that allowed agents to quietly circulate listings by email within their own networks before ever opening them to the public — a practice that preserved the appearance of compliance while undermining the spirit of open marketing. It also ensures that any platform used to market a home can’t restrict access to benefit a single brokerage’s bottom line.
We didn’t get here alone. Washington and Wisconsin moved first; New York has now passed its own version. Legislators from both parties have backed these bills, because making sure buyers can see what’s for sale isn’t a partisan question — it’s a basic fairness question. But Connecticut’s law sets a higher bar than what came before it, and that matters.
The families I represent didn’t create this crisis. They deserve a law that doesn’t make it worse — and now they have one.
State Sen. Jorge Cabrera represents the 17th State Senate District, covering Ansonia, Beacon Falls, Bethany, Derby, Hamden, Naugatuck and Woodbridge. He is Senate Chair of the  Insurance and Real Estate Committee.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Protect Revolution Wind from the feds
description: Offshore wind is the single largest source of low-cost zero-carbon domestic energy available to New England in the near term.
text:
As the Northeast heads into the winter heating season, we are facing record-high costs for home heating oil, with prices almost double what they were last year. That’s on top of the burden of continued volatility in the natural gas markets, contributing to soaring heating and electricity bills that will hit consumers hard this winter. 
Meanwhile, the federal government has continued relentless attacks against one of the best solutions to address the region’s winter woes: offshore wind.
Offshore wind is the single largest source of low-cost zero-carbon domestic energy available to New England in the near term. It is ideally suited to improve winter reliability and save ratepayers money by displacing higher-priced and more polluting sources, lowering wholesale energy prices and insulating customers from the impacts of spiking natural gas prices.
Despite two failed legal challenges by the Trump administration to stop the project, Revolution Wind is fully online and delivering power to Connecticut and Rhode Island just in time to make a substantial contribution to our winter energy reliability. Despite this success, the federal administration recently launched another attack on Revolution Wind, seeking to revoke the approval of this fully vetted, permitted, and constructed energy facility. 
No one on either side of the political divide in Connecticut thinks that shutting down a completed energy project makes sense.
While the administration probably won’t be able to halt Revolution Wind entirely, they may be able to delay sending its electricity to the grid — and that means delaying power to customers who need it. The project is forecasted to save Connecticut ratepayers $125 million; customers across the region can save as much as $500 million. However, rather than supporting that effort, the federal government’s actions continue to undermine that goal. If the flow of power from the project is delayed or terminated, families in New England could see electricity costs rise by 5-7 percent as a result. 
Together, New England and New York have established an aggregate target of securing 21.2 GWs of offshore wind. We are currently nearing the finish line on 3.4 GW of generation capacity in the region. However, due to the federal government’s actions, another 8 GW of projects have been stalled for the last two years.
If the midterm elections taught us anything, it’s that Connecticut consumers are sick and tired of high energy prices and a slipping economy. Continued attacks on offshore wind make these problems worse and impose real costs on our communities. Offshore wind projects support about 1,200 local jobs right here in Connecticut. At the State Pier in New London alone, nearly 200 existing jobs are tied directly to staging and assembly. 
There’s an entire supply chain of at least 50 Connecticut companies involved in offshore wind and related port development projects. When prices are high and people are living paycheck to paycheck, we can’t afford unnecessary and unwarranted disruptions to this vital engine of economic growth. 
We all agree that we need to improve the resilience and reliability of our electricity system while also addressing the rising energy costs that households are facing. That means securing the advantages of the abundant domestic wind energy resources off the shores of New England.
Revolution Wind is an essential piece of the affordability and reliability solution. Now that it is fully online, we must ensure it stays that way. But policy makers and state leaders across the region must also work to unlock remaining offshore wind potential so that no matter what energy market volatility happens around the globe, ratepayers have access to affordable, reliable energy.
Charles Rothenberger is the Director of Connecticut Government Relations at Save the Sound.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Forest Service says Sheep Creek mine proposal needs an environmental assessment
description: A controversial mine proposed at the headwaters of the Bitterroot River will undergo a more robust environmental evaluation following more than 6,500 comments, mostly urging scrutiny. The Bitterroot National Forest announced Friday it determined the U.S. Forest Service will conduct an environmental assessment for the project, the Sheep Creek Rare Earth Explo[...]
text:
Painted Rocks Reservoir delivers 32,000 acre feet of water annually to the Bitterroot Valley and its economies, or 10 billion gallons, according to the Bitterroot Water Partnership. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan/Aerial support provided by LightHawk)A controversial mine proposed at the headwaters of the Bitterroot River will undergo a more robust environmental evaluation following more than 6,500 comments, mostly urging scrutiny.
The Bitterroot National Forest announced Friday it determined the U.S. Forest Service will conduct an environmental assessment for the project, the Sheep Creek Rare Earth Exploration Project.
The project, from U.S. Critical Materials, calls for pulling 3,000 short tons of raw material out of a sensitive area for wildlife and at the water source that feeds the Bitterroot Valley.
Opponents in the Bitterroot Valley span the political spectrum and argue mine exploration should never take place in such a location and would harm the environment and economy.
Company representatives argue it could provide jobs and economic development.
U.S. Critical Materials CEO Scott Osterman said the company already has been doing the work needed for the environmental assessment, and it will have “no impact on our compliance work in progress.”
The Bitterroot Water Partnership, with a mission to lead conservation initiatives that promote clean water, said the decision brings a more thorough review and “facilitates greater transparency and public engagement.”
The greater scrutiny comes in a state that has seen a long history of mining impacts, including drinking water contamination, habitat loss and acid mine drainage, Bitterroot Water Partnership said.
Earlier this summer, the U.S. Forest Service announced it planned to consider a “categorical exclusion” for the project, for activities that don’t result in significant impacts under the National Environmental Policy Act.
The news release Friday from the Bitterroot National Forest said public comments and additional review showed the need for an environmental analysis.
“The next step is for the U.S. Forest Service to conduct an environmental assessment and develop one NEPA decision document that can support both federal and state permitting needs,” the news release said.
An environmental assessment is a public document prepared to determine the significance of environmental effects and how to move ahead based on those findings.
It can determine the project won’t have significant impacts, or find a more detailed environmental review is needed.
Bitterrooters praised the Forest Service decision.
Nicole Norton, of Darby, said fellow area residents know what it means to treat their land and water well.
“I’m really proud that thousands of people of the Bitterroot have upheld that for our waters, and our community well-being, only the highest level of respect and review is acceptable,” Norton said in a statement provided by Bitterroot Water Partnership.
Alex Hibala, a fishing guide and owner of Montana Headwaters Guide Service, said exploration, “let alone a full-blown hard rock mine, is a massive issue.”
“Those of us who work in Montana’s fishing industry are acutely aware of how even one mining mistake, one little oversight, can cause long-lasting damage to the health of our waters,” Hibala said in a statement from Bitterroot Water Partnership.
The Forest Service news release said the agency will coordinate with other involved agencies to develop a FAST-41 schedule that meets environmental assessment and permitting process requirements.
Fast-41 is a federal program based on the Fixing America’s Surface Transportation Act that aims to increase transparency, efficiency and predictability of environmental reviews.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Environmental groups double down on calls to halt Army’s lead azide detonation
description: The U.S. Justice Department on Sunday urged a federal appeals court to lift the administrative stay on a permit that would allow the Army to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in southeast Iowa. The DOJ arguments came the same day that environmental groups in the court case filed affidavits from scientists and officials […]
text:
Lead azide is set to be detonated at the Iowa Aarmy Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Ia. (Photo courtesy of Lori McFate/Iowa Army Ammunition Plant)The U.S. Justice Department on Sunday urged a federal appeals court to lift the administrative stay on a permit that would allow the Army to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in southeast Iowa.
The DOJ arguments came the same day that environmental groups in the court case filed affidavits from scientists and officials who argued against the Army’s reasons to go ahead with the detonation, which the government said would occur on Nov. 24.
While the lawsuit and stay ordered by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit focus on an emergency permit issued by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the DOJ informed the court late Saturday that the Army intends to invoke an exclusion to the law allowing it to detonate without the permit. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The DOJ’s Sunday filing opposing the environmental groups’ motion on the permit emphasized that a controlled detonation of the lead azide was “necessary now to respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion at” the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. 
“EPA’s regulations allow the Army’s planned action without the need for a permit, and the Army intends to act on November 24, 2026,” the filing said. 
A public affairs contact with the U.S. Army did not respond immediately Sunday to a request for confirmation of the new detonation date. 
The lead azide, located at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, was originally set for detonation on Nov. 20, then was pushed back to Nov. 23 amid concern from the public and the lawsuit. 


State of Iowa launches website for detonation information
Gov. Kim Reynolds announced Sunday the state had created a website for Iowans seeking more information about the Army’s planned detonation.
A news release from Reynolds’ office said state partners have had “several meetings” over the weekend to “gather information and ensure readiness in advance of the planned detonation.”
This collaboration across state agencies follows Reynolds’ decision Friday to initiate a State Emergency Operations Center.
“While the detonation is a federal operation, it’s important for the state to be engaged in the preparation process so we can support the work of our federal partners in responding to the needs of Iowans,” Reynolds said. “Protecting the health and safety of our people and communities is our highest priority.”


As of Sunday afternoon, the Army had not posted updated models for the new detonation date, nor announced an official schedule since the original postponement was announced. 
A Sunday news release from the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club Iowa Chapter and Earthjustice – the environmental groups suing over the EPA petition – criticized the lack of public information as the Army intends to move forward. 
“The Army has clearly mishandled this situation, and Iowans and residents in our neighboring states deserve a full review of all of the missteps that led us to this point,” Sierra Club Iowa Chapter Legal Chair Wally Taylor said in the release. “However, if detonation is now the only option, it is imperative that everyone impacted has access to the full range of testing, mitigation, and remediation resources.”
What outside scientists said
In its filing Saturday night, the DOJ said the Army intends to detonate regardless of the court stay because of the “immediate risk” that the degraded lead azide “will explode” when temperatures drop in the next several days.
A declaration from an Army munitions expert informed the court that changes in temperature can further destabilize the lead azide by causing more crystallization.
One of the scientists who filed affidavits supporting the environmental groups’ requests to halt the detonation, challenged this point, arguing the barrels were insulated from drastic temperature changes by the earthen structures the Army had put up around the material. 
Mark Thomas, an environmental health science researcher who formerly worked for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, argued in his affidavit that the anticipated drop in temperature, which the Army has cited as a reason to go ahead with the detonation, “would not translate into an immediate or comparable change in temperature inside the earth covered magazines where the material is stored.”
Protective barriers in place around the detonation site, according to a U.S. Army slideshow shared at an open house in Middletown. (Screenshot of U.S. Army slides)
Another scientist, Ranajit Sahu, a “combustion and heat transfer expert” and consultant,  said he “cannot rule out the potential formation and release of a wider range of combustion toxics” in addition to the lead, when the lead azide is detonated. 
“Given the lack of detail provided to the public, it is clear that the potential for release of such dangerous chemicals and their impacts have not been fully assessed in planning for this detonation,” Sahu said in his filing. 
He also emphasized that the option to chemically neutralize the lead azide was “hastily rejected” by EPA and the Army. In a filing late Saturday, DOJ said even removing the lids of the barrels to administer a chemical for treatment posed too great a risk for spontaneous detonation. 
 Concerns in Iowa City

Iowa City City Manager Geoff Fruin also submitted a declaration stating residents have voiced concerns to the city, which sits about 62 miles northwest of Middletown, about air quality, residual lead and the potential for short and long-term health impacts. 
The city has received no formal notification of the detonation beyond a Nov. 20 email letting Fruin know about the deployment of an EPA team to gather a pre-detonation surface water sample, as the city sits within a 100-mile radius of the detonation zone, he said.
The Iowa City Water Treatment Plant produces around 6 million gallons of drinking water daily, Fruin stated, with a raw water source in the Iowa River and distributions across the city, University Heights and other nearby areas. The city is concerned about impacts to the river, as well as those to the “several thousand children aged six and under” and around 12,850 people ages 65 and up living in the area. 
“Iowa City has been discussing possible protocols to address impacts from the detonation; however, it is difficult due to the lack of notice and information that has been provided,” Fruin said in his declaration. “The City of Iowa City supports the Iowa Environmental Council and Iowa Sierra Club in taking legal action to ensure that the lead azide is disposed of safely, with adequate and accurate information provided to allow the public to prepare, with adequate follow-up and support for any post-detonation impacts, and with a minimum of harm to the environment and population.”
Some residents in Middletown have said they’d rather the Army go ahead with the detonation than risk an unplanned detonation, according to reporting.
A separate Sunday filing from the DOJ, on behalf of the EPA, which is named in the lawsuit, opposed the environmental groups’ request to add the testimonies to the record, stating they were made after the EPA’s permit decision and sit “plainly outside the record for judicial review.” 
DOJ urges court to end the administrative stay 
The DOJ responded in opposition to the environmental groups’ request to pause and reevaluate an emergency permit issued by EPA allowing the Army to intentionally detonate the degraded explosives. 
The DOJ argues environmental groups didn’t fully demonstrate that a stay would “serve the public interest” nor their likelihood for success in the motion. 
In the initial filing, environmental groups acknowledged the risk involved in leaving the lead azide at the IAAAP untreated, though they argued about the EPA’s determination that detonation was the best course of action. DOJ pointed to this in its most recent filing. 
“Petitioners do not challenge that determination. Instead, they ask this Court to second-guess the agencies’ technical judgments about the specific permit terms needed to protect human health and the environment during a controlled detonation,” DOJ said. 
DOJ emphasized that a controlled detonation, as determined by EPA and the Army, is the best method to avert “a more damaging uncontrolled explosion.” 
“Petitioners cannot show that the public will not be harmed if the Permit is stayed,” the DOJ said. 
In a news conference Friday, Taylor, with the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, said it was a “lame excuse,” considering the material had been sitting in the Middletown plant for decades. 
Much of the public concern centers around the release of lead particles into the air with the detonation, as lead is toxic to humans and animals. 
The DOJ brief said the environmental groups fault EPA for “authorizing any release of lead dust.” 
“But no option prevents every release here; the only choice is between a release the Army can manage and one it cannot,” DOJ said. 
The government argues the EPA permit was “reasonable” and that the environmental groups are “not likely to prevail” in their request for a stay of the permit. The DOJ urges the court to lift the administrative stay and deny environmental groups’ motion. 
“The Army has delayed detonation by three days now,” the filing said. “But every day of delay increases the risk of an uncontrolled explosion that will cause far greater public health and environmental harm than the planned, controlled detonation initiated under the protective terms of the Permit.”

title: Virginia Foxx concedes congressional seat in NC’s closely watched 5th Congressional District

Virginia Foxx wrote on Sunday as she conceded her seat to Democratic challenger Chuck Hubbard.
